Greenpeace files EU complaint against Austria over anti-greenwashing rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:18:58 UTC
21:18:58 KST

Timo Kirez
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Greenpeace filed a complaint with the European Commission against Austria on Friday, alleging that the country's implementation of new EU rules against misleading environmental claims violates European law.
The environmental group said products already manufactured in Austria could continue to be marketed with environmental claims for another three years even if those claims do not meet the new EU requirements.
The EU's Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition (EmpCo) directive, aimed at combating "greenwashing" -- the practice of making misleading or unsubstantiated environmental claims -- takes effect Sunday.
Under the rules, environmental claims must be verifiable, while sustainability labels will be permitted only if they meet certification requirements. The rules also tighten requirements surrounding claims of climate neutrality.
Advertising environmental benefits based merely on minimum legal standards will also be prohibited, along with misleading claims about products' durability and repairability.
"The EmpCo guideline is a milestone in the fight against greenwashing," Greenpeace Austria economic expert Ursula Bittner said in a statement.
However, she accused Austria's federal government of "undermining the EU's efforts."
Greenpeace also cited a legal opinion it commissioned that concluded Austria's implementation of the rules violated EU law.
According to the group, the EU directive does not provide for the three-year transition period that Austria plans to apply to goods already on the market.
Greenpeace called on Austrian Economy Minister Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer of the Austrian People's Party (OVP) to amend the legislation to comply with EU law and eliminate the three-year transition period.

Türkiye’s Customs Union with EU provides edge over Chinese competition in EVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:18:31 UTC
21:18:31 KST

Emirhan Yilmaz,  Emir Yildirim  
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Türkiye’s customs union with the EU gives it a significant competitive edge over Chinese automakers seeking to enter the European market without facing heavy import tariffs, Polish automotive executives said during the two-day New Mobility Congress in southern Poland.  
Bartosz Mielecki, executive director of the Polish Automotive Group (PGM), said that while the two countries began developing their auto sectors at the same time in the 1970s, Türkiye ultimately established its own brand while Poland focused on becoming a leading European component maker.
He noted that the Polish auto industry produced goods worth €52 billion ($59.3 billion) in 2025, while parts and components made up half of the output and exports exceeded 75%.
Domestic vehicle sales in Poland reached 463,000 units in January-August, up 10% year-on-year and above the EU average.
He said Chinese automakers doubled their Polish market share from 6% to 13% over the past year, while European import tariffs will benefit tariff-exempt Turkish vehicles as regional suppliers face rising energy costs and income pressures.
Mielecki said that while Türkiye’s market-leading EV brand Togg began mass production in 2022 and entered Europe last year, Poland’s own Izera initiative transitioned to a joint venture model in late 2024 after a decade of development, highlighting the different national strategies of the two countries.
Aleksander Rajch, a board member of the New Mobility Association (PSNM), said work is underway to expand this electric and hydrogen mobility ecosystem to include the aviation and maritime sectors.
Rajch noted that EV registrations in Poland surged 240-fold since 2016, bringing the total number of EVs in the country’s fleet to 152,000 units.
He added that properly implementing a comprehensive mobility strategy could add 5% to Poland’s overall gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

Researchers explore sparkling wine from bushfire smoke-affected grapes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:17:11 CST
21:17:11 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in the Australian island state of Tasmania have made progress toward producing quality sparkling wine from grapes affected by bushfire smoke, which can make wine unpalatable.
The 10-year research trial, led by the Tasmanian Institute of Agriculture (TIA) in partnership with the University of Tasmania's (UTAS) Fire Center Bushfire Research Hub, is assessing the production of sparkling wine from smoke-affected grapes and the sensory impact of smoke compounds on sparkling wine during ageing, according to a recent UTAS statement.
In a specialized trial, grapes were exposed to smoke for three hours using local native wood and leaf litter to simulate conditions during a bushfire. The grapes were then processed into sparkling wine with controlled levels of smoke taint, the statement said.
TIA food scientist Naomi Vinden said the research could help Tasmanian wine producers prepare for "extreme climate events and the risk of bushfires," and prevent major financial losses from unpalatable smoke-affected wine.
PhD researcher Alison Ctercteko said results so far were "very promising," with methods showing the ability to remove smoke-taint compounds while retaining desirable wine aromas and flavors.
"I've got to make sure I'm retaining the lovely Pinot Noir or Chardonnay fruit flavors in the wine, and I'm not stripping them out," Ctercteko said, adding the research was expected to provide solutions to help growers and producers mitigate smoke impacts from future bushfires. ■

Feature: Date palm climbers embrace harvest, carry on family tradition in war-torn Sudan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:16:48 CST
21:16:48 KST

AL-BAJA, Sudan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- As dawn broke over Al-Baja village in northern Sudan's Al-Dabba locality, 50-year-old Salim Bilal gripped the trunk of a towering palm and began to climb -- his agility the product of more than three decades in the trade.
Below, workers waited to gather the bunches as they fell.
Known locally as "Hash al-Balh," the date harvest season is more than the end of an agricultural cycle for people in northern Sudan. It marks the beginning of an entire economic and social cycle, setting villages, markets, families, and workers in motion.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Sudan produced about 443,000 tons of dates in 2024 from roughly 37,100 hectares, or about 88,000 feddans, ranking seventh globally. The date palm provides food, income and employment for thousands of farmers and families along the Nile.
From high above the ground, Bilal moved carefully among the bunches of dates. He said he can harvest more than 50 palms a day, though the work has grown harder with age.
Climbers are now generally paid through a share of the harvest -- about one-seventh of the crop -- rather than a fixed wage.
Farm owner Awad Saleh, whose land holds more than 400 palm trees, expects 500 to 600 sacks this season, each weighing about 100 kg.
A sack sells for around 100,000 Sudanese pounds (about 166 U.S. dollars). Yet rising costs of fuel, electricity, labor and transportation have sharply reduced farmers' returns.
"Production costs have risen sharply, with higher fuel prices and insufficient electricity supplies, in addition to the costs of tending the palms, harvesting and transportation," Saleh said. "As a result, the farm's expected output will not cover all the costs of the season."
The numbers tell the story. Before the war erupted in April 2023, a 100-kg sack sold for around 25,000 pounds; today it fetches about 100,000. But the Sudanese pound has depreciated sharply since the conflict began, while production costs have continued to rise. The higher nominal price, in other words, has not translated into better returns for farmers.
Production has fallen too. Farmers say a feddan could yield up to 100 sacks, or 10 tons, before the war, compared with roughly 50 sacks today. Falling output, a weaker currency and rising costs of labor, irrigation, harvesting and transportation have combined to squeeze earnings from every direction.
The war has also redrawn the trade map. Before the conflict, part of the region's dates were transported from Northern State to markets in western Sudan. Saleh said the route has changed because of the fighting and road closures, making farmers more dependent on markets within the state. Transportation costs have soared, the movement of workers has been disrupted, and access to former markets has narrowed.
Yet for some families, the date palm has become an even more important source of income as other livelihoods have declined or been disrupted even more severely.
In Al-Baja, the harvest season means more than the yield from hundreds of palm trees. For a few weeks at least, it brings the village back to life and restores something of the rhythm it knew before the war.
As the sun dipped toward the horizon, Bilal was still working among the palms, with his two sons, both palm climbers themselves, climbing nearby. Below, freshly cut bunches of dates lay on the ground, waiting to be sorted and carried to market -- holding the hope of another good harvest.
For Bilal, there was another satisfaction. After more than three decades climbing these palms, he could now watch his sons working beside him, carrying on a trade that had sustained his family into another generation. ■

China Focus: Same moon, shared stories: Foreigners find reunion in China's Mid-Autumn Festival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:16:26 CST
21:16:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- For Kubanychbekova Bermet, an international student in north China's Tianjin Municipality, inviting her family in Kyrgyzstan to admire the moon has become a regular habit.
This simple gesture captures the spirit of the Mid-Autumn Festival, one of China's most treasured traditional holidays. Celebrated annually on the 15th day of the eighth month in the Chinese lunar calendar, it falls on Sept. 25 this year.
Beneath the same moon and sharing its gentle glow, the festival centers on one powerful idea: reunion. A sentiment once seen as distinctly Chinese is now resonating far beyond the country's borders.
As China's inbound travel booms, foreigners are not just experiencing the Mid-Autumn Festival, but embracing it deeply, finding their own meaning in its traditions.
For many, the journey into the Mid-Autumn Festival begins with a mooncake and Chang'e, the moon goddess in a Chinese fairy tale.
"When I celebrated Mid-Autumn Festival for the first time in China, our teacher told us the story of Chang'e, saying that no matter how far apart family members are, as long as they gaze at the same moon, they are together," said Bermet. "I missed home so much that day, almost to tears, but my heart felt warm."
Back then, Bermet had never even heard of mooncakes. That changed when a classmate handed her one filled with lotus paste and a salted egg yolk.
"Desserts are always sweet in Kyrgyzstan, so I never imagined a mooncake could hide something salty inside," she recalled. "Now I can tell all kinds of mooncakes apart. It gives me a real sense of accomplishment."
"The mooncake's round shape stands for reunion, and the egg yolk is like the moon," Bermet said. "During China's traditional festivals, even the food tells a story."
At Northwestern Polytechnical University in northwest China's Shaanxi Province, Russian student Dubiniwa Viktoriia pressed dough and shaped it in a mold. Her face lit up as she finished making a mooncake.
"I thought it would be hard. But with my teacher's help, it was fun. The mooncake I made tastes perfect," Viktoriia said. "Here, a mooncake is not just food. It's a symbol of family coming together."
Nearly 300 international students joined the campus festival, listening to stories about the holiday, making mooncakes and lanterns.
The festival's appeal extends to foreign travelers as well. With China making it easier to visit by expanding visa-free policies, more international visitors are getting firsthand experience of the country and its culture.
Official data showed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period, up 19.5 percent from a year earlier.
Popular tourist spots and restaurants in Xi'an, the capital of Shaanxi, have rolled out various Mid-Autumn cultural experiences. Foreign visitors have flocked to enjoy China's traditional song-and-dance performances and local delicacies.
They also got hands-on with making mooncakes, dumplings and lacquer fans. German visitor Laura is one of them.
"The round shape symbolizes reunion and the patterns pressed into its crust carry wishes for a good life," Laura told Xinhua when making a mooncake for the first time. "You can see how much Chinese people treasure family. That feels very close to us Germans."
"The Mid-Autumn Festival embraces both personal moments and human aspirations. It carries the warmth of everyday life, as well as a broader vision for global harmony and peace," said Li Nan, vice dean of the School of Communication at Tianjin Foreign Studies University.
Beatrice Faustina Jesslyn, an Indonesian student who has spent two years in China, shared a similar sentiment. This year, she joined the Mid-Autumn Festival gala at Tianjin University, having rehearsed for the performance for days.
"We come from different countries, yet we sing together in Chinese. To me, that itself feels like 'reunion,'" Jesslyn said. "Besides the performance, we also make mooncakes, guess riddles and admire the moon."
But what touched her most was being invited into a Chinese friend's home for a Mid-Autumn Festival meal.
"Though far from my family in Indonesia, I felt at home in China," Jesslyn said. "It was that experience that helped me truly embrace the festival and understand why it means so much to Chinese people."
This deepening cultural connection mirrors a broader shift in how the world views China. A July survey by the Pew Research Center found that a median of 46 percent of respondents across the 20 countries surveyed annually since 2023 held a favorable view of China, up from 32 percent in 2023.
As the festival night settles over China, thousands of lanterns glow and countless phones are raised toward the same bright disc.
"It speaks of a single moon, yet reflects the longing and hopes we all share. It tells the story of home, yet stirs a universal human yearning for belonging," said Wang Yi, an associate professor at Tianjin University. "That is why this festival can touch everyone."
Bermet added that the moon is even woven into their language. Many Kyrgyz girls carry the word for moon in their names. "In my country, the moon also stands for longing. So when Chinese people look up and miss home, I understand it at once."
As they told Xinhua, the moon knows no borders, and neither does longing. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's Yang Liuyue set world records in the snatch and total on her way to winning the women's 61-kilogram weightlifting title at the 20th Asian Games on Friday.
Yang lifted 112kg in the snatch to see a world record before adding 139kg in the clean and jerk for a winning total of 251kg.
DPR Korea's Pak Jin-hae refreshed a world record of 139kg in the clean and jerk, which Yang later matched to secure the gold medal.
The 19-year-old Yang had chalked up a world record in the snatch in the women's 63kg category at this year's Asian Weightlifting Championships. Pak took the silver with 248kg, while Kuo Hsing-chu from Chinese Taipei finished third with 237kg.
As the youngest competitor in the final, Yang said afterward that she did not focus on breaking records during the competition, but concentrated on her own lifts.
"I panicked a bit after my failed second clean-and-jerk attempt," she admitted. "I went all out on the third. I told myself to give it everything before stepping onto the platform. Once I started lifting, I couldn't think anything else."
Friday marked the Mid-Autumn Festival, a traditional Chinese festival. Yang said the weightlifting team planned to admire the moon from the deck of the cruise ship where the athletes are accommodating, and she would send her best wishes to her family.
"Before we left, my teammates even said they would post photos of us watching the moon on social media," she said.
Earlier in the day, 24-year-old Oh Kwang-ok of DPR Korea stood out in the women's 57kg, posting 104kg in the snatch and 134kg in the clean and jerk for a winning total of 238kg, creating three world records.
Thailand lifter Suratwadee Yodsarn settled for silver with 219kg, while Chen Guan-ling of Chinese Taipei came third with 217kg. ■

Raising taxes on passive income could bring Russia’s budget an additional 700 billion rubles a year, economist says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:16:04 UTC
21:16:04 KST

Raising taxes on passive income could bring Russia’s budget an additional 700 billion rubles a year, economist says
Applying Russia’s progressive personal income tax to income from deposits, dividends, investments, and property sales could bring the budget roughly 500–700 billion rubles in additional revenue a year, economist Dmitry Polevoy estimated.
Russians currently pay a 13-15% tax on passive income. Under the changes, a progressive scale of 13% to 22% would apply. The Finance Ministry estimates the increase will affect no more than 6% of Russians with such income, or about four million people. War veterans and people with deposit income up to one million rubles would not be affected by the changes.
Polevoy says raising taxes on investment and interest income could affect inflation differently than a standard personal income tax hike. A tax increase typically curbs demand and slows inflation, but here the disinflationary effect could be weaker or even turn slightly proinflationary.
High earners typically reinvest a large share of the profits they make on deposits and investments, Polevoy says. The new tax will shift some of that money from savings into consumption, since it will fund social payments and other budget spending.
The government needs the additional revenue to cover rising spending. Budget revenues for 2027 are planned at 43.3 trillion rubles, with a deficit of about 5.5 trillion rubles, or 2% of GDP. Authorities plan to spend 48.8 trillion rubles, 5.7% more than in 2026.

US seeking to revive Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks
President Zelenskyy said that eight regions have come under attack by Russian forces since the start of the day.
The United States is working to arrange a new round of talks in a bid to end the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war.
Kyiv and Moscow both confirmed the plan to relaunch trilateral talks on Friday. The move follows negotiations that started earlier this year before the US efforts to broker an end to hostilities petered out amid Washington’s war on Iran.

The United Arab Emirates is mooted as the host of the new talks.
“The American side has proposed meeting at a technical level in a three-way format,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters. “We are awaiting a proposal from the United States regarding the date and the US has suggested the Emirates as a possible location.”
Later, the Kremlin confirmed that a trilateral meeting could be soon, although spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there were no details to add currently.
President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Russia and Ukraine earlier this month in a bid to jump-start the bid to secure a ceasefire.
The US stance has previously been criticised for favouring Russia’s narrative, with Moscow insisting that Ukraine cede territory that Russia has illegally occupied, demilitarise and drop ambitions to join NATO.
Russia’s presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev reportedly met with Witkoff and Kushner in the US on September 24. Peskov said those talks were about potential economic cooperation.
Zelenskyy said that Trump told him that Ukraine will be granted permission to produce advanced Patriot air defence missiles.
Kyiv desperately needs additional air defences to counter Russia’s increasing drone and missile attacks, but Trump has delayed approval.
Should a licence be issued, it would be more than a year before Kyiv could put any new Patriot systems into service, leaving Zelenskyy, in the US to attend the United Nations General Assembly, to continue his pleas for additional support from allies.
“In recent days, during our meetings, Ukraine has openly informed our partners: Russia will only escalate as winter approaches unless there is pressure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X on Friday. “For diplomacy to work, US sanctions must be implemented and European sanctions must be strengthened.”
Kyiv is also talking with European Union representatives about the need to accelerate budget support for the military, warning that Ukraine risks running out of missiles and drones early next year.
Overnight barrages
Both Moscow and Kyiv continue to launch nightly barrages against one another.
Overnight attacks struck a 16-floor building in Kyiv’s central Pechersk district, killing a 14-year-old boy and injuring at least seven other people.
In the southern Odesa region, Governor Oleh Kiper said one person was killed and another injured in a series of “massive” Russian strikes on a residential area and logistics premises of a postal operator.
Russia said its air defence units destroyed about 50 drones over the Rostov region overnight and a drone attack damaged the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, forcing it to suspend operations.
Ukraine recently struck two other major Russian oil refineries in Moscow and Yaroslavl. Zelenskyy asserted that refineries in Bashkortostan and the Samara region had also been hit in the past 24-hours.
The Ukrainian leader also reported unspecified strikes in the Black Sea. He added that he has held talks with India, Turkiye, Egypt and other Middle Eastern countries concerning efforts to unblock shipping in the Black Sea, where Russia has targeted cargo vessels.

US arms sales to Israel surge to $21.6 bn in 20 months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:07:35 UTC
21:07:35 KST

Breadcrumb
US arms sales to Israel worth $21.6 billion in 20 months
Notifications submitted by the US President Donald Trump administration to Congress, along with US State Department data covering the period from 20 January 2025 to 17 September 2026, show that the Trump administration has approved arms deals for Israel worth $21.6 billion in just 20 months.
The value of military aid, funded by US taxpayers, and arms deals approved by former President Joe Biden for Israel between October 2023 and early 2025 exceeded $17.9 billion, according to a study by Brown University.
These weapons were used in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of more than 50,000 civilians, children and women during this period.
September 2026: $2.8 billion in weapons
The US State Department informally notified the offices of the four top Republican and Democratic members in the House of Representatives and Senate last week of a $2.8 billion military aid deal involving new weapons for Israel that Washington is preparing to conclude.
The deal includes 40,000 2,000-pound bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrating warheads.
A 2,000-pound bomb is considered one of the most destructive munitions in the world, as its explosion sends metal fragments thousands of feet in all directions and can penetrate metal and thick concrete.
Despite opposition from Democrats, the deal is expected to pass as usual under emergency authority that allows the administration to bypass congressional objections.
Historically, Congress has failed to stop any arms deal.
The following are the main previous large deals:
January 2025: $2.04 billion
After the Biden administration had previously sent shipments of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, and as criticism mounted following their use in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of children and women, his administration suspended one shipment in 2024.
In the first week of the Trump administration after his return to the White House in January 2025, he announced the immediate lifting of the ban on that shipment.
The shipment was valued at $2.04 billion.
February 2025: $7.4 billion
In the first week of February 2025, the US State Department informed Congress in two separate statements that it had approved an arms deal for Israel worth $7.4 billion.
It included 20,000 bombs, guidance systems and equipment worth $6.75 billion, and 3,000 Hellfire air-to-ground missiles worth $660 million.
The administration bypassed congressional notification to obtain approval.
The Trump administration used emergency powers that allow for immediate sales, citing national security interests, to bypass the usual congressional review procedures.
It provided Israel with a $675 million deal including 5,000 1,000-pound bombs and guidance kits and a $295 million deal including Caterpillar bulldozers.
The deal was announced at a value of $3.01 billion, but it included what the administration had announced in January 2025.
June 2025: $510 million
Following the US-Israeli attack on Iran in June 2025, and to rebuild Israel's stockpile, the Trump administration approved the provision of high-precision guidance systems to the Israeli military, worth $510 million.
The deal included more than 7,000 guidance kits for offensive munitions.
January 2026: $6.67 billion
In September 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources, that the Trump administration was seeking congressional approval for an arms deal with Israel worth more than $6 billion.
The deal would be funded through the Foreign Military Financing programme, or military aid.
In January, the deal was announced with a total value of $6.67 billion. It includes 30 Apache helicopters, doubling Israel's fleet of this type of aircraft, 3,250 assault vehicles and other equipment.
March 2026: $650 million
One week after the US-Israeli war on Iran began this year, Israel requested more than 20,000 bombs.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as stated in a statement in March 2026, determined that an emergency existed requiring the sale to Israel to be completed immediately and the deal to be exempted from congressional review.
The deal was announced at a value of $650 million and included 12,000 1,000-pound bombs, as well as 500-pound bombs.
Reuters also quoted an official as saying that Israel would purchase an additional $298 million worth of munitions through direct sales.
May 2026: $992 million
On 1 May, Rubio again used emergency powers to approve a deal for Israel to purchase 10,000 APKWS laser-guided rocket systems worth $992.4 million.
These rockets have been used as countermeasures against Iranian drones because of their lower cost compared with expensive weapons.
This means that the total value of the deals announced and approved by the administration so far is $19.2 billion.
It will rise to $21.6 billion when the administration completes procedures for the latest deal, with at least half of the amount being military aid funded by US taxpayers.

Hackers steal $352 million from major crypto exchange
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Hackers steal $352 million from major crypto exchange
Hackers have stolen nearly $352 million from major cryptocurrency exchange Bitget, prompting the company to suspend withdrawals. The breach comes amid mounting concern that AI is making cyberattacks easier to carry out.
Bitget detected unauthorized transfers from its wallets on Thursday evening, CEO Gracy Chen said. She stressed, however, that customer funds are safe and that the loss is covered by the company’s User Protection Fund, which holds more than $464 million.
The stolen assets came from parts of Bitget’s “hot” and “warm” wallets, which are used to process transactions and hold funds readily available for transfer. Its offline “cold” wallets were not affected, according to Chen.
She added that although withdrawals have been temporarily suspended, deposits and trading remain available while the company investigates the breach.
Bitget has not identified the perpetrators, but Chen said, without elaborating, that the company suspects North Korean involvement.
Blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain has estimated that the attackers have already converted about $183 million of the stolen assets into Ether tokens.
The theft follows other major attacks on cryptocurrency infrastructure this year. Earlier this month, around $320 million in Bitcoin was drained from a wallet used by the Liquid Network, although most of it was later returned.
In August, users of Coldcard hardware wallets also lost at least $89 million after attackers exploited a flaw in how the devices generated the secret keys protecting their funds. Coldcard’s maker has warned that AI-assisted code review could uncover old software flaws faster than developers can address them.
The growing capabilities of AI have also been linked to an overall increase in cyberattacks on cryptocurrency platforms. Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said it has recorded a 440% increase in AI-assisted malicious entries since powerful open-source coding tools became widely available, from about two a day to 11.
Beyond cryptocurrency, reports of AI agents gaining unauthorized access to real systems during unrelated tasks and security tests have raised questions about whether developers can reliably keep them within their assigned limits, or prevent malicious actors from using more capable models to find vulnerabilities and carry out attacks on a larger scale.
Executives at Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and xAI have backed calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful systems.

Trai launches platform to rate buildings on digital connectivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:04:45 UTC
21:04:45 KST

NEW DELHI: You will soon be able to check if receiving a mobile call will mean running to the balcony of your home in the hope of getting network coverage just as you do in your current residence. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) Friday launched a platform that will rate buildings based on their digital connectivity, enabling people to choose accordingly.Trai Friday launched a "digital connectivity rating" (DCR) platform for the same and also a mobile app for testing digital connectivity. Which means like being rated on green parameters like water and power usage, buildings will have a new rating too that could mean avoiding homes where taking a call means standing in an open balcony.Trai chairman Anil Kumar Lahoti said: “The Digital Connectivity Rating Platform establishes a transparent and standardised framework for assessing the digital connectivity readiness of properties. By making ratings publicly searchable and verify the certificates, the platform will empower consumers with credible and comparable information. It will help them make more informed choices about homes and offices with strong and reliable connectivity, supporting smoother calls, downloads and access to online services.
It will also enable consumers to recognise the value of digital connectivity infrastructure built into a property, while encouraging property managers to plan such infrastructure at the appropriate stage of property development.”The platform offers a public rating search page where consumers can search for a rated property by property name, or location. They can view the property’s digitally signed rating certificate and verify its authenticity through the QR code provided on the certificate. Based on this information consumer can make an informed choice while selecting the desired property prior to making the final purchase or lease decision."The platform provides a public interface for consumers to view the properties rated for digital connectivity. It brings property managers (PMs) registered Digital Connectivity Rating Agency (DCRA) and consumer onto a common digital interface. Property managers can register their properties in category of public, govt, commercial, private, submit rating applications, upload the prescribed information and documents, select a registered DCRA and track the status of their application through the platform. The platform supports the prescribed assessment workflow for both constructed and under-construction properties," Trai said in a statement .The platform enables the digital workflow relating to assessment, report generation, certification and publication of ratings. Consumers and other stakeholders will be able to search rated properties, view published ratings, verify the corresponding certificates and compare the properties of interest." Field assessments will be facilitated through a dedicated DCRA mobile app. The app will enable authorised DCRA to undertake in-building digital connectivity measurements in accordance with the prescribed testing methodology. Property information received through the web portal and the assessment data captured through the mobile application will be synchronised in the platform," said the statement .
The DCR framework provides a standardised method for evaluating digital connectivity within properties. The assessment considers prescribed parameters relating to fibre readiness, mobile network availability, in-building solutions and Wi-Fi infrastructure, with applicable benchmarks for different categories of properties." The framework seeks to encourage the consideration of Digital Connectivity Infrastructure at appropriate stages of property development and facilitate the assessment of infrastructure and connectivity performance in existing properties. The Digital Connectivity Rating (DCR) Platform can be accessed at: https://dcrp.trai.gov.in," it added.

Air Force, Pentagon Work to Boost Military Spouse Employment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:01:00 UTC
21:01:00 KST

New Air Force, Pentagon, and White House initiatives are taking a new swing at an issue that has long frustrated military families: barriers to spouse employment.
Unemployment and underemployment have plagued military spouses for years, with the unemployment rate among military spouses holding steady at around 20 percent—despite initiatives to promote spouse preferences for hiring on base, support for remote work, and advocacy for making professional licenses more portable across state borders.
Improving spouses employment is not a “charitable initiative,” but a major retention and readiness incentive, argued Lyndsey Akers, a consultant with AFA’s United Forces & Families program.
“When military spouses have greater access to meaningful and sustainable careers, we strengthen the economic stability of military families,” Akers said at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last week. “We support the conditions that enable continued service, and we connect employers with an experienced, adaptable, and often overlooked talent pool.”
Top-down interest from the White House’s new Military Spouse Commission is driving renewed interest in the topic.
Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen Simmons said at the conference that the nation “has admired” the problem for too long; but “we haven’t done enough about it, and to get an issue the attention it needs, usually, first off, you have to elevate.”
Cindy Wilsbach, wife of Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach and a senior writer for presidential correspondence at the White House employee, said the new commission President Donald Trump’s interest.
“It was marching orders from the leader of the free world to say, ‘We see the military spouse family and we recognize there are some longstanding generational problems that we need to get after,’” Cindy Wilsbach said during a panel discussion.
Both Wilsbachs are members of the commission, as are all the service chiefs, their spouses, and their senior enlisted advisors, and their spouses, including:
- Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas A. Schiess and his wife Debbie Schiess
- Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe and his wife, Dr. Doniel Wolfe
- Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John F. Bentivegna and his wife Cathy Bentivegna
“With the four spouses here going to be involved with the Military Spouse Commission, we’ve got an opportunity to make some real change to laws that prevent us from hiring people fast enough and putting people into jobs and places and moving positions around,” said CMSAF David Wolfe during a panel discussion.
Cindy Wilsbach said the commission won’t try to reinvent efforts already underway but instead “will add to the work that’s being done,” while raising the profile of the issue to give advocates access to the President and other high-level decision-makers.
Global Military Spouse Connection
One program that’s newly in place and starting to grow is the Air Force’s Global Military Spouse Connection, which started in June as a pilot program for just a few installations.
Officials say the program is meant to serve as a “bridge” between Active-Duty military spouses who have PCSed to a new location and local hiring managers.
“Using career field administrators, GMSC creates a structured, active pipeline to connect the military spouse talent pool with employment opportunities,” according to an Air Force release.
“We are assisting hiring managers in finding the best-qualified individual,” said career field administrator Wyteeshia McRoberts, in a statement. “We’re not contacting them to do favors. We are looking at resumes, seeing what they qualify for and making recommendations for the right jobs.”
CMSAF Wolfe highlighted the program in his Sept. 14 keynote address to the conference, noting how the program “went from idea to first action in only 60 days,” and promising rapid expansion. On Sept. 22, the Air Force announced the program was already available for spouses moving to the following locations:
- Luke Air Force Base, Ariz.
- Goodfellow Air Force Base, Texas
- Laughlin Air Force Base, Texas
- Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho
- Travis Air Force Base, Calif.
- Patrick Space Force Base, Fla.
- Ramstein Air Base, Germany
- RAF Croughton, U.K.
- RAF Mildenhall, U.K.
- RAF Lakenheath, U.K.
- RAF Feltwell, U.K.
- Kadena Air Base, Japan
SpouseWorks
While the Department of the Air Force has launched the new connection program, the Office of the Secretary of Defense is focused on better publicizing the programs it already has, said Simmons.
Until recently, spouses looking for Pentagon help to land jobs, scholarships, or fellowships were on their own navigating a confusing sea of acronyms: SECO, MyCAA, MSEP.
SECO stood for Spouse Education and Career Opportunities, but wasn’t visible enough to leaders or community members, Simmons said. So his team rebranded to “SpouseWorks” and changed the organization. Before, the program “was buried in one of our directorships through no fault of their own,” Simmons said. “But in my mind, … it needed to report directly to me, so we turned it from a sub-office to a directorship.”
Other programs were folded in, so that now there are also SpouseWorks Fellowship and SpouseWorks Scholarship programs. “We’re trying to make it very simple and easy to use.”
SpouseWorks offers training, education, and professional development; career coaches; and a job board. Simmons said the goal is to be a one-stop shop for military spouses and a resource for employers seeking high-quality employees.
Early returns are promising. “We’re up well over 50 to 80 percent usage year over year,” he said. “And we’re only about halfway through the first year of the SpouseWorks rebrand.”
Challenges Remain
Headwinds continue, however. “I wish we could say that we had a lot of consistency, but what happens is with every change of leadership, somebody has a bright idea and then a great program goes away,” said Sue Luangkhot Hoppin, president of the National Military Spouse Network. “We don’t dot the Is and cross the Ts and we don’t necessarily solidify the programs before we move on to the next one.”
Lack of consistency from base to base, due to different commanders’ priorities, is also a challenge, he said. Elevating the issue to department leaders can raise the profile and relieve operational commanders of an extra burden.
One policy change that had unintended consequences for families was the widespread rollback of remote work options for federal civilians. Because of frequent PCS moves, remote work is an ideal option for many military spouses. “Remote work is a lifeline for a lot of military spouses,” Luangkhot Hoppin said. “It allows them to work even if they have childcare issues. But if they have to go back to the office, all of a sudden they need to have access to affordable child care, and that’s become an issue.”
Liz O’Brien, senior vice president at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation, argued that remote work is only a piece of the equation, noting that during the COVID-19 pandemic, when remote work options surged, spouse unemployment stayed stubbornly high. Childcare is one of the biggest barriers to better spouse employment, O’Brien, Luangkhot Hoppin, and Simmons agreed. Simmons sees an “intrinsic relationship” between the two; without ready and available childcare, many spouses can’t work. If they have to wait months for childcare openings to materialize, their window for employment can begin to close down.
Simmons said the Pentagon is working multiple fronts to reduce the wait times for childcare, both through expanded capacity at its Child Development Centers as well as through partnerships with the Armed Forces YMCA, private industry, and support for informal childcare support.
“Year over year … our childcare wait lists are down 25 percent, which is phenomenal,” Simmons said. And the tie to spouse employment is clear. “As a result, you see that wait list drop, you also see the spouse employment drop.”

It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

In recent weeks, concerns about AI have forged unlikely alliances in the tech and policy worlds. Tech moguls such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis joined Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella and Bill Gates in sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI and called for a slowdown of the technology’s development despite years of racing for dominance. The senator Bernie Sanders teamed up with Steve Bannon to urge Congress to regulate AI, which has become one of the very few issues to unite Americans across the political spectrum.
The latest moves were sparked in part by the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s warnings on Twitter/X that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and believe that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
The reality is, we don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing.
Bill Gates’s nearly 6,000-word essay in late August warning about AI and its potential harms to humanity doesn’t come as a surprise. One of us has been a Microsoft employee for nearly a decade, witnessing all the dangers unfold in real time. Together, we’ve spent the past two years organizing with other Microsoft employees and activists to uncover the company’s role in the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. We have collectively called on Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military.
But it’s not just Microsoft that is involved in AI-driven destruction.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza was a testing ground for the use of AI in warfare and the results were deeply disturbing. Israel’s military used AI to identify people to kill, with 12,000 targets generated and bombed in the first month alone. This was done with little to no meaningful human oversight, as documented in an investigation by Oscar-winning Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham, whose latest film NAZA includes chilling testimonials by the soldiers involved.
Earlier this year in Iran, the US military launched an AI-involved airstrike that hit Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, killing 156 children, teachers and other civilians. The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.
The horrors wrought by AI aren’t limited to people overseas – they’re already being felt by vulnerable communities in the US The Department of Homeland Security is using AI tools – including Microsoft’s Azure – to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants at a massive scale. Law enforcement agencies nationwide are deploying facial recognition technology despite evidence of algorithmic bias that has led to the wrongful arrest and incarceration of Latino and Black Americans. The NYPD also partnered with Microsoft to build its Domain Awareness System, using Azure to connect to 18,000 security cameras, according to the New York Daily News, creating a mass surveillance system that has expanded to Georgia and other parts of the world, including Brazil and Singapore. Datacenters that power AI are being built in rural and low-income neighborhoods throughout the US where many are living under the poverty line and are now facing significant health threats from air pollution caused by these facilities.
Though many of these harms have been documented over the years, rightwing government leaders are continuing to shut down dissent through dishonest and draconian measures. Donald Trump has called AI risks a “hoax” and said any attempts to limit the power of the technology were part of a “sick conspiracy”. House Republicans have dismissed the public’s concerns about AI, blaming Chinese government disinformation for public opposition to datacenters. Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, has threatened to revoke the citizenship of NAZA film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
One thing is clear: the dangerous future that Gates, Amodei, and others are warning us about is already here, and we must act now to prevent further harm. Those of us with families in Gaza, Lebanon, Iran and US neighborhoods terrorized by ICE already know people living through the nightmare.
In the last few weeks, we’ve seen promising efforts from US policymakers attempting to curtail the potential harms of AI technology. The House recently proposed the Frontier Act to embed third-party evaluators within tech companies to conduct safety assessments, and earlier this month, Sanders and the representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop tech leaders from building and developing technologies that humans cannot control.
These bills are a good starting point. But they could take years to pass and don’t address the devastation already being caused. Frontier AI companies and governments must act now to ban the selling and use of AI technologies in military targeting, autonomous weapons systems, and mass surveillance. This is what employees from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind are calling for.
We are living through a precious and fleeting moment when we can still confront the harms AI has already caused to the most vulnerable and course-correct before they become irreversible, spreading into more communities. We need to establish clear guardrails right now and shape the future of AI so that it protects everyone, not just a privileged few.
- 
  Mohamed Hussein organizes with No Azure for Apartheid, an employee-led movement calling on Microsoft to end its involvement with the Israeli military. He is also a leader in Palestinians and Allies at Microsoft, an internal employee group.
- 
  Granate Kim works with No Azure for Apartheid and is the Campaigns Director at MPower Change, an organization that mobilizes Muslim communities in defense of human rights.

DNA database of UK dogs could help police collar criminals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

From tracking criminals to sniffing out drugs, dogs have long helped police crack cases. Now experts are hoping a database of canine DNA could offer vital leads.
While hair, saliva and other canine material may be found at crime scenes, or on individuals connected to incidents, scientists say they are often not fully investigated.
Yet such traces could provide valuable clues, from the identity of a canine perpetrator to evidence a dog’s owner was present at a crime scene.
“You might have a human case, kidnapping, for example,” said Prof Denise Syndercombe Court, a forensics expert at King’s College London who is leading the work. “Lots of us have dogs. We live with dogs all the time. And so if you can identify canine material associated with a crime like that, then that can be very powerful in being able to provide intelligence to help solve a human case where there’s no other evidence.”
As a result, researchers at King’s College London and the Royal Veterinary College have teamed up to harness the potential of canine DNA.
It is not without its challenges.
“Forensically, we don’t have loads of DNA,” said Syndercombe Court. “You have a few cells that are left at a crime scene … So you’ve got to make something useful out of that.”
One approach is similar to that employed in the forensic analysis of human DNA, which is to focus on very small segments called short tandem repeats (STRs).
This technique involves looking at the number of times these small segments are repeated in the DNA, resulting in two numbers for each STR – one inherited from each parent.
Syndercombe Court noted the set of numbers provided a virtually unique profile – be it for a human or a dog. What is more, in dogs some sets of numbers are more common in some breeds than others.
By focusing on STRs the team has built a database covering 80 different breeds – the first of its kind in the UK. For the 10 most common breeds, including labradors, cocker spaniels and miniature schnauzers, samples were taken from at least 50 dogs of each breed.
The upshot is that canine DNA from a crime scene can be analysed and the results either compared with those from a particular dog – allowing that animal to be confirmed or ruled out as being linked to a crime – or screened against the database, potentially allowing experts to identify the breed of dog from which it came.
The latter could be particularly useful where the dog thought to be linked to a crime is unknown, or where samples cannot be taken from a canine suspect, or where the sample does not match the DNA of a dog under suspicion.
Syndercombe Court said her team now hoped to expand their database to include breeds such as pitbull terriers, American XL bullies and Japanese tosas that are banned in the UK.
While the STR analysis focuses on DNA from the nucleus of a cell, the team have also created a database using another approach: sequencing DNA from within mitochondria – the tiny structures that power cells.
With many mitochondria per cell, this approach can be useful where there is very little material to work with – although it is more limited as this DNA is only passed from mother to offspring.
The focus on doggy DNA has already offered insights for police investigations. In one case, the approach shed light on whether serious injuries sustained by a man were down to another person – as he claimed – or occurred when he tripped over his own dogs as they attacked the accused.
Forensic analysis supported the latter. “We looked at the T-shirt [of the accused] and there were holes in the T-shirt,” Syndercombe Court said, adding the team also found DNA from two different dogs on the garment.
In another case, the DNA analysis shed light on a sheep attack.
“We got some decent DNA from the crime scene, and the police thought it was a particular person’s dogs,” said Syndercombe Court.
However the DNA from those dogs did not match the DNA recovered from the crime scene.
“So we were not only able to exclude his dogs, which were of a particular breed, but also say the breed of dog that [did] this attack was very likely to be [another breed],” said Syndercombe Court.
Dr Nicholas Dawnay, an expert in forensics at Liverpool John Moores University – who was not involved in the work – said research assessing how best to use canine DNA collected from crime scenes was hugely important.
“Whether it is a dog attacking a human or livestock or wildlife species, the ability to match the individual dog back to the attack is the primary goal. Obtaining breed information at the early stages of an investigation may help narrow down the pool of possible dogs, which is exciting,” he said.
But Dawnay said a big challenge remained regarding the funding of canine forensic casework: “Police budgets are stretched and without effective funding, the benefits of this research may struggle to be realised.”

Cocktail of the week: Eleanore’s apple highball – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

I adore calvados, and this highball was built off the back of a love for calvados and tonic. This refreshing aperitif expands on that idea andfeels really quite sophisticated in comparison.
Apple highball
Serves 1
For the apple syrup
250g eating apples, washed – we use braeburns
250g caster sugar
For the drink 
25ml calvados – we use Avallen
20ml Lillet Blanc 
15ml apple syrup (see above and method)
15ml fresh lemon juice
   1 dash orange bitters – we use Regans’
1 dash champagne, to taste
1 dash tonic water, to taste
1 twist lemon zest, to finish
First make the syrup. Dice the apples, core, peel and all, put them in a saucepan, and add the sugar and 100ml water. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring, for about 10 minutes, until the apples are soft and the sugar has dissolved. Fine strain into a clean jar, seal and store in the fridge, where the syrup will keep for up to four weeks (it’s also lovely diluted with sparkling water).
To build the drink, put all the liquids bar the champagne and tonic into a cocktail tin filled with ice and give it a short shake. Strain into a small chilled highball glass filled with fresh ice and top with a dash each of champagne and tonic. Give it a quick stir, squeeze the lemon zest over the top, to express the oils (if you like, drop it into the drink afterwards), and serve.
- 
  Johanna Cole, general manager, Eleanore, Edinburgh

A baby girl appears to alter a father’s relationship priorities in one highly specific way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:07 UTC
21:00:07 KST

Having a daughter appears to shift a father’s focus toward maintaining a strong romantic relationship with the child’s mother. The research suggests that fathers of daughters show higher levels of commitment and relationship satisfaction compared to fathers of sons. These findings, published in Personality and Individual Differences, provide evidence that a child’s sex can influence a father’s psychology in ways that promote long-term family stability.
The foundation of this research rests on paternal investment theory, a framework suggesting that fathers serve as an early model of male behavior for their children. For daughters in particular, a father’s presence and level of involvement provide information about whether men in the broader social environment are reliable and likely to invest in long-term relationships. When a father is absent or uninvolved, daughters tend to adjust their expectations and sexual strategies to fit a world where male support is unpredictable.
For instance, a 2003 longitudinal study found that girls who grew up with an absent father were more likely to engage in early sexual activity and experience teenage pregnancy. Along similar lines, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 indicated that an earlier age of father absence is linked to a higher number of casual sexual encounters during college. Another line of research, such as a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, has found that father absence during specific developmental windows is associated with accelerated physical maturation, including an earlier onset of puberty.
Because daughters bear the higher physical costs of pregnancy and childcare, their reproductive success is especially sensitive to signs of reliable male support. The researchers hypothesized that having a daughter might prompt fathers to maintain a stronger pair-bond with the mother. By demonstrating a stable relationship, fathers model reliable male investment, which might encourage daughters to delay reproduction and seek out committed partners.
“But no prior study had looked at the reverse, the impact having a daughter has on a man,” Kristina M. Durante, a professor of marketing and research fellow at the Center for Women in Business at Rutgers Business School, told PsyPost. “This was a significant gap, especially given that one of the leading theories for why father absence negatively impacts daughters is because fathers send a message to a daughter about what to expect from a future partner.” The research, led by Krystal Duarte alongside Durante, aimed to test whether fathers of daughters display stronger pair-bond motivation than fathers of sons.
To investigate this dynamic, the researchers conducted three separate studies. In the first study, the team surveyed 184 parents with a single child under the age of 18. The sample included 101 fathers and 83 mothers. Participants completed questionnaires assessing their emotional attachment to their partner and various components of their relationship quality, such as satisfaction, commitment, and trust.
The results indicated that fathers of daughters reported stronger attachment bonds to the child’s mother than fathers of sons. On a 9-point scale measuring attachment strength, fathers with daughters averaged a score of 8.04, compared to 7.37 for fathers of sons. Fathers of daughters also reported higher levels of relationship commitment, satisfaction, and trust. In contrast, mothers’ reports of relationship quality and attachment did not differ based on whether they had a son or a daughter.
For the second study, the researchers analyzed data from a large, long-term project called the Fragile Families and Child Wellbeing Study. This dataset allowed them to examine how mothers perceived their partners’ behavior over several years, from the child’s birth up to age nine. The final sample included 587 couples. The team measured both partner-directed support, such as showing affection and fairness toward the mother, and parenting-focused support, such as cooperating on childcare rules.
Mothers who had a daughter reported receiving more partner-directed support from fathers shortly after childbirth compared to mothers who had a son. This difference in romantic relationship support was specific to the parents’ dynamic as a couple, as the researchers found no differences in general parenting or co-parenting behaviors based on the child’s sex. Additionally, fathers’ perceptions of the mothers’ supportiveness did not vary depending on whether they had a boy or a girl.
“Outside of finding that daughters have an impact on dads, we were surprised and delighted to see that dads of daughters were reported to be better partners by the mother,” Durante noted. “So, this isn’t just dad ‘reporting’ that he is a more committed partner, moms are feeling that commitment through his behavior.” Over time, the gap in partner support between fathers of daughters and fathers of sons appeared to narrow as the children grew older.
The third study aimed to rule out the possibility that preexisting personality differences between men who have daughters and men who have sons were driving the results. The researchers tracked 168 first-time parent couples from their third trimester of pregnancy through the first two years of their child’s life. Participants reported on their relationship satisfaction, romantic attachment styles, and feelings about childcare at multiple points before and after the birth.
Before the babies were born, there were no differences in relationship quality or attachment between the expectant fathers of sons and those expecting daughters. After childbirth, however, fathers of daughters reported greater relationship satisfaction and provided more support to their partners. They also showed decreases in attachment anxiety, meaning they became more secure and less worried about their relationship.
Meanwhile, fathers of sons tended to become more avoidant, pulling away emotionally, and less satisfied with their relationship over time. Once again, these shifts were specific to the romantic pair-bond, as satisfaction with childcare duties did not change based on the child’s sex. By tracking these changes across the transition to parenthood, the study provides evidence that the birth of a daughter directly relates to a reconfiguration of a father’s romantic motivations.
“Having a daughter seems to shift dads toward greater investment in their relationship with the child’s mother, not just toward the kid, but toward the marriage/partnership itself,” Durante explained. “This showed up across three different methods (self-report, partner-report over time, and before-vs-after having the baby), which is what makes it compelling: it’s not just ‘dads of daughters say nice things,’ it’s that fathers’ actual relationship behavior appears to change after a daughter is born.”
“These are small-to-medium effects, which means differences of about half a standard deviation on measures like commitment and relationship satisfaction, not full standard deviations,” she added. “The effect isn’t large enough to predict any single father’s behavior, but it’s consistent enough, showing up across three independent studies using different methods, to suggest something real and biologically patterned is going on beneath the surface.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “It’s not that dads love daughters more than sons,” Durante clarified. “It’s not that fathers of sons are bad partners. Sons’ fathers didn’t get worse, so much as daughters’ fathers showed a distinctive uptick in pair-bond-focused behavior.”
“This is an effect we found in the US and may not translate to other non-Western populations,” Durante pointed out. In societies where fathers are less involved in daily family life, or in places with a strong cultural preference for sons, the effects of a child’s sex on a father’s relationship behavior might look quite different. The research also focused on heterosexual couples, leaving it an open question whether similar dynamics exist in non-heterosexual partnerships.
Future studies could explore the exact biological or social mechanisms that relate to this shift in fathers. For instance, the transition to fatherhood is known to correspond with drops in testosterone, which encourages caregiving. However, it is not yet known if having a daughter influences these hormonal changes more than having a son. Exploring how the sex of multiple siblings interacts to influence a father’s relationship behavior could also provide a more detailed picture of family dynamics.
“We are continuing to look at how a person’s early experience with mom and dad impacts their behavior in adulthood,” Durante said. “We are looking closely at how moms may differentially influence the development of sons versus daughters.”
“Becoming a father to a daughter may recalibrate a man’s relationship priorities, nudging him to be a more visibly committed partner, possibly because daughters are especially attuned to what their father’s relationship teaches them about what to expect for a future partner,” she concluded.
The study, “Daughters promote pair-bonding in fathers in modern Western cultures,” was authored by Krystal Duarte, Kristina M. Durante, Jeffrey Gassen, Americus Reed, Steven Rholes, and Jeffry A. Simpson.

Mahershala Ali Balances Tenderness and Swagger in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

No one really wants to talk about religious rage, the complex resentment when you feel your God has abandoned you: We like our faith to be tidy and count-your-blessings clean, not clouded with doubt and fury. In writer-director Bassam Tariq’s action thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, Mahershala Ali plays Latif, a Houston, Texas, hit man who’s also, ostensibly, a devout Muslim: He strives to be a man of faith even as he’s breaking bones (and more) in the name of Allah. Then his wife dies suddenly, making him a single dad with three kids to care for, teenager Fatiha (Adia), her younger brother Qadir (Jahleel Kamara), and an infant, Aziza, who can’t tolerate baby formula; only her mother’s breast milk will do, and supplies are quickly running out. That’s a workaday problem Latif has got to solve, and prayer takes a backseat to his feelings of betrayal. “You take her from me,” he rages in voiceover, “and you expect me to bow down to you?”
A crisis of faith and a desperate search for breast milk: As plot drivers go, that’s a pretty novel combination, but Tariq and Ali pull it off here. The tone is equal parts sacred, profane, and comical. Tariq opens the film with a skull-crushing action sequence in which Latif, dressed in swirling robes, beats the heck out of a baddie in a public bathroom; the sequence is exhilarating and brutal, not least because Ali, wrapped in quasi-Samurai warrior garb and wielding a menacing knife, makes such a dashing, beguiling figure. When his wife dies, he realizes his priorities must shift toward his family, but he can’t free himself from his longtime boss Mike (Laith Nakli), who has a special job for him: Mike’s porn-king nephew Hatty (Abubakr Ali) is being harassed by a (Christian) religious fanatic, Pastor Hwan Yoon (John Cho). Can Tariq take care of that? He can—but meanwhile, baby Aziza is yowling with hunger, and it turns out that a sex worker formerly in Hatty’s stable, Tiffany Boone’s Fugazi, is lactating and has a bountiful supply of what baby needs. If Latif’s life of spirituality mingled with bloody violence seemed complicated before, it has now entered the realm of the surreal.
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is most entertaining when it indulges its tawdry side. Hatty, with his tacky sex mansion and bevy of "halal-certified" cuties, is a particularly clever invention, and Cho, decked out in spangled western shirts and sporting a row of gold teeth, appears to be having a blast as a sleazy operator who’s more interested in power than in Jesus. The action sequences are sharp and swift. In his quest for milk, his tiny daughter strapped snugly to his chest, Ali’s Latif is a new kind of action hero. (Some of the movie’s visuals echo the climactic baby-rescue scene of John Woo’s magnificent Hard Boiled, in which Chow Yun Fat descends the wall of a multi-story hospital building while fending off a hail of bullets, even as he cradles a gurgling mite with one arm.)
But Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother also tangles with complex issues of faith. It’s clear that Latif’s daughter Fatiha, who breaks fast when she shouldn’t and has a crush on one of the family’s young Mormon neighbors, is straying from the path. But the movie doesn’t judge her for it. The suggestion is that doubt is part of faith—you can’t have the second without the occasional tension of the first—and even Latif will have to face that crisis.
The Pakistani-born Tariq previously co-directed (with Omar Mullick) the 2013 documentary These Birds Walk, and he was one of the filmmakers in talks to direct the ill-fated Marvel reboot of Blade, with Ali set to star. In a world where blessings, even mixed ones, are sparse, it’s not a terrible thing that Ali was saved from potentially being chewed up by a Marvel vehicle; he’s a superb actor who deserves better, and Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother gives him plenty to work with. The movie’s title refers to a hadith in which a man approaches the Prophet Muhammad and asks, “To whom should I give the best of me?” The prophet’s answer, so emphatic he repeats it three times, is “Your mother”; only when the man asks the question for a fourth time does the prophet respond, “Your father.” As Latif, Ali captures the spirit of the movie’s title: he seems powered by a contradictory blend of male privilege and humility. Early on, he sees, as if for the first time, the little notes his wife had left all over the house, reminders for herself and the kids of all the minuscule things that need to be taken care of in a household. She had handled all these tasks quietly, and seemingly with ease. Now those things—essentially women’s work—are left to him, including sustaining an infant who needs something he can’t provide.
As Latif, always spoiling for a fight, Ali swaggers through the film. But there’s another man inside, a gentle, God-fearing one, and that’s the one you see in the somber beauty of Ali’s eyes. Out of necessity, Latif needs to reconcile with his feminine side. Suddenly, he’s both father and mother, and he finds that filling the role of the latter is the greater challenge. It’s the tenderness he carries within that makes Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother both distinctive and thought provoking. The thrills are just a fringe benefit.

‘Gamechanging’ brain tumour test reduces diagnosis from eight weeks to two hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:53:43 UTC
20:53:43 KST

A rapid new test for brain tumours can diagnose patients while they are still on the operating table.
Scientists have called the development “gamechanging” and said it could secure early treatment for those who “do not have time on their side”.
The test was developed by the Brain Tumour Research Centre of Excellence at the University of Nottingham and can diagnose forms of cancer while the patient is still undergoing surgery.
The NHS has begun using the diagnostic tool, which can cut waiting times for a diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours. It could also secure early access for clinical trials for certain patients.
Prof Frankie Swords, the NHS medical director, said the rapid test was “a huge leap forward for patients” with the “potential to completely transform how we diagnose brain tumours”.
It also means patients can start having treatment earlier, which could save lives, and also prevents uncertainty.
It is a genomic test, which means it analyses the genetic code of a sample of a tumour in a matter of hours. NHS England will be piloting the new tool in five specialist centres around the country, before rolling it out more widely.
Stuart Smith, a consultant neurosurgeon at Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust and co-lead of the university’s research centre of excellence, said: “I am very proud to have been part of this exceptional team creating this rapid genomic testing, which will save valuable waiting time for patients who potentially are being told they don’t have time on their side.
“The ability to have detailed information about the tumour at the point when decisions are being made in the operating theatre is gamechanging.”
Rather than looking down a microscope at a tumour, the test allows doctors to get faster and more accurate results. Small tissue samples are sent from the tumour to a pathology lab, where they are put into a shoebox-sized sequencing machine made by Oxford Nanopore. Inside, the molecules of DNA pass through a nanopore – a tiny hole – and this reveals the unique genome, which defines the type of tumour.
Primary brain tumours are the single biggest killer of children and adults under 40 in the UK.
The specialist centres where the test is first rolled out will be Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust, University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, Great Ormond Street hospital NHS foundation trust, King’s College hospital and Newcastle hospitals NHS foundation trust.
The test will then be brought to sites in Bristol, Oxford, Leeds and Manchester.

Satellite Imagery Reveals Damage at Russia’s Kuibyshev Oil Refinery Following Ukrainian Drone Strike
Following a recent Ukrainian drone attack that sparked massive fires at the Kuibyshev Oil Refinery in Russia’s Samara region, new satellite imagery has revealed the specific damage that forced the facility to suspend operations, the OSINT project “Absolutely Reliable Source” reported on September 25.
The new visual evidence follows the overnight attack on September 22, when Ukrainian drones struck the Rosneft-operated facility in retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, triggering explosions and massive fires. The Kuibyshev plant is one of the leading refineries in the Volga region, with an annual design capacity of 7 million tons of crude oil.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the “Absolutely Reliable Source,” the drone strike hit the refinery’s oil tank farm. The visual analysis confirmed that three storage tanks were destroyed by fire, with a fourth tank likely sustaining damage.
Additionally, the OSINT assessment identified a “scorched” pumping station and confirmed structural damage to the critical pipelines feeding the facility’s primary crude distillation units, designated as AVT-4 and AVT-5.
While the satellite imagery showed no signs of direct strikes or damage on the primary or secondary processing units themselves, the destruction of the supply infrastructure has effectively paralyzed the plant, the “Absolutely Reliable Source” wrote.
Based on the available information, the OSINT project noted that the refinery has completely halted operations, observing that it is nearly impossible for the distillation units to function without a stable supply of raw materials.
Ukrainian drones have also recently targeted Russia’s Rostov and Krasnodar regions overnight on September 24, striking facilities linked to oil storage. In the Rostov region, falling drone debris damaged administrative buildings at an oil depot in the Kagalnitsky district, though Governor Yury Slyusar reported no fire or casualties.
Meanwhile, in the Krasnodar region, a drone-induced fire broke out at an industrial facility identified by monitors as an oil depot in the village of Novotitarovskaya. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted a total of 40 Ukrainian drones across multiple regions and occupied Crimea during the nighttime barrage.

Number of Sudanese fleeing to Chad surges 20-fold as aid runs dry, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:52:02 UTC
20:52:02 KST

Number of Sudanese fleeing to Chad surges 20-fold as aid runs dry, UN says
GENEVA, Sept 25 - There has been a sharp increase in the number of people fleeing from Sudan to Chad to escape fighting and dire conditions, and aid funding is failing to keep up with needs, the United Nations refugee agency said on Friday.
More than 400 people a day have been crossing into eastern Chad over the past week, a 20-fold increase from the numbers seen in recent months, UNHCR said.
They were fleeing Sudan's Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile regions — which have all been hit by clashes between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in a more than three-year-old civil war.
There were "people who tell us that they flee the conflict, they flee the aerial bombardments, they flee the drone attacks," Mamadou Dian Balde, UN Regional Refugee Coordinator for the Sudan Situation, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Nairobi.
Only 18% of the $1.6 billion funding it needed this year had come in, UNHCR said.
“It means less food. It means less capacity for people to be relocated to safer areas. It means less capacity to shelter themselves,” Dian Balde said.
The agency warned of potential knock-on effects if Sudanese refugees’ basic needs are not met in Chad, saying its analysis shows many move on towards Europe after repeated failed attempts to find safety.
The civil war has devastated wide swathes of Sudan, displacing up to 14 million people, ruining harvests and decimating the economy, according to UN estimates.
Drought and other harsh conditions were also forcing people to move, UNHCR said.
Almost 1 million refugees have crossed into Chad since the conflict began, more than 55,000 so far this year, according to UNHCR data.
Aid groups like UNHCR face major funding shortfalls after the administration of US President Donald Trump and other donor countries cut billions of dollars in foreign assistance over the past year. REUTERS

Australia urges global cooperation on climate, AI checks and international law
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese underlined the need for countries to work together to address the climate crisis, emerging technologies such as AI, and the breakdown of international rules, at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He said that cooperating on urgent challenges that confront every country, creating solutions that work for citizens and staying true to the UN’s founding purpose “remains the test of our time” which “we can and we must pass”.
The UN was established eight decades ago “from the ruins of war” by citizens and leaders who vowed to work together to prevent another global conflict, Mr. Albanese stressed.
Uniting nations
“We can seize and share and shape the opportunities this moment holds in the interests of our citizens. But we can only do it together,” he said.
Mr. Albanese insisted that “the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone, nor can it be subcontracted to the world’s richest companies or dictated by the pace of technology.”
He stressed that “shaping a secure, peaceful and prosperous world is a task for all of us”, which is why Australia is seeking a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2029-2030.
Promoting wider perspectives
If successful, “Australia will safeguard the rules that protect us all by upholding international law, including the UN Charter and the sovereignty of all States,” he said.
“We will amplify the voices of small States and middle powers to ensure a wider range of perspectives shape the Council's decisions.”
The Australian premier noted that the world is rapidly changing and new issues – including climate change, emerging technologies such as AI, and the breakdown of trust, civility and social cohesion – demand the full attention of the international community.
He also emphasized the need to “embrace” change and reform multilateralism.
Cooperation, not coercion
“As a middle power, Australia is showing leadership and working with others on fresh ideas to tackle the big issues now facing the world in our region,” the Prime Minister said.
He highlighted how his Government is “elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability and offer nations sovereign choice free from coercion”.
That way, partners can address the “big issues” they face such as economic and energy security, development and transnational crime, among others.
Social media ban
Mr. Albanese also recalled that last year Australia instituted a social media ban for people under 16, following the campaign by grieving parents who addressed the General Assembly that turned into global action.
“Already, more than 20 countries are bringing in or have brought in age restrictions on social media,” he said, “and with the European community taking action, there are many more to come.”
