Pakistan, Turkiye edge closer towards joining Saudi war against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:22:45 UTC
20:22:45 KST

Pakistan, Turkiye edge closer towards joining Saudi war against Houthis
Pakistani and Turkish military chiefs head to Riyadh for urgent talks, but both countries remain cautious about the extent of their involvement.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Turkiye and Pakistan are rushing their military chiefs to Riyadh in response to a call from Saudi Arabia for an urgent meeting on implementing their mutual defence agreement, amid the escalating war against the Houthis in Yemen that has spilled over into Saudi territory.
Turkiye’s Defence Ministry confirmed on Friday that General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu, the chief of general staff, will be travelling to Saudi Arabia.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Saudi, Turkish, Pakistani chiefs plan urgent talks amid Yemen fighting
- list 2 of 4Saudi Arabia’s King Salman slams targeting of Mecca by ‘terrorist’ Houthis
- list 3 of 4How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?
- list 4 of 4Saudi Arabia allies line up support as Houthi attacks mount
Pakistan’s chief of defence forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir, is also expected to arrive in the Saudi capital soon, Al Jazeera has learned, though the Inter-Services Public Relations, Pakistan’s military media wing, did not respond to a request for confirmation on whether Munir had departed for Riyadh.
The developments follow a Saudi request to Turkiye and Pakistan for their military chiefs to convene, following weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory.
The Houthis said on Thursday they had fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets, including a claimed strike on a “sensitive target” in Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Saudi authorities said air defences intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu, and issued emergency alerts for Mecca, Jeddah and Yanbu.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on August 7, treats an attack on any one of Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan as an attack on all three.
Saudi Arabia’s account of the days before Friday’s meeting showed how urgently Riyadh sees the crisis.
Three different reactions
The meeting between three chiefs of staff was first announced after a meeting in New York on September 24 between the Saudi Foreign Minister, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Ishaq Dar, and Turkish Foreign Minister, Hakan Fidan.
According to the Saudi foreign ministry, they discussed arrangements for an urgent chiefs of staff meeting to explore ways of supporting Saudi Arabia under the pact.
The statement condemned attacks targeting Mecca and civilian and economic facilities in the kingdom, and affirmed Saudi Arabia’s right to defend itself under Article 51 of the UN Charter.
Pakistan’s account of the same meeting sounded more cautious.
“Under the framework of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), we reviewed progress towards establishing the institutional structures under the agreement and exchanged views on regional and international security issues,” Dar posted on X.
Turkiye’s foreign ministry struck a similarly measured tone at the New York meeting. Turkish state media described it as a review of ongoing “technical negotiations” towards institutionalising the pact, ahead of a future meeting of its Strategic Political and Defence Committee.
Days earlier, Fidan had struck a notably different note in a live interview with Turkish broadcaster NTV.
“Our agreement includes an alliance commitment, we stand by our word,” he said. “Their military needs could particularly be in certain technical areas and we wouldn’t have any problem meeting that.”
Neither Islamabad’s nor Ankara’s account of the New York meeting mentioned the Houthi attacks that had prompted the Saudi statement.
Houthi warnings
That caution may be connected to direct warnings the Houthis have issued to both countries, say analysts.
The Iran-backed Houthis have in recent days made dramatic territorial gains against Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government forces. They seized the strategic port city of Mocha and then almost the entire Red Sea coast, including several islands. That has given the group greater control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the critically important maritime passage that Saudi Arabia was using to ship oil out after the US-Iran war effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz. This week, the Houthis also made advances towards Yemen’s highlands, even as battles with Saudi-backed government forces have escalated.
They have launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia — and threatened allies.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi movement’s political bureau, told an Iraqi television programme this week that Pakistan and Turkiye would be met with an “iron fist” if they entered the war.
Tughral Yamin, a retired brigadier and senior associate at Islamabad’s Institute of Policy Studies, told Al Jazeera the constraints run on both sides of the pact.
“Sending troops would be difficult because the Pakistan Army is stretched thin on ground due to external and internal threats,” he said, referring to ongoing border clashes with Afghanistan, persistent tensions with India and mounting attacks domestically by armed groups. “It is also subject to speculation if Turkiye would be willing to divert troops to Saudi Arabia. Turkiye has its commitments to NATO and its border with Syria is not entirely secure.”
Urgency in Riyadh
The Saudi religious establishment has struck an even more urgent note than the foreign ministry.
Grand Mufti Sheikh Saleh Al-Fawzan called on forces to “stand united against this misguided sect and deviant group”, referring to the Houthis.
He described defending the kingdom’s borders as a duty “for which lives and souls are sacrificed”.
In a rare message, Saudi King Salman struck a similar note days earlier, accusing the Houthis of attempting to strike Mecca again and telling a cabinet meeting in Jeddah that the attempt violated Islam’s holiest sites.
Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera that the mufti’s message was significant domestically, even if its practical effect on Pakistan and Turkiye is limited.
“The mufti’s authority actually carries real weight in Saudi Arabia domestically, and this statement works above all as a mobilisation tool aimed at soldiers on the front line, giving a long, costly war a spiritual, religious anchor that makes sacrifices easier to accept,” he said.
“For Pakistan and Turkiye, the effect is more about tone than the obligation. Both governments already engage with Riyadh through existing security arrangements, and religious framing mainly reinforces the language of solidarity without altering the formal terms of those commitments,” the academic added.
A regional diplomat told Al Jazeera the messaging reflects a broader shift.
“The [Saudi] public have become increasingly aware of the threat of the Houthis, regularly receiving sirens warning of Houthi missile strikes usually aimed at civilian infrastructure,” the diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity. “But this speech signifies a broader approach to raising civilian awareness and a reflection that things are likely to get worse, not better.”
Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus said on Friday that the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement had not yet been submitted for parliamentary approval. He expected it to be formally submitted when the assembly returns from recess on October 1.
Under Turkiye’s constitution, international agreements only take effect once parliament ratifies them.
Two days before the New York meeting, Pakistan’s Foreign Office announced that retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood had been appointed as the pact’s first secretary general.
Mahmood is a former senior officer at the Inter-Services Intelligence, Pakistan’s main spy agency, and will lead the pact’s General Secretariat being set up in Riyadh.
“In practical terms, Pakistan has just sent a retired three-star general to Riyadh to assume the office of the secretary general of the Joint Defence Alliance,” Yamin said. “The task before him would be to assess the situation quickly and come up with some realistic answers.”
Pakistan “already has advisers, trainers, logisticians and technicians on the ground [in Saudi Arabia] under past bilateral protocols,” he added.
In April, Riyadh confirmed the arrival of a Pakistani military force, including fighter and support aircraft, at King Abdulaziz airbase in the kingdom’s Eastern province. That deployment under the two countries’ Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, signed last September, came amid attacks on Saudi Arabia from Iran.
Pakistan has trained thousands of Saudi military personnel since 1967 and stationed troops in the kingdom since the 1970s, including to protect oil infrastructure in the Eastern Province.
A stretched coalition
Ereli said Saudi Arabia’s difficulty was not a lack of resources.
“Saudi Arabia’s resources, airpower and the years of external backing are there,” he said. “The real difficulty here lies in a fragmented, multi-actor coalition on the ground [in Yemen]. Limited US military commitment has left Riyadh carrying most of the operational weight on its own, straining its air defence capacity.”
France and Britain have offered defensive support. Britain agreed this week to refuel Saudi jets on defensive missions. France confirmed on Friday that it is sending troops to guard the major oil terminal at Yanbu, the Red Sea port that Saudi Arabia has been using to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
Despite the mounting show of support from Pakistan, Turkiye, France and Britain, the regional diplomat said the Houthis show no sign of easing off in their campaign against Saudi Arabia and the forces it backs in Yemen.
“The Houthis have demonstrated their willingness and ability to target both civilian and military targets in Saudi Arabia and intend to continue to do so,” the diplomat said. “It’s clear Saudi Arabia is preparing for a sustained increase in tempo of operations which may include further loss of life.”
“Fighting is more contested than most think,” the diplomat added. “[Saudi-backed] coalition forces suffered a major logistical and operational setback in Mocha but are progressing slowly on the remaining fronts, and a battle may have been lost, but the war is yet to be decided.”
Yamin, for his part, said he was hopeful cooler heads would prevail.
“I hope a diplomatic solution would resolve the conflict, because none of us would like our country to get entangled in a war that is not of our making,” he said.

'It's up to the players now': Ireland urged to boycott Israel games
Ireland’s football team must take responsibility for whether they play Israel rather than leaving the decision to footballing institutions, a prominent campaigner has told The New Arab, as pressure mounts on players ahead of their upcoming Nations League fixtures.
Ashish Prashar, a former adviser to the Middle East peace envoy and a leading voice in the #StopTheGame campaign, said Irish players now faced a "moral question" over whether to take part in the matches.
“Evil happens when good men do nothing. It’s up to the players now,” Prashar told The New Arab. “We can have a conversation about what is fair or what is not fair, but if you’re faced with this moral question, it doesn’t matter who passed the buck to you. It’s about what you’re going to do.
“We don’t get to choose what we face in life. We decide who we are.”
Ireland and Israel were drawn in the same group in League B of the UEFA Nations League 2026-2027, prompting backlash from Irish fans, activists and public figures over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The #StopTheGame campaign on X is calling on Ireland to boycott the matches, with more than 160 Irish sportspeople signing an open letter backing the demand.
The campaign has drawn comparisons with Ireland’s decision to deny visas to the Yugoslav team in June 1999 amid the Kosovo crisis, which led to a Euro qualifier being cancelled and a fine from UEFA.
While the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) passed a motion in November requesting that UEFA suspend Israel from international competitions, the body said it had no choice but to play Israel to avoid sporting or financial sanctions following a vote this summer.
Prashar argued that meaningful action was unlikely to come from football's governing bodies and that pressure therefore needed to come from players and the public.
“It’s never going to come from the institutions; it’s always going to come from the people. The people inside the institution are normalising the genocide and should be held accountable,” Prashar said.
“[FAI] have normalised the mass slaughter of children, they have normalised mass rape of detainees, they have normalised ethnic cleansing, and they have normalised genocide.”
He added: “[FAI] have to be reminded every day that they put their own self-interest first. They have no dignity.”
Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson also drew attention this week after describing the fixture as “playing against genocide”, comments that received support from Prime Minister Micheál Martin.
“We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We’re playing against Israel, we’re not playing with Israel,” Hallgrímsson said.
Protests have also been held outside the Irish team’s hotel in Dublin, with further demonstrations planned in the run-up to the games.
The Irish squad is due to meet on Thursday to discuss its approach to Sunday’s game against Israel and could consider protest protocols, including whether players will shake hands with their Israeli counterparts.
Ireland’s women’s basketball team refused to shake hands with Israeli players before a EuroBasket qualifier in February 2024.
Ireland and Israel are due to play twice in eight days, with the fixtures held on a home-and-away basis.
Ireland’s designated home match on 4 October was moved from Dublin’s Aviva Stadium to Backa Topola, Serbia, while the 27 September fixture is due to be played in Debrecen, Hungary.
The Israeli team and its players have also faced controversy ahead of the fixtures, with Israel’s Saied Abu Farchi shown a red card after making a gun-firing gesture with a corner flag while celebrating a goal.

UK companies to use Ukrainian battlefield data to train AI-powered drone swarms
British companies will be allowed to use battlefield data from Ukraine to develop new artificial intelligence models for drone swarms.
Source: Reuters citing the UK government
Details: An agreement between UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy provides access to a database of images and videos collected by drones in Ukraine. It includes more than 6 million instances of objects being detected, including tanks, artillery, air defence systems, infantry and aerial assets.
Drone swarms can fly, sail or move autonomously, using artificial intelligence to work together, identify threats and targets and make decisions, the UK government said. It added that a human remains involved in such operations.
"This world-first access to real battlefield data will allow British companies to continue pushing the frontier of defence innovation, deterring our enemies and making us safer at home as well as further strengthening Ukraine," UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement.
Access to the database will be granted to no more than 12 British companies. Applicants will be required to submit proposals demonstrating how their work would meet both Ukrainian and British defence requirements.
The UK government expects proposals to include AI-based autonomous target recognition and distributed decision-making systems that would allow drone routes, priorities and behaviour to adapt without relying on a single command centre.
Background: Technology giant OpenAI will provide the Ukrainian government with free access to its AI-powered cybersecurity system Daybreak to help protect civilian infrastructure such as hospitals and power plants from cyberattacks.

One in 10 Russian POWs in Ukraine Is a Foreign Citizen, Kyiv Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:15:19 UTC
20:15:19 KST

One in 10 Russian prisoners of war (POWs) held in Ukraine is a citizen of another country, according to Ukraine’s “I Want to Live” project that helps Russian soldiers surrender.
As of September, Russian POWs in Ukraine include citizens of 55 countries, the project said. Nearly 29,000 foreign nationals have signed contracts with Russia’s armed forces since 2022, according to Ukrainian data.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The figures point to the growing international outreach of Russia’s military recruitment campaign, which Ukraine says increasingly targets economically vulnerable people in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
Russia has faced diplomatic pressure over the recruitment of foreign nationals. According to “I Want to Live,” Moscow has halted recruitment in 39 countries, including China, India, Egypt, Kenya and Pakistan.
The Kremlin has nevertheless shifted its focus toward South America, Central Asia and Africa, according to the Ukrainian project.
Foreign nationals captured by Ukraine in the first nine months of 2026 already outnumber those captured during the whole of 2025. They include citizens of Argentina, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Honduras, Vietnam and Mongolia.
Ukraine has previously captured foreign fighters from countries including North Korea. Two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces during fighting in Russia’s Kursk region were later handed over to South Korea.
Russian Drones, Missiles or Troops Could Test NATO Within Months, Danish Intelligence Says
Promises of jobs, citizenship
Ukraine says Russia’s recruitment campaign often begins far from the battlefield, with promises of well-paid work, Russian citizenship or opportunities to study.
By August, Ukraine’s foreign ministry said it had identified at least 2,982 recruits from 37 African countries serving in Russia’s armed forces, including 486 confirmed dead. Ukraine also held 35 African citizens from 17 countries as POWs.
The largest contingents came from Kenya, Egypt, Cameroon, Ghana, Nigeria, Uganda, Algeria and Mali.
The number has grown rapidly. Ukrainian officials identified around 1,400 recruits from 36 countries in November 2025, more than 1,700 by February 2026 and almost 3,000 by August.
International organizations have also raised concerns about the recruitment system.
Amnesty International reported in September that Russia’s recruitment of foreign nationals relies on deceptive and coercive practices and, in some cases, amounts to human trafficking.
Recruits interviewed by the organization said they had been promised civilian jobs in areas including security, logistics, construction and IT, as well as high salaries and expedited Russian citizenship.
Some said their passports and phones were confiscated after they signed military contracts.
The International Federation for Human Rights reported in April that Russia had developed an organized recruitment pipeline targeting undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers and foreign students across Asia, Africa and Latin America.
What foreign POWs told Kyiv Post
Kyiv Post has also interviewed foreign nationals captured after joining Russia’s military.
In September 2025, Kyiv Post gained exclusive access to one of Ukraine’s largest POW camps and spoke with two foreign fighters, one from Ghana and another from Egypt.
Joshua, from Ghana, said he had been studying in Moscow and was struggling financially when he signed a contract with Russia’s defense ministry.
Mohammed Salah, from Egypt, said visa problems had pushed him to join the Russian army in exchange for citizenship.
A similar pattern emerged in a 2024 Kyiv Post interview with a Somali national identified as Bashiir.
Bashiir said he had traveled to Russia looking for work after earning about $100 a month in Somalia. He told Kyiv Post he saw advertisements for the Russian armed forces and believed he would be trained to work as a security guard inside Russia.
“No shooting, no killing, no other things,” he said.
Bashiir said he did not realize he had been taken across the border into Ukraine until he was already there.
Ukrainian authorities told Kyiv Post at the time that his account resembled explanations frequently given by captured Russian personnel, who often claim they were drivers, cooks, rear-guard troops or ammunition carriers rather than combatants.
Petro Yatsenko, a representative of Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, told Kyiv Post that captured soldiers routinely say they did not participate in fighting.
The recruitment campaign has already prompted governments in Africa and elsewhere to intervene on behalf of their citizens.
South Africa has repatriated citizens recruited into Russia’s military, while Kenya has sought assurances from Moscow that its nationals would no longer be recruited. Ghana has also pressed Russia over the recruitment and deaths of its citizens.

While the railway line is not the reason the hotel is being built at this specific location, accessibility is crucial for tourism, and a rail connection would certainly be useful. She particularly emphasized the benefits of connecting Pärnu to two international airports, noting that this would be a fantastic asset for her sector.
According to Pärnu Mayor Kristel Voltenberg, Pärnu had been promised that the railway line would begin operations this year, but the deadlines subsequently began to slip. The latest pledge was that train services would begin in 2030, and all planning was consequently aligned with that deadline. Now, publicly available information suggests that this deadline is once again turning into an empty promise – one that could vanish into thin air – and Pärnu cannot be satisfied with this situation.
Estonian Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis noted that it is possible to complete the Tallinn–Pärnu line first, allowing domestic services to commence. This matter is set to be discussed during budget planning, but it is clear that this section will open before the entire line is completed.

Although land routes are available, Iraq remains one of the top destinations for Iranian airlines, especially after Iraqi airlines stopped flying to Iran at the start of the Iran war in February.
CBS/AFP
Walkouts during Netanyahu's U.N. address were "louder than any speech," senior Iranian diplomat says
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to the U.N. General Assembly to use the podium in front of other world leaders as a "loudspeaker for justifying war and aggression," but he argued the mass walkout by dozens of other delegations "spoke louder than any speech."
"The world is not fooled by narrative-building," Gharibabadi wrote in a post on X Thursday evening. "History will judge crime, occupation and aggression, not propaganda displays in New York."

Iran's president wants a deal with the U.S. before November midterm elections
Iran wants to make a deal with the U.S. before the midterm elections in November, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told journalists from several news organizations Thursday in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
"We don't want it to get to the midterm elections," Pezeshkian said. "We wish Americans to return to the MoU before the midterms," he added, referring to the memorandum of understanding signed between the two countries in June. That agreement formed the basis of a ceasefire that collapsed within several weeks, as Iran accused the U.S. of breaching the deal by keeping its naval blockade in place.

"This has not been the position of the Iranian government, that we seek to assassinate President Trump or his family members," Pezeshkian said.
Commander rejected plans to rebase farther from Iran before deadly drone strike, sources say
The dozens of U.S. troops bombarded by Iranian drones at a small Kuwaiti port in the opening days of the Iran war could have relocated to safer positions in western Saudi Arabia, multiple sources told CBS News, but those plans were rejected by the unit's commanding general despite intelligence warning of a potential attack on their post.
About one week before the launch of Operation Epic Fury, most American soldiers and Air Force personnel stationed in Kuwait were moved to Jordan and Saudi Arabia — farther away from Iranian missile range. At least two options were scouted, planned and presented to the leadership of the 103rd Sustainment Command, the Army Reserve unit that ran logistics for U.S. Central Command: one was Logistical Support Area Jenkins, a U.S. military base near the southwest port city of Yanbu, and another was Prince Sultan Air Force Base, just southeast of the Saudi capital city Riyadh.
A third option, supported by the commander, Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, was to follow the playbook from the unit that was previously deployed to Kuwait before the 103rd arrived in September 2025. During the 12-day war between Israel and Iran that July, the active unit briefly moved its home base at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait to Port of Shuaiba, roughly 30 miles south of Kuwait City and just 65 miles southwest of Iran.
"That was a totally different scenario," one service member, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak with the media, told CBS News. "Missiles and drones were flying overhead between Iran and Israel and we were more worried about one of them being intercepted and falling out of the sky."
Iran delivered 7-day plan to U.S. this week, foreign minister says
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Aragchi told a group of reporters in New York City that Iran shared a 7-day plan with U.S. mediators this week. If certain conditions of that proposal are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be opened at the end of the seven days and talks would be restarted to try to get a final deal.
The terms of the proposal mimic large portions of what was in the 14-point Memorandum of Understanding that was signed by President Trump back in June.
A mediator in the talks told CBS News on Thursday that the talks are positive, but still in an early phase.
Earlier this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was more circumspect about the diplomacy, saying there had been no breakthroughs. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Mr. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, have been handling the shuttling back-and-forth with the mediators on the possible terms of a hypothetical truce with follow-on talks.
Israel's Netanyahu addresses U.N. as many leaders walk out
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday as his country faces broad condemnation and growing isolation.
As Netanyahu took the stage, many attendees walked out.
"If there are any other moral cowards who haven't yet left this hall, please do so now," Netanyahu began.
Netanyahu launched a defense of his country's actions in Iran and across the Middle East.
"With our great American friends, we crushed Iran's army, navy, air force and nuclear facilities," he said, later thanking President Trump for his "bold leadership."

US backs Musk’s X in legal battle with EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:12:03 UTC
20:12:03 KST

US backs Musk’s X in legal battle with EU
The US government has joined Elon Musk’s appeal against an EU fine imposed on X, accusing Brussels of “regulatory overreach” and escalating a transatlantic clash over its regulation of US tech firms.
The European Commission fined X €120 million ($136.51 million) for alleged violations of its 2022 Digital Services Act, the first such penalty under the bloc’s Digital Services Act (DSA), a vast legislative censorship and media control apparatus. Brussels accused the platform of breaching rules on transparency, advertising, and data access, as well as using a deceptive blue-tick system for verified accounts.
Musk, who has claimed the EU’s tech regulations stall technological progress and equated the bloc to a “Fourth Reich” over them, appealed the decision in February, seeking to overturn the fine.
On Thursday, the US Department of Justice said it had filed an application to intervene in support of Musk’s legal challenge.
“The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said. “We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory over-reach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth.”
🚨 United States Files Request to Intervene in Case Brought by X Corp. and Elon Musk Seeking to Annul Decision by European Commission
“The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within…
The Justice Department warned that the case – the first DSA enforcement challenge to reach the General Court – could set a precedent for US tech firms. Citing “significant concerns” over Brussels’ approach to liability and jurisdiction, it said Washington has an interest in “protecting American companies from foreign extraterritorial enforcement action.”
Separately, the EU is investigating X for other potential DSA breaches, including its approach to content moderation and explicit images generated by its Grok AI chatbot. Under the DSA, the EU has also probed Meta Platforms and Amazon, while Apple was fined under a sister law, the Digital Markets Act, over alleged anti-competitive behavior in its App Store. Apple is appealing a €500 million fine under the regulation.
Neither the European Commission nor X responded to media requests for comment on the US intervention.
US-EU clash over Big Tech
EU scrutiny of US tech firms has become a major source of friction between Brussels and the administration of President Donald Trump, which has backed claims that the bloc unfairly targets American tech giants and harms digital free speech. Senior administration figures, including Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have criticized the EU’s fine on X as an attack on American companies. Musk previously accused the EU of trying to shut down X, claiming in 2024 that the commission had offered him an “illegal secret deal” to “quietly censor speech” to avoid a fine.
Trump has railed against the X fine, calling it “nasty” and warning that “Europe is going in some bad direction.” He has strongly condemned the DSA and related tech regulations, repeatedly labeling them “overseas extortion” and a “form of taxation.” He has threatened new tariffs on European goods unless the EU rolls back the regulatory penalties. The European Commission has rejected Trump’s criticism, insisting the DSA is non-discriminatory and applies equally to all large tech platforms operating in Europe.
DSA: Online safety or censorship?
Brussels sells the DSA as an online-safety law meant to fight illegal content and “disinformation.” Critics see something far more sinister: an expanding censorship and narrative-control regime that gives unelected EU officials sweeping leverage over political speech – and over the largely American tech platforms that carry it.
That criticism gained ammunition from a 2026 report by Republicans on the US House Judiciary Committee.
They have accused the bloc of a “clear bias” toward censoring conservative and populist parties, pointing to its intervention in Romania’s election, then in Hungary, where arch EU critic Viktor Orban was heavily defeated by pro-EU Peter Magyar. It also cited pressure on platforms in Slovakia, the Netherlands, France, Moldova, and Ireland, as well as at EU level.
Brussels has also gone beyond pressuring platforms. The EU banned RT and Sputnik in 2022 and has sought tighter controls on what it considers Russian disinformation, and has since pushed platforms to clamp down on what Brussels labels Russian disinformation. The commission itself admitted DSA-linked mechanisms are being used to address Ukraine-related content and election risks. Critics argue that, backed by the threat of massive fines, the system gives Brussels powerful leverage over narratives that challenge its political and foreign-policy consensus.
That leaves a stark divide over what Brussels’ flagship internet law actually does. The EU calls it online safety; its critics see a censorship architecture capable of suppressing dissenting narratives, shaping the information environment around elections, and forcing global tech platforms to police political speech on Brussels’ terms.

It will be recalled

Turkish parliament to oversee anti-terror bid: Speaker

20:11:02 KST

The Turkish parliament will swiftly establish a monitoring committee to oversee the implementation of the “terror-free Türkiye” project in the new legislative year that will start on Oct. 1, the assembly’s speaker has said.
“With the opening of the parliament, the monitoring commission will be established quickly and will fulfill its responsibility regarding supervising the process,” Numan Kurtulmuş said at a press conference on Sept. 25.
According to a framework law adopted by lawmakers in early August, the parliament has to create a new committee to monitor the implementation of the “terror-free Türkiye” project in the name of the Turkish people.
Launched in late 2024, the anti-terror bid stipulates the full disarmament and dissolution of PKK. In case all the weapons are laid down and the disarmament process is completed, the framework law will take effect and postpone legal procedures against certain members of the terror group for five to 10 years.
“The Turkish parliament will have three main responsibilities during this process,” the speaker said, citing them as “monitoring the process through the parliamentary committee, aligning the committee’s activities with the governmental bodies and making legal arrangements if deemed necessary.”
However, Kurtulmuş recalled that the disarmament and dissolution processes should be entirely accomplished and confirmed by the National Security Organization (MGK). He also stressed that PKK members who are mostly located in Iraq should begin soon to hand over their weapons to the Iraqi security institutions.
New constitution an obligation
On a question, the speaker reiterated that Türkiye should not miss the opportunity to rewrite a fully civilian brand-new constitution.
“It’s time for Türkiye to own a constitution that reflects and embraces all of its people. It’s a must,” he stated.
The speaker stressed that Türkiye urgently needs an inclusive, democratic constitution grounded in human rights, noting that broad political consensus makes this an ideal moment to achieve it.
Snap election discussions
On a question about the timing of the next presidential and parliamentary elections, Kurtulmuş said the ultimate decision about the date of the polls belongs to the Turkish parliament.
“The authority to call an early election rests solely with parliament, and now is not the time for that discussion,” he said.
Kurtulmuş’s statement comes amid discussions about whether the ruling alliance might opt for early polls in order for President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to run for the office for another term. Normally, Erdoğan is ineligible to run for the next presidential elections.
However, if 360 lawmakers vote to dissolve parliament and call elections before May 2028, the president becomes eligible to run for a third consecutive term.

National Chengchi University Distinguished Professor Wang Hsin-hsien (王信賢) said Xi placed Taiwan within the wider framework of stable US-China ties. Beijing sees Taiwan as a key concern that could affect cooperation on trade, fentanyl, artificial intelligence, and other issues, he said, per UDN.

Chang said Taiwan was therefore discussed to keep disagreements under control rather than reach a “grand bargain.” Beijing believes careful handling of the issue is necessary to prevent it from disrupting wider bilateral ties, he added.
China is also concerned about US arms sales to Taiwan, possible US transit arrangements for Lai, and high-level exchanges between both sides, Chang said. However, Beijing’s concerns do not mean Washington will stop selling weapons to the country, he added.
Chang said Washington and Beijing have fundamentally different positions on Taipei. As a result, the talks were focused on preventing the issue from becoming a source of conflict rather than trying to reach a major agreement.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Average household water bills exceed €500 a year for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:02:04 UTC
20:02:04 KST

The water bill for an average household in Flanders has risen above €500 for the first time this year, according to a report by the region’s utilities regulator, VNR. A rise in water bills is being discussed during the Flemish government’s budget talks.
Average household water bills exceed €500 a year for first time
This is the first time the VNR has published figures on the average water bill. Since the start of the year, the agency has also been acting as a watchdog for the water sector.
The findings show that an average household – 2.3 people, according to the VNR – has seen its water bill rise from €489 in 2025 to €507 this year. For a family of four, the average water bill this year is €716; for a family of five, it is €836. The regulator will soon announce its decision on next year’s tariffs.
To burden families with a higher water bill – which has only recently been increased – is simply unacceptable to me
Water bills have risen significantly over the past few years. In 2020, an average household paid €352, rising to €410 in 2023. Water treatment and sewerage management, in particular, have become more expensive over the past two years.
A 2.3-person household in Flanders consumes around 70 cubic metres of water per year.
It emerged on Friday that the rise in water bills is on the table during the Flemish budget negotiations. This could amount to an extra €40-€60 per year for a household, which could generate €80 million for the region’s budget.
Christian democrats CD&V, the party responsible for water bills through Environment minister Jo Brouns, is not in favour of the plan.
“People are already afraid to go to the petrol station these days; petrol prices are at an all-time high, and the cost of the weekly shop is rising,” he told VRT. “To then burden families with a higher water bill – which has only recently been increased – is simply unacceptable to me.”
He believes savings can be found elsewhere. “We need to look at ourselves, the Flemish government. We can be leaner and more efficient. As for the rest, we must examine all the proposals on the table over the coming days and hours, in a spirit of constructive dialogue.”
The budget must be finalised by Monday, when minister-president Matthias Diependaele of N-VA delivers his September declaration to parliament. The region is seeking between €1.5 and €2 billion to balance the budget.

Details

The new, as-yet-unnamed product will be a first for OpenAI and will continue a paradigm first applied by OpenAI in its consumer products, where ChatGPT serves as a gateway through which many users access new models such as GPT-6 Astra. It is intended to help customers create automated workflows and eliminate vulnerabilities amid increasingly sophisticated AI-enabled cyberattacks. It also gives OpenAI greater control over how its models are used for security monitoring.

Daybreak is the company’s cybersecurity program, divided into two access levels—red (Red) and blue (Blue). The release of new cybersecurity products comes amid criticism of OpenAI and other leading AI laboratories over a series of alarming incidents in which "unauthorized" agents escaped their "sandboxes" and hacked external websites, including the Hugging Face website and the Australian government’s website. But while these incidents have raised concerns about AI security risks, OpenAI’s new cybersecurity tools are part of the company’s ongoing efforts to develop security products for AI, the publication notes.

OpenAI has focused on enterprise sales of cybersecurity products, and this work is now led by Chief Revenue Officer Dali Raich, who joined the company in August.
Earlier this month, OpenAI said it would invest $1 billion to subsidize the use of its cybersecurity products for critical services.
Next week, OpenAI also plans to release a dozen or more other products at its annual DevDay event, which will take place on September 29, according to another source familiar with the agenda. Most of these releases are unrelated to cybersecurity and instead concern other areas of the business aimed at both the enterprise and consumer segments.
According to the source, OpenAI has paused all major launches over the past two weeks, with the exception of the affordable GPT-6 Sol and Luna models, in order to release them at DevDay. Earlier this month, CEO Sam Altman hinted at a large number of new releases at DevDay in a tweet featuring several ship emojis.

====================================================================================================

Children’s math and reading skills are linked to better maternal health in midlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:00:06 UTC
20:00:06 KST

An analysis of National Longitudinal Survey of Youth data found that mothers whose children were better at math and reading tended to be healthier. On the other hand, low levels of math and reading comprehension in children were related to larger declines in mothers’ physical health between 40 and 50 years of age. The paper was published in Intelligence.
Intelligence is the general capacity to learn, reason, solve problems, understand complex information, and adapt effectively to new situations. It has been linked to a wide range of health outcomes, with higher intelligence and cognitive ability generally associated with better physical health, better mental health, and a lower risk of death. These associations have helped give rise to cognitive epidemiology, a field that examines how cognitive abilities relate to health and disease across the lifespan.
The relationship between intelligence and health likely begins early, as childhood intelligence has been associated with health outcomes many decades later. At the same time, parental health can influence children’s cognitive development, with maternal depression, physical health problems, and other adverse conditions sometimes associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in children. Because influences can run in both directions, researchers increasingly view the family rather than the individual as an important unit for understanding the relationship between intelligence and health.
Study author Linda Wänström and her colleagues explored the relationship between family intelligence and maternal health. More specifically, they focused on the association between the intelligence of children and the health of their mothers.
These researchers used data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (NLSY79). This is a longitudinal survey of 12,686 US adolescents and young adults from 8,770 households, initially aged 14 to 21 at the end of 1978. The NLSY Children (NLSYC) dataset includes all biological children of the NLSY79 mothers, totaling 11,504 individuals. NLSYC participants have been surveyed every two years since 1986 and their familial connections with the NLSY79 participants tracked. About 51% of the NLSYC participants were male.
The NLSYC participants completed the Peabody Individual Achievement Test (PIAT) in mathematics, reading recognition, and reading comprehension every two years from ages 5 to 15, between 1986 and 2014. Each eligible child underwent up to five assessments.
Study authors used scores on these tests as a measure of intelligence. In the NLSY79 group, health assessments of mothers were conducted as they reached ages 40 and 50, starting during the survey years of 1998 and 2008, respectively. These assessments included a self-report measure of physical and mental health, and a depression scale. For mothers, there was also an intelligence assessment done when they were between 15 and 23 years old using the Armed Forces Qualifying Test, an achievement test often used as a proxy for an intelligence test.
The results showed that, on average, mothers’ depression symptoms increased between 40 and 50 years of age, while their physical health scores decreased. As expected, children’s math and reading scores increased as they grew up.
Mothers whose children had stronger math and reading scores tended to have better physical and mental health. On the other hand, low levels of math and reading comprehension in children were associated with larger declines in mothers’ physical health between 40 and 50 years of age.
“The results indicated that family-level intelligence is positively related to maternal health at middle-age,” the study authors wrote. They discussed the notion of a “Flynn effect transfer” within families. The Flynn effect is the well-documented historical phenomenon where intelligence test scores increase from generation to generation. The authors suggested that families with higher cognitive levels and gains, possibly due to mothers starting families later and belonging to later cohorts, exhibit better maternal health outcomes in midlife, which could be studied in future research.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the links between health and cognitive abilities. However, it should be noted that although the study originally talks about intelligence, it did not use a dedicated test of cognitive abilities, but used achievement tests as proxy indicators of intelligence. Such a decision is defensible as achievement test scores tend to be highly correlated with intelligence, but this view is not universally accepted among researchers.
The paper, “Family-level intelligence and maternal health: A cross-cohort, cross-generational longitudinal study using the NLSY,” was authored by Linda Wänström, Patrick O’Keefe, Graciela Muniz-Terrera, Stacey Voll, Frank D. Mann, Sean Clouston, Scott Hofer, and Joseph L. Rodgers.

====================================================================================================

Party Invite Phishing Scams Are the New Missed Connections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

This past April, while attending his nephew’s bar mitzvah on Cape Cod, Eric Umansky woke up to an inbox full of emails from people from his past. They all wanted to know the same thing: Was he actually throwing a party Saturday night?
The New York–based journalist wasn’t sure what party they were referring to, or why random acquaintances he’d met in passing 15 years ago were emailing him. On deadline and already stressed about work, he checked his phone, where more messages inquired about a supposed Paperless Post invite he’d sent for a “Special Private Dinner Party” at 7 pm on May 2.
Except Umansky hadn't sent the invite, and he wasn’t planning to host a party anytime soon.
As it turned out, he was an early victim of an email scam that has since become more widespread. What Umansky didn’t expect was the positive effect it would have on his social life.
In May, after receiving increased reports, the Federal Trade Commission issued a consumer alert warning about scammers sending “unexpected messages that look like they’re from well-known invitation platforms like Evite or Paperless Post,” noting how some messages “make you enter your email username and password to see event details” while others “tell you to enter a phone number and share a special code to RSVP.”
Umansky wasn’t sure how it happened; he thought he'd taken the necessary precautions to safeguard his email, including using two-factor authentication. All he could think to do was post a message on Facebook, LinkedIn, and his other social networks to notify people that he was, in fact, not having a party and, more importantly, “don’t come to my house.”
Phishing scams, which have proliferated across the last two decades, remain one of the biggest security risks faced both by individuals and companies. Email scams, in particular, can now be highly sophisticated, incorporating social engineering techniques like creating urgency or fear in a target and even leveraging the personal relationships between two people to manipulate a victim, what’s known as “spear phishing.” AI has only made those deceptions harder to weed out.
But in some recent cases, like Umansky’s, the fake party invite is having an unintended outcome: It is encouraging people to check in to see whether the message was actually real and, in doing so, has reignited dormant relationships.
“It was so striking to me after it happened that I actually had a thought that I was like, ‘Oh, is this a net positive?’” says Umansky, who over the last several months has reconnected with a handful of old friends and colleagues over lunch and via text. He recently spent an hour on Zoom with a former coworker who now lives in Mexico City. They hadn’t talked to each other in over a decade. “I was like, Oh, you know, I actually want to catch up with you about something. There was an idea I wanted to bat around with him, which we talked about for maybe 10 minutes. The rest of the time we talked about our lives.”
According to a 2024 study published in the scientific journal Communications Psychology examining social withdrawal, which surveyed 2,400 adults in the US, UK, and Canada, people are sometimes unwilling to contact old friends because they believe the other person won’t want to hear from them or they fear the interaction will be awkward. The research noted that “high priority placed on work and productivity in North America has led people to cut back on social connections and social time to meet increasing demands at work,” in addition to other life transitions, such as parenthood or moving to a new city.
But a suspicious party invite is exactly the kind of low-stakes incentive that has made initiating contact easier because it represents the one thing we all crave: a sense of belonging.
According to Lara Aknin, a professor of psychology at Simon Fraser University whose research has explored the hesitancy around reconnecting with lapsed contacts, only 30 percent of people actually check in with an old friend “even when we make doing so as easy as possible by helping them identify a desirable, feasible, and low-risk contact.”
With email scams, “people are motivated and willing to reach out to an old friend because the scam provides a legitimate excuse or social cover to do so,” she says. “In fact, people may even be slightly grateful for the reconnection opportunity this context affords, even though they hope the scam is false.”
Most people will only have a small number of close relationships in their lifetime, and it is even fewer these days; nearly half of the population (44 percent) have five or fewer acquaintances. “In the course of [scammers] taking advantage of that real desire, they are actually helping fill it,” Umansky says.
He’s not the only one who has reignited old relationships after being targeted by a scam. “I heard from a friend of more than 30 years,” Larry Persily wrote in the Wrangell Sentinel, a local newspaper in Alaska, of the trend. One source confirms with WIRED that they are back in touch with an ex they haven’t spoken to in years after receiving a fake invite.
To be clear, the unintended consequence of scam attempts may be reconnecting with lost friends, but they’re not all Zoom reunions and brunch. The FBI estimates that scammers tricked Americans out of $21 billion in 2025 alone, with help from AI.
Some of us remain impervious to the lure of the phishing trap invite. In late August, I received an unexpected Paperless Post invite—“Raise a Glass! Dinner & Drinks” the subject line read—from an acquaintance I hadn’t spoken to since 2017, though I immediately deleted it because I could barely remember who he was or why we even exchanged emails. I probably should have reached out. Maybe we both would’ve enjoyed the catch-up.

Socialism is More Popular Than Ever in the U.S., According to Polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

It’s undeniable. Socialism is on the rise—or at least growing in popularity in the U.S.
Forty-three percent of Americans have a positive view of socialism, the highest share since Gallup began tracking the measure since 2010. The latest survey, conducted Aug. 3-24, found that socialism has gained ground over time as several market-oriented economic concepts have lost favor. It now ranks ahead of big business, which has fallen to a positive rating of 35% from a peak of 58% in 2012.
Capitalism and free enterprise are still more popular than socialism. Capitalism’s positive rating, however, has fallen to 55% from a peak of 61% in 2010 and 2012. Free enterprise is now favored at 77%, compared to its peak of 89% in 2012. Small business remains the most favored economic system at 95%, relatively unchanged in 2010.
Those figures, however, mask sharp partisan differences. Democrats view socialism much more favorably than Republicans do, and their views have become more positive over time.
This shift has come as progressives and democratic socialists have defeated establishment candidates in several key Democratic primary contests. Zohran Mamdani’s election as New York City Mayor last year marked a breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). In June, all three of his endorsed candidates won against establishment Democrats in congressional primaries in New York City.
Read More: Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
Progressives also won high-profile primaries elsewhere, including Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, both of whom have not adopted the socialist label, as well as DSA members and House candidates Melat Kiros in Colorado and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. Democratic socialist Francesca Hong narrowly lost in the gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin, a battleground state.
What Brookings analysts dubbed a “DSA summer” serves to “signal that unhappiness with the Democratic establishment and, in the post-Biden world, opposition to elderly officeholders can be leveraged by young, charismatic DSA candidates—and reflect an impatience with party leadership that transcends ideology.”
Republicans have sought to portray those victories as evidence that the Democratic Party is moving too far left ahead of the November midterm elections, while Democratic leaders have tried to temper concerns about the party’s direction. In November 2025, the House voted 285-98 to approve a resolution denouncing the “horrors of socialism,” which was followed by another resolution condemning socialism that passed 220-192 earlier this month. A July analysis by the Cook Political Report found that center-left candidates dominated primaries in the competitive House seats most likely to determine control of Congress, suggesting that progressive victories may not signal a leftward shift across the country.
“If left-wing nominees manage to win in swing districts, their overall movement will be strengthened,” the August Brookings analysis said. “If they lose districts deemed winnable and cost Democrats control of the House and Senate, their mainstream presence will likely be diminished.”
Still, changing views among the American public could indicate growing openness to what was once a political red line.
Here’s what the latest polls say.
Partisan split
Socialism isn’t gaining popularity universally in the U.S.
Most of the increase in socialism’s positive rating through 2025 came from growing favorability among Democrats. In 2010, 50% of Democrats viewed socialism positively, according to Gallup. That rose to 66% last year, and remained relatively unchanged at 65% this year. Socialism now matches free enterprise in favorability among Democrats, following a sharp decline in their positive views of free enterprise since 2021.
Democrats have also viewed socialism more favorably than capitalism since 2016, when 54% of Democrats viewed capitalism positively, while 60% viewed socialism positively. That year marked a breakthrough for the DSA as longtime Senator Bernie Sanders (I, Vt.) brought the organization to national attention during his presidential run.
Capitalism’s positive rating has further fallen among Democrats, declining from 42% last year to 35%.
Other polls have found a similar pattern among Democrats. A CBS/YouGov poll, conducted Aug. 12-14, found that 58% of Democrats viewed socialism positively, compared to 32% for capitalism. College-educated Democrats were especially positive about socialism, with 71% viewing it favorably.
Meanwhile, 50% of Democrats viewed capitalism negatively, compared with 18% for socialism. That contrasts with the broader public, which overall favored capitalism to socialism.
The poll also found that half of Democrats viewed the label “democratic socialist” positively.
A Marquette Law School poll highlighted by CNN in June similarly found that the DSA had a higher net favorability among Democrats and Democrat-leaning independents than Democrats in Congress by 13 points. A national survey conducted by Data for Progress in August 2025 found that Democrats preferred democratic socialism to capitalism by a 58-percentage-point margin.
Socialism has also grown in popularity among political independents, accounting for the overall boost to socialism’s favorability in the latest Gallup poll. The share of independents rating socialism positively rose from 37% last year to 45%, surpassing big business which fell to a record low of 32%. Capitalism, free enterprise, and small business still ranked above socialism in favorability among independents.
Republicans remained overwhelmingly skeptical of socialism, with just 14% viewing it positively. Large majorities of Republicans continued to have positive views of small business, free enterprise, and capitalism, while 62% of Republicans viewed big business positively.
Still, Americans’ economic views are more complicated than the results might initially suggest, according to a Gallup analysis from August. The report, based on open-ended survey responses, found there is broad support for free-market principles like economic competition and market choice, despite concerns about capitalism spurring economic inequality and excessive corporate power.
The CBS/YouGov poll, meanwhile, found that support for government intervention crossed party lines, with 75% of Democrats, 62% of independents, and 54% of Republicans supporting government price controls.
And the Data for Progress survey showed 70% of 1,257 respondents said the U.S. economic system is “rigged in favor of corporations and the wealthy” and favored replacing it with one that “gives working people a fair shot,” including 67% of independents and 58% of Republicans. Additionally, 83% of respondents, including 81% of independents and 80% of Republicans, agreed that social work and mental health are necessary parts of a public safety budget.
Generational differences
Younger Americans are more receptive to socialism, polls show.
According to Gallup, 57% of Americans aged 18 to 34 viewed socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism. The pattern was reversed among older adults: 65% of those aged 55 and older viewed capitalism positively, while 34% viewed socialism positively. Of Americans aged 35 to 54, 50% rated capitalism positively, while 45% rated socialism positively.
The August CBS/YouGov poll also found that younger Americans were more likely to perceive shrinking economic opportunities. Fifty-four percent of American adults under 30 said their opportunities to succeed are worse than their parents’ generation’s, compared with 31% of those aged 65 and older. Of those under 30, 80% also said buying or owning a home is harder for their generation than previous generations, while 71% saw worse prospects for financial security and 64% for having a good job.
Among those under 30, 61% described the U.S. economic system as somewhat or very unfair. Socialism was viewed positively by 43%, compared with 38% for capitalism. By contrast, 30% of those 65 and older viewed socialism positively and 59% viewed capitalism positively.

Abbas by video, Netanyahu in person: two messages at UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:57:48 UTC
19:57:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Abbas by pre-recorded video, Netanyahu in person: two contrasting messages at the UN
On Thursday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly from behind a screen, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu prepared to take the same podium in person, highlighting a disparity that went beyond the two leaders' contrasting messages.
Abbas spoke by pre-recorded video after the Palestinian delegation was denied the necessary US entry visas to attend the gathering in person, according to Palestinian officials.
His address focused on the war in Gaza, Israel's occupation, settlement expansion and the displacement of Palestinians, while calling for an end to the war, an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, reconstruction and a political process leading to an independent Palestinian state.
"We will not leave our homeland, nor will we accept displacement," Abbas vowed.
The Palestinian Authority president also pointed to the growing number of countries recognising the State of Palestine, saying 160 had now done so.
He called on other countries to follow suit and reiterated the Palestinian demand for full UN membership.
Abbas also called for the implementation of international resolutions concerning the Palestinian cause and stressed that recognition should be accompanied by a political process capable of establishing an independent Palestinian state.
His speech came as the Gaza war remained the centre of international attention, with the humanitarian crisis, destruction and displacement continuing to dominate discussions surrounding the UN gathering.
Limits of international recognition
Abbas devoted part of his address to the Israel's genocide of Gaza and the humanitarian conditions facing Palestinians there, while also warning about Israel's settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.
He argued that settlement projects threaten the possibility of establishing a geographically contiguous Palestinian state and called for international efforts to address what he described as continuing violations of Palestinian rights.
The Palestinian president also called for implementation of the 20-point plan proposed by the US administration and the UN resolution on Gaza, presenting them as elements of a broader political framework for ending the war and addressing its aftermath.
Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Ahed Ferwana told The New Arab that "Abbas's speech sought to reinforce the Palestinian position through international law, diplomatic recognition and the growing number of countries supporting Palestinian statehood."
Ferwana said the Palestinian president delivered clear messages on halting the war, rejecting displacement, ending the occupation, stopping settlement expansion and establishing a Palestinian state.
But Abbas's absence from the UN hall itself illustrated what Ferwana described as an imbalance in the political and diplomatic tools available to the two sides.
The Palestinian leadership has expanded its diplomatic presence in recent years, particularly as more countries have recognised Palestine, but Ferwana said recognition alone could not alter conditions on the ground without mechanisms capable of exerting political pressure.
"The gap between international support for Palestinian statehood and developments in the occupied Palestinian territories remains one of the central challenges facing the Palestinian leadership," he added.
He also pointed to the diplomatic significance of physical presence at the General Assembly, saying a head of state or government attending the gathering has opportunities that a recorded speech cannot fully replicate.
"A leader attending in person can interact directly with foreign delegations, international media and diplomats and respond to developments surrounding the gathering," he explained.
In Abbas's case, however, his message reached the General Assembly through a screen, while the Palestinian delegation's inability to attend became part of the wider political story surrounding his address, according to Ferwana.
"The contrast became more pronounced when Netanyahu arrived at UN headquarters to deliver his own speech from the podium," he said.
Netanyahu focuses on 'security'
When Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes and crimes against humanity, took the podium, several delegations walked out in protest against his government's policies and its conduct of the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu responded by describing those who left as "moral cowards", while continuing with an address that devoted substantial attention to Israel's security concerns, Iran, Hezbollah and Israel's military operations in the region.
He argued that Israel's military action against Iran had been necessary for the country's survival and presented the broader regional confrontation through the lens of threats facing Israel.
Palestinian political analyst Akram Atallah told TNA that Netanyahu's address represented an attempt to shift the focus of international discussion away from the destruction in Gaza and towards Israel's security concerns.
"Netanyahu entered the General Assembly knowing that the Gaza war, civilian casualties and destruction would remain central to international criticism of Israel," he said.
"The Israeli prime minister therefore sought to frame the discussion around threats facing Israel, particularly Iran and armed groups in the region," Atallah added.
Netanyahu's presentation placed the Gaza war within a broader security narrative, allowing him to address audiences concerned about Iran, Hezbollah and the possibility of a wider regional confrontation while defending Israel's military conduct.
Atallah said, "The strategy was not simply about responding to criticism but about establishing the framework through which Netanyahu's speech would be understood."
Despite the walkouts, Netanyahu was able to use the UN platform directly and speak to international media gathered around the General Assembly, he believes.
"That physical access stood in contrast to Abbas's participation by video […] The difference was particularly visible because the two leaders addressed the same international institution during the same high-level gathering but approached the conflict from fundamentally different starting points," he said.
For Abbas, the central issues were the occupation, Palestinian statehood, settlement expansion, displacement and the humanitarian consequences of the Gaza war, he added.
For Netanyahu, the emphasis was on Israel's security, Iran, regional threats and the justification of Israeli military action, he continued.
Between rhetoric, law and political power
But Gaza-based political analyst Tayseer Abdullah criticised Netanyahu's speech in a Facebook post, arguing that the Israeli prime minister sought to present himself as the victim despite the international criticism directed at his government over the war in Gaza.
Abdullah wrote that Netanyahu had "dons the guise of the oppressed, the downtrodden, and the weak", describing what he considered a reversal of the positions of victim and perpetrator.
Abdullah also referred to the International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Netanyahu and questioned how the Israeli prime minister was able to travel to New York and address the General Assembly.
At the same time, Abdullah criticised statements by some Palestinian officials, including rhetoric about repeating the events of 7 October, arguing that such language could shift international attention away from the occupation, destruction and war and allow Israel to portray itself as the threatened party.
The 81st session of the General Assembly again provided a global stage for competing narratives over the Israel's ongoing genocide of the Palestinian people.
It also spotlighted how access, diplomatic leverage and the ability to shape the international conversation surrounding a war that has continued to define the region's politics.

UN coordinator calls for joint action to protect Caspian Sea

UN coordinator calls for joint action to protect Caspian Sea
TEHRAN – Protecting the Caspian Sea is not only an environmental priority but also a priority for sustainable development, UN Resident Coordinator in Iran Christine Weigand has said, noting that the environmental challenges facing the transboundary body of water require joint and collaborative solutions.
Weigand made the remarks at the seventh meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP7) to the Tehran Convention on the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea in Tehran on Wednesday.
The gathering of the five littoral states around a shared ecosystem provides an important opportunity to strengthen regional cooperation and translate common commitments into practical measures to protect the Caspian Sea, she said.
Noting that 2026 marks the 20th anniversary of the entry into force of the Tehran Convention, the UN official said the Caspian Sea has sustained human life and civilizations for thousands of years and remains a source of livelihoods and well-being, an important transportation route, a valuable reservoir of natural resources and a habitat for unique marine biodiversity.
“Protecting the Caspian Sea is not only an environmental priority, but a sustainable development priority,” she said, stressing that the health of the sea is directly linked to the livelihoods and well-being of surrounding communities, economic activities, sustainable natural resource management and regional resilience.
Environmental challenges, she added, do not stop at national borders. Marine pollution, biodiversity loss and mounting pressure on shared ecosystems have transboundary consequences and therefore require cross-border and participatory solutions.
Weigand described the Tehran Convention as an important framework for joint action by the littoral states, saying it facilitates the advancement of scientific knowledge, the exchange of data and experience, the development of effective policies and the translation of shared commitments into collective action.
She also highlighted the UN’s role in supporting environmental cooperation in the region, noting that the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) hosts the Tehran Convention Secretariat, while various UN agencies operating in the region draw on their complementary expertise to support the littoral states in advancing the convention’s objectives.
In Iran, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and UNEP are working with national and local partners under the broader Caspian Sea initiative to translate regional commitments on marine litter and plastic pollution into concrete action, she said.
Strengthening waste separation and recycling in coastal communities, promoting circular approaches to plastics and providing community-based grants for local solutions are among the measures being pursued under the initiative, she added.
The UN Resident Coordinator also underscored the need to engage the private sector and local communities, including women and young people, in improving waste management systems.
 
 “Protecting our seas is a shared responsibility, and no country, institution or organization can protect this unique ecosystem alone,” she said.

autonomous robotic hand walks on its fingertips like the addams family’s thing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:55:53 UTC
19:55:53 KST

ETH ZURICH TRAINS ROBOTIC HAND TO WALK ON ITS FINGERS
A robotic hand has apparently decided it no longer needs the rest of the robot. Researchers at ETH Zurich’s Soft Robotics Lab have developed an autonomous five-fingered hand that can walk across different surfaces, steer itself, recover after falling over and interact with objects — all using the same fingers normally reserved for grasping. Rather than adding wheels or legs to the system, the team turns the hand itself into a mobile robot, allowing its fingers to alternate between supporting, moving and manipulating its body.
The prototype is based on a commercially available anthropomorphic hand equipped with five fingers and 20 actuated joints, four for each finger. Researchers Amirhossein Kazemipour, Hehui Zheng and Robert K. Katzschmann added a compact onboard system containing a battery, sensors and computing hardware, bringing the complete untethered robot to 818 grams. The resulting machine needs no external arm to carry it around and, despite looking suspiciously ready for a role in The Addams Family, is intended as a practical experiment in mobile manipulation.
the robotic hand walks using its five fingers | all images courtesy of ETH Zurich
REINFORCEMENT LEARNING PUTS FIVE FINGERS TO WORK
Teaching a hand to walk is slightly more complicated than asking it to behave like a very small quadruped. Unlike legs, its five fingers have different geometries and ranges of motion, while the palm naturally sits at an angle. When one finger leaves the ground to take a step or interact with something, the others must continue balancing the robot’s entire weight. The researchers addressed this asymmetry through reinforcement learning, training locomotion policies in simulation before transferring them to the physical hand.
The results take the robot well beyond a tabletop demonstration. ETH Zurich’s hand was able to move untethered across 14 indoor and outdoor surfaces, including carpet, tile, metal grating, asphalt, grass, gravel and weathered stone. When deliberately placed on its side, it successfully pushed itself back upright in 21 of 25 trials. Its fingers can also switch from locomotion to manipulation: in one experiment, the robot supported itself while pressing keyboard arrow keys, correctly hitting 29 out of 32 targets. It then put those keyboard skills to excellent use by completing moves in the puzzle game Sokoban.
the autonomous system weighs 818 grams
AUTONOMOUS ROBOTIC HAND BECOMES ITS OWN MOBILE MANIPULATOR
Other experiments asked the hand to approach and push a small object toward a target, demonstrating how locomotion and manipulation can operate as part of the same system. This dual role is central to the research. Conventional robotic hands generally arrive at a task attached to an arm, which itself may need a larger mobile platform to move through space. Giving the end effector its own means of locomotion removes some of that hardware and could allow a larger robot to leave its hand close to an otherwise inaccessible area.
The researchers imagine a future system in which a robot places the hand near a narrow opening or confined workspace, letting it crawl independently toward a control or object, perform the required task and return to be collected. Further development will require better onboard perception and a broader range of movement, but the experiment already reframes a familiar piece of robotic anatomy: instead of designing another mechanism to carry the hand where it needs to go, ETH Zurich simply taught the fingers to take it there.
all five fingers double as legs
20 actuated joints control the hand’s movement
the hand navigates indoor and outdoor surfaces
project info:
name: Fingers as legs, Anthropomorphic hand design: Amirhossein Kazemipour, Hehui Zheng, Robert K. Katzschmann location: Soft Robotics Lab, ETH Zurich
