What’s the point of the interstellar Fermi Explorer mission?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:54:39 UTC
19:54:39 KST

How many interstellar probes has humanity launched? If you’re not a die-hard space geek, the answer will probably surprise you: five. Yes, we currently have five spacecraft, all launched by NASA, heading out into the great beyond. Pioneers 10 and 11, along with the New Horizons probe that passed Pluto in 2015, are well on their way to crossing the fuzzy boundary between our solar system and the rest of the galaxy. They’ll eventually join Voyagers 1 and 2, which are already plying the black void between stars.
That makes me wonder: What’s the point of the Fermi Explorer mission?
Fermi Explorer is a private space venture dreamed up by entrepreneur Philip Johnston and a small team of like-minded people who want to send a small, relatively inexpensive spacecraft on a flyby trajectory past the sun’s nearest neighboring star system, Alpha Centauri. As you might expect, given the target distance of more than 40 trillion kilometers, it’ll be a while before the mission gets there: Fermi Explorer’s trip is projected to take just under 80,000 years.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Mark your calendars.
The mission’s specific objectives for its (as-yet-unbuilt) 100-kilogram spacecraft are to carry a payload mass of at least one kilogram, to pass by Alpha Centauri within 500,000 years at a distance of less than about 400 billion km and to launch sometime in 2029—all for a price tag below $15 million.
Mind you, none of this is infeasible. I dare say it’s not even improbable. Launch costs for such a trip used to be prohibitive, but rideshare programs—in which several small satellites are launched at the same time in a single rocket, like people sharing a cab—lower the cost significantly. Launch for such a mission could easily be less than $1 million, and by using off-the-shelf technology, the spacecraft could be designed and built relatively cheaply.
The most expensive part of Fermi Explorer would probably be operation cost, such as salaries for personnel, and that’s because of the mission’s duration, which in turn depends on the propulsion and trajectory needed to leave the solar system. While chemical rockets could be used to give the spacecraft the kick it would need to escape the sun’s gravity, that approach would violate the mission’s mass—and budget—constraints.
Instead Fermi Explorer will use solar-electric propulsion: solar panels will power a small thruster that ionizes atoms of xenon and employs a powerful electric field to shoot them at very high speed out the back of the spacecraft. The thrust from such engines is low—just a whisper of force, about the same as the weight of a sheet of paper resting in your hand. But this thrust can be maintained for days, weeks or even months, allowing the spacecraft to build up a terrific velocity. All that additional time adds to the operation cost, however.
Moreover, the trajectory out of the solar system takes years. The plan is not to simply fling Fermi Explorer out toward Alpha Centauri. Instead the idea is that the spacecraft will use a well-understood process utilizing the Oberth effect. The maneuver will start with the spacecraft thrusting backward, opposite the direction of Earth’s motion around the sun, so that Fermi Explorer will drop closer to the sun in a series of ever more elongated, elliptical paths. The spacecraft will move fastest when at its perihelion, or closest point to the sun; thrusting forward will then maximize the increase in its speed. This is very similar to pumping your legs on a playground swing to increase the height of your arc.
After a half-dozen such maneuvers, a final long burn at perihelion would give the spacecraft enough oomph to achieve escape velocity, eventually allowing it to leave the solar system at a speed of about 24 kilometers per second relative to the sun. That final perihelion thrust would occur in the year 2043, and Fermi Explorer would take roughly 15 to 20 more years to pass what is generally accepted as the boundary between the solar system and interstellar space. From there, it would be a quick 80 millennium jaunt to Alpha Centauri.
Again, to be clear, all of this is technologically doable right now.
That brings me back to my original question: Why do this?
According to Johnston and his collaborators, the point is in the name. The Fermi paradox is an apparent—but so far still unexplained—contradiction between how seemingly easy it is for intelligent life to explore the entire galaxy in cosmically short times and how there’s no compelling evidence that aliens have visited Earth. (The paradox is attributed to physicist Enrico Fermi, who allegedly stated this conundrum succinctly at a lunch with colleagues discussing aliens: “But where is everybody?”)
The team behind Fermi Explorer wants to show that the holdup is not linked to any lack of ability to send probes to other stars—one of the potential roadblocks to galactic exploration. Thus, the team’s proposal for a demonstrative mission to Alpha Centauri.
I’m scratching my head about this, however, because we’ve already blown through that roadblock by sending five probes on interstellar trajectories.
Now, to be fair, those NASA spacecraft are just heading out into space somewhat willy-nilly after flying by their planetary targets in our own solar system; none is bound for Alpha Centauri or any other nearby star. But sending something to a specific interstellar destination isn’t that much harder. Missions from NASA, the European Space Agency and others have threaded interplanetary trajectory needles with incredible precision. Targeting a star, even one that’s thousands of times farther away than anything we’ve previously visited, isn’t that big a leap.
The team also makes a point of inspiring people to think about space exploration and the Fermi paradox, as well as the possibility of “great filters,” which are potentially extinction-level barriers to a species achieving space travel. But I’m not convinced of the efficacy of its plan here. Again, we already have probes on their way to the stars, and we also know public interest in a specific mission can wane. I’d wager Fermi Explorer is especially prone to this because of its mass and cost constraints, which prohibit it from carrying equipment for maintaining long-term contact with Earth; it wouldn’t get very far before slipping permanently out of communication range. And just to state the obvious, it would beam back no science from or about Alpha Centauri itself. Out of sight, out of mind.
If inspiration is the goal, I’d argue that setting up a scholarship for young students (especially in underserved communities) to study interstellar space exploration could be more effective—and easier, too.
The timing on this announcement is a bit ironic as well: right now the New Horizons team is struggling with a NASA decision that may force it to switch off two important instruments that measure the space environment around the probe. Unlike the Voyager spacecraft, which are running out of power and need to conserve it, New Horizons’ woes are linked to budgetary shenanigans brought on, at least in part, by the Trump administration’s peculiar antipathy to many areas of scientific research. The White House has repeatedly proposed devastating cuts to NASA’s science budget, leaving the agency scrambling to essentially look for loose change between the sofa cushions. The New Horizons instruments only need about $2 million a year to operate—less than a ten thousandth of NASA’s annual budget.
And New Horizons actually returns valuable science from deep space. Fermi Explorer won’t be able to carry much in the way of scientific instrumentation and wouldn’t be able to do much actual exploration with them even if it did—again thanks to the limited range of its communications.
I am not exactly against this mission—people and private ventures are free to spend their money as they wish—but I do have serious doubts about what exactly is new here, why it’s being done and what will really be accomplished.
Is interstellar space worth exploring? Absolutely. But not all missions to get there are equal.

Egypt rolls out first homegrown robot (VIDEO)

Egypt rolls out first homegrown robot (VIDEO)
Egypt has unveiled the first locally developed industrial robot, as the country seeks to expand domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on imported industrial technology.
The robot was officially launched and handed over at a ceremony attended by Industry Minister Khaled Hashem on Wednesday. According to the Ministry of Trade and Industry, it was developed by Egyptian engineers using locally produced technology. Local media reported that around 80% of its components are domestically produced, with developers aiming for 90% once motor production is localized.
The robotic arm is already being used commercially. It is being integrated into packaging equipment operated by Egyptian manufacturer QB and is designed for industrial packaging and automation on production lines.
Hashem said localizing the production of machinery and manufacturing lines is a key part of Egypt’s national industrial strategy. He added that the ‘Made in Egypt’ label is intended to reflect the country’s ability to develop technology and integrate into global supply chains.
The ministry said it will monitor the robot’s performance in industrial operations to assess its effectiveness and encourage wider adoption by Egyptian factories.
Egypt is not the only African country developing local expertise in industrial robotics. Tunisia’s TIRA Robots has developed robotic arms for integration into production lines, while other local engineering companies, including XPERT-MECA, design automated machinery and integrate industrial robots produced by global manufacturers such as KUKA.
Industrial automation is also well established in South Africa and Morocco, particularly in the automotive sector. Local companies integrate foreign-made robots into production lines. Morocco-based MTS Robotics develops automated systems for welding, assembly, handling, and packaging.
Cairo has also seen locally developed robots outside the industrial sector. In September, a team from Tanta University won the national RoboDam 2026 competition with an autonomous robot designed for cleaning operations. The university said the system could be manufactured locally at a significantly lower cost than imported alternatives.

the flâneur and the birth of the modern urban spectator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:50:29 UTC
19:50:29 KST

paris becomes a city to look at
The flâneur wanders through Paris, a city that is changing quickly, with new streets and boulevards, covered passages, cafés, department stores, advertisements, and shop windows reshaping the experience of the French capital. Walking is no longer only a way of getting from one place to another; it also becomes a way of watching what is happening around you, from the people moving through the streets to the buildings, fashions, signs, and goods on display.
This change is particularly clear in the Parisian arcades, where the street moves indoors and becomes a covered passage lined with shops, cafés, and other places to stop and look. Structures such as the Passage des Panoramas and Galerie Vivienne create a space between the street and the interior, giving pedestrians somewhere to walk without necessarily having a destination. The design of these passages draws attention to what is around them, whether it is a shop window, another pedestrian, the details of the building, or the movement between the enclosed passage and the street outside.
During the transformation of Paris under Georges-Eugène Haussmann in the mid-19th century, wider streets and longer views change how people see and move through the city. The boulevard becomes a place where the city can be observed, with pedestrians, traffic, architecture, and everyday life unfolding in front of those passing through. The rise of the department store adds another layer to this experience, bringing looking and shopping closer together. The shop window, in particular, gives pedestrians a reason to pause, look, and imagine the life associated with the objects on display before they even enter the store. It is within this growing mix of streets, crowds, shops, and visual distractions that the flâneur takes shape as a particular kind of urban observer. He can move through the city without rushing toward a destination, using the freedom to wander as a way of paying attention to the changing life around him.
Boulevard de Sébastopol ca. 1853–70 | Charles Marville, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
baudelaire’s ‘passionate spectator’
In The Painter of Modern Life, written in the 1860s, Charles Baudelaire describes the flâneur as the figure of the modern observer, someone who is deeply engaged with the transient character of contemporary life. He wanders the city without looking for timeless beauty but finds significance in its changing appearances, its fashions, crowds, gestures, and fleeting encounters, treating the everyday metropolis as material for observation. Baudelaire’s understanding of modernity is important because it shifts attention toward what is temporary and unstable, suggesting that the modern city is defined precisely by its constant transformation. The flâneur walks with no purpose; his apparent idleness allows him to remain attentive to the city as it changes around him, moving between the positions of participant and observer without fully belonging to either.
This distinction also separates the flâneur from the merely curious pedestrian or the crowd gawker, since the figure described by the French poet possesses a more deliberate form of attention in which observation becomes almost a method of understanding the city. The flâneur reads the street as a collection of signs, interpreting clothing, architecture, advertisements, gestures, and crowds as evidence of a larger social world. Yet the freedom associated with this figure is also inseparable from privilege, since the ability to wander without an immediate destination requires time, mobility, and a degree of anonymity that was not equally available to everyone in the modern city. The flâneur is overwhelmingly imagined as male, while women and working-class pedestrians encountered the same streets under very different social and economic conditions, making the history of flânerie as much a history of who was permitted to observe as it is a history of urban freedom.
image © Ossip Van Duivenbode
the arcade becomes a theory of modern life
Several decades after Baudelaire, German philosopher Walter Benjamin returns to the flâneur while developing The Arcades Project, an unfinished study of 19th-century Paris in which architecture, commodities, advertising, fashion, literature, and urban experience are brought together as fragments of modern life. For Benjamin, the Parisian arcade becomes more than an architectural type, because it represents a larger transformation in the relationship between the city and its inhabitants, bringing together public movement and commercial display within an environment organized around looking. The arcade offers the flâneur an ideal setting, as it allows observation to take place alongside consumption, producing a peculiar tension between the detached pedestrian and the commodity world surrounding him. The flâneur appears to move freely through the city, yet the city he observes is increasingly organized by commercial interests, with shop windows and displays turning objects into images before they become purchases.
Benjamin’s reading complicates the romantic image of the solitary urban wanderer, revealing how spectatorship is entangled with the emerging culture of commodities. To look at the modern city is also to encounter a system designed to attract attention, desire, and consumption, meaning that the observer who believes he is simply watching may already be participating in the economic and visual structures that shape what he sees. This is one reason the flâneur remains useful beyond the specific streets of 19th-century Paris, because the figure provides an early model for understanding how urban environments can turn everyday movement into a form of spectatorship.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s Pont Neuf Wrapped, Paris, 1975-85. Courtesy of Christo and Jeanne-Claude Foundation | image by Wolfgang Volz
from flâneur to modern spectator
During the 20th century, this relationship between urban space and spectatorship expands far beyond the street, as cinema, photography, advertising, radio, television, illuminated signage, exhibitions, and mass-produced images introduce sophisticated ways of directing attention. The experience of the city becomes inseparable from a wider visual culture in which architecture is encountered alongside images of architecture, products are experienced through advertising, and public space becomes a surface for communication as much as a place of movement. The spectator no longer needs to physically wander through the city to encounter its images, while the city itself becomes mediated through technologies of representation. The boulevard, arcade, and department store establish early conditions for this transformation by bringing movement, commerce, and visual attention together, while later forms of media extend the same logic across increasingly large distances.
The flâneur can therefore be understood as an early prototype of the modern urban spectator rather than as a historical figure who simply disappears once the 19th century ends. His particular form of walking may belong to another era, but the underlying activity of observing, interpreting, and consuming the city through images continues to evolve as new technologies and spatial environments change the conditions of urban experience.
image by Maximilian Orlowsky
when the observer becomes part of the image
The contemporary city allows the spectator to become a producer and distributor of images at the same time, so that walking through an urban environment increasingly involves not only seeing but photographing, recording, sharing, tagging, mapping, and publishing what has been seen. This changes the position of the observer in ways that distinguish contemporary spectatorship from the classical flâneur, since the person moving through the city is no longer necessarily anonymous or detached but may instead be consciously performing the experience for an audience. A street, building, café, installation, or public square can become part of the image as much as part of the experience, with people moving through the city while also thinking about how it will appear in a photograph or on a screen. The contemporary spectator is part of a much larger network in which urban experiences are captured and recirculated, creating a city that exists simultaneously as physical space and as an enormous collection of images. What began with the flâneur as an individual practice of looking becomes, through digital media, a collective and continuously updated form of urban spectatorship.
Galerie Vivienne – interior, 1905 | Brown University Library, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
designing the gaze
The spaces of the modern city have always had a role in shaping the way we look, whether through the long views created by Haussmann’s boulevards, the shop-lined passages of the arcades, the café terraces that turn the street into something to be watched, or the department stores that bring pedestrians into carefully arranged worlds of displays and commodities. What changes over time is the ways in which that relationship is presented and mediated, from the shop window and the museum interior to the illuminated facade, the digital screen, and the camera in our pockets.
This is where the flâneur remains useful as a way of thinking about urban experience, because his wandering is less important than the attention he gives to the life around him. The city becomes something to observe while moving through it, and that habit has become so familiar that it is easy to overlook how much the spaces contribute to what we notice, where we stop, and what stays in our view. The flâneur belongs to a particular moment in the history of Paris, but the condition he represents has continued to develop as cities have become shaped by commerce, media, and technology. We still move through streets, although the experience now extends into the images we make of it, leaving the modern pedestrian somewhere between observer and participant, moving through a city that is constantly presenting itself as a spectacle.
image by Adrien Olichon
image © Ossip Van Duivenbode

What’s in Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:49:48 UTC
19:49:48 KST

What’s in Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
Tehran’s offer comes as high fuel prices put pressure on Trump ahead of the US midterm elections.
Iran says it has put forward a plan to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, as Qatar passes messages between the two countries at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Speaking on the sidelines on Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the timetable could begin as soon as Washington accepted the proposal.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pope Leo heads to France amid assisted dying, abuse debates
- list 2 of 4Mamdani plants olive tree with Gaza families
- list 3 of 4Saudi Arabia allies line up support as Houthi attacks mount
- list 4 of 4Nepal PM says global order is broken in fighting climate crisis
Both sides have described the indirect contact facilitated by Qatar in New York positively, but neither has indicated any diplomatic breakthrough as the war approaches its seven-month mark.
Analysts have told Al Jazeera a firm peace deal remains unlikely, with Iran still wanting to follow the approach set out in an earlier agreement, which would give it and Oman a main role in managing the strait before moving on to discussing terms for a broader peace deal.
For its part, the US, which has claimed to be “in total control” of the Strait of Hormuz, wants Iran’s nuclear programme to be the subject of discussions straight away.
Iran has previously made clear that it will not engage with broader peace talks, including addressing the issue of its nuclear programme, until the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Hormuz strait is lifted, sanctions are repealed and the US provides a guarantee of an end to strikes, among other conditions.
Here’s what we know.
What has Iran proposed?
Araghchi told reporters in New York that Iran had presented its plan to the US through intermediaries. “If certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be open on the end of the seventh day and [peace] talks would restart,” he said.
He did not give details but said the proposal resembles the June 17 memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by Iran and the US, which briefly eased the conflict before breaking down. “The moment they accept this plan, from the next day, this timetable can start, and after seven days, the strait will be open,” he said.
Under the June agreement, Iran undertook to allow ships to pass through the strait without paying tolls for 60 days – that was the period of time given for peace talks to take place. But the MoU left open what would happen after that period.
Araghchi did not say whether the same arrangement formed part of his new proposal. Nor did he spell out what Washington would have to do before the seven-day timetable began, how either side would verify those steps, or what rules would govern shipping once the strait reopened.
It is highly unlikely Iran would be offering to cede control of the Strait of Hormuz, analysts say.
Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera that Tehran is unlikely to receive the sanction relief it has previously demanded and, therefore, sees the strait as its primary ticket to helping it recover from the war economically.
“Hormuz is a clear Iranian red line,” he told Al Jazeera. “The Iranians will not get reparations for the war, so control of the strait is the only way they can recover economically. I cannot see them backing down from that.”
Why does the June agreement matter?
The MoU signed in June set out an immediate halt to military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon, where Israel has launched strikes and occupied part of the country, and triggered a 60-day period for negotiations on a lasting peace settlement. It included US waivers for Iranian oil exports and provisions to restore maritime traffic through the strait.
It deferred other issues, including the future of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile, to broader peace talks.
But the agreement unravelled the following month amid renewed confrontation over shipping routes through the strait.
Coningham told Al Jazeera that Iran’s latest proposal follows this earlier model: “Open the strait within seven days, then start talks on the nuclear file.”
But “the US does not want to compartmentalise the issues, it wants them discussed as one package”, he said.
How else does this new proposal place pressure on the US?
Coningham also sees a political calculation in making the offer publicly at the UN as Americans contend with high fuel prices. “By explicitly saying this may be the only chance before the midterms, Iran is putting pressure on Trump over oil and gas prices and the strait,” he said. “It is a tactic to put more pressure on the US.”
The strait, which runs between Iran and Oman, is a vital route for oil and gas exports from the Gulf. Disruption to shipping has driven up energy prices far beyond the region, giving both governments an economic reason to reach an agreement despite their differences.
With the US midterm elections approaching, a deal to get it reopened could give Trump a chance to bring down fuel prices before voters go to the polls – potentially giving the Republican Party a much-needed electoral boost before the midterms.
Trump has presented the electoral calculation differently, however. In his address to the General Assembly on Tuesday, he accused Iran of waiting to see how his Republican Party performs in November and predicted a deal would happen after the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if there was no agreement.
Trump claimed the election did not affect his own decision-making on Iran: “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
That leaves an open question about whether the prospect of lower energy prices is enough to persuade his administration to accept Iran’s proposed order of talks. Coningham doubts it. “Trump is prepared for this to go on through the midterms,” he said. “The same problem remains where the proposal does not answer questions about the nuclear file.”
Where do broader US-Iran peace talks stand?
Araghchi met US envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Tuesday in talks mediated by Qatar. The Iranian foreign minister described the exchange as productive and said messages continued to pass between the sides.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it would be wrong to describe the meeting as a major breakthrough, however.
Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security, told Al Jazeera that the major blockage for Washington and Tehran is that each is making different assumptions about how much pressure they can exert on the other. The Trump administration is unlikely to revive the failed MoU, she said, because it assesses its naval blockade and tighter sanctions as working.
“The US appears to believe it can wait this out until Tehran is prepared to make meaningful concessions,” Ozcelik said.
“But Iran remains defiant despite indications that it is hurting economically.”

The Italian Ambassador to the United Kingdom, Fabio Cassese, undertook a two-day mission to the East Midlands and South Yorkshire, where he visited some of the most important Italian industrial companies operating in the country. In Alfreton, the ambassador visited the Ferrero plant—the heart of production for the historic Thorntons chocolate brand, following the merger of the Italian group with the British brand. The ambassador then visited the Danieli Group’s facility in Sheffield, where the company has been present for over 25 years. Its new headquarters, located in the Advanced Manufacturing Park and featuring state-of-the-art laboratories and a distribution center, supports the UK’s iron and steel industry on its path toward zero emissions. Also in Sheffield, Cassese visited the Marcegaglia Group’s facility, where stainless steel is produced from recycled waste using a method that reduces emissions and increases both production capacity and jobs. A subsequent meeting between the ambassador and representatives of Sheffield’s industrial sector and the Hallamshire Cutlers’ Company confirmed the deep ties between Italian industry and the “City of Iron.” The mission concluded with a meeting with the mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, with whom Cassese discussed strengthening cooperation between Italy and the region in the areas of investment, industry, and innovation. Finally, the ambassador emphasized how Italian companies create jobs and build skills in the United Kingdom, driving innovation and contributing to the growth of bilateral trade.

OPINION - Removing the punchbowl: Kevin Warsh's first test as Fed chair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:49:33 UTC
19:49:33 KST

- Christopher Smart is managing partner of the Arbroath Group, an investment strategy consultancy, and was a senior economic policy adviser in the Obama administration
In its simplest form, the role of a central banker is little more than the description offered by William McChesney Martin Jr., whose term as chairman of the US Federal Reserve spanned from Harry Truman to Richard Nixon. The job, he famously said, is "to serve as the chaperone who has ordered the punchbowl removed just when the party was really warming up."
Just four months into the job, Kevin Warsh seems to be taking the challenge seriously, and investors appear pleased. Bond yields have edged higher since the decision last week to raise the federal funds rate by 0.25%, but the stock market took it all in stride, rebounding nicely after an initial selloff.
To be clear, few Americans believe they are living through a party, with just 28% feeling the country is on the right track, according to a recent YouGov poll. The S&P 500 may be up 13% so far this year, but plenty of signs suggest the world is unraveling. Protracted wars in Ukraine and the Gulf have driven gasoline and diesel prices higher. Electricity costs have spiked amid a binge of data center construction to support artificial intelligence. Meanwhile, the US government has imposed tariffs on imports and shows few signs of controlling its carefree spending habits as borrowing costs edge higher than at any time since 2007.
Dodging the White House
Warsh refused to cite any of these specific causes of the persistent inflationary pressures when he explained that the Federal Open Market Committee had "removed a dose of accommodation." He has said from the start that he believes too much guidance from the Fed may distract investors from focusing on economic data. But he may also be trying to avoid anything that sounds like blaming the president of the United States.
For investors, the decision comes as a pleasant, reassuring surprise after months of Donald Trump's broadsides on the Federal Reserve. First came relentless social media posts criticizing Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, for refusing to cut rates. Then prosecutors launched an investigation into cost overruns for the renovation of the Fed’s headquarters, and Trump tried to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook on barely credible grounds.
Before Warsh's appointment, his published views also suggested that he had turned noticeably more dovish, arguing that artificial intelligence would ultimately improve productivity and relieve price pressures. In his confirmation hearings, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts accused Warsh of being the president’s "sock puppet."
Complicating matters further was Warsh’s longstanding concern about central bankers offering too much "forward guidance" about their intentions, which he argues shifts market attention away from actual economic fundamentals as traders try to guess what the Fed will do next. Thus, his first news conference as chair was widely panned when he refused to engage reporters on the likely causes of inflation, leading to a bond selloff.
But a more hawkish speech at the Fed’s conference in Jackson Hole in August was apparently enough to rally the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) behind a unanimous decision. He cited too many inflation subcomponents running above 3%, as the Fed has now failed to achieve its 2% inflation target for more than five years. "We removed a dose of accommodation," were his bland words.
Trump’s response was not so bland in a social media post: "Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR. Our Country is BOOMING with new Investment!" Investors have come to overlook a president who misunderstands that a "booming" economy requires guardrails against inflation, but they were grateful he chose not to attack Warsh personally. There was also relief that senior Republicans held their fire, even with a tightening decision coming just a few weeks before difficult midterm elections.
Restoring credibility in an era of shocks
Warsh has cleared this initial hurdle in bolstering the Fed’s credibility, and market inflation expectations have remained steady through the rate announcement. But the challenges ahead may be even more daunting than resisting pressure from the White House as the FOMC navigates commodity price spikes, the uncertain impact of artificial intelligence and the continuing profligacy of the US government.
Warsh lumped all these pressures into the blandest of descriptions, attributing inflationary pressures to "the geopolitical landscape of shocks and uncertainty." Single price shocks from oil, tariffs or borrowing rates can be absorbed as buyers, sellers and investors adjust their expectations. The problem these days is that the shocks have become a permanent feature of the emerging order. They just keep coming.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

‘Primetime’ Exposes the Ego-Driven Core of Vigilante Pedophile Hunting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Child predators are arguably the most reviled demographic in society.
So when someone like Chris Hansen, the former NBC Dateline journalist and host of the To Catch a Predator series, decides to take up the mantle of exposing them to the public, he is naturally praised as a hero.
But, as is revealed in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime—a dramatized snapshot of Hansen’s life at the show’s peak—it’s not as simple as that. Exposing allegedly bad people for public entertainment brings up a lot of ethical concerns and unintended consequences. And while many of the vigilantes carrying out these sting operations claim they are doing a public service, their motivations become a lot more suspect when fame and money are involved.
To Catch a Predator launched in 2004. In the show, Hansen’s team would pair up with civilian watchdog group Perverted Justice, using adult “decoys” to pose as minors online and exchange messages with men in chatrooms and private DMs. After the conversations became sexual, the crew would set up a sting, inviting these men to a home to meet the decoy, only to have Hansen confront them, uttering his catchphrase, “Have a seat.” The men were technically free to leave instead of sitting for an on-camera interview, but often police were waiting outside to arrest them.
The show developed an intense fandom that remains active to this day in subreddits like r/tcap, which has 52,000 weekly visitors, despite the fact that NBC stopped airing the original series in 2007.
In A24's Primetime, a darkly told character study in theaters September 25, Hansen (Robert Pattinson) clearly enjoys the praise and seems desperate for more accolades. He brags to his two young sons that he’s about to be on prime-time television, despite them not understanding the importance of that, and complains that the show has “never won an Emmy or any of the significance it deserves.” When a fan recognizes Hansen on a flight and becomes bloodthirsty, asking the TV host if he ever wants to “bleed” the predators he’s outing, Hansen smiles and admits that what he does by disgracing them on national television is “a little worse.”
In real life, Hansen cofounded the streaming service Trublu in November 2022, where he continues his investigations into alleged child predators. But these days, he’s far from alone. His work has inspired copycats, who thrive on social media and streaming platforms like YouTube, Kick, and Facebook. These groups and individuals are largely disorganized, and as such, hard to track, but a 2022 Washington Post investigation identified at least 160 in the US. Arguably, the people running these operations are more reckless, in part because they’re driven by virality.
One of them, who goes by Skeet Hansen, was featured in the 2025 MTV documentary Predators, about the Dateline show. In the film, directed by David Osit, Skeet Hansen responds to the criticism of the movement by saying, “There’s never been a detective that solved a murder that didn't get paid for it. So why shouldn't I be able to monetize off of catching these guys like the original show and making this content for people’s entertainment?”
One of many issues with that argument is that these hunters aren’t professional investigators—and sometimes they get things wrong.
In April, YouTuber and Kick streamer Vitaly Zdorovetskiy apologized after publicly—and wrongly— accosting a man of Indian descent. He accused the man of wanting to “rape a 16-year-old” in a mock Indian accent and called him “Mr. Mumbai.” In March 2025, The New York Times reported that Zdorovetskiy’s tactics for ambushing suspected creeps included beating some of them up, dressing like the Joker; the Times piece found that there have been more than 170 violent vigilante attacks by predator-hunting groups since 2023.
I spent over a year investigating similar groups in Canada for Vice, starting in 2015, and found that some of the people being targeted in stings had severe intellectual and physical disabilities.
Law enforcement groups, meanwhile, have repeatedly denounced vigilantes, noting that their evidence often can’t be used within the criminal justice system and that confronting alleged pedophiles can allow the targeted person to escape before police can step in. In some cases, the so-called predator hunters have ended up being charged with child-porn offenses themselves.
Warning: The following contains spoilers for Primetime.
In Primetime, the catastrophic consequences of these rogue busts culminate in a sting taking down Louis William “Bill” Conradt Jr., a chief felony assistant district attorney in Rockwall County, Texas. Conradt doesn’t agree to come to a decoy house, so both the TV crew and police show up at his home, where he shoots and kills himself. (The real-life Hansen told the Hollywood Reporter he doesn’t regret the November 2006 sting. Neither he nor NBC responded to a request for comment for this story.)
There are no heroes in Primetime, and the movie doesn’t wrap up any of these threads neatly.
At the end, struggling actor “Decoy Dan,” played excellently by Skyler Gisondo, finally gets career validation when his appearances on the show earn him a SAG-AFTRA card, but it’s clear from his expression that he’s not comfortable with what he had to do to get it.
Meanwhile, Hansen’s character, who repeats the phrase “What would have happened if I wasn’t here?” to suspected predators throughout the film, leaves the audience to grapple with that question. The answers are far from black-and-white.

US intervenes to stop $136 million fine imposed by EU on X social media, Elon Musk's companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:43:57 UTC
19:43:57 KST

The United States challenged the €120 million ($136.51 million) fine the European Union imposed on Elon Musk's X (formerly Twitter) over alleged breaches of online rules.
The alleged breach falls under a new series of regulations imposed by the EU, which has caused more friction with Washington, with the US arguing that the fines cannot be imposed on American companies operating outside the EU.
“The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction,” said US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.
“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” he added.
According to the US Department of Justice, the fine also stepped over the "corporate veil" principle and targeted not only X as the company committing the breaches, but Musk himself and other companies he owns.
It also warned that the approach could "have significant implications for 'very large online platforms' and other similar entities operating in the digital services sector within the EU."
Musk-EU clash erupts after two-year-long investigation
The legal battle began in December 2025, after an almost two-year investigation found that X was not doing enough to tackle illegal and harmful content posted on the platform.
The case also represents a wider crackdown on Big Tech in the EU that aims to regulate the industry in order to allow smaller companies to compete and, in exchange, offer more choice to European consumers, something that has been widely criticized by the Trump administration.
Reuters reported that the European Commission, which acts as the EU's executive arm, issued a response saying that the case didn't target any specific nationality, making the US argument to intervene on the grounds of the Article 40 of the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU void.
The article, according to the US Department of Justice, "provides that a natural or legal person, including a State, may intervene in disputes before the Court where that person 'can establish an interest in the result of the case to the Court.'"
The European Commission also said that the case aims to "defend its digital and democratic standards, which it says serve as the benchmark for the rest of the world."

German prosecutors investigate alleged 105-year-old former-Nazi PoW camp guard over WWII crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:43:45 UTC
19:43:45 KST

A 105-year-old German citizen is being investigated over crimes committed at a Nazi prisoner of war (PoW) camp during World War II, German prosecutors announced on Thursday, the BBC reported.
The prosecutors allege that the man was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at the Stalag VI K PoW camp in Senne, northwestern Germany, the BBC explained. Futher details about the former guard have been kept private.
Prosecutors attempting to investigate Nazi-era crimes face a host of challenges as most of the remaining suspects and witnesses are already dead. Of the 5.3 million Red Army soldiers held by the Germans during WWII, only 50% are thought to have made it home.
A similar case involving a seperate former guard at Senne had been underway when the supect died, aged 99, prosecutors explained. Many cases have been abandoned in recent years after the accused died or became physically unable to stand trial.
Germany hasn't had a statute of limitations for murder or accessory to murder since 1979, allowing the prosecution of Nazi crimes from WWII.
Stalag VI Prisoner of War camp, one of Nazi Germany's largest
According to records, one in three Soviet PoWs were processed through Senne, which was one of the largest PoW camps in Nazi Germany.
Approximately 300,000 prisoners, including 180,000 to 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war were held in the camp during WWII. When American troops liberated Senne in 1945, only 9,000 living prisoners were still inside.
Many of the surviving PoWs were treated like traitors when they finally returned to their home countries.
Precedent for investigating former Nazi Guards
A 100-year-old guard from Stalag VI A (Helmer) is also currently under investigation on suspicion that he served as a Nazi camp guard and took part in executions during the final years of World War II.
The legal landscape for prosecuting former guards shifted in 2011 with the conviction of John Demjanjuk, a former Sobibor death camp guard. Prior to his conviction, the courts had required evidence of direct involvement in the atrocities committed during WWII.
Since then, several former concentration camp guards have been found guilty of being accessories to murder, on the same basis as Demjanjuk.
In 2020, a 93-year-old former concentration camp guard was found guilty of being complicit in the murders of more than 5,000 people held in the camp.
These cases set a legal precedent for charging former Nazi camp guards; however, with each passing year, the window for further prosecutions narrows.
 
More than 80 years after the end of WWII, most former guards who are still alive are at least 100 years old, and time is running out to convict them for their involvement in crimes during the war.

====================================================================================================

'I had not truly come home': Israeli psychologist turns Gaza, Lebanon battlefield trauma into art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:43:31 UTC
19:43:31 KST

Michael Feuerstein, a Jerusalem psychologist who has done 400 days of reserve duty in Lebanon and Gaza and this week left for another 500 days – this time in Syria – is an unusual and very sensitive person.
Stopping off for a few minutes at the capital’s Malha Mall after the first bout of 100 days in places of destruction and death, he saw Israelis laughing, eating, and buying.
“I returned home, but I had not truly come home,” he told the Magazine in a long interview. “I was plunged into a feeling of strangeness, with a gap between me and other people. I didn’t understand what happened to me. I didn’t understand what people were doing. I felt like an alien from space. I went home, and I cried – even though no combat soldiers I knew had been killed in battle. I couldn’t look my wife in the eyes. I wondered: ‘Am I crazy, am I imagining?’ Men are taught not to show weakness.
“Understanding did not come clearly or all at once. It arrived slowly, in fragments, always accompanied by questions: ‘Did it really happen? Why are you exaggerating? Are you the only one who feels this way?’”
On the battlefield, everything appeared to him to be under control. “We carried out our missions. We maintained our friendships, our smiles, and our humor. But beneath that surface, other experiences continued to emerge: images of destruction and devastation, feelings of terror, annihilation, and loss,” he recalled.
His next birthday will come after the High Holy Days. Being in Syria, it will be “the fourth time in a row that I’ll miss celebrating it at home. I’ll also vote on October 27 from there.”
Asked if he thought about his own possible death in battle, Feuerstein said he did. “We have ammunition, but in war, most of the threats are explosions, artillery. There is nothing that really protects you. We went through minefields. Soldiers understand the statistics. Ninety-nine percent of the time I wasn’t afraid, but I felt a ‘little death’ when I returned.”
“I really couldn’t explain it in words, so I decided to create an exhibition entitled From the battlefield to home, an intimate journey, comprised of texts, poems, and images. The exhibition gives visual and emotional form to this journey – from war to home, from silence to expression, from fragmentation toward reconstruction, and from pain toward the possibility of healing. The book and the exhibition are dedicated to them – and to all those who have lost what was most precious to them on the battlefields.”
It has already been presented in a variety of medical, academic, therapeutic, and community settings in Israel, including the lobby of the Hadassah-University Medical Center in Ein Kerem and the University of Haifa. On Monday, September 28, at 6:30 p.m., it will be presented in the sukkah booth of the Feuerstein Institute at 17 Diskin Street, Jerusalem.
FEUERSTEIN IS the grandson of the late, world-renowned developmental psychologist and Israel Prize winner Prof. Reuven Feuerstein, who was acclaimed around the world for the clinical methodologies he pioneered – Structural Cognitive Modifiability (SCM) and Mediated Learning Experience (MLE).
In 1965, the senior Feuerstein established a research unit to process data from his historic psychological work with young Holocaust survivors and mass immigrant populations. These techniques continue to be used to treat children with neurodevelopmental conditions such as Down syndrome and autism, as well as adults recovering from traumatic brain injuries and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
He is the son of Dr. Rabbi Refael (Rafi) Feuerstein, who is today president of Jerusalem’s Feuerstein Institute, where he directs the mission and focus of the organization’s work. Rafi holds degrees in psychology and philosophy from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and earned his doctorate in psychology from Paris V University. Since 1993, he has been a valuable member of the Feuerstein Institute staff, specializing in cognitive-dynamic assessment.
A psychologist at the Feuerstein Institute while doing his specialist work at Hadassah-University Medical Center in Ein Kerem, Michael is married to Margalit, who works in teaching dance and informal education, and is the father of three children aged nine, six, and 18 months. His sister, Chava Dardik, also works at the institute as an occupational therapist and oversees its five rehabilitation centers around the country, working closely with people dealing with PTSD and the transition back to life after combat.
“These centers, financed by the Defense Ministry and the National Insurance Institute, are caring for 230 men and women. They are mostly young families with small children. Many institutions have sprouted up since October 7, but many still feel it’s hard for them to function,” Dardik explained.
“Our aim is to help them return to normal functioning. It’s not enough to just take young kids to kindergarten. Some complain they don’t interact with them. Our program is multidisciplinary, combining physical and emotional rehabilitation, dealing with trauma. We use the Feuerstein techniques of planning, being organized, and flexible, and not being impulsive. Those who want to study are helped. They are with us for a whole year, two or three times a week for four hours each time. We even use dogs as animal therapy to calm them down.”
Thus, the family legacy and professional history are deeply intertwined across generations, spanning groundbreaking work in cognitive psychology.
“I had a month after returning when I created more and more, but I thought I’d save it in a drawer at home. Later, I sat with my sisters. They were worried about me, that I was different. They came to encourage me. I brought a collection of what I had written and showed it to them. They were shocked – so I realized that publicizing it at an exhibition would help me heal,” Feuerstein recalled.
“I have a young brother in the regular army who is going to Lebanon. My wife has six brothers and brothers-in-law who are also going. As a result of spending the High Holy Days in Syria and continuing through December, it will probably take me about two months to get better. I went to a private psychologist for counseling who himself served in the Second Lebanon War. He understood me, and I felt better.”
Asked whether he mourned not only Israelis who were murdered and killed since Oct. 7, 2023, but also children, women, and men who were not involved in Hamas terror, Feuerstein said: “Yes. It’s all very violent. We did things we had to do. We had to decide in seconds whether to kill a terrorist who endangers you. It’s justified. But you are like a god who decides who will live or die.
“Suddenly, there are no clear borders of what’s right or wrong. Everything is black and white there. You sit in a house in Gaza and know that in a few minutes, I will destroy it. In one, I saw a heart-shaped pillow with a picture of a couple who had lived there. It takes a lot of effort to keep your own heart alive in such situations.”
As a psychologist, he didn’t feel he was supposed to cope better than other soldiers. “I am more sensitive. When we treat patients, we have to be a mirror for their pain. Most people who were there pushed it away.”
Feuerstein and his family are sure that he didn’t and doesn’t suffer from PTSD. “But my experiences have influenced my personality. I changed. At first, I couldn’t go to synagogue minyans, because I needed distance because of my feeling of being alone. I will miss the Shabbat, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Sukkot prayers, but there are not holidays on the battlefield. You don’t feel them, and somebody has to protect Israel even on holy days.”
'The exhibition helped me to be understood, to tell my story'
ASKED WHAT IMAGE in the exhibition was most meaningful for him, he said: “Drawings, like one in which I lie in sand. They came before words. It was dissociation, like Rabbi Shimon, after Bar Kochba’s revolt, who remained in a cave for a year or two. I am very private and shy. My family wanted to know what happened to me as a result of the battlefield, and since I couldn’t explain it to them, the exhibition helped me to be understood, to tell my story.”
In this sense, “art became a form of archaeology – bringing to the surface experiences that had no name and no recognized place. It was a process of excavating from the depths of the psyche, from the very fabric of the body, words and images that had been buried there, and slowly attempting to reconstruct them on the page.”
The exhibition was born out of a need to give words and images to the experience of war and to the difficult journey home. “Through the creative process, I was able to approach and touch the most delicate materials of the psyche. What my body and mind were telling me was profoundly different from the narrative I had experienced during the events themselves.”
A very powerful image and symbol was the bulldozer, “because in a few hours, in a sea of destruction, we had to clear everything up.” So was the ceramic vest: “It is strong, but underneath there is a storm, so I felt I was dripping into the floor.”
Feuerstein knows that his endless reserve duty hurts his wife and children. “My connection with the kids is less, but if I’m called, I have to go. My soul won’t let me stay.”
His wife contributed poems to the exhibition. “She saw the pain; she paid the price. She has run our home for many months alone, and it hasn’t been easy for her. She asked me not to return to reserve duty. Through the reflection in her eyes, I rediscovered my own face. Her perspective completes the mirror, allowing another dimension of the experience to emerge and helping tell a fuller story – one that is not only about the person who went to war but also about those who waited for him to return.”
Feuerstein has a friend with whom he’s served together in reserve duty, who decided to stop because his family was hurt so much.
'Why am I on the battlefield and they aren’t?'
When Feuerstein saw haredi young men near him after returning from battle, he felt angry. “It doesn’t do me any good. They won’t pay attention to me. But I see them in the street, and I want to yell at them. Why am I on the battlefield and they aren’t? They say they are responsible for miracles because of their religious studies. Maybe there were miracles, but not because they are in yeshiva.”
Despite all his experiences on the front lines, Feuerstein emerges with optimism and a positive outlook. “When I made room for the pain, allowing myself to touch it and even wallow in it, I discovered its healing power. I discovered how authentic life, hope, and joy are revealed, renewed, and capable of filling the heart. The pain and sorrow enabled me to deconstruct and process the fragments of reality, ultimately building a more complete and complex self.”■
The exhibition of Michael Feuerstein will be on view, free of charge, through Hol Hamoed Succot at the Feuerstein Institute, 47 Narkis Street, in Jerusalem’s Nahlaot neighborhood.

In the coming days, the Shin Bet’s Unit 730, which is responsible for protecting public figures, will begin providing security for Gadi Eisenkot, one of the opposition's main candidates to aim for the prime minister role in the upcoming elections, Maariv reported on Friday.
Security officials told Maariv that final discussions have been held in recent days within the Shin Bet regarding the security plan and the scope of protection Eisenkot will receive. The assessment is that the Shin Bet’s VIP protection unit will assume full responsibility for his security in the coming days. The decision to protect Eisenkot was made following the advisory committee's recommendation and in light of the threat assessments against him.

Yariv Levin transfers authority to Shin Bet
The move comes after the Ministerial Committee on Shin Bet Affairs was expected to convene to decide whether to adopt the advisory committee's recommendation on personal security and grant state protection to Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot until election day. However, none of the ministers attended the meeting except for the committee’s chairman, Justice Minister Yariv Levin. Following the ministers’ absence, Levin decided to transfer authority to the Shin Bet to independently determine what security measures are required.

Committee discusses positions of Shin Bet, police

At the end of the discussion, it was recommended that Eisenkot be provided with security until election day. The decision was approved by a majority vote, not unanimously.
One of the significant pieces of information presented to committee members was the police’s updated threat assessment. In the days before the discussion, the threat level facing Eisenkot was raised to level 4 out of 6, considered a high threat level. The police commissioner submitted an assessment to the committee recommending that Eisenkot receive immediate armed protection. Police did not point to information indicating an immediate danger to life, but determined that the level of threat justified taking protective measures.

Latvia moves to buy Anduril’s Barracuda cruise missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:42:29 UTC
19:42:29 KST

- Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said Latvia expects to complete the purchase of Anduril's Barracuda long-range cruise missiles after visiting the company.
- He also witnessed the signing of cooperation memoranda involving Latvia's Ministry of Defense and Latvian drone maker Origin Robotics.
Latvia is working to buy Anduril’s Barracuda long-range cruise missiles, President Edgars Rinkēvičs said after visiting the American defense company and meeting its founder, Palmer Luckey.
Rinkēvičs wrote that he looked forward to completing the acquisition of the missiles and to further defense industry cooperation. During the visit he also witnessed the signing of memoranda of cooperation involving Latvia’s Ministry of Defense and Origin Robotics, a Latvian drone maker. Neither Latvia nor Anduril has disclosed which Barracuda version Latvia wants, how many missiles it plans to buy, the price or a delivery date. The terms of the memoranda were not made public.
Barracuda is a family of turbojet-powered, subsonic cruise missiles that Anduril unveiled in September 2024 in three sizes: Barracuda-100, -250 and -500. The largest carries a warhead of more than 45 kg (99 pounds) over 926 km (575 miles). Anduril designed the missiles to be built quickly and in large numbers, and says the three versions share more than 90% of their components. The company claims Barracuda costs about 30% less and takes half the time to produce compared with similar cruise missiles.
The missiles can be launched from fighter jets, helicopters, cargo aircraft, ships and ground launchers. Anduril says they can fly together and split roles on a single mission, with some acting as decoys or scouts while others strike.
Barracuda is moving into large-scale production. In May, the U.S. Department of War signed a framework agreement for Anduril to deliver at least 1,000 surface-launched Barracuda-500Ms a year for three years to the U.S. Army, starting in 2027. In July, Poland’s state-owned defense group PGZ signed an agreement to assemble and later produce the Barracuda-500M at its Military Aviation Works No. 2 plant in Bydgoszcz. PGZ said European production could make the missile eligible for purchase by other EU countries under the bloc’s SAFE defense loan program.
Origin Robotics, based in Riga, builds drones for military use. Its BEAK drone is already in combat service in Ukraine. The company has also developed BLAZE, a briefcase-sized drone interceptor that uses radar and AI-based cameras to find and hit enemy drones on its own after launch.
Latvia borders Russia and Belarus. Its longest-range strike weapon on order is the Army Tactical Missile System, a ballistic missile with a range of about 300 km (186 miles) that Latvia is buying along with six HIMARS launchers under a deal approved by the U.S. State Department in 2023. The Barracuda-500 would give Latvian forces roughly three times that reach.

Türkiye at UNGA 81: Masterclass in 360-degree foreign policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:42:25 UTC
19:42:25 KST

- Klaus Jurgens is the director of Economyfirst Limited London
Much has been said and written about the dysfunctionality of the United Nations, with some external analysts going so far as to argue its entire structure is not fit for purpose. Fair enough, an academic exercise. Yet real change can only come from within; member states themselves must get ready to reform the UN. Enter the Republic of Türkiye and its unwavering desire to do just that – not abolish it but make it better, or, as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan rightfully insists, "the world is bigger than five." The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, if seen from Ankara’s perspective, might just have become a milestone in this undertaking. Through Türkiye's empathy, global commitment and solidarity with the oppressed, the Turkish roadmap took center stage. Quick explainer: UNGA runs for an entire year, from September 2026 until September 2027. Yet what makes the headlines is the so-called high-level meetings week that takes place now.
Calling a spade a spade – President Erdogan speaks
How important UNGA 81 is for Ankara was underlined by the fact that a book has swiftly been published in English, Arabic and Turkish by the Presidency featuring the president’s speech. Türkiye has come full circle, from splendid isolation two and a half decades ago to being a globally recognized and trusted foreign policy-making actor or, in the words of the head of Türkiye's National Intelligence Organization (MIT), Ibrahim Kalin, in 2018, when he was the president’s spokesperson, Türkiye sees foreign policy from a 360-degree angle.
What can we take home from Erdogan's speech? In a journalistic nutshell and based on excerpts from listening live via translation, he reiterated that not inviting Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to speak in person but only via video link is an injustice. Erdogan described the past 30 years as the bloodiest ever seen, mentioning Myanmar, Darfur, Ukraine, Palestine and Lebanon. Referring to Gaza, he said that 74,000 innocent citizens were killed, mostly women and children, and Gaza has become the world’s largest graveyard. Saying that none of this is a personal matter only of interest to himself but concerns the collective conscience of humanity, he went on to say the United Nations rendered itself unable to work. Asian workers, as well as African nations facing a capitalist threat, came up, as did the need for a new paradigm for the world based on income equality. Another focus was the keyword connectivity – this implies roads, transport and energy in regions of the world where they are still lacking; only then would society follow.
But while addressing those issues of worldwide concern, Erdogan made sure that, as mentioned above, his nation is appreciated as a leading global actor by underlining that Türkiye has a resilient economy, a top defense industry and is an integral part of Europe. Of course, the recent Ankara NATO Summit and Türkiye’s commitment to security came up too. And the impressive list of topics went on, including COP 31 in Antalya and the suggestion to have a Turkish director at the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
Handshakes that shift the global order
And Türkiye led the way with a remarkable number of exactly those important face-to-face meetings. Naming only a selection, Erdogan spoke, for example, with leaders from Poland, Japan, Bangladesh, Senegal and Qatar, as well as UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. If we then take into account that he met with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of UNGA as well, besides attending the annual reception for heads of state and government hosted by Trump at a famous downtown hotel, it is only fair to say that Türkiye was in high demand from all four corners of the world indeed.
And one of those four corners of the world is most naturally the United Kingdom. The president met face-to-face with Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who just settled into his new role. But the fascinating dimension is that regardless of whether a conservative or socialist prime minister resides at 10 Downing Street, cooperation is going from strength to strength. Defense, trade, tourism, education, you name it. A government in Ankara that can proudly be categorized as moderate conservative can successfully deal with either a staunchly left-leaning British government or with an almost sister-party counterpart hailing from the Conservatives. Could Burnham become an ally with regard to UN reform? Could he agree on condemning West Bank "settler" violence? What about the two-state solution? Why not! In diplomacy, bilateral relations often pave the way for bigger multilateral efforts.
Attending with a powerful top-level delegation headed by the president, clearly outlining the country's foreign policy-making objectives, engaging in face-to-face diplomacy with leaders from around the world and, for example, connecting with the Turkish business community in New York and beyond all contribute to a successful four-day trip. But the real "tangible" benefit is that Erdogan and his delegation did not play to their domestic gallery, so to speak, like most other nations; Türkiye addressed its global audience instead. Diplomacy 2.0, certainly. Can the UN be reformed into a working institution promoting peace, justice and no more genocides? Figuratively speaking, for this to happen, it needs many more Türkiyes; copycats very welcome.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

The Backstory: When 'Tau' Devi Lal won the PM race, and then gave it away with a twist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:40:26 UTC
19:40:26 KST

Chaudhary Devi Lal, the former Haryana chief minister and deputy prime minister, who turned down the Prime Minister's post in 1989 in favour of VP Singh.
NEW DELHI: On December 1, 1989, the newly elected Janata Dal parliamentary party gathered in Parliament's Central Hall to decide who would lead the government that was about to replace Rajiv Gandhi's Congress. The leadership contest had already become a tug-of-war between VP Singh and Chandra Shekhar, with neither side willing to concede the top job.Then came an extraordinary political manoeuvre.VP Singh proposed Chaudhary Devi Lal's name. Chandra Shekhar seconded it. Devi Lal was declared elected as leader of the Janata Dal parliamentary party. And then the 75-year-old Haryana veteran stood up and proposed VP Singh for the Prime Minister post.Within minutes, the man who had just been chosen to lead the government had handed the job to someone else.VP Singh was elected leader and would become India's seventh Prime Minister. Devi Lal became deputy Prime Minister.
The episode, one of the more remarkable leadership reversals in political history, has been recounted in several accounts of the 1989 transition. But this story is about Chaudhary Devi Lal, a man whose influence was built far from Delhi's power corridors and whose appeal rested heavily on Haryana's farmers and rural voters.
The Central Hall manoeuvre
The drama of December 1 was the culmination of days of uncertainty following the 1989 Lok Sabha election, which had ended Rajiv Gandhi's five-year tenure and produced a fractured mandate.The National Front, led by the Janata Dal, was in a position to form the government with outside support from the BJP and the Left parties. But before the government could be formed, the Janata Dal had to settle its own leadership question.VP Singh was the obvious national face of the anti-Congress campaign, having broken with Rajiv Gandhi and built his reputation around allegations of corruption in the previous government. Chandra Shekhar, meanwhile, had his own ambitions and was deeply reluctant to accept Singh as the party's leader.Devi Lal sat at the centre of the equation.A detailed account of the episode in journalist Neerja Chowdhury's 'How Prime Ministers Decide' describes a political formula worked out at Odisha Bhavan shortly before the parliamentary party meeting. The plan was simple but dramatic: Singh would propose Devi Lal's name, Devi Lal would then withdraw and propose Singh, and Chandra Shekhar would be persuaded to second Devi Lal's nomination.Chandra Shekhar agreed to second Devi Lal's name after being told that Devi Lal would be the candidate. He did not, however, know the full plan.When the meeting began in Central Hall, the arrangement played out almost exactly as planned. Singh proposed Devi Lal. Chandra Shekhar seconded him. But after Devi Lal's nomination, the Haryana leader proposed Singh instead. The assembled parliamentarians broke into applause and Singh was declared leader of the Janata Dal Parliamentary Party.Chandra Shekhar was furious.According to the account, he believed he had been assured that Devi Lal would become Prime Minister. After the meeting, he reportedly warned that the episode would have consequences for the future.That warning proved prescient. Less than a year later, Chandra Shekhar and Devi Lal would join forces against VP Singh, helping bring down the government they had helped create.
The OG 'Tau'
Born on September 25, 1914, in what was then Punjab, Devi Lal entered politics through the freedom movement and went on to become one of Haryana's most influential leaders.He served as Haryana chief minister twice, from 1977 to 1979 and again from 1987 to 1989, before becoming deputy Prime Minister at the Centre.His political persona was very different from that of the Delhi establishment. Devi Lal cultivated the image of a rustic, accessible farmer leader and became popularly known as 'Tau', or elder uncle.Former IAS officer Ram Varma, who spent more than three decades in Haryana's administration and worked under all three of the state's famous political Lals, provides an insider's account of Devi Lal in his 2017 memoir 'Life in the IAS: My Encounters with the Three Lals of Haryana'.Varma describes Devi Lal as having the "aura of a kingmaker" and as a "leader of farmers", while portraying him as a warm and genial personality with an exceptionally strong mass following.Varma's description also places Devi Lal in the distinctive political tradition of Haryana's three Lals. In the book's foreword, he notes that Bansi Lal was the only one of the three to possess a university degree, while Devi Lal and Bhajan Lal acquired their political education through the "rough and tumble" of village-level politics. He records that Devi Lal had earlier served as parliamentary secretary under Punjab CM Partap Singh Kairon, giving him administrative experience before Haryana was created in 1966.That combination of grassroots politics and governmental experience helped turn Devi Lal into a formidable political operator.
From Haryana's farmer leader to national kingmaker
Devi Lal's influence had grown sharply by the late 1980s, when opposition parties were attempting to unite against Rajiv Gandhi's Congress.He became one of the principal forces behind the formation of the Janata Dal and helped bring disparate opposition groups into a common political platform. His enormous rural base in Haryana gave the anti-Congress coalition an organisational strength that leaders in Delhi could not easily ignore.His political stature was also on display in September 1989, when his 75th birthday became the occasion for a massive opposition rally in Delhi. VP Singh and several other opposition leaders attended, underlining the importance of Devi Lal in the emerging National Front coalition.Yet the relationship between the two men was more complicated than their public alliance suggested.VP Singh was the face of the anti-Rajiv Gandhi campaign at the national level, while Devi Lal possessed something Singh lacked: a formidable rural organisation and an established mass base in north India.By the time the election results were out, the question was no longer simply whether the opposition could form a government. It was who would control it.
The shifting dynamics
At around 7 pm on December 1, 1989, VP Singh met President R Venkataraman at Rashtrapati Bhavan with the documents establishing his election as leader of the National Front parliamentary party, along with letters of support from the BJP and Left parties. Venkataraman invited Singh to form the government and set December 2 for the swearing-in.The following day, VP Singh took oath as Prime Minister and Devi Lal took oath as deputy Prime Minister.But the political bargain did not bring lasting peace.The relationship between Singh and Devi Lal deteriorated rapidly as their competing political interests collided. Devi Lal became increasingly critical of the Prime Minister and emerged as the most powerful internal challenger to Singh.In August 1990, Singh removed Devi Lal from the Union cabinet. The following months saw the Janata Dal split, the BJP withdraw support and the VP Singh government fall.On November 9, 1990, Chandra Shekhar became Prime Minister with Devi Lal once again serving as deputy Prime Minister.
Legacy that became a political dynasty
Devi Lal's influence did not end with his death. It flowed into one of Haryana's most prominent political families.His son Om Parkash Chautala became one of Haryana's most consequential politicians and served as CM five times. Devi Lal's political legacy was subsequently carried through the Indian National Lok Dal, the party associated with the Chautala family.The next generation entered politics as well. Om Parkash Chautala's sons Ajay and Abhay Chautala became prominent leaders, while Ajay's sons Dushyant and Digvijay Chautala also entered electoral politics.
But the family eventually split politically. Ajay Chautala and Dushyant Chautala broke away and formed the Jannayak Janta Party in 2018, while the INLD remained with Om Parkash Chautala and Abhay Chautala.The split fractured what had once been a formidable political inheritance. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, neither the INLD nor the JJP won a seat in Haryana, while the BJP and Congress won five seats each in the state.The contrast with Devi Lal's own era is striking. The man whose political clout once helped determine who would become India's Prime Minister left behind a family whose branches now operate through separate political formations.Devi Lal died in New Delhi on April 6, 2001, aged 86, after a political career that had taken him from the freedom movement and Haryana's villages to the centre of national coalition politics.
News desk journalist, digital, at The Times of India, with a focus on Indian politics. Over a decade of chasing stories, taming headlines and arguing with commas like they're part of the opposition. Tracks elections, policy pivots, party drama and the fine print of power, where every word can tilt the narrative. Believes good journalism is clarity under pressure, ideally filed before the next breaking alert crashes in. Powered by deadlines, context, sharp edits and a steady supply of strong tea.
