====================================================================================================

China Focus: Beijing Culture Forum highlights closer connection between young people, cultural heritage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:26:16 CST
14:26:16 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Cultural heritage often conjures images of the distant past: yellowed, crumpled pages, dust-covered artifacts, or centuries-old techniques that seem far removed from younger generations. But Li Ziqi, 36, has a different perspective.
Through her poetic portrayal of rural life and traditional crafts, the Chinese video creator has helped China's cultural heritage reach a global audience, amassing over 30 million YouTube subscribers.
At the 2026 Beijing Culture Forum, held earlier this week in Beijing, Li encouraged everyone, especially young people, to forge a closer bond with cultural heritage. "Culture does not exist solely in museum display cases. It lives in the fabric of everyday life," she said.
Her remarks echoed a broader discussion at the two-day forum, which brought together more than 600 guests from 44 countries and regions to discuss cultural heritage and mutual learning among civilizations.
For the first time since its 2022 debut, this year's event held a parallel forum focused on young people, highlighting their role in cultural heritage protection.
"For a long time, heritage protection was mainly a matter for older people, but young people are the future and should be aware of the importance of heritage," said Leonardo Barci Castriota, vice president of the International Council on Monuments and Sites.
While school education is essential to raise young people's awareness, it is also important to make cultural heritage more accessible by providing hands-on experiences beyond the classroom, Adam Green, a senior lecturer in sustainability at the University of York in Britain, told Xinhua.
Green cited a cultural program at York Minster, a historic cathedral, where young people were invited to design their own architectural creations with LEGO bricks, inspired by the building itself.
"It gets children thinking about the material in a creative, proactive, and critical way," he said, adding that such activities can "create an inclusive environment" for young people to engage with heritage resources and generate new visions.
In China, innovative programs are encouraging greater youth involvement in cultural heritage protection, with technology making it easier than ever for young people to take part.
One example is an initiative under the "Digital Central Axis" project, which uses digital tools to protect the Beijing Central Axis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Young people can photograph cultural landmarks along the axis and upload pictures to an online monitoring platform in real time.
To date, the initiative has collected more than 180,000 monitoring photos from nearly 30,000 participants, most aged 10 to 16. It offers young people a simple yet effective way to protect cultural heritage, said Li Wenxuan, head of the "Digital Central Axis" project.
Meanwhile, the forum also put the spotlight on young people pursuing careers in cultural heritage.
Zhong Fangrong, a Gen-Z researcher at the Institute of Archaeology of the Dunhuang Academy, once drew widespread attention on Chinese social media after choosing to study archaeology at Peking University, despite long-standing stereotypes that the field offered limited earning potential, particularly for students from low-income families.
Six years later, Zhong has no regrets over her decision and feels a strong sense of achievement from her excavation and recording work in the caves of Dunhuang, a key hub on the ancient Silk Road in Gansu Province, northwest China.
"What we document may have never been recorded before, but by preserving it today, we may leave something that people a hundred years from now can still draw on," she said.
Zhong is not alone. At the Dunhuang Academy, for example, Ding Xiaohong, deputy director of the Cultural Heritage Digitalization Research Institute, said most members of his team are young people from diverse academic backgrounds.
For young people, simply preserving what has been passed down is just the beginning of the story.
Lang Jiaziyu, a 31-year-old forum participant, is the third-generation inheritor of "Dough Figurine Lang," a folk art recognized as a national intangible cultural heritage (ICH) item in China. He believes that being an inheritor involves more than mastering the craft itself.
"On the one hand, we need to innovate our techniques and incorporate new elements into our works. On the other hand, an important task for our generation is to explore the potential of ICH and unlock its value across different industries," he said.
The tech-savvy inheritor now uses AI, 3D scanning, and other technologies to create short videos about his work and daily life for social media. He also plans to promote the traditional craft through video games and micro dramas.
In addition, Lang has taken his craft abroad through international cultural exchanges, introducing audiences across Asia, Europe and the Americas not only to his intricate figurines but also to the stories and cultural ideas behind them.
"As a young Chinese ICH inheritor, I feel proud and confident to showcase our culture on the global stage," he said.
These efforts cannot be sustained without national support for ICH protection, including policies, funding, and platforms, Lang added.
Li echoed this point at the forum, noting that the government, media, ICH inheritors, online content creators, and supportive netizens are all working together to create a positive environment for young people to grow in the cultural heritage sector.
Recently, China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism released a plan for carrying forward ICH during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The document specifies major tasks, including strengthening the cultivation of young talent in the sector.
"Whether in the online or offline world, cultural heritage is never carried forward by one person alone. It takes an entire chain of efforts, with every link essential and every part closely connected to the others," she said. ■

Tata v Tata: What’s behind India’s big boardroom brawl?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:22:23 UTC
14:22:23 KST

Tata v Tata: What’s behind India’s big boardroom brawl?
India’s most famous conglomerate is knee-deep in feuds over who gets to decide the Tata Group’s future.
New Delhi, India – An unprecedented power struggle has erupted at the top of one of India’s largest conglomerates, pitting the board of its holding company Tata Sons against its majority shareholder Tata Trusts.
Last week, Tata Sons extended Chairman N Chandrasekaran’s term and said it would consider publicly listing the holding company, flying in the face of the family charity that controls the 158-year-old Tata Group.
Extending Chandrasekaran’s chairmanship and taking Tata public is at the heart of the family-linked feud – and its outcome will not be limited merely to the group’s headquarters at Bombay House.
Collectively, listed Tata companies have a market capitalisation of $277bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders apart from pension funds, insurers and mutual funds, investment advisory firm InGovern said.
So what’s behind the bitter brawl inside one of the corporate world’s most consequential boardrooms?
How big is the Tata Group?
The Tata Group business conglomerate spans industries from information technology and automobiles to steel, power, aviation, chemicals and consumer goods.
It has 26 publicly listed companies, including TCS and Tata Motors. They have a combined market capitalisation of $277bn and operate across more than 100 countries. Tata Sons serves as the group’s principal holding and investment company.
The group’s humble beginnings go back more than 150 years when Nusserwanji Tata, born into a Parsi priest’s family in Gujarat, moved to Mumbai (then Bombay) in the mid-19th century and entered the trading business.
He later expanded into trade with China before his son Jamsetji Tata built the business into an industrial group, riding on deals in cotton and opium. Opium was then banned by China’s Qing rulers, and Nusserwanji found a way to smuggle it.
The conglomerate’s real breakthrough came when the United States Civil War broke out in 1861. The disruption to US cotton supplies sent Indian cotton prices soaring and transformed the fortunes of Bombay’s merchants, including the Tatas.
Their businesses turned into an empire over coming generations. Jamsetji Tata died in 1904, and his sons Dorabji and Ratanji Tata carried his businesses forward. The family’s charitable trusts became major shareholders of Tata Sons.
JRD Tata, who became chairman in 1938, transformed the group into a diversified industrial enterprise, expanding into aviation, including India’s flagship carrier, Air India; chemicals; and engineering. In 1991, Ratan Tata succeeded JRD, taking over as India began economic liberalisation.
Under Ratan, the Tata Group consolidated a sprawling group under a more unified corporate identity and pushed it onto the global stage with landmark acquisitions, including Tetley, Corus and Jaguar Land Rover. Tata is now pushing into the next generation of global manufacturing with a major iPhone assembly operation in India and a semiconductor fabrication and chip-assembly business.
Ratan was the chairman of both Tata Sons and its majority stakeholder, Tata Trusts, and remained a bridge between the two. After he died in 2024, a widening schism gradually became apparent.
Tata Trusts is an umbrella of family-linked charities that own 66 percent of Tata Sons.
So what’s Tata v Tata about?
The face-off was triggered on September 17 when Tata Sons reappointed Chandrasekaran as its chairman over the Tata Trusts’ nominee on the board, Noel Tata, in a 4-to-1 vote.
Noel Tata is the sitting chairman of Tata Trusts and the only family-linked senior executive sitting in the top echelons of Tata Sons today. Noel is the half-brother of Ratan Tata and became Tata Trusts’ chairman after Ratan’s death in 2024.
But the divisions between the company and majority shareholder run deeper – and include questions of taking Tata Sons public and providing a planned exit to Tata Sons’ second-largest shareholder, Shapoorji Pallonji.
Chandrasekaran’s reappointment
Last month, Chandrasekaran said he would not seek another term as chairman after February 2027. But Tata Group said in a statement the board asked him to reconsider the group’s “larger interests”, a request that he accepted.
The 68-year-old Noel Tata called the reappointment “illegal” under Tata Sons’ articles of association, adding in a statement that both trust nominees on the board were required to vote in coordination, whereas only Noel Tata voted against. The other trust nominee, Venu Srinivasan, voted in favour of Chandrasekaran’s reappointment.
This matter is now expected to be decided by the courts.
Listing of Tata Sons
India’s central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), requires companies with assets exceeding $10.45bn to publicly list.
Tata Sons tried to skirt the requirements by deregistering as a nonbank finance company. But days before its board meeting this month, the RBI rejected the company’s request, bringing it closer to a public listing.
Tata’s structure is unusual because the holding company at the very top of the empire is at the moment not itself subject to public-market scrutiny, even though many of the companies beneath it are.
At the board meeting, Tata Sons said it would take steps to comply with the RBI’s requirements. But Noel Tata opposed the move, arguing that listing would alter the character of a group that also supports extensive philanthropic activities.
Shapoorji Pallonji’s proposed exit
The Shapoorji Pallonji Group holds an 18.4 percent stake in Tata Sons and is its second-largest shareholder.
The infrastructure and construction conglomerate is knee-deep in debt and is seeking to monetise its shareholding in Tata Sons.
Tata Trusts said Noel Tata tabled a plan to sell a part of the Shapoorji Pallonji Group’s stake in the holding company worth $2.61bn. Tata Sons has not yet commented on the plan.
Shapoor Mistry, the group’s patriarch, is also Noel Tata’s brother-in-law. The Shapoorji Pallonji Group backs Tata Sons going public and is opposed to Noel’s position.
What does the dispute mean for India’s economy?
The central question in the showdown that is captivating millions of Indians involves the public listing of Tata Sons.
Noel Tata said in a statement that the Tata Group “was conceived as a national service carried on through business”. The unusual privately owned structure of Tata Sons, Noel argued, has allowed the company to remain in the country’s service and “act repeatedly in ways that a purely commercial calculus would not have supported”.
“A listing will destroy its character and strike at the heart of this principle,” Tata Trusts has argued.
However, Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian development economist, told Al Jazeera that Tata Sons needs to be listed publicly, no matter what. “There is a law for everyone, and Tata cannot be an exception to that,” he said.
“We are at a stage as a country when top business houses cannot be allowed to continue to behave in whatever manner they have managed to behave in over the last 100 years,” Mehrotra said.
Mehrotra argued that over the past decade under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India’s top business houses, including the empires of billionaires Gauran Adani and Mukesh Ambani, “have been permitted by the government to grow the concentration of industries across sectors in a historically unprecedented manner”.
“India’s biggest business houses have grown horizontally, capturing all sectors, which have come at the cost of people below them in the pyramid,” Mehrotra said.
“That means that the core inflation is being driven essentially by these handful of businesses because their horizontal and vertical control gives them the ability to mock up prices that are unprecedented in our economy’s history while their profits mount,” he said.
Mehrotra said that while the Tata boardroom drama could be captivating for some, “ordinary Indians’ concerns are rooted in regulating the unchecked growth [of conglomerates] backed by the government.”
InGovern, a governance advisory firm, said in a note that a holding company like Tata Sons that exercises “influence over businesses of such scale cannot reasonably remain outside the governance and transparency expectations increasingly associated with systemically important financial and industrial conglomerates”.
What’s the future of Tata Group?
That is slated to be decided in the courtroom now.
Both sides have lawyered up with some of India’s top legal eagles. Harish Salve, a former solicitor general of India, is leading the Tata Sons legal team while Abhishek Singhvi, a member of parliament from the opposition Indian National Congress party, is representing Tata Trusts.
The Tata Group is no stranger to boardroom tussles and dramas. After Ratan Tata stepped down from the Tata Sons chairmanship in December 2012, Cyrus Mistry was appointed to the top job, becoming the first person from outside the Tata family to lead Tata Sons in decades.
However, differences grew between Mistry and Ratan Tata, who was then still heading Tata Trusts, over strategy, governance and capital allocation. Tata Sons pulled off a stunning coup, removing Mistry as the chairman in October 2016.
Cyrus is the younger brother of Shapoor Mistry and also the brother-in-law of Noel Tata. In bitterly fought legal battles, Cyrus eventually lost his case in 2021 before the Supreme Court. At that time, lawyers Salve and Singhvi found themselves on the same side, fighting for Tata Sons against Mistry.
That judgement upheld “that the affirmative voting rights given to Tata Trusts-nominated directors are legal, valid and a globally accepted corporate norm for majority-trust-held institutions”, said Nitin Potdar, a senior company lawyer based in Mumbai.
Currently, the Tata Sons board has two nominated members from Tata Trusts: Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan. While Noel Tata opposed the reinstatement of Chandrasekaran as the chairman of the holding company, Srinivasan voted in favour.
“Even if the two Tata Trusts nominees give their votes differently, that does not give rise to any [legal] deadlock,” Potdar told Al Jazeera.
Singhvi, who will now represent Noel Tata, wrote in an X post that his reaction to the tussle “is one of sadness and regret that these issues could not be solved amicably”.
“But in the ultimate analysis, fundamental rights of shareholder-owners cannot be nullified in the manner in which they have been,” he wrote. “To stultify shareholder ownership rights would spell doomsday for corporate governance across hundreds of Indian companies.”
“Rupturing the over hundred years of Tata Trust and Tata Sons established hyphenated relationship and divorcing one from the other seems unthinkable,” Singhvi said.

“Is the cause of Man that of each man? That is what utilitarian ethics has been striving to…”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:19:59 UTC
14:19:59 KST

“Is the cause of Man that of each man? That is what utilitarian ethics has been striving to demonstrate since Hegel; if one wishes to give the word useful a universal and absolute meaning, it is always a question of reabsorbing each man into the bosom of mankind; it is said that despite the weaknesses of the flesh and that particular fear which each one experiences in the face of his particular death, the real interest of each one is mingled with the general interest. And it is true that each is bound to all; but that is precisely the ambiguity of his condition: in his surpassing toward others, each one exists absolutely as for himself; each is interested in the liberation of all, but as a separate existence engaged in his own projects. So much so that the terms “useful to Man,” “useful to this man,” do not overlap. Universal, absolute man exists nowhere.”
– Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity

Pope Leo arrives in France with AI, apologies for clergy abuse on agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:12:16 UTC
14:12:16 KST

Pope Leo arrives in France with AI, apologies for clergy abuse on agenda
PARIS, Sept 25 - Pope Leo arrived in France on Friday for a whirlwind four-day visit, saying he wished to be a pilgrim of peace for a world at war, on a trip during which he is also hoping to repair the Catholic Church's standing after abuse scandals.
Leo was greeted at the Paris Orly airport, under a clear blue sky, by President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte, and by children who sang for him and asked for autographs. He will also travel to the famed Catholic shrine at Lourdes, in the southwest, and to Metz, on the German border.
During the September 25 to 28 trip, he is set to renew calls for global rules on AI development, while laying out a vision for Europe's future.
Telling reporters on the plane to Paris that he was coming to convey a message of peace, Leo added: "It is a message which at this time, as we all may know, is particularly important."
Leading Leo's agenda on Friday are speeches to Macron and other French leaders at the Elysee Palace and to staff at the headquarters of the UN culture and education body, UNESCO, which is facing budget shortfalls after US President Donald Trump withdrew from the agency in 2025.
The first US pope attracted Trump's ire earlier this year after criticizing the Iran war.
Asked about Trump's attempt to bar CNN and several other outlets from the White House, Leo, aboard the plane to Paris, reaffirmed his support for freedom of the press, saying all were welcome to cover his visit.
'MESSAGE OF PEACE'
People lining the streets Leo was due to pass through on his way to the Elysee held up phones and waved flags and signs.
"He brings a message of peace and hope that is very, very positive. His visit to France sends a wonderful signal to the country," a Catholic passer-by, Antoine Barxias-Casties, said in front of Notre-Dame cathedral on the eve of Leo's visit.
France, a secular nation where the separation of church and state is enshrined in a 1905 law, has witnessed a steady decline in affiliation to the Catholic Church during the post-war era, mirroring a trend in other traditionally Catholic countries.
Although the French Bishops' Conference points to an increase in baptisms of adults, a report published by the official statistics agency INSEE showed that only 25% of French 18-to-49-year-olds identified as Catholic, compared with 43% a decade earlier. Only 8% of Catholics said they regularly attended a place of worship.
AI AT TOP OF PAPAL AGENDA
Leo, who has made the risks associated with AI a major concern of his papacy and has called on world leaders for global rules to oversee the industry, is expected to address the issue at UNESCO.
In a speech at the Vatican on Thursday, the pope said AI could benefit humanity, but has introduced "new dangers to security and international peace". He urged global leaders to "govern wisely" in overseeing the technology.
Leo's visit comes as Catholic leaders in France have been at odds with the government over the 2024 enshrining of a right to abortion in the French constitution, a world first, and the passage of a law earlier this year legalizing assisted dying for adults with incurable illnesses.
The Catholic Church teaches that all human life is sacred and opposes abortion, assisted dying and capital punishment.
Leo will also lead a prayer service in Paris on Friday at the restored Notre-Dame cathedral, in the first visit by a pope since a devastating fire nearly destroyed the Gothic masterpiece in 2019.
POPE TO MEET ABUSE SURVIVORS
Leo is the first pope to make an official visit to France in nearly 20 years. Local Church leaders hope the trip will repair the Church's standing after a crushing 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.
French bishops have since introduced compensation and safeguarding measures, but survivors have continued to press Church leaders to demonstrate accountability.
"Leo bears the immense responsibility of 'declaring enough is enough'," Alain Esquerre, 66, a spokesperson for victims at the Notre-Dame de Bétharram Catholic institution, told Reuters.
The pope will meet seven French victims of abuse by Catholic clergy on Sunday in Lourdes. The Vatican, which usually only issues statements about the pope's meetings with abuse victims afterwards, has not provided further details.
Leo's French tour will culminate in Metz on Sunday with a speech on "the roots of Europe for peace and unity". REUTERS

Trump to wrap up Xi summit with a tour of US archives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

Trump to wrap up Xi summit with a tour of US archives
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 - US President Donald Trump will follow up his summit with Xi Jinping by taking the Chinese leader on Friday to the US National Archives, where they are expected to stress views about the history and direction of ties between their countries.
Thursday's lavish state summit at the White House appeared heavy on symbolism but light on substance, with no sign of major breakthroughs between the world's biggest economies.
Still, Trump highlighted progress under a bilateral trade mechanism, citing what he described as increased market access for US farmers and ranchers, while both leaders identified artificial intelligence as an area for cooperation.
Trump said in remarks welcoming Xi they would see some of the greatest treasures of US history at the National Archives, including the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution and the Bill of Rights.
They would also see "artifacts testifying to the long and cherished relationship" between China and the United States and their "cultural exchanges," he said.
"Just as our ancestors reached across the ocean centuries ago to trade, to learn, and to build a better world, our two countries do really the same thing, and we're very proud of it and the relationship," Trump said.
China has not commented on the visit to the archives, but analysts say Xi may be keen to see records relating to the US switch of recognition to communist China from Taiwan in 1979.
CHINA PRESSES ON TAIWAN
China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own and Xi has long sought to persuade Trump to state publicly that the United States opposes Taiwan's independence, rather than saying only that it does not support independence, which has been Washington's formulation for decades.
He is also keen to get the US to halt arms sales to the island.
As expected, Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan on Thursday, saying he hoped the United States would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence." China's state news agency also reported that Xi "hopes the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing 'Taiwan independence'."
While the United States, like most countries, has no formal diplomatic relations with Taipei, Washington is its most important international backer and is bound by US law to provide it with the means to defend itself.
America's Asian allies will watch closely to see how Trump talks about Taiwan following Xi's visit.
After his May summit with Xi, Trump, whose administration in December approved an $11 billion arms sale package to Taiwan, said he was holding a second package, worth some $14 billion, in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip."
Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank said Beijing may believe it has established a new baseline on Taiwan with Trump.
He said Xi's use of the word "adhere" was revealing because "it implies Beijing believes Washington is already behaving in ways it wants."
"In the context of the current standdown on Taiwan arms sales, China may increasingly view that restraint as a new baseline rather than a temporary pause," he said.
"Beijing's objective is to get Trump to absorb Chinese red lines into his own definition of a stable relationship."
On Thursday, Senate Democrats criticized the summit, saying Trump had failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, artificial intelligence or human rights.
They also criticized Trump for failing to publicly address China's military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island. REUTERS

Robber gets life for binding elderly man, leaving him to suffocate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:07:38 UTC
14:07:38 KST

The Nazareth District Court on Thursday sentenced Mohammed Sabih, a resident of Kafr Misr in northern Israel, to life in prison after he was convicted of the aggravated murder of Abdullah Saadi, 76, from the village of Muqeible, in 2023.
The court also ordered Sabih to pay 258,000 shekels (about $85,140) in compensation to the victim’s family.
Sabih, together with another man whose trial is still ongoing, broke into the victim’s apartment late at night, bound him with adhesive tape and wrapped the tape around his head in a way that blocked Saadi’s airways.
The two searched for the victim’s safe and stole money and jewelry. They remained in the apartment for about 50 minutes before leaving and abandoning Saadi while he was still bound, causing him to suffocate to death.
Another accomplice, Yakub “Samir” Zoabi, also a resident of Kafr Misr, was convicted of planning the robbery and sentenced to 4.5 years in prison.
Zoabi, who was not present during the robbery, knew Saadi beforehand and had visited his home the day before the murder.

A week in diplomacy: Trump talks tough, and the world calls his bluff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:06:59 UTC
14:06:59 KST

News analysis
A week in diplomacy: Trump talks tough, and the world calls his bluff
- President Trump aimed to reassert US power with a tough UN speech and a summit with China, but faced growing resistance from world leaders amid his domestic and international challenges.
- The US-Iran war has stalled, raising global energy prices and dividing Trump’s base, while his midterm election outlook dims due to unpopular foreign policies.
- World leaders appear to be preparing for a time when the US president’s influence could begin to wane following the midterms, and with less than two-and-a-half years left in office.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – From his high-profile address to the UN General Assembly to his high-stakes White House summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump this week was looking to reassert himself on the world stage.
But Trump’s diplomatic flurry has done little to dispel the view among many analysts of a president beset by problems at home and abroad. Those include a widening Iran war that has driven up US petrol prices and cratered his approval ratings, while his relations with allies worsen and the AI challenge from China intensifies.
With the limits of his power exposed, Trump has begun facing pushback from world leaders on issues ranging from the crisis in the Middle East to Russia’s war in Ukraine, leaving the impression of a foreign policy agenda that has stalled.
This comes as Trump’s Republican Party faces midterm elections in November that could further constrain him politically.
Even so, Trump’s speech to the United Nations on Sept 22 was a stark reminder of how, since returning to the White House in 2025, he has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped to create from the ashes of World War II.
Standing atop the rostrum of a world body dedicated to peacemaking, he issued a fresh threat to “annihilate” Iran if it does not agree to a deal, defended his coercive approach to OPEC member Venezuela by asserting “to the victor belong the spoils”, and signalled he may not be done deploying the US military to achieve his international aims.
Despite that strident stance, Trump’s talks with Xi on Sept 24 put the US president up against a Chinese counterpart who appeared to be in a stronger position, overseeing a surge in his country’s trade with the world while the US grapples with the economic fallout from the Iran conflict.
Limited results
That was the backdrop for a state visit by Xi that was heavy on pomp and ceremony but light on substance, despite a host of thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and Iran.
The most tangible outcome appeared limited to a two-month extension of a trade truce, originally due to expire in November, between the world’s two biggest economies.
While Trump showed little interest in publicly airing any differences between the two powers, Chinese state media reported that, behind closed doors, Xi urged him to oppose independence for Taiwan. The democratically governed island claimed by China remains the most contentious topic in relations between Washington and Beijing.
Trump’s seemingly non-confrontational attitude was a far cry from his previously hawkish, tariffs-driven approach, which has been tempered by Beijing’s control over rare earth minerals, a key input for technology and auto manufacturing that Beijing has shown the ability to withhold in retaliation.
“Trump sees himself taking us back to a world where might makes right,” said Brett Bruen, who was a foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and now heads the Global Situation Room strategic consultancy. “But it’s noteworthy that he goes all wobbly when it comes to Xi Jinping and ascendant Chinese power.”
A White House official rejected the notion that Trump’s foreign policy has hit a wall and said his UN remarks “highlighted his various wins in advancing US interests around the world”, including preventing Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. Tehran has always said its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes.
Iran war stalemate
Looming over Trump’s packed week of diplomacy was the war with Iran, which he started alongside Israel on Feb 28.
It has dragged on for nearly seven months, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region, most recently to Yemen and the Red Sea shipping corridor.
Iran’s defiance, despite the economic and military beating it has taken, has become the most intractable foreign policy challenge of Trump’s second term.
Trump used his address at the UN to defend his attack on Iran and to declare that “America is back”, stronger than ever.
But after a string of early foreign policy achievements, including a Gaza ceasefire and the capture of Venezuela’s leader, Trump’s record in his second term in office is increasingly defined by stalemates.
With the Iran war deeply unpopular and dividing Trump’s political base, he could pay a price in the midterm congressional elections when his Republican Party’s control of Congress is at risk.
World leaders appear to be preparing for a time when the US president’s influence could begin to wane following the midterms, and with less than two-and-a-half years left in office.
Most European and Asian allies have already spurned Trump’s demands for assistance in an Iran conflict he launched without consulting them.
At this year’s UN gathering, some US partners took aim at Trump, though mostly without mentioning him by name.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron warned against a global “return to the law of the jungle”, saying countries faced a choice between a world governed by power and coercion, and a “civilised international society”.
In a rebuke to Trump, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva decried foreign interference in his country’s October election and insisted that “we do not need aircraft carriers patrolling our waters. We need cooperation to stem the flow of weapons and money that fuel crime”.
The White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump was “not concerned with posturing but about results”, and that some leaders’ public comments did not match what they told the president in private.
Resisting Trump
In another sign of diminished clout, Trump’s effort to pressure Ukraine and Russia to agree to even a limited energy ceasefire failed to gain much traction.
And while Trump touted a deal with Denmark and Greenland for an expanded US military presence in the vast Arctic island, it fell short of his initial demand to “own” the territory and his threat, if necessary, to take it by force from a fellow NATO member.
“A year ago, few countries dared cross Trump,” Ian Bremmer, president of the Eurasia Group, wrote on X. “Now, Canada, Europe, China, Iran, Russia and others are all more willing to say no.”
At one point, Trump himself seemed to wonder how much international sway he actually possessed.
In his speech, he told world leaders he wanted to rebrand AI as “super intelligence”.
“Let’s see if I have any power,” he said. “Maybe I do and maybe I don’t. We’re going to find out pretty soon.” REUTERS

A week in diplomacy: Trump talks tough, and the world calls his bluff
- President Trump aimed to reassert US power with a tough UN speech and a summit with China, but faced growing resistance from world leaders amid his domestic and international challenges.
- The US-Iran war has stalled, raising global energy prices and dividing Trump’s base, while his midterm election outlook dims due to unpopular foreign policies.
- World leaders appear to be preparing for a time when the US president’s influence could begin to wane following the midterms, and with less than two-and-a-half years left in office.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – From his high-profile address to the UN General Assembly to his high-stakes White House summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump this week was looking to reassert himself on the world stage.
But Trump’s diplomatic flurry has done little to dispel the view among many analysts of a president beset by problems at home and abroad. Those include a widening Iran war that has driven up US petrol prices and cratered his approval ratings, while his relations with allies worsen and the AI challenge from China intensifies.
With the limits of his power exposed, Trump has begun facing pushback from world leaders on issues ranging from the crisis in the Middle East to Russia’s war in Ukraine, leaving the impression of a foreign policy agenda that has stalled.
This comes as Trump’s Republican Party faces midterm elections in November that could further constrain him politically.
Even so, Trump’s speech to the United Nations on Sept 22 was a stark reminder of how, since returning to the White House in 2025, he has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped to create from the ashes of World War II.
Standing atop the rostrum of a world body dedicated to peacemaking, he issued a fresh threat to “annihilate” Iran if it does not agree to a deal, defended his coercive approach to OPEC member Venezuela by asserting “to the victor belong the spoils”, and signalled he may not be done deploying the US military to achieve his international aims.
Despite that strident stance, Trump’s talks with Xi on Sept 24 put the US president up against a Chinese counterpart who appeared to be in a stronger position, overseeing a surge in his country’s trade with the world while the US grapples with the economic fallout from the Iran conflict.
Limited results
That was the backdrop for a state visit by Xi that was heavy on pomp and ceremony but light on substance, despite a host of thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and Iran.
The most tangible outcome appeared limited to a two-month extension of a trade truce, originally due to expire in November, between the world’s two biggest economies.
While Trump showed little interest in publicly airing any differences between the two powers, Chinese state media reported that, behind closed doors, Xi urged him to oppose independence for Taiwan. The democratically governed island claimed by China remains the most contentious topic in relations between Washington and Beijing.
Trump’s seemingly non-confrontational attitude was a far cry from his previously hawkish, tariffs-driven approach, which has been tempered by Beijing’s control over rare earth minerals, a key input for technology and auto manufacturing that Beijing has shown the ability to withhold in retaliation.
“Trump sees himself taking us back to a world where might makes right,” said Brett Bruen, who was a foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and now heads the Global Situation Room strategic consultancy. “But it’s noteworthy that he goes all wobbly when it comes to Xi Jinping and ascendant Chinese power.”
A White House official rejected the notion that Trump’s foreign policy has hit a wall and said his UN remarks “highlighted his various wins in advancing US interests around the world”, including preventing Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. Tehran has always said its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes.
Iran war stalemate
Looming over Trump’s packed week of diplomacy was the war with Iran, which he started alongside Israel on Feb 28.
It has dragged on for nearly seven months, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region, most recently to Yemen and the Red Sea shipping corridor.
Iran’s defiance, despite the economic and military beating it has taken, has become the most intractable foreign policy challenge of Trump’s second term.
Trump used his address at the UN to defend his attack on Iran and to declare that “America is back”, stronger than ever.
But after a string of early foreign policy achievements, including a Gaza ceasefire and the capture of Venezuela’s leader, Trump’s record in his second term in office is increasingly defined by stalemates.
With the Iran war deeply unpopular and dividing Trump’s political base, he could pay a price in the midterm congressional elections when his Republican Party’s control of Congress is at risk.
World leaders appear to be preparing for a time when the US president’s influence could begin to wane following the midterms, and with less than two-and-a-half years left in office.
Most European and Asian allies have already spurned Trump’s demands for assistance in an Iran conflict he launched without consulting them.
At this year’s UN gathering, some US partners took aim at Trump, though mostly without mentioning him by name.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron warned against a global “return to the law of the jungle”, saying countries faced a choice between a world governed by power and coercion, and a “civilised international society”.
In a rebuke to Trump, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva decried foreign interference in his country’s October election and insisted that “we do not need aircraft carriers patrolling our waters. We need cooperation to stem the flow of weapons and money that fuel crime”.
The White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump was “not concerned with posturing but about results”, and that some leaders’ public comments did not match what they told the president in private.
Resisting Trump
In another sign of diminished clout, Trump’s effort to pressure Ukraine and Russia to agree to even a limited energy ceasefire failed to gain much traction.
And while Trump touted a deal with Denmark and Greenland for an expanded US military presence in the vast Arctic island, it fell short of his initial demand to “own” the territory and his threat, if necessary, to take it by force from a fellow NATO member.
“A year ago, few countries dared cross Trump,” Ian Bremmer, president of the Eurasia Group, wrote on X. “Now, Canada, Europe, China, Iran, Russia and others are all more willing to say no.”
At one point, Trump himself seemed to wonder how much international sway he actually possessed.
In his speech, he told world leaders he wanted to rebrand AI as “super intelligence”.
“Let’s see if I have any power,” he said. “Maybe I do and maybe I don’t. We’re going to find out pretty soon.” REUTERS

Jesse Butterfield marries paper and metal in A Veiled Boundary exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:49 UTC
14:00:49 KST

Jesse Butterfield marries paper and metal in A Veiled Boundary exhibition
Sewn paper and hand-hammered steel sit side by side in these lighting pieces and stools by designer Jesse Butterfield, displayed during London Design Festival 2026.
The aptly named Sew Paper Lighting and Stool Des Pois series premiered during Butterfield's A Veil Boundary exhibition, curated by Alex Tieghi-Walker, in the city-wide festival's Brompton Design District.
The paper lanterns continue the centuries-old tradition of using the material to make lampshades, as a result of its physical lightness as well as its translucency.
To realise the Sew Paper Lighting series, Butterfield teamed up with The Paper Foundation, a Lake District-based paper mill, founded by sixth-generation papermaker Mark Cropper.
"We got to visit The Paper Foundation and see their process, then select six or seven different papers," said Butterfield.
"We went through their archive and chose what we thought would have nice drapage and lighting effects, as well as selecting different papers for different applications."
Slim stainless steel frames dictate each piece's general form and purpose: from pendants and wall lights to floor and table lamps.
Beyond this, the lanterns strewn around the space comprise folded, draped and otherwise physically manipulated handmade paper, hand-stitched into amorphous shapes.
In dialogue with the paper lamps, Butterfield's Stool Des Pois series explores the sheet metal's capacity to behave in a similar way to paper.
A paper model was the natural starting point for the stool, which was then scaled up and recreated in steel, heated and hammered by hand until a thinness and lightness akin to paper was achieved.
The stools are based on the same initial model and dimensions, with natural variations owing to their handmade nature, ensuring that no two are entirely alike.
Further distinction is made through the polka dot patterning, a result of intentional blackening of the metal which introduces further visual interest while telling the story of their manufacturing process.
"This is the first time where I'm leaving the dots on the surface," said Butterfield.
"They come from the making process – in the past I've sanded them away, but I wanted to bring them in now as they fit with the theme of things being perfectly imperfect," he added, nodding to the leitmotif of this year's Brompton Design District programme.
Elsewhere in the district, RCA students exhibited a series of stools created with a single tool and Isamaya French launched her second-ever Studio Iron show.
The photography is by Andy Stagg.
A Veil Boundary was on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Unknown

04:46:24 UTC
13:46:24 KST

Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin told world leaders at the UN General Assembly on Thursday that the international community had failed Palestinians, warning that continued violence and settlement expansion were undermining prospects for a lasting peace.
Addressing the 81st session of the General Assembly in New York, Martin said the international legal order was under “tremendous strain” and described the denial of fundamental human rights as one of the defining challenges of the era.
“We, the collective international community, have failed Palestine,” Martin said, referring to the continuing suffering of civilians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Martin said the first phase of the Gaza peace plan agreed by Israel and Hamas last October was welcome but had not fundamentally changed conditions on the ground.
He pointed to continued Israeli attacks, restrictions on humanitarian assistance and the ongoing suffering of civilians.
Martin warns two-state solution is being eroded
He also condemned the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, saying developments there were damaging prospects for a just and lasting peace.
“What we are witnessing on the ground is a deliberate attempt by some to make the prospect of a two-state solution impossible,” Martin said, citing statements attributed to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu opposing the establishment of a Palestinian state and Israel’s approval of development in the E1 area.
The UN secretary-general has similarly warned that illegal settlement expansion and other developments in the occupied Palestinian territory are eroding the conditions needed for a viable Palestinian state and called for renewed efforts toward a two-state solution.
Ireland backs international legal accountability
Martin also reaffirmed Ireland’s support for the International Criminal Court, saying there could be “no impunity for war crimes” and calling for measures aimed at undermining the court to be withdrawn.
His remarks came amid broader debate at the UN over Gaza, Palestinian statehood and the future of the two-state solution.
The UN secretary-general has urged an end to the fighting, expanded humanitarian access and compliance with international law.
Martin said the international community would ultimately have to confront the record of what has happened in Gaza, warning that the consequences would carry a lasting moral and political weight.
Ireland has been among the countries advocating for Palestinian rights and a negotiated two-state settlement, while Martin’s address placed the issue at the centre of his appeal for a stronger international commitment to human rights and international law.

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Russia’s Central Election Commission (CEC) will convene on Friday to establish the final results of elections to the ninth convocation of the Russian parliament’s lower chamber, the State Duma.
The commission will announce the exact distribution of all 450 mandates and sum up the results of over 2,200 lower-level electoral campaigns, also held on September 18-20.
The results of the vote were not immediately announced after the polls closed. CEC Chair Ella Pamfilova said that regional commissions were given time until September 25 to conclusively review all incoming complaints and requests, conduct the necessary inquires and only then establish the official outcomes of the campaigns.
Who will make it into the new Duma?
According to preliminary results, five parties crossed the five-percent threshold: the United Russia party, the Communist Party, LDPR, the New People and A Just Russia.
The 225 seats designated for party lists will be distributed among them. The other half of the State Duma will be determined by the voting results in single-seat constituencies.
The United Russia is poised to form the largest faction. Party Chairman Dmitry Medvedev said on September 24 that it is expected to secure 349 seats in total, according to preliminary allocation: 140 via the federal list and 209 in single-seat constituencies.
If the CEC confirms this distribution, it will mark the largest number of seats won by a single party in a legislative election in the entire modern history of the State Duma. The current record is also held by United Russia, which secured 343 seats in the 2016 elections. In 2021, it got 324 mandates.

Chinese President Xi Jinping addresses a welcome banquet at the White House in Washington, D.C., the United States, Sept. 24, 2026. Xi on Thursday attended a welcome banquet held by U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
WASHINGTON, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Thursday evening attended a state dinner held by U.S. President Donald Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, at the White House.
Xi and Peng were warmly greeted by the U.S. presidential couple upon their arrival. The two presidential couples posed for photos and met with guests attending the dinner.
Xi and Trump delivered remarks respectively after the dinner began.
Xi extended sincere greetings and best wishes for the Mid-Autumn Festival to Americans from all sectors of society who care about and support the further growth of China-U.S. relations.
Xi noted that Trump paid a successful visit to China in May, and that the two heads of state exchanged state visits within six months, making history in bilateral engagement.
He said common understanding on many issues have been reached during his visit this time, adding new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and providing fresh strategic guidance for bilateral ties.
Xi stressed that over 200 years ago, soon after its independence, the United States turned its eyes to China. The two countries started trading with each other, exchanging goods to meet each other's needs and drawing on their complementary strengths.
Noting that more than 80 years ago, the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in the fight against Japanese militarist aggressors, Xi said such a friendship forged in blood and fire will surely live on through the generations.
Over 50 years ago, Ping-Pong Diplomacy between the two countries reopened the door to bilateral exchanges that had been closed for years, Xi said. The older generation of Chinese and U.S. statesmen, with the political wisdom of "a small ball moving the globe," set in motion the historic process of normalizing China-U.S. relations.
Xi said the story of an American named Ronald Sakolsky, who more than 20 years ago gave financial support to Chinese desert control worker Yin Yuzhen for her tree-planting effort, touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between the two peoples.
Xi noted that bilateral exchanges have helped promote heart-to-heart communication between the two peoples and cemented public support for China-U.S. friendship and cooperation.
Today, China-U.S. relations have come to another historical juncture, Xi said.
Trump's pledge to make America great again and China's commitment to achieving great national rejuvenation are both ambitious goals that can surely be mutually reinforcing, he said.
He said China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of the two peoples, keep pace with the trend of the times, and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other.
Like a river that never stops flowing, history never stands still, Xi said, adding that the friendship between the two peoples is a worthy cause that holds great promise.
The two sides should join hands and move forward side by side, nurture the beautiful flowers of China-U.S. friendship, and write a new chapter in their friendly relations, he added.
The state dinner was held in a warm and cordial atmosphere, featuring wonderful performances put on by American artists. ■

Indonesian Minister of Marine Affairs and Fisheries Sakti Wahyu Trenggono delivers a speech during a launching ceremony of a capture fisheries cooperation program between China and Indonesia in Tual, Indonesia, Sept. 24, 2026. China and Indonesia on Thursday launched a capture fisheries cooperation program in Tual, a coastal city in Indonesia's Maluku Province. (Xinhua/Cheng Yiheng)
TUAL, Indonesia, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- China and Indonesia on Thursday launched a capture fisheries cooperation program in Tual, a coastal city in Indonesia's Maluku Province.
More than 100 representatives from the two countries' governments, businesses and local fisheries associations attended the launch ceremony at a prime fishing harbor near the junction of the Banda and Arafura seas. After the launch, several modern Chinese fishing vessels sounded their horns and set out for the open sea.
Li Hongwei, minister counselor of the Chinese Embassy in Indonesia, said at the ceremony that the China-proposed 21st Century Maritime Silk Road, a key component of the Belt and Road Initiative, is highly compatible with Indonesia's Global Maritime Fulcrum strategy. The two sides have been advancing the alignment of strategies, plans, industries and projects to build a maritime community with a shared future, he said.
China is ready to use the launch as an opportunity to strengthen technical cooperation, resource conservation and coordination across the fisheries value chain with Indonesia, Li said.
Indonesian Minister of Marine Affairs and Fisheries Sakti Wahyu Trenggono told Xinhua that the ministry's five blue economy initiatives are aligned with China's vision for sustainable global fisheries. He said Indonesia hopes to deepen cooperation with China in capture fisheries, aquaculture and marine conservation.
More than 90 percent of Maluku Province is covered by sea, and local communities depend heavily on marine and fisheries resources.
The project will improve the value chain for fish landing, cold-chain storage, processing and exports. It is expected to create about 1,100 jobs at sea and on land, while also spurring supporting investment in ship repair, cold storage, quality testing and skills training, according to project information. ■

Rodd said the efforts of Constables Jeff Smith and Michael McCurdy prevented the attacker from using the explosive materials he had with him, as well as a “significant” amount of ammunition.
Police describe confrontation with armed synagogue attacker, security officer remains in critical condition
Smith, who was stationed outside of Sons of Jacob to provide security, remains in critical condition but is making progress, according to Rodd. Ward later died of his wounds from the exchange with police.
“[The shooter] had the means, the mechanism, and the motive to perpetrate a greater act. The only thing that stopped entry into the synagogue to execute the intent were the two officers,” said Rodd. “He was equipped with other weapons and the means to carry on a gun battle for a long period of time.”
Authorities reveal suspect scoped out synagogue before attack
The CBC reported that police obtained a video of the attack in Belleville, a town over 100 miles east of Toronto on the north shore of Lake Ontario. On the video, Ward is heard shouting. Police report he is saying, “You are going to die for the Jews.”
Rodd confirmed that before Ward targeted the Sons of Jacob, he scoped out the synagogue grounds. “We know that there was a reconnaissance in the presence of our officer, but nothing that would have alarmed him or would have triggered him to be on the defensive,” Rodd said.
Ward was a former member of the Canadian Armed Forces. Rodd noted.
“He was shot multiple times in multiple places,” Rodd said. “He has everything extending from fractures to wounds, and is still bearing shrapnel.”

EU seeking to curb Russian athletes’ return to international competitions – media

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

13:29:42 KST

EU seeking to curb Russian athletes’ return to international competitions – media
The EU is considering measures to curb the return of Russian and Belarusian athletes to international sports under their national flags following a decision by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) to ease restrictions, Euractiv reported on Thursday, citing EU diplomats.
The proposals were outlined by the EU diplomatic service and the European Commission in a non-paper and have yet to become a formal EC proposal, according to the outlet.
Measures under discussion include targeted sanctions and visa restrictions against individuals linked to Russian and Belarusian sports. Brussels is also considering using EU funding as leverage by restricting financial support for organizations that allow athletes from the two countries to compete under their national symbols.
Another option would seek to curb media revenues linked to Russian athletes, although diplomats have acknowledged that the measure could be difficult to implement. The EU could also approach third countries in an effort to discourage them from facilitating the return of Russian and Belarusian competitors under their national flags.
The proposals have already faced resistance within the bloc. Slovakia blocked a draft set of conclusions discussed by EU security ambassadors on Tuesday, Euractiv reported, citing three diplomats. EU governments reportedly remain divided over how far they should intervene in decisions traditionally made by independent sports federations.
The Commission and the EU diplomatic service are expected to develop further proposals ahead of an EU ministerial meeting on education, sport and culture on November 20.
The discussions follow the IOC’s July decision to provisionally lift restrictions on the Russian and Belarusian Olympic committees, potentially opening the way for their athletes to compete at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics under national symbols. The IOC has said decisions concerning flags, anthems and other national identification at future Games will be made later.
Russian and Belarusian athletes were barred from many international competitions after the Ukraine conflict escalated in February 2022, although a number of sports federations have since eased restrictions.
Russian athletes have subsequently secured several major international titles. In July, 19-year-old Pavel Graudyn won the men’s individual saber title at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong.
In August, Evgeniia Chikunova won the women’s 200-meter breaststroke at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris, setting a championship record of 2:19.32 while competing under neutral status.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.

Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The announcement comes as the global education fund faces financial pressure, with several donors expected to reduce their contributions.
Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.
“When more children in the world’s poorest countries go to school and learn to read and do math, it creates fertile ground for economic growth and new markets for Danish business,” he said.
The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.
