Still healthy labour market?
Here's a super brief note from Westpac on the Australian jobs market.
It follows this week's employment report from the ABS for the month of August.
Employment rebounded in August, but so did labour force participation, resulting in the unemployment rate lifting to a cycle high of 4.6%.
The result points to a labour market that is gradually building slack, with labour supply continuing to outstrip labour demand.
Netwealth shares tank after announcing it will defend First Guardian class action
ASX-listed investment management giant Netwealth has announced plans to defend against a class action over its alleged failures in the First Guardian superannuation fund collapse.
Netwealth said it received a letter on Monday "alleging breaches of duties in connection with the offering and monitoring of certain First Guardian investment options".
The company said it had already entered into a court-enforceable undertaking with ASIC in January, where $101 million in compensation was paid to affected members.
Off the back of the news on Friday of its plans to defend the case, Netwealth's share price sunk.
At time of writing, it stands at $17.06, a price that represents a two-and-a-half year low.
My colleague Nassim Khadem wrote several months ago about investors considering a class action, you can read more below.
ANZ considering restructure of 400 New Zealand roles
Around 400 technology jobs in the New Zealand arm of ANZ are being scrutinised under a new restructure plan with at least 100 facing the chopping block.
ANZ told the ABC on Friday afternoon that they "are making a number of changes" in their tech team as part of their 2030 strategy and that they "will continue to support our teams during this process".
It's understood that there are 1,500 jobs in the tech division of ANZ's New Zealand offices, and of those, around 10 per cent will be slashed.
ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos last year said the bank wanted to “put our house in order” and was looking to cut 3,500 jobs by September 2026.
It comes amid broader concerns in the banking sector on the push to move work offshore.

Pentagon probing how shipment of F-35 fighter jet parts was diverted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:30:49 UTC
06:30:49 KST

Pentagon probing how shipment of F-35 fighter jet parts was diverted
The Pentagon is investigating how a shipment of F-35 fighter jet parts on its way to the U.S. from overseas was diverted, and the military is now trying to retrieve the parts, a defense official confirmed to CBS News.
A source briefed on the incident told CBS News a shipment was diverted to Hong Kong. According to Bloomberg News, the parts are now in China's hands, although the Pentagon declined to confirm this.
A defense official said in a statement, "The F-35 Joint Program Office and Department of War are aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components." The parts were in transit to the U.S. from Australia either for replacement or repair when they were diverted.
"We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence," the defense official said.
The F-35A Lightning II is the newest version of the plane and the most advanced fighter jet in the military's arsenal. It travels up to 1,200 miles per hour and can carry a payload of 18,000 pounds.
The missing parts are said to be related to the plane's canopy and weapons bay door. If this is the case, they do not contain the kind of advanced avionics that would be advantageous for an adversary to obtain. Nonetheless, they could provide information about the F-35's stealth technology: Even the canopy contains elements of the stealth systems — it's coated with radar-absorbent material that helps the plane hide from enemy radar.
It's not clear whether the U.S. raised the missing plane parts with China during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit with President Trump on Thursday, but military issues almost certainly came up during their meeting. Xi was expected to press Mr. Trump to curb U.S. support for Taiwan. China wants the U.S. to halt all arms sales to the self-governed island and oppose Taiwanese independence.
Doing so would effectively end the longstanding policy of strategic ambiguity, that is, refusing to state whether the U.S. would intervene militarily if China were to attack Taiwan.
After their summit in May, Mr. Trump said he had made "no commitment either way" on whether to move forward with a pending arms sale to Taiwan. Democratic and Republican lawmakers have urged him to approve the arms package, but it has remained in limbo since Mr. Trump and Xi last met.
On Wednesday, Republican Sens. Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn and Lisa Murkowski wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to ask why the State Department did not obligate $300 million in foreign military financing Congress had approved for 2026 and the Defense Department did not provide Taiwan with $1 billion appropriated by Congress for security cooperation. They also wanted to know why the administration did not approve the $14 billion in military sales to Taiwan that Congress passed earlier this year.
The senators said in their letter that the appropriations "are critical to the kind of deterrence by denial that will prevent conflict," and said "it is especially confusing that the Administration would withhold approval of the very arms purchases it aggressively pushed Taiwan to make."

Protecting Bab al Mandab shared regional, international responsibility — Yemen tells UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:28:01 UTC
06:28:01 KST

Protecting the strategic Bab al Mandab Strait is a shared regional and international responsibility and should not be borne by Yemen alone, Presidential Leadership Council Vice President Abdullah al-Alimi said.
Al-Alimi told the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday that Houthi attacks on maritime navigation have turned the security of one of the world's most important shipping routes into a tool of pressure and bargaining.
"The Houthis' use of maritime security as a tool of blackmail is not only a threat to Yemen, but is holding the global economy hostage," he said.
Al-Alimi said years of conflict had demonstrated that supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government and strengthening its economic, security and military capabilities amounted to an investment in international security and stability.
"Protecting this strategic passage is a shared regional and international responsibility that Yemen cannot bear alone," he said.
Al-Alimi said a secure Red Sea depended on a stable Yemen, while stability in Yemen required restoring effective state authority.
"There can be no sustainable peace as long as an armed militia remains above the state and outside the law," he said, adding that restoring the Yemeni state will contribute directly to regional stability and the protection of one of the world's most important maritime corridors.
'Iranian agenda'
He said the government had dealt "responsibly and positively" with regional and international initiatives and made major concessions in an effort to reach peace and alleviate the suffering of Yemenis.
Al-Alimi accused the Houthis of responding to those efforts with intransigence and using periods of a humanitarian truce to strengthen their military arsenal at the expense of Yemenis.
He also accused the group of rejecting peace initiatives and escalating attacks in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab in service of "an Iranian agenda" extending beyond Yemen's national interests.
Al-Alimi said the threat posed by the Houthis is also being strengthened by "the absence of an effective and decisive international position."
He urged the international community to move toward a "strategic partnership" with Yemen to strengthen security and stability in the region, saying the government is capable of ending the threat posed by the Houthis.

'No lie' will change Netanyahu's ICC arrest warrant: NY Mayor Mamdani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:23:00 UTC
06:23:00 KST

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani hit back at Benjamin Netanyahu's criticism of him at the U.N. General Assembly Thursday, saying that "no lie" will alter the International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister.
"As he has done time and again, Prime Minister Netanyahu used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians," Mamdani said in a statement.
"Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity."
Ahead of Netanyahu's visit, Mamdani urged his arrest, saying the U.S. should honor a warrant for Netanyahu issued by the International Criminal Court in late 2024.
Israel's attacks killed more than 73,000 people in the Palestinian enclave since October 2023, mostly women and children. It displaced virtually the entire population and damaged or destroyed most of its buildings.
Inside the General Assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech.
New York City's first Muslim mayor has long been a vocal critic of Israel's military actions in Gaza and has called Netanyahu a war criminal and an architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people.
In November 2024, the ICC, based in The Hague, issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.
This July, Mamdani urged U.S. federal authorities to enforce the ICC arrest warrant for Netanyahu, acknowledging that New York City authorities lack the legal power to carry it out.

Insane catch helps South Africa beat Australia in one-day clash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:20:56 UTC
06:20:56 KST

A remarkable one-handed diving catch from all-rounder Marco Jansen has helped South Africa claim a 67-run win over Australia in a one-day clash in Durban.
Jansen was named the Player of the Match after scoring 75 off 59 deliveries with the bat before picking up one wicket with the ball. Mitch Marsh top scored for Australia with 60 off just 36 deliveries.
What's next?
South Africa leads 1-0 in the three-match series ahead of the second ODI in Johannesberg on Sunday night AEST.
Mitch Marsh could not hide his dismay at how Australia capitulated tamely in their opening ODI in South Africa, who were helped to victory by an incredible catch by Marco Jansen that needs to be seen to be believed.
The Aussies ended up succumbing to a 67-run defeat to the disappointment of their stand-in skipper after a succession of cheap dismissals in a sorry run chase in Durban.
Marsh himself seemed to have laid the foundations for victory with his blistering opening knock of 60, but after he had perished needlessly to the spinning wiles of Kehav Maharaj, none of his team could cement the partnerships to get them anywhere near the hosts' 298-run target.
After watching the world champs collapse to 230 all out off just 41.2 overs, Marsh sighed: "I'm pretty disappointed. South Africa outplayed us. It was a good game of cricket, but we fell well short.
"We had our opportunities. I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."
The South Africans had set a challenging target after being inserted by Marsh, compiling 8-297 thanks largely to a brilliant 112 from Matthew Breetzke and a spectacular 75 off 59 balls from pace-bowling all-rounder Jansen.
Marsh, standing in as skipper again for the rested Pat Cummins, then led from the front in response with his 36-ball pyrotechnics, which featured three sixes, one of which sailed for 104 metres over the dressing room roof at Kingsmead and landed at the roadside.
He shared a blistering opening stand of 90 in just 9.2 overs with Travis Head, but like Head (36), Cooper Connolly, who'd looked supreme in making 38, and Matt Renshaw (44), he got out to an airy shot when the Australians were up with the required rate and under no real pressure.
The superb spinning of the two slow left-armers Maharaj (4-20) and Bjorn Fortuin (2-34) soon put them under that pressure, though.
Loading Twitter content
Discomfited, Josh Inglis got out to a poorly executed reverse sweep on the eighth ball he faced and Australia lost their last six wickets for just 54 to allow the Proteas to draw first blood in the three-match series.
The key moment may have been when Jansen took a sensational running, diving, one-handed catch in the outfield, stretching out his long telescopic arm to scoop up the ball just above the turf to get rid of key man Renshaw off Gerald Coetzee. It left Australia on 7-215, and there was no way back.
So, after the three-match sweep of the Zimbabwe series, this really did feel like a proper test of Australia with the defence of their 50-over World Cup in southern Africa just a year away.
The first part of the reconnaissance mission demonstrated just how much they still have to work on, and the weakness against spin was again shown up even while South Africa had five top-line pace bowlers sidelined through injury.
Man-of-the-match could easily have been Jansen, with his one wicket, four catches and big-hitting or the superb 36-year-old veteran tweaker Maharaj, but batting at No.4, Breetzke's superb 106-ball knock, before being run out by Connolly, deservedly won the day.
All-rounder Jack Edwards had an uncomfortable debut — 0-56 off 10 overs, followed by scoring five off 15 balls — but there was encouragement again in the display of paceman Nathan Ellis, who, fresh from his outstanding series against Zimbabwe, was again the bowling pick with 3-57.
All-rounder Cameron Green, back in the side after missing the series against Zimbabwe as he recovered from a shoulder injury, had a poor day with the bat, falling for five while trying to belt Maharaj over cow corner and getting caught in the deep.
The opening loss has really put pressure on Australia to turn the series round at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on Sunday, when Cummins is set to be recalled. They haven't won a bilateral series against South Africa since 2014.

Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
NEW YORK, Sept 24 - Finnish President Alexander Stubb said on Thursday he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory.
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defenses to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
"That's why ... I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers, either in the occupied territory of Ukraine or in Russia for strategic purposes because that would save lives," Stubb said.
The Finnish leader, a staunch ally of Ukraine who also has good relations with US President Donald Trump, made the remark in an interview with Reuters in New York where world leaders have converged for the annual gathering at the United Nations.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy used the event to press hard for ceasefires that would cover strikes on targets related to energy infrastructure and vessels in the Black Sea. Russia has given no public indication it wants to see such arrangements.
Four-and-a-half years since the full-scale Russian invasion, the Ukrainians fear Moscow plans to systematically target and destroy power and heating sites in the depth of winter. Russia's use of ballistic missiles hit record levels this summer.
Only Ukraine's Patriot air defenses are able to intercept such missiles, but ammunition is severely depleted and it is unclear where new supplies could come from.
Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine's battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones.
Starlink does not work over Russian territory, but Ukrainian officials believe turning it on for Ukraine's use inside Russia would allow its weapons to strike mobile ballistic launchers located within several hundred kilometres of the border.
Looking ahead to winter, Stubb said there were three things that Ukraine needed.
"One is air defenses and even Starlink would be to a certain extent a good air defense there. And the second one is energy installations for the winter."
"The third one is money. So those are the things that we're working on. We're working on putting up a winter package because I don't see the war ending, you know, before the winter."
Stubb said it was good that US-led peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine had restarted in August with the visits of US envoys to both Moscow and Kyiv.
"I still think that the easiest solution would be to call an unconditional ceasefire, basically stop the killing, as President Trump reiterated in his speech in the UN General Assembly," he said.
Such a step, he continued, would be followed by negotiations on security, territory, reconstruction and compensation and other topics.
The war could be frozen along the line of contact with 30-kilometre buffer zones east and west, he said, adding that the next best option was the idea of the partial ceasefire on energy and grain related targets. REUTERS

The death toll from the sinking of the KM Virgo Transport 8 in Indonesia's Java Sea has risen to 42 after search and rescue teams recovered 14 more bodies from inside the vessel, media reports said Thursday.
The victims were retrieved during diving operations inside the wreckage, state-run Antara News Agency reported, citing Mohammad Syafii, the head of the National Search and Rescue Agency (SAR), or Basarnas.
“The joint SAR team's efforts have once again yielded results,” said Syafii.
He said divers from the Basarnas Special Group, the Indonesian Navy and other search and rescue units recovered all 14 bodies from inside the ship.
The bodies were initially transferred to the KN SAR Pacitan search and rescue vessel for emergency handling before being flown to Banjarmasin.
A Basarnas HR-3604 helicopter and an Indonesian Navy Panther helicopter were used to transport the victims, according to the Antara News Agency.
Upon arrival in Banjarmasin, the bodies were handed to the Disaster Victim Identification team and authorities for medical identification and additional procedures.
As of Thursday, authorities had found 150 people from the vessel's passenger manifest.
Of them, 108 survived, while 42 were confirmed dead.
Search and rescue operations are continuing for 93 people who are missing, according to the latest figures.

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- European Council President Antonio Costa Thursday reiterated his support for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) in defense of international law.
In delivering his speech in the general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Costa said there can be no double standards in terms of international law and "we are witnessing deliberate violations of international law."
Following and defending international law is not an option but a responsibility, according to Costa.
"We stand firmly behind them and will uphold their independence, their integrity and their ability to fully exercise their mandate," said Costa, referring to ICJ and ICC.
"It is unacceptable to threaten or attack the International Criminal Court, its officials and its staff. Accountability cannot depend on political convenience," he added.

Costa urged for strong, effective, representative and deliverable multilateralism in a bid to address challenges of today around peace, climate emergency, economic insecurity and artificial intelligence (AI).
Costa called for an accountable, transparent and regulated architecture on AI and its governance.
"We need an AI that serves humanity, not controls it," said Costa, who added that the United Nations must play a central role in setting global standards on AI governance.
Moreover, Costa stressed the need to reform the global financial architecture with an eye on sustainable development.
The 2027 Sustainable Development Goals Summit must be a "turning point" to correct course, regain momentum and meet the targets for 2030 and beyond, said Costa. ■

SANAA, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Thursday evening that it had launched missile and drone attacks at a "sensitive target" in the Saudi capital Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, marking another round of long-range attacks amid an escalating confrontation with Saudi Arabia.
In a televised statement aired by Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV, the group's military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the Houthi armed forces carried out two separate operations, one targeting a site in Riyadh and the other targeting an Aramco facility in Yanbu.
Sarea said the attacks were carried out with "a number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," claiming that both operations "successfully achieved their objectives." He did not identify the target in Riyadh or provide details of any damage or casualties.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the two claimed strikes, and the Houthi account could not be independently verified.
Sarea said the attacks were launched in response to continuing Saudi air and missile strikes against Houthi-held areas in Yemen.
He claimed Saudi forces had carried out a total of 1,018 air and missile strikes since the latest escalation began, causing civilian casualties and damage to infrastructure.
The Houthi spokesperson vowed that the group would continue retaliatory operations as long as Saudi military action continued, reiterating what he described as an "escalation for escalation" policy.
The fresh announcement came only hours after the Houthis claimed a separate large-scale missile and drone operation against Saudi military positions in the southwestern border region of Jazan.
The latest Houthi claims also followed an announcement by the Saudi Arabia-led coalition earlier Thursday that its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed six ballistic missiles, thwarting attempts to strike Taif and Yanbu in Saudi Arabia.
The latest exchanges underscore the widening confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with both sides stepping up long-range attacks in recent weeks alongside intensified ground fighting in Yemen.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

Trump and Xi Meet Ahead of State Dinner With Top A.I. Leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:51:12 UTC
05:51:12 KST

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad.
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

Feature: Chinese craftsmen turn press-on nails into high-value art in Milan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:50:51 CST
05:50:51 KST

MILAN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- As the Italian model slowly moved her fingers under the spotlight, the green tourmaline stones on the translucent, green-gradient nails glittered, drawing the visitors' attention at Milan Fashion Week.
The showcase was part of a special event held Wednesday on the sidelines of Milan Fashion Week, featuring handmade nail art products -- specifically press-on nails -- from Donghai County in East China's Jiangsu Province.
Far from ordinary disposable press-on nails, the Donghai products combine art with techniques such as crystal carving, filigree and enamel work. Some elaborate sets carry price tags of thousands of U.S. dollars.
Li Xiao, general manager of Jiangsu Jingyiyi Supply Chain Management Co., Ltd., said a hand-painted Sun Wukong (Monkey King) press-on nail set brought to the event proved especially popular. A local tour guide spotted it on the first day and pre-ordered it.
Li said Sun Wukong's popularity overseas gives the design cross-cultural appeal. Since Donghai is closely associated with Huaguo Mountain, the legendary home of the Monkey King, designers drew inspiration from a story tied to the area and made this characteristic authentic creation.
"Handcrafting is central to the products' character," said Li. Painting, the layers of carving, and the placement of inlaid crystals all reflect the maker's individual artistry, while traditional techniques such as filigree have also been incorporated into modern nail art, giving the products their distinctive character and value.
"Unlike disposable options, these intricate press-on nails can be carefully removed, stored, and reused," Li noted. "This makes them a high-value alternative to traditional manicures done at a nail salon."
A Chinese press-on nail company told Xinhua that a hand-painted set can range in price from several hundred RMB to several thousand U.S. dollars. A set inspired by the famous Chinese painting A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains has been priced at 2,000 U.S. dollars. Some people have begun treating the nails as collectibles.
"I'm deeply drawn to Chinese press-on nail design. I think this is something novel for Italy, since designs like these are rarely seen on the market here," said Italian fashion blogger Katerina Kutsak, adding that the motifs incorporating Chinese culture felt especially distinctive.
Behind the products on display in Milan is an industry that emerged around 2019, after investors noticed that small crystal stones could be attached to artificial nails. The industry expanded rapidly, drawing on the crystal resources of Donghai, which is globally recognized as a World Craft City for Crystal.
Donghai has since become China's largest press-on nail production center, with its products exported to over 30 countries and regions, according to the county government. ■

But, if you remove one, 10 more pop up in their stead. That's just the way the internet works.
Zoë Schiffer: As things stand now, has anyone specifically been held accountable for what happened to Maddie?
EJ Dickson: So, the men are being charged with sexual cyberharassment which is a misdemeanor that is punishable by up to one year in prison and an $1,000 fine. I believe one of them is ... The police department is alleging that he'd financially profited off of her humiliation. When I reached out to Theta Chi, their fraternity, they said that they were on interim suspension and completely disavowed their activities and said, "This is not what Theta Chi is about." I don't know if that was prompted by my reaching out or if that had already been underway prior. I don't want to speculate, but I had said that she will see them posting from parties and stuff.
Zoë Schiffer: And where does this leave Maddie?
EJ Dickson: She's traumatized. I mean, can you imagine the worst moment of your life goes viral when you're 19 years old, and you don't even remember it? She doesn't think she'll be able to date and find love. She thinks this is going to follow her wherever she goes for the rest of her life. And the first time I met her, she wasn't even particularly emotional about it. It was just fact for her. And I was just sitting there. I'm a parent. It broke my heart. And that's the thing that really haunted me after reporting this and what really stuck with me when I spoke to her best friend who's quoted in the article. They stole her youth. They stole her girlhood. They stole her optimism and her sense of hope and belief that she could do something great with her life. Because that's what college is all about, right? You're kind of on the precipice of all of that. And that just seems like the most egregious theft of all.
Zoë Schiffer: Her experience also isn't an isolated incident, right? How far-reaching is this? How many people has this happened to?
EJ Dickson: So, there are degrees of it. All told, I was able to identify about a little less than a dozen women across the country who had been doxed in this fashion and on this scale. They were all young women in their late teens, early 20s, college students or recently graduated from college, conventionally attractive, and they had all been subject to some sort of salacious rumor or had nonconsensual videos or images of them circulating and were perceived to have transgressed the boundaries of sexual norms, I guess, in some way was kind of the unifying criteria. But, the burner accounts were also doing this on a much smaller scale to teenage girls whose photos were posted on college's incoming students' Instagram pages. They were taking their photos and posting them and making fun of their bodies and the way they looked and posting their full names. Girls who weren't even in college yet, incoming freshmen, they were doxing on a much smaller scale. And they do that pretty regularly. Or, they'll take photos of somebody's dating profile, some girl's dating profile or a message, and they'll post it, and they'll release her name and make fun of her. So, it happens all the time. I think that it's really the scale that differs, but the exposure aspect of it happens all the time.
Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, I'm curious how she felt. Like you said, you talked to her after the article came out. Obviously, it's this decision that I think a lot of sources face where it's like, do you not speak out and hope that the story kind of goes away? Or, do you take the chance and try and take back a little of the narrative?
EJ Dickson: That was really difficult. That was something I was really concerned about because I thought that there was a possibility that it could renew the harassment against her. And we had a number of conversations about that. And I think she understood and understands the impact that her story has and that she has an opportunity to speak for other women who have been through this and to sort of ensure that shame switches sides, that she doesn't need to be ashamed of what happened to her. I think she was a little overwhelmed, but she's a very strong person.
Maddie Kowalski: I'd like to end this with something really important. Although I don't have control over what happened to me, I can control what I do moving forward, and I want to move forward with healing.
Zoë Schiffer: Here's Maddie again. We thought she should close out the story in her own words.
Maddie Kowalski: These last few weeks have been the darkest and hardest moments of my life, but I'm still here, and that's something that I'm really learning to be proud of. I'm taking steps to rebuild myself, to feel safe again, and to understand that what happened to me doesn't define me. And I know that this is a long path. I've unfortunately also realized that there are so many women and girls as well as men who go through things like this in silence, feeling alone or ashamed or afraid to speak. And if sharing my story can help even one person feel seen or teach one person why consent and decency matter, then it's worth it.
Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was fact-checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

Former Houthi spokesman tells i24NEWS he welcomes cooperation between Israel, Saudi Arabia ‘when it comes to defeating Houthis’
Unknown

- i24NEWS
- Middle East
- The Houthi advance in Yemen may revive Israel-Saudi relations
The Houthi advance in Yemen may revive Israel-Saudi relations
In an interview with i24NEWS, former Houthi spokesman Ali al-Bukhaiti discusses Iran’s role in the group’s advance and the possibility of Saudi-Israeli cooperation
As the Houthis push toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait and continue to take ground from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, the question of Saudi-Israeli cooperation against the Iranian-backed group is back on the table.
Riyadh and Jerusalem have quietly worked together before, and the Houthis' latest advance may give them good reason to do so again.
In a special interview, Ali al-Bukhaiti, a former Houthi spokesman, told me he knows of no publicly announced coordination between Riyadh and Jerusalem. But he doesn't see a problem with it.
"In my personal view, cooperation is not something wrong when it comes to defeating the Houthis," he said. "Just as Saudi Arabia cooperates with the United States and European countries. If it is possible for them to cooperate with the Israelis on this issue, personally, I don't see anything wrong with that."
Why the urgency? According to al-Bukhaiti, this is no longer just a Yemeni war. "I believe that the Battle of Bab al-Mandab is the first battle in which the Iranians and Hezbollah personnel are directly participating," he said. Not as fighters, but "in a management capacity. Intelligence management. Intercepting the communications of the other side. As well as coordinating between the fronts and information warfare."
For Tehran, the timing makes sense. Hezbollah is weakened, Assad is gone, and the Iraqi militias are weak. "Therefore, its winning card is the Houthi group," al-Bukhaiti said, "because of its proximity to the region's most important strait."
For more than two decades, the Houthis have built their entire identity around one slogan: "Death to America, Death to Israel." Yet now that they finally stand at the gates of one of the world's most important shipping lanes, with real leverage over American and Israeli interests, they are rushing to reassure both.
According to al-Bukhaiti, Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdulsalam said the Bab al-Mandab blockade targets only Saudi ships. American and Israeli vessels will be left alone.
"The Houthis' slogan for 20 years or more has been, 'Death to America, death to Israel.' But when they reached the Bab al-Mandab Strait, they said, 'We have nothing to do with either America or Israel. Our problem is with Saudi Arabia and the Muslims,'" he said.
So much for the resistance. The group that claimed to fight for Gaza and against "global arrogance" has, when it truly mattered, chosen to aim its guns at fellow Arabs and Muslims instead.
On the Saudi-backed side, one absence stands out. "The absence of the Southern Transitional Council has nothing to do with the defeat. There may be a connection to the absence of the UAE," al-Bukhaiti said. Abu Dhabi built the forces of Tariq Saleh along the coast and backed them with continuous air cover and naval vessels near al-Mokha. Without the Emiratis, that front didn't hold.
So the Houthis have spared Israel, turned their guns on Riyadh, and let Tehran run the show. If al-Bukhaiti is right, Saudi Arabia and Israel may have more in common in Yemen than either is ready to admit.

About 60 ships passed through Strait of Hormuz on September 23 — Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:49:40 UTC
05:49:40 KST

LONDON, September 24. /TASS/. About 60 commercial vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, transporting 22 million barrels of oil, the largest daily volume since the beginning of July, Reuters quoted an unnamed US official as saying.
The source also said that about 40 of these vessels coordinated their actions with the US military to ensure protection.
Reuters said it could not verify this data from independent sources.
Before the war with Iran began on February 28, about 125 large commercial vessels per day typically passed through the strait, including bulk carriers and container ships, tankers and gas carriers, which transported about 20% of the world’s daily supplies of oil and liquefied natural gas.
In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the United States resumed large·scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the agreements on the Strait of Hormuz.

UN education officials call for urgent action for Gaza children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:41:36 UTC
05:41:36 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Education officials at the UN urged governments and donors on Thursday to step up support for children caught in conflicts and disasters, highlighting the devastating effect of the war in the Gaza Strip on access to education.
Gordon Brown, the UN special envoy for global education, said hundreds of millions of children worldwide are being denied education because of conflict, displacement and climate-related disasters.
“Instead of the world developing only some of the potential of some children in some countries, we must be determined to develop the potential of all children,” Brown told reporters at a UN briefing.
He highlighted Gaza, where hundreds of thousands of children remain out of school, and tens of thousands of young children have no access to preschool.
Maysa Jalbout, director of Education Cannot Wait (ECW), which touts itself as the first global fund dedicated to education in emergencies, said the organization was committing $3 million in emergency funding for vulnerable children in Gaza, including those with conflict-related injuries and disabilities.
The program is expected to reach up to 13,000 children and will be implemented through local organizations.
Jalbout said Gaza has more child amputees per capita than anywhere in the world, underscoring the severe toll the conflict has taken on children.
ECW is also responding to disasters elsewhere. In Nepal, where floods and landslides recently damaged or destroyed 29 schools, the organization committed $1 million to help children return to learning.
Jalbout said the crises in Gaza and Nepal are different, but the consequences for children can be similar: “School stops, protection disappears, and the future is put on hold.”
ECW is seeking $600 million in new funding to reach 10 million more children affected by crises worldwide.

Netanyahu claims Mamdani endangers Jewish New Yorkers by 'spreading lies' about Israel
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Mayor Zohran Mamdani of endangering Jewish New Yorkers with his criticism of Israel's military actions in Gaza, saying during a speech at the United Nations on Thursday that the mayor has spread lies about Israel.
Calling Mamdani “the antisemitic mayor of New York,” Netanyahu spent part of his time speaking to the United Nations General Assembly to assail the man who threatened to have him arrested if he came to the city.
“Mr. Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York. They talk to me, they tell me ‘this isn’t the city we remember, it changed so quickly,’” Netanyahu said.
Mamdani replied, saying Netanyahu used his speech at the UN to repeat “baseless lies” aimed at sanitising Israel's genocide of Palestinians.
"No lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant," the mayor continued.
It's the latest in a back-and-forth between Netanyahu and New York City's first Muslim mayor, who has long been a vocal critic of Israel's genocide in Gaza and has called Netanyahu “the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people.” Mamdani has said that his criticism of Israel and advocacy for Palestinian rights don't amount to antisemitism.
The mayor met with U.S. President Donald Trump this week in New York. Netanyahu, during his speech Thursday, praised the president for his support of Israel, saying “we’ve had no greater partner than President Trump.”
During his mayoral campaign last year, Mamdani said he would direct police in New York to execute an arrest warrant against Netanyahu issued by the International Criminal Court, but has more recently acknowledged the city does not have the authority to take him into custody.
The mayor has since encouraged the federal government to arrest Netanyahu, though Trump has said the prime minister will not be arrested.
“Mr. Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me. Well, you can’t silence me and you can’t silence the truth,” Netanyahu said in his speech.

Two Palestinians were killed and at least 27 others injured Thursday in Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip, including seven Palestinians wounded by Israeli gunfire in Jabalia and Rafah.
The attacks came amid continued Israeli violations of a ceasefire agreement in force since Oct. 10, 2025.
Four Palestinians, including two women, were injured when Israeli military vehicles opened fire toward tents sheltering displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area northwest of Rafah, a medical source told Anadolu. One of the women was critically injured.
In northern Gaza, three Palestinians sustained injuries after Israeli forces opened fire toward tents sheltering displaced people in the Halawa camp east of Jabalia town, another medical source told Anadolu.
An Israeli drone struck a vehicle on Al-Rashid Street in the Al-Baidar area of the Sheikh Ajlin neighborhood southwest of Gaza City, medical sources told Anadolu.

The vehicle was transporting the body of a Palestinian killed in an Israeli airstrike earlier Thursday in Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip, they added.

The fire continued for some time before passersby managed to extinguish it.
Earlier Thursday, four injured Palestinians were brought to Nasser Hospital, one of them in critical condition, after an Israeli drone struck a group of civilians in central Khan Younis, in southern Gaza.
In a separate attack, a Palestinian was killed and another injured in an Israeli strike on a civilian vehicle west of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, a medical source told Anadolu.

In the northern enclave, the Israeli army carried out a large-scale demolition of homes and residential buildings in areas where its forces are deployed east of Gaza City. The explosions were heard across large parts of the enclave, witnesses said.

hundreds of feet of cable and steel reimagine rodin’s thinker for networked age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:35:32 UTC
05:35:32 KST

Kasey McMahon rebuilds The Thinker from steel and cable
Artist Kasey McMahon reimagines the contemplative figure for the networked age, constructing a life-size Thinker by hand from steel and hundreds of feet of network cable, the physical infrastructure through which contemporary information travels.
A nod to Rodin’s iconic contemplative figure, the work replaces the solidity of bronze with the tangled physical infrastructure of the networked world. McMahon began working with network cable as a sculpturalmaterial more than a decade ago, drawn to the idea of turning the infrastructure behind our digital lives into something physical.
all images by Aaron Wessling – Single File Studio unless stated otherwise
Hundreds of feet of network cable form The Human Figure
The Thinker is the fourth life-size human figure in that ongoing body of work and the first male figure. The sculpture began with a welded steel armature that established the anatomy and seated posture. Artist Kasey McMahon then wrapped and layered hundreds of feet of CAT5 and CAT6 network cable by hand until the figure took shape.
Rather than concealing the material, the construction leaves connectors, printed markings, and individual lengths of cable visible. Blue, gray and white dominate the figure, punctuated by strands of red. The work was fabricated in McMahon’s Portland-area studio, a converted 120-year-old garage. The process moved between welding and metal fabrication, anatomical adjustment, and the slower work of wrapping and layering cable to give the figure its final mass and gesture.
Kasey McMahon reimagines Rodin’s Thinker using network cable
The Thinker is a reflection on bodies, networks, and technology
The pose is familiar, but the material changes the question. The figure is unmistakably human, yet its body is made from the infrastructure through which human communication and information travel. The Thinker arrives amid an increasingly charged conversation about artificial intelligence and our relationship with technology. It doesn’t attempt to resolve that tension. The figure simply sits, and thinks. The sculpture was privately commissioned and is now installed in Austin, Texas.

'Keep praying': Friends rally for Neriya Leiter as he remains seriously wounded after terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:35:26 UTC
05:35:26 KST

“We need a miracle and for everyone to rally together,” said Elkana Ariel, a friend of Neriya Leiter, who is fighting for his life after being critically wounded Wednesday in a terrorist attack on Highway 433.
Ariel, from the community of Havat Yair, told ynet about Neriya: “He is the kind of friend everyone wants. He is all heart, beloved in the community, always walking around with a smile and taking life lightly. Just this past Yom Kippur, he led the Ne’ilah prayer that closes the day.”
Ariel added that the entire family is deeply involved in giving and volunteering.
“Just a month and a half ago, he and his family returned from a trip to the United States, joined by the widow of his older brother Moshe and their children. One of his sisters is married to a career soldier. They all serve in the reserves, and even after his brother fell, they did not stop.
“Neriya is an amazing father who is present in the lives of his family and children and in the community. The situation requires a lot of prayers. We are hoping for the best and calling on all the people of Israel to keep praying,” he said.
Neriya’s father, Israel’s ambassador to the United States, Yechiel Leiter, landed in Israel Thursday morning and went to the hospital, where Neriya's mother and other family members were already gathered.
“They grew up in the same room. They were best friends. Neriya has led the family since Moshe’s death,” his father said.
Neria’s mother, Chana, also spoke Thursday morning in an interview with Army Radio.
“After Moshe fell, Neriya wanted so much to gather all of us together, and he helped all of us. He held our hand. He was amazing. He had a good relationship with almost all of us. Whoever needed help — he was there,” she said.
After his brother’s death, Neriya moved to a rear-echelon role in an elite unit. In a post on social media, he described the tension between the price his family had already paid and the fact that the fighting was continuing and he still wanted to feel part of it.
Neriya understood the high cost, but after several months, he returned to combat reserve duty. At the time he was wounded Wednesday, he was attached to a battalion carrying out reserve service in Judea and Samaria.
Neriya underwent complex brain surgery Wednesday night that lasted for hours.
Professor Alexander Yoskovich of Shaare Zedek Medical Center gave an update Thursday morning on his condition.
“After a series of tests and a series of surgeries, we can say that his condition is stable. His condition is still serious and his life remains in danger, but we are full of hope,” he said.
Neriya Leiter was wounded in the attack at the Bell checkpoint, an IDF inspection point on Highway 443. A terrorist drove his vehicle toward a police car and struck him. The attacker, 29, was killed by forces at the scene.
Yechiel Leiter was born in Pennsylvania in the United States and immigrated to Israel after being deeply influenced by Zionist values. He was named after Rabbi Yechiel Michel Leiter, his great-great-grandfather, a prominent European rabbi and halachic authority who later immigrated to the United States and served as a community rabbi, where he wrote the responsa work “Darkei Shalom.”
Yechiel’s grandfather, Moshe, was a well-known Torah scholar. Beyond his extensive religious learning, he was also known as a public activist. He published articles in the Orthodox Jewish press and founded a refugee association and a Talmud study organization in Zurich.
Because he felt the positions of Agudat Yisrael were not sufficiently enthusiastic about immigration to the Land of Israel and Zionism, he left the movement and remained active in Mizrachi.
He later immigrated to the United States, where his father served as a community rabbi and where he also held a rabbinic position.
In 1925, he immigrated to the Land of Israel but returned to Vienna after several months. He lived in Vienna until 1938, when he fled the threat of the Holocaust and moved to the United States. He was appointed rabbi of the Ahavat Re’im synagogue.
The father of Rabbi Yechiel Michel, Rabbi Shalom Leiter, was himself a rabbinical judge and halachic authority. His children, in addition to Rabbi Yechiel, also served as rabbis, heads of rabbinical courts, city rabbis and public activists.

Urging ministers to engage with officials at all levels, PM Modi reportedly said it had come to his notice that a minister did not interact with officials below the secretary in the department while suggesting that interaction with officials of levels was necessary for better performance.
PM, in his brief address, has asked ministers to ensure saturation of around 40-45 major welfare schemes and communicating their benefits effectively to the intended beneficiaries.

'Won't leave until Zionist regime destroyed': Iran marks 200 nights of pro-regime rallies amid war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:17:46 UTC
05:17:46 KST

Since the start of the war with Iran, Iranian television channels aligned with the Islamic Republic have broadcast nightly images and videos of rallies supporting the country’s leadership and armed forces, part of a sustained effort by state media to project national unity and public backing for the government.
The displays come as much of Iran’s population of about 92 million contends with a worsening economic crisis and severe government repression. But the Islamic Republic also retains a significant base of genuine supporters who continue to turn out for pro-government rallies.
Throughout recent months, whether amid talk of a possible return to negotiations between Washington and Tehran or during periods of heightened regional tensions, nightly gatherings have continued in public squares across Iranian cities.
Last week, Iran marked what state-affiliated media described as the 200th consecutive day of pro-government street gatherings, with events beginning Sept. 15 and continuing for several days in cities across the country. Iranian officials and state institutions used the milestone to praise participants and emphasize what they described as the population’s resilience and support for the government.
The Basij, the paramilitary force that played a central role in the violent suppression of mass anti-government protests earlier this year, issued a statement marking the 200th day.
“The Iranian nation will remain in the streets and squares for as long as necessary, and for as long as the interests of the regime dictate,” the Basij said.
Iranian military Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi also praised the demonstrators.
“Dear Iranian people, I bring you news from the battlefield: Your presence and unity are what strengthened the morale of the fighters, enhanced national resilience and sowed fear in the heart of the enemy,” he said.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the public as the country’s most important national security asset, saying Iranians had “defended the homeland, its territorial integrity and its independence through their presence and resilience.”
One of the most prominent gathering points has been Tehran’s Revolution Square, known in Persian as Enqelab Square. In recent days, Iranian channels have continued broadcasting videos showing crowds there waving Iranian and Hezbollah flags, praying and singing.
Reporting from the square last Wednesday, an Iranian television correspondent described the gathering as the 200th night of what he called “spontaneous public gatherings.”
“People gathered here to demonstrate solidarity and unity,” he said. “Two hundred nights have passed since the first days of the ‘Ramadan War’” — the Iranian name for Israel’s Operation Roaring Lion — “but not a single moment has passed in which these people have not thought about the slain leader, Ali Khamenei. Mourning for the leader continues to be felt deeply in people’s hearts.”
The reporter said those gathered behind him had come to the square for 200 consecutive nights.
“They will not leave the square until the Zionist regime is destroyed,” he said.
Another event marking the 200th day was held last week in Tehran’s Abu Zar Square, where a statue of Amir Ali Hajizadeh, the former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Aerospace Force who was killed during the war, was unveiled.
Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani attended the ceremony. Images from the event showed participants holding portraits of slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. The ceremony also featured fireworks, a display of a Zelzal rocket and balloons shaped to form the number 200.
The nightly gatherings across Iran have taken different forms in recent months, at times reflecting developments elsewhere in the region. Some have included demonstrations supporting Yemen’s Houthis during their escalation with Saudi Arabia.
Anti-American and anti-Israel chants have also remained a regular feature, much as they were during the war. Video published from Abu Zar Square on Sept. 15 showed demonstrators chanting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
“Death to America” chants were also heard at Revolution Square that day, shortly after a mass wedding ceremony involving several couples from the pro-government community. The couples arrived at the square in vehicles decorated with flowers.
The nightly displays have not been limited to rallies and slogans. They have periodically included military exhibits. Iran’s Mehr news agency published videos Sept. 14 showing drones on display in Quds Square in Isfahan during a nighttime rally.
Iranian state news agencies have also reported that some participants in the rallies have joined what authorities call the “Sacrifice of Life” campaign. The government claims more than 30 million people have signed up and declared themselves willing to sacrifice their lives and “defend the country’s territory,” although it remains unclear what participation in the campaign entails in practice.
A drill involving male and female campaign volunteers was held in Tehran last Friday morning. Iranian media aligned with the government said many thousands participated, though images from the event appeared to show something closer to a mass procession.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended the event and was quoted as saying, “Unity and cohesion, on every issue, will shatter the enemy’s hopes.”
Iranian reports said similar exercises would be held in other cities.
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch in the IDF’s Intelligence Directorate research division and now a senior researcher in the Iran and Shiite Axis program at the Institute for National Security Studies, cautioned against using the rallies as a measure of the government’s overall popularity or stability.
Iran faces mounting economic difficulties amid continued U.S. pressure and is still dealing with the aftermath of widespread protests earlier this year that were violently suppressed. Nevertheless, Citrinowicz said the government retains millions of supporters whose significance should not be dismissed.
“There is real distress in Iran, and it is very evident, including in the statements of President Pezeshkian, who sees himself as a representative of the population,” Citrinowicz said. “The situation is difficult, but at the same time, I would not dismiss these demonstrations. Ultimately, there is a significant core that supports this regime, even in the current economic situation and amid the economic and social complexity Iran is experiencing because of the war.”
Citrinowicz said the latest gatherings were a direct continuation of the demonstrations held during the war, when tens of thousands of people took to the streets each night in Iran’s major cities, including Tehran.
The rallies, he said, served two purposes: projecting an image abroad that the government retained the confidence of the Iranian public while sending a message to Iranians opposed to the Islamic Republic.
The message to government opponents, he said, was that “there is no point in going out” to protest, even if they were considering taking to the streets, because public spaces had already been filled by government supporters and the leadership retained enough backing to make an uprising appear futile.
“We are seeing the same logic in the current demonstrations,” Citrinowicz said.
He said the government’s promotion of the “Sacrifice of Life” campaign fit the same strategy.
“The regime’s entire focus right now is on demonstrating both the support it enjoys and the Iranian citizen’s willingness to make sacrifices, in the sense of, ‘You will not break us. People will be willing to fight if necessary,’” Citrinowicz said. “It all serves the same strategic purpose. Even when the numbers are exaggerated, I would not underestimate the base of support the regime has.”

New York sues Polymarket over allegations of illegal gambling operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:15:25 UTC
05:15:25 KST

New York, Polymarket file dueling lawsuits amid illegal gambling claims
New York attorney general accuses prediction market platform of targeting ‘most vulnerable’ residents.
The US state of New York and prediction market company Polymarket have filed dueling lawsuits amid claims the betting platform is in violation of gambling laws.
In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, New York State Attorney General Letitia James said that Polymarket has been operating as an unlicensed gambling operation due to its failure to obtain a licence from the New York State Gaming Commission.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Google employee charged with insider trading over Polymarket bets
- list 2 of 4Prediction platform Kalshi to collect job details to combat insider trading
- list 3 of 4Who has profited most from the war on Iran?
- list 4 of 4New York sues Kalshi, says its prediction markets are ‘illegal gambling’
The move comes after James’ office launched similar suits against Polymarket competitors Kalshi, Coinbase and Gemini Titan.
“Our gambling laws exist to protect New Yorkers, prevent the potential harms of problem gambling, and ensure funding for educational and public benefit programs,” James said in a statement announcing the suit.
“By skirting New York’s laws, Polymarket is targeting the most vulnerable and depriving New York families of critical services and support. My office will never hesitate to take action to defend our laws and keep New Yorkers safe.”
The suit also alleges that the company encouraged gambling among young people.
It accuses Polymarket of targeting users as young as 18, while state law requires users to be at least 21 years old to take part in mobile sports betting.
“By running an unlicensed gambling operation, Polymarket has done more than just knowingly violate state law, they have put New Yorkers at risk, especially those underage who are most vulnerable to problem gaming,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement.
The more than 30-page lawsuit claims that Polymarket, which is valued at more than $20bn, has advertised sports betting in particular since July 2025.
It pointed to a post on X from August 17, 2025, about the launch of its US mobile app that said it was “BAD NEWS (For sportsbooks)”.
Polymarket filed a countersuit hours later, arguing the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive authority to regulate prediction markets.
The betting platform said New York had left it with an “impossible choice” between obeying state regulators, or continuing operations and facing potentially “huge” criminal liability.
“This is an extraordinary assertion of state power squarely foreclosed by federal law,” Polymarket said in its lawsuit in Manhattan federal court.
Chief Legal Officer Neal Kumar said Polymarket tried to work out its differences with state officials, but “they preferred the media hit”.
“We chose to engage with them directly on the substance and address their concerns,” Kumar said.
Polymarket’s main rival Kalshi is facing similar allegations in New York.
Kalshi has been critical of reporting on lawsuits against it and allegations that it is akin to a sports betting or gambling platform.
Polymarket did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The Polymarket lawsuit comes days after reporting from the Wall Street Journal that alleged a wave of users had linked stolen bank debit cards and then used them to make wagers, effectively draining the accounts.
According to the report, when CEO Shayne Coplan was made aware of the issue, he responded: “Just keep growing and pay a fine if regulators ever find out.”
Political pressure
Prediction markets allow users to wager on so-called event contracts, covering political events, sports, elections and even award shows.
Concerns about the role of prediction markets came to a head earlier this year when wagers were made in the hours before the United States and Israel first struck Iran, prompting widespread backlash in Washington.
New York’s lawsuit joins a growing list of states that have sued prediction market platforms, including Arizona, Massachusetts, Nevada and many others.
Those states are at odds with the federal government, as the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has claimed that the federal agency exerts authority over the regulation of prediction markets.
Polymarket has close ties with the family of US President Donald Trump.
The prediction market platform has investment from 1789 Capital, a venture capital firm backed by Donald Trump Jr, the president’s eldest son, who also serves on the company’s advisory board.

Officer fended off Ontario synagogue gunman despite being shot multiple times, authorities say
One of the officers who helped prevent a shooting at an Ontario synagogue on Yom Kippur continued fighting off the gunman despite being shot multiple times, officials revealed Thursday. Police also confirmed the shooter was targeting the Jewish community in a "hate-motivated" attack.
Constable Jeff Smith was shot several times, suffering wounds to his head and torso, but continued fending off the attack until a second officer, Constable Mike McCurdy, arrived, Belleville Police Service Chief Murray Rodd said at a Thursday news conference.
Smith was shot almost immediately with a shotgun, Rodd said, before he was even able to get out of his car.
"Despite suffering life-threatening injuries, within moments of encountering the armed suspect, Constable Smith exited his vehicle and engaged the attacker," Rodd said. This went on for almost three minutes before McCurdy arrived.
Rodd said Smith and McCurdy's actions prevented "what would have become an unimaginable tragedy" and that they were the only thing that prevented the gunman from getting into the synagogue.
Smith remains hospitalized and is set to undergo several surgeries related to "serious head trauma," Rodd said, adding: "While his recovery will be lengthy and challenging, he is making progress every day."
Smith's injuries include bone fractures, and he still has shrapnel inside him, officials said.
The shooting took place Sunday near Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario. The gunman, identified as Sean Ward, 29, from Quinte West, was hospitalized with serious injuries after the shooting and later died, police said earlier this week.
Rodd said Thursday the attempted attack was a "hate-motivated crime."
"This was a deliberate attack directed at members of the Jewish community during one of the holiest observances of the year," he said.
Rodd also noted the shooter "had the means, the motive, and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue. The loss of life and irreversible damage that could have been rippled through our community for generations cannot be overstated."
Rodd said the shooter had several firearms with him, in addition to the shotgun, and enough ammunition to continue a gun battle for a "long period of time," along with containers of gasoline in his car.

UNCTAD identified three main priorities: transferring withheld Palestinian revenues, protecting the banking system and aligning reconstruction support with the scale of the damage, the report said.

Each rate rise locking aspiring homebuyers out for a decade, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:48:59 UTC
04:48:59 KST

Each rate rise locks tens of thousands out of home ownership, research finds
In short:
A rate rise is estimated to cause an immediate 5 per cent reduction in home purchases.
Economic modelling suggests the home ownership rate would fall by 0.3 of a percentage point and take more than a decade to recover.
What's next?
Markets and economists are almost certain the RBA will announce a rate rise on Tuesday.
Each standard interest rate increase could be locking close to 30,000 households out of home ownership, some of them for more than a decade, research suggests.
The modelling was conducted by James Graham, a senior lecturer in economics at the University of Sydney, along with Avish Sharma, a PhD candidate at Northwestern University who is a former analyst at the Reserve Bank of Australia.
Dr Graham said early findings from the study showed a typical 0.25 percentage point increase in interest rates caused an immediate 5 per cent decline in home purchases — a phenomenon in evidence in Australia's housing market downturn.
The research finds buying remains lower for up to two years after a rate increase.
That fall in housing purchases translates to a 0.1 percentage point decline in the home ownership rate within weeks of the rate rise, peaking at 0.3 per cent four years later.
"To put that in context, the home ownership rate at the moment sits at about 66 per cent," Dr Graham told The Business in an exclusive interview about his yet-to-be-published research.
"So you're talking about maybe one-third of a per cent knocked off that 66 per cent."
Loading...
That may not sound like a lot, but with close to 10 million households in Australia, each rate rise could be locking up to 30,000 households out of home ownership for years.
But Dr Graham said each subsequent rate rise produced a smaller shock than those before it.
"Those first rate rises, they were probably the most damaging. They were the ones that pushed a bunch of people out who missed out for a very long time," he said.
"The subsequent rate rises, though, you're sort of pushing into a part of the population that's likely more and more able to cope."
Even so, with three rate rises already this year and the high likelihood of more to come as soon as next Tuesday, the research suggests the RBA's monetary policy actions could reduce home ownership by more than Treasury forecasts the federal government's investment tax changes will boost it.
Loading...
Locked out for 'many, many years'
The modelling suggests home ownership rates eventually recover from the interest rate shock, but take more than a decade to fully do so.
Dr Graham said that was because changing life circumstances meant many prospective buyers locked out by rate rises remained excluded from ownership for years, some permanently.
"If you miss out on that ideal time, maybe next month or next year, you've changed jobs by then, new kids have come along, or the bank has changed its mind about how much it will lend," he said.
"It often means that you've missed out now, but you've actually missed out for many, many years to come."
Potential homebuyers do get a benefit from the housing value declines typically associated with interest rate increases, however.
"If you're sitting there with a bunch of cash or your mortgage ready to go, that's a great time to buy," Dr Graham said.
"But what we find is that a lot of people are not sitting there with all their money ready to go, necessarily."
For this group, the research finds the benefit of lower prices is more than outweighed by the increased cost of borrowing, tighter serviceability tests on loan applications, and reduced income growth due to the general economic slowdown from higher rates.
"If you're struggling to get that mortgage or your income's falling, so you're going to struggle to repay that mortgage, the fact that the house is cheaper doesn't help," Dr Graham said.
The research also suggests that younger first home buyers and those on lower incomes are disproportionately affected by rate rises.
Dr Graham said there were several things changes policymakers could consider to minimise the impact of rate rises on the home ownership rate.
"Do we need such a large serviceability buffer given that we're already very high into the interest rate hiking cycle?" he asked, questioning banking regulator APRA's 3 percentage point buffer above current mortgage rates, which has remained unchanged as rates have climbed off their post-COVID lows.
"States can look at do they need such large stamp duties, could they sort of like change those into land taxes or something like that instead?"

Syria recovers 36 looted antiquities from US worth over $5M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:47:59 UTC
04:47:59 KST

Laith Al-jnaidi, Lina Altawell
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
- Recovered artifacts include massive funerary relief from Palmyra, 14 rare mosaics looted from 
- Roman villa in Syria Damascus credits Syrian-US cooperation, efforts by Manhattan District Attorney's Office for return of cultural heritage
Syria recovered 36 looted antiquities from the US worth more than $5 million, including a massive funerary relief from the ancient city of Palmyra and 14 rare mosaics stolen from a Roman villa in the country.
The artifacts were returned during a ceremony in New York this week as part of efforts to combat the illicit trafficking of antiquities and recover looted cultural property, Syrian news agency SANA reported.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, and US Special Envoy to Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack attended the ceremony, along with Syria's charge d'affaires in Washington Mohammad Nasser Qanatri, its UN Ambassador Ibrahim Olabi, and other officials and diplomats.
“Repatriation ceremonies are a powerful reminder that preserving cultural heritage transcends any border or nationality,” Bragg said in a statement published by his office.
He described the investigation that led to their recovery as “incredibly complicated, multi-faceted.”
The return of the artifacts would not have been possible without “close partnerships that spanned the globe," Bragg added.
Among the recovered pieces are a massive stone relief looted from the archaeological site of Palmyra and 14 rare mosaics stolen from a Roman villa in Syria, he said.
Bragg said his office's Antiquities Trafficking Unit seized 31 antiquities from the Middle East and North Africa as part of the investigations.
The Palmyra relief was smuggled from its original site during a period when the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh) was responsible for systematic looting of archaeological sites in Syria, he added.   
Funerary relief from Palmyra
The Palmyrene funerary relief dates to the late second century and consists of a massive limestone sculpture depicting a reclining man surrounded by a woman and three children, according to the Manhattan District Attorney's Office.
The relief once decorated the wall of a burial chamber in ancient Palmyra and weighs more than 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms).
The artifact appears to have been carefully removed from the wall to avoid damaging the figures carved into it, according to the same source. 
Mosaic dating to 3rd century BC
The recovered collection also includes the "Telete and Eros" mosaic, a large section of a mosaic floor dating to the third century BC.
The piece depicts the mythological wedding of Telete and Eros, made from hundreds of small colored stone cubes known as tesserae.
The Manhattan District Attorney's Office said it seized the piece in July 2021 along with 22 other mosaics stolen from Syria and Lebanon.
The recovered antiquities also include three female "Syro-Hittite" figurines dating to the second millennium BC and made in northwestern Syria.
The three figurines first appeared on the art market in the late 1980s and early 1990s in the possession of New York art dealer Edward Merrin, who was later convicted in federal court of crimes related to antiquities trafficking, before they were sold to the collection of antiquities collector Michael Steinhardt, according to the source.
Bragg said four of the artifacts returned to Syria were among 180 antiquities worth a total of $70 million seized by his office from the Steinhardt collection following a years-long criminal investigation spanning several countries.   
‘Part of Syria’s history is finally returning home’  
“Through Syrian-American cooperation, a part of Syria’s history is finally returning home thanks to the efforts of the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office,” Qanatri said.  
“This achievement demonstrates how mutual respect and a shared commitment to protecting cultural heritage can build lasting bridges between our two countries,” he added.  
Syrian archaeological sites suffered widespread looting, trafficking, and destruction during years of civil war, including Palmyra, which is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site.  
In 2015, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2199, imposing binding measures to combat the illicit trafficking of Syrian antiquities and cultural property amid concerns that proceeds from such trade could be used to finance armed groups.  
The US imposed emergency restrictions in 2016 on imports of Syrian archaeological and ethnological materials illegally removed from the country on or after March 15, 2011, referring to the start of the long civil war.  
Washington said at the time that the measures were intended to curb the looting and trafficking of Syrian cultural heritage.  
The US restrictions cover objects made of stone, metal, ceramics, glass, ivory, bone, and textiles, as well as paintings, mosaics, and other Syrian cultural property.  
Palmyra was particularly subjected to looting and destruction during ISIS’ control of the city in 2015, while UNESCO later documented the destruction of the temples of Bel and Baalshamin, the Arch of Triumph, and parts of the city's museum and its collections.
