03:46:39 KST

Students accuse top college of deceptive conduct in class action over unaccredited degree
In short:
The International College of Management Sydney is being sued by former students whose degrees lacked professional accreditation, despite claims in promotional material.
The college has blamed "an administrative oversight" and will defend the Supreme Court proceedings.
The students' lawyer say higher education regulators need to ensure universities live up to their promises to students.
A leading private college has been accused of misleading and deceptive conduct in a Supreme Court class action by students who were shocked to discover their degrees were not professionally accredited.
Lead plaintiff Tessa Coddington initiated the lawsuit against The International College of Management Sydney (ICMS) after reading an ABC News article about other accreditation class actions launched against three public universities last year.
"These are pivotal years of your life, and [the ordeal has caused] so much financial strain," Ms Coddington said.
"To take, like, a pay cut is one thing, but to delay your career is another."
Ms Coddington accrued a $45,000 student debt to complete the three-year ICMS Bachelor of Property (Management, Valuation and Development) degree she graduated from in late 2022, an investment of time and money she has come to regret.
She was shocked to discover after graduating that the degree was never accredited by the Australian Property Institute (API), which she said left her unable to progress beyond an entry-level graduate role in property valuation, or have her qualifications recognised overseas.
"I was like, 'What do you mean this property degree doesn't get me what it says it does?'"
Ms Coddington said it took years of emailing with ICMS to confirm the degree had never been accredited, after employers raised concerns about it. Over that time, her anxiety grew.
ICMS representatives initially said they were still seeking accreditation from API, which has not been accused of any wrongdoing.
Only in December last year did API confirm the degree had not met its standards and reject the college's accreditation application.
In March this year, Ms Coddington commenced a diploma at Deakin University to gain accreditation, which involves studying the same subjects again.
"I shouldn't have to do this. My original degree should have been enough," she said.
"It's been a huge burden, emotionally, just to prepare yourself after a full day of work to go and study more and do a 7pm lecture.
"It's exhausting and … it feels like the hurdles just keep moving."
Students are seeking compensation for their distress, their HECS debts, and the costs of further study.
'Administrative oversight' blamed
ICMS declined a request for an interview but in a statement said students were not "materially affected" by promotional material on its website that wrongly claimed the course was accredited with API.
ICMS said this incorrect claim was made in 2024 and removed in 2026.
"ICMS identified one recent news article on its website, which stated that the degree was accredited by the Australian Property Institute," an ICMS spokesperson said.
"That statement occurred due to an administrative oversight and was immediately removed once identified. "
The college said it reported its "oversight" to the higher education regulator, the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA), and removed the article earlier this year.
ICMS said it "denies the claims being made against it", and that it would defend the class action and had met its legal obligations.
"ICMS is not required, by TEQSA or any other regulator, to hold separate course accreditation or recognition with any professional valuer bodies," the spokesperson said.
"Working as a property valuer in NSW does not require a degree accredited by such a body, and obtaining certification from them is an optional professional credential."
ICMS said the Australian Valuers Institute recognised its degree.
It added a disclaimer to its website earlier this year to clarify the degree did not have professional accreditation for property valuers.
The college also said the degree had a full-time employment average above the national average, according to a long-running survey of university graduates.
Ms Coddington said even with the disclaimer, high school students choosing a course would be unaware of the ramifications.
"What I struggle to understand is how ICMS can still offer this degree and call it a Bachelor of Property (Management, Valuation and Development)," she said.
International student spent $100k on degree
Mauritian international student Yuvarassee Moothoosamy, who has also joined the class action, was shattered by the lack of accreditation.
She estimated the degree cost her $97,000, plus tens of thousands extra for accommodation in Sydney, with her parents going into debt to fund her studies.
"There was a bit of guilt because I already spent that much money and my parents paid it all … some of it was a loan as well," she said.
Ms Moothoosamy said she was furious that she would need further study to gain professional accreditation to work as a valuer.
"I'm in a completely different career path now. I do want to get back at some point … because I eventually do want to do [property] valuation," she said.
"For the moment, I have to find something else to be able to have a life and pay bills."
Without the resources to study further, she is now working in hospitality.
"I wouldn't say I was sad, I was quite angry with the whole thing and felt quite used. Because as an international student, I think it was just a money grab."
ABC investigation revealed hundreds of careers in limbo
Ten students have already signed onto the ICMS class action, but lawyers expect those numbers to grow as they identify other students.
Last year, ABC News revealed 160 students from a University of Newcastle engineering degree and 115 from a Western Sydney University master's had started separate class actions after a similar lack of accreditation curtailed their careers.
ABC News understands the University of Newcastle class action may reach a settlement by the end of this month.
Mediation in the Western Sydney University (WSU) class action is continuing. WSU declined to comment.
Twenty-seven students from James Cook University also settled a fourth Supreme Court class action last year over an unaccredited financial services major.
Australian Law Partners ran all the cases, saying TEQSA needed to be "on top of its game" to ensure representations to students were accurate.
"The federal regulator has a critical role to ensure compliance with the threshold standards," solicitor Duke Myrteza said.
"Without that oversight … students are exposed to potential hardship through enrolling in courses that don't offer the outcomes that are represented to them."
Mr Myrteza declined to comment on the regulator's performance but noted there were a "significant" number of claims alleging higher education providers had not met threshold standards under federal law.
In a statement, TEQSA said providers must provide students with "accurate and current information" about accreditation status.
"Where a course is intended and advertised as meeting professional accreditation requirements, the necessary accreditation must be in place," a spokesperson said.
"If it is not, TEQSA expects the provider to identify any students who may have been disadvantaged and take appropriate action to remediate any adverse impact on these students."

Merz government wants ‘secret police’ – opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:46:09 UTC
03:46:09 KST

Merz government wants ‘secret police’ – opposition
Germany’s opposition lawmakers have accused Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government of seeking to create a “secret police” by dramatically expanding the powers of the country’s intelligence agencies.
The accusations came during the first parliamentary debate on the reform on Thursday, with lawmakers from the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the Left and the Greens raising concerns over surveillance and fundamental rights. The government argues that the changes are needed to counter growing security threats.
Under a reform approved by the cabinet last month, the BND foreign intelligence agency and the BfV domestic security service would gain broader operational powers, allowing them to move beyond primarily gathering and analyzing information.
Among the proposed changes, the BND could sabotage foreign companies, penetrate foreign IT systems and disable weapons deemed a threat to Germany. The BfV, meanwhile, could secretly enter homes and access computers and mobile phones under certain circumstances.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the reform would usher in a “new era” by turning the country’s intelligence services into “genuine intelligence agencies” capable of actively countering threats. He said Germany must bring its services to the level of its European partners.
AfD MP Gottfried Curio branded the proposed overhaul of the BfV “Stasi 2.0,” referring to East Germany’s notorious secret police, and called the reform a “coup against the rule of law.” The AfD, however, supports granting the BND greater operational powers.
The BfV has itself been locked in a legal battle with the AfD. In 2025, the agency designated Germany’s most popular party a “confirmed right-wing extremist” organization, but a Cologne court in February barred it from applying that classification while the case proceeds.
The ruling came months before the AfD scored major gains in regional elections. It won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and 38.3% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday.
Green MP Konstantin von Notz said granting the BfV such extensive powers would be a “grave mistake” and questioned whether parts of the reform would survive scrutiny by the Constitutional Court. He nevertheless backed giving the BND greater powers.
Left Party MP Clara Buenger went further, warning that the BfV could become a “new German secret police.”
“Fundamental rights are being trampled on here,” she said, arguing that the agency would gain powers traditionally reserved for police.
The debate comes as Merz’s government braces for growing AfD influence at the regional level. The Telegraph and Die Welt reported in July that Berlin was developing a “secret plan” to counter potential “obstructionism” by regional authorities, allowing the federal government to bypass them in a crisis.
The German government wants the intelligence reform to take effect at the beginning of 2027. It still requires approval from both the Bundestag and Bundesrat.

What 17,000 Australians have to say about money, housing and mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:44:33 UTC
03:44:33 KST

The ups and downs of modern life in Australia
How stressed out are we about housing? Are we happy in our long-term relationships? And are we getting smarter?
Every year since 2001, researchers have followed the lives of more than 17,000 people across Australia to answer questions like these.
It's called the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey, and data for 2024 has just been released.
Across nearly a quarter of a century, it gives us a window into how Australian life has changed.
Let's take a look at some of the ups and downs.
We'll go one step at a time. Just tap "show me another" to see each insight.
New dads are taking (slightly) longer leave
Across two surveys, both mothers and fathers have taken more paid parental leave.
In 2024, women took more than four months on average, while fathers took just four weeks.
It may not look like it in the chart, but the amount of leave men are taking has actually climbed at a faster rate than for women.
The report says the increases could be due to the federal government extending paid parental leave during this period.
Mental health has declined for young women
As part of the survey, participants' self-reported mental health is ranked from 0 to 100, and the results show a startling change over time.
On average, mental health for women across most age groups has declined since 2001, particularly for young women aged between 15 and 24.
Older men report better mental wellness
The trend among men is similar, with younger age groups reporting declining mental health across decades, although the levels are overall higher than for women.
But one group, men aged 65 and over, has bucked the general trend and seen an increase in self-reported mental health.
More under-30s are living with their parents
The proportion of young people living with their parents has climbed since the turn of the century.
While the increase was greatest for 18- to 21-year-olds — lifting to 85 per cent — it also rose for other younger age brackets.
The researchers say most of this growth had happened up until the mid-2010s, and has remained fairly stable ever since.
Thinking skills have decreased for the youngest
Survey participants have to do two cognitive tests, called backwards digits span (BDS), which involve reciting back long strings of single-digit numbers, and symbol digits modalities (SDM), where symbols are matched to numbers.
In both tests, average performance has declined for Australians aged between 15 and 24.
But older Australians are showing more brain power
While younger people are faring worse, older Australians are performing better on these tests compared to in 2012.
Those aged 45 and older did better on average on both tests across time.
But keep in mind that this chart only displays change within age groups. Overall, the survey shows cognitive ability declines as you get older.
Fewer people are receiving benefits
Across the board, a smaller share of Australians are receiving government income support payments, a broad category which includes the pension, JobSeeker and Youth Allowance.
About 13 per cent of 18- to 64-year-olds received income support, down from 24 per cent in 2001, which researchers attribute to the tightening of eligibility and growth in employment.
Australians aged 65 and over rely more on benefits, given this group encompasses retirees, but that share has also dropped across the survey period.
The education gap is widening
The percentage of people with a university degree has risen across decades, for all ages and genders.
But it has risen much faster for women, with the biggest gender gap emerging in the 35—44 age groups.
Men consistently pocket more
Since 2001, average hourly earnings for workers have risen, despite a surge and dip around the COVID-19 pandemic due to changes in working hours.
But the chart indicates the gender pay gap has persisted across the survey period, with women earning less on average.
More Aussies can't put food on the table
In four years, the share of Australians over 15 who experienced food insecurity increased.
More people reported they could not "obtain adequate food" in the past year due to a lack of money.
Older Aussies struggle less with 'problematic' social media use
To determine "problematic" social media use, participants answer questions that capture their preoccupation with and negative emotions when using online platforms.
The percentage of people above the "at-risk" threshold was greatest for teenagers, but steadily declined across older ages.
Single parents are in the most housing stress
A higher proportion of Australians are reporting housing stress, but when you break it down into types of households, it reveals some are driving the increase more than others.
Housing stress has consistently been higher for single parents with kids, but has also surged for single older men and couples with kids in recent years.
Middle age is the roughest patch for relationships
As you age, the data shows that relationship quality increases, but not before it plummets in your 30s and 40s.
Women also consistently report a lower relationship quality than men across their lifetimes.
But it's worth noting that even at the lowest dip for women, the average rating for relationship quality is about a four out of five.

Rogue agent hack vindicates Albanese's push for tough AI guardrails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:42:57 UTC
03:42:57 KST

analysis
When rogue AI agent 'scaled a fence', it reinforced Albanese's case for tough guardrails
The revelation that an AI agent turned rogue and breached a firewall to get at Medicare statistics has strongly reinforced Anthony Albanese's case for tough guardrails on this transformative technology.
The timing of the disclosure (and the incident itself) is fortuitous in a political sense, although the opposition's suggestion the announcement was delayed for political purposes doesn't hold water.
The government says ministers only learned late last week of the breach. The impact for Albanese's argument would have been the same even if it had been announced a few days ago.
During the United Nations' leaders week in New York, the prime minister has been heavily focused on AI — in concert with other like-minded countries stressing action is imperative.
The AI companies themselves have been looking for leadership from politicians. But US President Donald Trump has rejected the message, indeed scoffed at it. He believes what he's renamed "super intelligence" should run free.
But for the Australian audience, this relatively minor hack vindicates the warnings. As one government man put it, it was a real-life example of a science fiction scenario.
Taskforce to tackle AI incidents
In a training exercise, an OpenAI agent broke loose, refusing to be deterred when it couldn't get its way with the Services Australia Medicare statistics portal.
The AI agent, tasked to undertake research on medicine spending, interacted with four sites: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health, and the Services Australia Medicare portal.
When it found itself frustrated by the Services Australia site, it successfully sought a way to outsmart the obstacle.
As Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles described it, the data "was behind a fence — the AI agent climbed the fence".
There are different levels of protection for different sorts of data. "When we're talking about the data of Australian individuals within the Australian government system, to continue the analogy, that sits inside a safe," Marles told reporters. "When you're talking about our national security — the most sensitive information that we have — it sits behind a fortress."
The information that was hacked concerned general statistics, not personal data, so in that sense the practical implications were limited. But the fact of the breach is serious and its message salutary.
The government has reacted with a taskforce led by the prime minister's own department.
It will make recommendations on:
- Reporting requirements when there are AI-driven cyber incidents.
- Commonwealth governance and information-sharing arrangements for managing incidents.
- Engagement and information-sharing obligations of AI firms.
- The adequacy of existing laws and penalties relating to incidents.
- How to strengthen the protections that departments and agencies have to prevent AI attacks.
The government has been angered by OpenAI's slowness in notifying it. The incident happened on June 18; OpenAI learned of it on August 11. On September 10, it emailed the Services Australia "Public Interest Disclosures" address, described as a "public mailbox".
On September 15, Services Australia notified the Australian Signals Directorate (which investigates cyber breaches). Minister for Government Services Katy Gallagher was told "around September 17".
In a Wednesday, US time, telephone conversation with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese registered the government's "disappointment" at the company's tardiness in informing the government.
However, Marles told his Thursday news conference that OpenAI was being "very cooperative".
Australia won't be alone in receiving unwelcome news about the activities of rogue agents. Following OpenAI agents escaping mid-year and hacking Hugging Face in a massive operation, the company has undertaken an extensive search for other incidents.
Loading
AI needs to be a priority
While the Australian incident vindicates the government's approach, it also underscores that the work on AI has to be given even higher priority.
Part of this should be to elevate Andrew Charlton to the ministry.
At present he's assistant minister for science, technology and the digital economy, as well as cabinet secretary. Charlton is not only highly expert in AI but an excellent communicator, and to have him as sidekick to Industry Minister Tim Ayres is to undervalue significant talent. Given the term is at its halfway mark, it is time for a ministerial reshuffle anyway.
While in the US, Albanese was also spruiking his Digital Duty of Care legislation, only to have the US embassy in Canberra issue a swingeing attack on it.
The intervention was unusual at one level, although the Trump administration has sent similar salvos to the United Kingdom and Europe in the name of "free speech".
Albanese dismissed the US criticism. But he gave grist to critics when, in unscripted remarks, he started to talk about misinformation and disinformation, triggering memories of earlier unpopular legislation that was eventually withdrawn.
"The truth is this is having an impact on our entire society and how it functions with misinformation, disinformation, with the increased polarisation that we're seeing as well in the political system, where people are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right," he said.
"And that is why we think that this is a very positive move that's being put forward."
Questioned about this, he distanced his comments from the Duty of Care bill. But those fearing "creep" will be unconvinced.
Parts of the Duty of Care legislation, notably enabling people to opt out of algorithms, will be widely supported.
While parts of the US critique are over the top, the US and other critics have a point when it comes to the power afforded to the minister to determine potential "harm". The US said it was concerned "how the Australian government, or the communications minister [Anika Wells], would designate what constitutes 'foreseeable harm'".
Although the government points out ministerial directions would be subject to disallowance, it has signalled it is ready to be flexible in negotiations.
Many will regard the disallowance provision as insufficient protection. At the very least, there is a strong argument for the parliament having to pass any new designations of harm proposed by the minister.
Wells on Thursday again flagged Labor was willing to give ground on this, saying if the power "needs to go to the parliament to secure Coalition support, I am more than open to that".
Like AI, ministerial discretion requires strict "guardrails".
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

Israel's growing diplomatic isolation was on stark display at the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday as scores of delegates walked out when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took the podium, leaving much of the hall empty as he defended Israel's wars and lashed out at his critics.
The protest began as Netanyahu approached the rostrum, with cheers and boos echoing through the chamber before scores of diplomats filed out. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman repeatedly called for order as the walkout unfolded.
The Palestinian Mission to the U.N. had urged delegations from the 193-member body to participate in a coordinated walkout, saying it would send a message that governments would not be complicit in "genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation."
Netanyahu responded defiantly from the podium.
"If there are any other moral cowards who have not yet left the hall, please do so now," he said.
The Israeli prime minister also defended his decision to attack Iran, calling it "one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make."
Netanyahu argued that Israel's military actions were protecting countries whose representatives had walked out of the chamber, claiming that some of their leaders had privately thanked Israel for its actions against Iran.
"In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall," Netanyahu said.
His address came as Israel faces mounting international pressure over its genocidal policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. At least 73,922 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's attacks in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023. Israel's indiscriminate attacks have left much of the territory devastated and reconstruction efforts have stalled.
At one point, he held up a pager while referring to Israel's September 2024 operation targeting Hezbollah members in Lebanon. The pager explosions wounded more than 3,000 people and killed 12, including two children.
The scenes inside the General Assembly contrasted sharply with Netanyahu's insistence that Israel would continue its military course.
"We will continue to win because we have no other choice," he said, while thanking U.S. President Donald Trump for his actions against Iran.
Earlier Thursday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the General Assembly by prerecorded video after the United States denied him and other senior Palestinian officials visas to attend the gathering for a second consecutive year.
"We will not leave our homeland. We will not accept displacement. And we will not allow anyone to decide our future on our behalf," Abbas said.
Abbas called for stronger international action against Israel and renewed his appeal for a two-state solution. Netanyahu has rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state while he remains prime minister.
Signs of Netanyahu's contentious reception extended beyond the U.N. headquarters. More than 100 protesters gathered in New York during his address, demanding that he face prosecution over Israel's military actions. Some demonstrators were detained by police.
The mass diplomatic walkout, protests outside the U.N. and growing international criticism underscored the widening divide between Netanyahu's government and many of Israel's traditional partners as the conflicts in Gaza and the wider region continue.

'Forced down our throats': Most of us never chose an AI world. Yet here we are
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:40:55 UTC
03:40:55 KST

Most Australians don't trust AI. Why do these countries feel differently?
• 中文版 | Indonesian •
Part 1: Who Really Controls AI?
Australians are the world's biggest sceptics of artificial intelligence, even as it increasingly becomes part of everyday life.
But across the Asia-Pacific, many people keep using AI despite their doubts, while nations go their own ways to protect against its risks.
__
Isabel Oar finds herself relieved these days to spot grammatical errors in an email.
It is a sign that she is reading something from a human, not artificial intelligence (AI).
"I get quite irritated if I feel like I'm responding to an email that's been written by AI," the Queensland-based teacher says.
"I feel that communication should be human. So I refuse to use it for writing."
After starting as an enthusiastic user of OpenAI's ChatGPT for coding and other tasks, Isabel has pulled back more recently, like many other early adopters she knows.
For a start, she has come to trust AI less after seeing it make mistakes in its responses and in coding.
"I don't really ask AI questions anymore. I still Google things," she says.
However, even the search engine's use of AI summaries makes the technology seem unavoidable.
"We're having this forced down our throats. It's in everything and we're not consenting to it," she says.
The ABC has been talking to Australians over the past year about their hopes, doubts and experiences as AI rapidly enters workplaces, homes and education.
Over that time, views have quickly changed from caution, excitement and concern to something different.
Isabel's experience is echoed in many of the hundreds of responses to a recent ABC call-out asking people how AI has changed their lives.
Here is how other respondents put it, which you can see by scrolling through their sentiments below.
"I don't trust AI; I use it daily as it gives me confidence with writing."
— Craig, Victoria
"AI has a way of being inherently addictive to use. The models are developed by companies who want you to use it more, in a similar way to social media."
— Harriet, Queensland
"I am not quite so trusting of the information served up to me and now tend to check with more than one product … I still find it extremely useful and use it daily."
— Laura, New South Wales
"I trust AI more than I did a year ago, but in a different way. I trust it as an exceptionally capable assistant, not as a substitute for experience, expertise or professional judgement."
— Mike, New South Wales
"Being told constantly at work 'just run it through [Microsoft] Copilot' is frustrating. I'm not an expert in these fields … so I'm relying on AI to produce accurate results, which often it does not."
— Ellie, Victoria
"I trust AI less than I did a year ago … not so much because of the technology but because of the lack of community care from the owners of AI companies, and the lack of lawmaking by governments to protect society."
— Darren, Victoria
"We need to tread more carefully ... The march of AI is not inevitable. It's a choice."
— Patricia, New South Wales
Australians are among the least trusting and accepting of AI in the world, in stark contrast to people in many neighbouring countries, according to a study by the University of Melbourne and consultancy firm KPMG.
Trust and acceptance were much higher in emerging economies like India and China, where AI was more likely to be seen as a pathway to prosperity, says Nicole Gillespie, a scholar on trust in organisations and professor of management at the University of Melbourne.
"In emerging economies, AI plays a stronger role in filling real resource gaps. It can help overcome shortages in skills, information and networks, and bridge barriers of language to open access to global markets," she says.
People in emerging economies were still aware of the risks of AI, and the survey found users in India and China reported slightly more experience of its harms, a result reflecting their higher use of the technology.
Rather than being more worried about AI's risks than others, Australians were simply much less likely to see the upside of AI, Professor Gillespie says.
Another survey suggests that people around the region are using AI even if they do not always trust it.
People in China, Indonesia and Malaysia had the highest rates on this measure, according to an online survey by market research firm Ipsos.
In Australia, New Zealand and Japan, more than half of people say the same.
Data from the same report also showed that China, South Korea and Indonesia were more excited about AI products and services, compared to Australia and New Zealand, who were more nervous.
"What this tells us is that trust is not necessarily a prerequisite for usage," says Hamish Munro, Ipsos chief executive in the Asia-Pacific.
"Adoption can move ahead of trust, with people willing to engage with the technology while still questioning how much they should rely on it."
'It's not turn-off-able'
Some respondents to the ABC's call-out say they wanted to opt out of the AI increasingly present in software or were abandoning programs that did not give them this option.
Emma Gerts, a writer and librarian from New South Wales, says she quit using Microsoft Word and Google Documents as she did not trust them not to scrape her work and use it for training AI models.
She sees AI as inherently untrustworthy because of its mistakes, the difficulty of verifying its responses, and the profit motive of AI companies.
While she believed it could be useful for tasks like coding, it had had no benefits for her work, including writing emails, she says.
"By the time I got through prompting it and re-prompting it and figuring out exactly the right words to say so that it would understand what I meant, I was just like, I could have written this email already," Emma says.
"I turn AI off anywhere I can turn AI off.
"But unfortunately, it's not turn-off-able in a lot of things."
In Western Australia, digital literacy educator Gabrielle Jolliffe says she had noticed her students become less open to the technology this year, a change she attributed to their experiences receiving some of its erroneous answers.
"This is the first time I have struck amongst my students a reluctance and suspicion to use it," she says.
Gabrielle would like to see providers of free generative AI programs stating clearly up-front how they would use information they gathered.
"Just like we have labelling requirements on alcohol, on what's inside food … they need to be very, very open and transparent about how the data is being used."
Meanwhile, Emma would like to see regulations requiring that software let people switch off AI.
"I don't think they should be allowed to force AI into a program," she says.
Such support for stricter rules is echoed in the University of Melbourne/KPMG survey, which showed most Australians backed regulating AI.
They were also less likely than people in other Asia-Pacific countries to say that current safeguards were adequate.
Professor Gillespie, from the University of Melbourne, says "thin institutional reassurance" was a factor in Australians' low trust in AI.
"Only around half express confidence in government, big tech firms or commercial organisations to develop and use AI in the public interest," she says.
From Go to 'whoa'
In Australia and other Western nations, the release of ChatGPT in 2022 is widely regarded as the event that began broad public discussions about the potential harms and benefits of AI.
For much of Asia, that moment arrived when Google DeepMind's AlphaGo program defeated the South Korean grandmaster Lee Se-Dol at the strategy board game Go in 2016, says Jian Xu, an associate professor and expert on China's AI governance at Deakin University.
"It marked an important stage in the longer trajectory of AI awareness and governance in Asia, well before the emergence of ChatGPT," Dr Xu says.
Since then, Asian nations have diverged in how they regulate AI and manage its risks.
At one end of the spectrum, China has developed one of the world's most comprehensive regulatory frameworks for AI governance, Dr Xu says.
Rather than relying on a single, overarching AI law, China has built a "layered regulatory framework" combining general laws for cybersecurity, data security and personal information with AI-specific regulations, he says.
Among them are the recent "Interim Measures for the Management of AI Anthropomorphic Interactive Services", taking effect in July and addressing risks associated with AI agents simulating human interaction and emotional relationships.
Another measure requires that AI upholds "socialist values" and refrains from generating content that incites the subversion of state power.
"The government seeks to promote AI development while ensuring that emerging technologies remain safe, controllable, politically compatible and aligned with broader national development objectives," Dr Xu says.
"This can be seen as 'AI governance with Chinese characteristics'."
At the other end of the spectrum, Singapore has pursued a "soft-law" approach balancing safety with realising AI's economic potential, according to Terence Lee, a professor and expert on Singapore's AI governance at the University of Nottingham Ningbo, China.
The city-state's government has prepared to embrace AI for more than a decade and wants the external business and investment community to see it as a place that lets businesses road-test new ideas with minimum restrictions, he says.
"Rather than passing restrictive, overarching legislation … Singapore relies on voluntary or self-regulatory frameworks, and it targets updates to existing laws (rather than rolling out new legislation), and offers technical testing tools and guidelines," Professor Lee says.
Australia's unanswered AI question
One Australian government official has called trust the single factor that will determine whether the country's AI industry thrives or stalls — more influential than chips, capital or energy.
"Why are Australians the most sceptical people on earth about this technology?" Assistant Minister for Technology Andrew Charlton said at an AI summit in Canberra earlier this year.
"Australians took up smartphones, contactless payments, and online banking faster than almost anyone. Adopting is in our DNA.
"Australians are not refusing the future. But they are asking a fair question: who is this actually for?
"And until we answer that question convincingly, scepticism is not irrational. It is the reasonable response of people who suspect they are being asked to carry the risks while someone else hoovers up the rewards."
The Australian government is hoping to build public trust in AI through reforms addressing its risks.
Among its priorities is legislating a "digital duty of care" requiring AI companies to make their products safe and proactively address potential harm, reforms to personal data protection laws, and safety testing of frontier AI systems through its newly-established AI Safety Institute.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in July also indicated Australia would change its fragmented approach to regulating AI.
He announced the Australian government would coordinate the design of "Australian standards" for the technology, and that legislation would be brought to parliament early next year.
Among the standards would be rules requiring data centres to minimise water use and underwrite new power supply to cover their consumption.
It was a response to growing backlash against data centres among local communities, a sentiment also reflected in audience responses to the ABC's recent call-out.
Gerard Goggin, professor and researcher on the cultural and social dynamics of digital technology at Western Sydney University, says awareness of data centres has helped bring about Australia's shift in regulating AI.
"That's something that's emerged in a way more palpable sense … in terms of environmental aspects, planning aspects, but also perhaps the strategic opportunity for Australia to harbour data centres," he says.
Professor Goggin says consumer protection, disability accessibility, and copyright would be among the most important pieces of legislation responding to the rise of AI in Australia.
There were also harmful uses of AI, such as "nudify" apps, that could and should be banned, he says.
"We shouldn't shy away from [doing] that when that comes," Professor Goggin says.
Meanwhile, in Queensland, Isabel still sees AI's benefits and believes it has a useful role for teachers, especially in speeding up tedious, time-consuming administrative tasks.
Still, she says there were benefits to adopting technology more slowly.
"You get to see the mistakes that everybody else makes and then adjust," she says.
"And I think maybe Australia needs to consider slowing things down."

IDF chief warns Iran remains a threat as Israel welcomes INS Drakon submarine into Navy service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:29:11 UTC
03:29:11 KST

IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir on Thursday called the arrival of Israel’s sixth submarine, the INS Drakon, a major step in strengthening the IDF’s capabilities during a ceremony at Haifa's naval base.
“Even these days, our eyes are open toward what is happening in Iran and among its proxies. The Iranian regime is hurt and wounded, but has not learned to change its intentions,” Zamir said at the ceremony.
“With the integration of the INS Drakon into the Navy, the Navy reaches improved maritime readiness and new heights in its capabilities and operational strength: more covert, farther-reaching, deeper and more lethal.”
Zamir added that Israel’s recent military achievements were “unprecedented,” citing operations against senior figures, strengthened defensive readiness, improved deterrence and expanded operational capabilities.
Herzog: 'INS Drakon' is a new chapter for Israel's Navy
President Isaac Herzog said the vessel represented a glimpse into the future of the Navy, and added that the submarine fleet would expand Israel's operational capabilities.
“Today, as we receive the INS Drakon into the ranks of the Navy, we look for a moment into the future,” Herzog said.
“The Drakon submarine joining the Navy today, like the additional submarines that will arrive after it, together reflect the bright future of the Navy. A future that means innovation, a future that means broader operational capabilities, a future that means immense power available to the State of Israel, more than ever before.
"Power that we will be able to use, and will not hesitate to use when necessary, even thousands of kilometers from Israel’s borders.”
Herzog said that in recent years, the Navy sailors and many others involved in the project had worked at the Kiel naval base in Germany.
“Over the past two years, Israeli Navy soldiers and many others connected to this enormous project worked at the Kiel port on German soil. Another almost unimaginable symbol,” he said.
“Eighty-one years since the terrible Holocaust, the nation-state of the Jewish people is building together with Germany the crown jewel of global defense engineering. At the same time, the State of Israel is not only importing security equipment from Germany, but is also exporting advanced defense systems to it, thereby contributing to the defense of all of Europe.”
Herzog thanked Zamir, Defense Minister Israel Katz, Ministry of Defense Director General Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram, Navy commanders and soldiers, and representatives of the German government and Thyssenkrupp for their roles in bringing the submarine into service.
Addressing the submarine crews, Herzog praised their work and said the arrival of the Drakon marked a new chapter in Israel’s naval capabilities.
“Above all, I want to thank you, the submarine fighters under the command of Cmdr. O. Two years of training and long weeks at sea have brought you here as heralds of a new chapter in Israel’s maritime strength,” he said.
“We hold in our hearts, with appreciation and pride, the memory of the 69 members of the Dakar crew, and send a comforting embrace to their families.”
He told the Drakon’s crew that the human element remained the decisive factor despite the submarine’s advanced technology.
“Today, when the Drakon submarine is entrusted to you, the fighters of the submarine flotilla, among the finest sons and daughters of Israeli society in all its diversity, we remember one clear principle: the person determines. The person operating the machine, whether it is the most advanced and expensive machine, is the one who will always bring victory and the ability to complete the mission in full,” Herzog said.
Herzog also referred to the legacy of the INS Dakar submarine, which disappeared in 1968 and whose crew of 69 sailors were lost.
“Even at this ceremony, especially at this ceremony, we remember well the painful journey of the Dakar submarine, whose name not only serves as inspiration for the Drakon submarine, but also represents the immense courage and strength of spirit that characterized its crew,” Herzog said.

Former England soccer star Wayne Rooney says grandma was Polish Jew during Auschwitz visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:28:56 UTC
03:28:56 KST

Wayne Rooney, the former English soccer star, revealed that his maternal grandmother was a Polish Jew during a family visit to Auschwitz.
Speaking in his Disney+ documentary, The Real Rooneys, Rooney explained that he "recently found out my mum's mum, my nan, her family was Polish Jews."
“Technically, if that’s true, you’re actually Jewish,” a producer called from off camera. Judaism is passed down maternally, and given Rooney's heritage comes from his "mum's mum," the former soccer player is considered Jewish by Halacha (Jewish law).
"I'm Catholic, but I've always asked questions like, 'Why aren't we Jewish?'" Rooney responded.
He explained that his mother told him that his great-grandmother had fled Poland for Liverpool, adding that they thought her original surname was Greenburg.
The Rooneys visit Auschwitz at their 10-year-old's request
The announcement came during a family trip to Poland, where the family aimed to learn more about World War II for their son's school project.
“Kit really wanted to go,” Rooney's wife, Coleen, told the Guardian when asked whose idea the trip had been.
Rooney added, “It’s really important to learn about history, good and bad. Sometimes with your kids, you only want to tell them the good stuff, and I don’t think that’s good for them."
"I've watched a lot of documentaries on it, and you just wouldn't think human beings could do that to other human beings. It's crazy," he told his taxi driver on the way to the concentration camp.
Although his sons hadn't been to Auschwitz before, Rooney himself had visited with his England teammates during the 2012 Euros, which were held in Poland and Ukraine.
Jewish organizations respond to Rooney's announcement
Rooney could usurp Nick Blackman, the Blackburn Rovers player who is officially recognized as the first English-born Jewish player in the UK's Premier League.
Blackman debuted in 2009 while Rooney, who has subsequently discovered his Jewish heritage, debuted for Everton in 2002.
Blackman played for Israel's Maccabi Tel Aviv towards the twilight of his career.
However, Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA), a UK-based charity dedicated to exposing and countering anti-Jewish hate, felt that Rooney's newfound history had bigger implications. In a statement on X/Twitter, CAA commented that "this news is a reminder that the idea that Jewish people are not sporty is a myth laced with antisemitic tropes about Jewish physical weakness."
"In fact, before the Second World War, Jewish people were at the pinnacle of European sport across a range of disciplines, including football," it added.
"It is taking time to rebuild that culture from the ashes of the Holocaust, and educate about how Jewish people and people with Jewish heritage have contributed, and continue to contribute to the world of sport."

Poet, author Yehuda Atlas passed away at age 89, Sourasky Medical Center announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:28:52 UTC
03:28:52 KST

The Israeli author and poet Yehuda Atlas died on Thursday at the age of 89, Sourasky Medical Center's Ichilov Hospital in Tel Aviv announced.
"Yehuda was an eternal child until his last moments. In his life, he acted and worked for people out of emotion and a desire to help. He was an editor, children's writer, and translator, and in his last years he wrote about children at risk out of a sense of mission. May his memory be blessed," read the statement.
Atlas, one of the most recognizable and beloved authors in Hebrew children's literature, left behind a work that became an integral part of the childhood of several generations in Israel.
His most recognizable book, And This Child Is Me (Vehayeled Haze Hu Any), was published in 1977 and introduced readers the a child's world in simple, direct, everyday language as he grapples with parents, friends, shame, love, jealousy, and frustration.
In an interview with Walla Culture, Atlas revealed the principles of his writing: "I write briefly, simply, understandably, and to tell the truth."
An inflation in children's books
In the same interview, Atlas said that he believed there was an "inflation" in children's books, criticizing books that he described as trying to be too educational or therapeutic.
"Everything in our lives is a long process, and by the time you get close to describing the problem, you're at the end of the book," he said.
He also spoke more than once about the importance of cooperation over competition, something he mentioned in another Walla interview, where he said the way to resolve disputes is to talk, "and this is true not only for children but also for the adult world and politics."
In his final years, he continued to engage with children and the voices of those who are not always heard. His family said after his death that "Yehuda was an eternal child until his last moments," and that in his final years he wrote about at-risk children out of a sense of mission.
Herzog commemorates Atlas
President Isaac Herzog published a social media post remembering Atlas, where he said: "'This child is me' - that exact feeling accompanied hundreds of thousands of girls and boys in Israel who grew up in the light of Yehuda Atlas's great talent, who passed away today."
"And indeed, the dozens of children's books that came from Yehuda Atlas's hand, alongside the many books that he translated, were an inseparable part of the world of Israel's children, and their parents too found in them, more than once, great pleasure and, above all, a longing for other years," he added.
"The Yehuda Atlas cluster, born to farmer parents and raised in green and blooming landscapes, remained, to a large extent, an eternal child, and so did we, who were moved each time anew by his precise ability to depict, with the hand of an artist, the soul of a child," Herzog continued.
"Atlas will be missed by many, women and men alike, but the fruits of his talent will surely continue to accompany Israel's children for generations to come," he added, and finished by sending his condolences to Atlas's family.

No More ‘Trump Avenue’: Canada’s Capital Moves to Rename Street Amid Tense Trade War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:27:50 UTC
03:27:50 KST

Ottawa's City Council voted unanimously on Wednesday to remove President Donald Trump’s name from a residential street in the Canadian capital amid an increasingly hostile trade war.
The motion to rename “Trump Avenue” in the city’s Central Park neighborhood was brought forward by River Ward councillor Riley Brockington on Sept. 9 and swiftly received support from other local officials. “I don't like the idea of anything that's named for Donald Trump, who's demonstrated hostility towards Canada,” Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe said at a news conference after the vote.
The move symbolizes the strained relations between the two countries, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney goes head-to-head with the Trump Administration in a trade standoff. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect on Sept. 8, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada and his insistence on referring to it as the “51st state” have significantly contributed to the tensions.
The streets in Ottawa’s Central Park neighborhood were named after New York City institutions in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when Trump was primarily known for his businesses and real estate ventures, long before his political aspirations came to fruition.
Brockington said a consultation with local residents will now follow, with alternative names proposed for “Trump Avenue” ahead of a vote.
“I could speak at great length why I believe, strongly, it is time to rename ‘Trump Avenue,’ but I don't want to give a platform anymore to the person who is on the current street sign blades,” Brockington said. “I do believe this is about a new beginning, and I want this to be a community-led process where the community ultimately will select and recommend to City Council what that new name will be.”
In a statement to TIME, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly referred to the name change as a “meaningless gesture” and said “these local governments should do right by the citizens they serve, thank President Trump for defending their country, and make a good deal to benefit Canadian and American citizens alike.”
TIME has reached out to Ottawa's City Council for comment.
The vote to cut the street name comes after President Trump recently pushed through controversial renaming efforts of his own.
In late August, he signed an Executive Order renaming Lake Ontario, which borders the Canadian province of Ontario and the U.S. state of New York, as “Lake America.” The order applies to U.S. federal references of the lake and does not determine how Canada—or others—refer to the body of water. Several lawmakers across both countries have rejected the new moniker.
Thomas Juneau, a professor of public and international affairs at the University of Ottawa, says the street name change in Ottawa is “illustrative of the mood” of Canadians.
“Polls have repeatedly [shown] how extremely unpopular Trump is, and how his targeting of Canada on trade, and his trolling on social media, have made him and the U.S. unpopular,” he tells TIME.
A poll by Politico, conducted Sept. 13-15, found that 83% of Canadians thought it was wrong for Trump to impose tariffs on their country, while 71% backed Carney’s retaliatory tariffs. Another poll, conducted by Abacus Data between Sept. 4-9, found that 82% of Canadians had a negative impression of Trump.
Carney says he studied risk of U.S.-led military action amid annexation threats
In a new interview, Carney admitted he had prepared over the past 12 months or so for the “extreme tail risk” that Trump might order military action against Canada, amid the U.S. President’s repeated mentions of his desire to annex the country.
“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney told the New York Times. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare.
Juneau says the “risk of American military intervention against Canada is extremely low,” but reasons that just because Canada “shouldn't take [Trump’s] threat literally, it doesn't mean they shouldn't take it seriously.”
In an April 2025 interview with TIME, Trump denied he was “trolling” when discussing annexation. “We’re taking care of their military. We're taking care of every aspect of their lives… We don't need anything from Canada. And I say the only way this thing really works is for Canada to become a state,” he argued.
Carney, in line with other Canadian officials, has vehemently pushed back against the idea, stressing that Canada is “not for sale.” In June, after Trump revived talk of his ambitions to annex Canada, Ontario Premier Doug Ford simply stated “Canada will never be the 51st state.”
Despite the tensions, Carney said he and Trump have spoken “frequently” since trade talks collapsed last month. However, there is no clear path toward an end to the trade standoff.
“Trump is actively trying to choke off the Canadian economy," says Juneau, noting that a key sticking point in trade negotiations, according to Carney, has been Washington's efforts to restrict Canada’s ability to negotiate trade deals abroad.
Canada seeks international alliances to remove reliance on U.S.
The U.S. accounted for 72.5% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, according to the country’s annual trade report, making it Canada's largest trading partner by a wide margin.
Canada and the U.S. are also deeply integrated through defense arrangements, including their membership in NATO and the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD)—a bilateral defense and national security arrangement involving the shared defense of the continent.
Amid the strained relations with the Trump Administration, Carney has sought to diversify Canada’s trade and security alliances to reduce its reliance on the U.S.
“The weaponization of that interdependence by the U.S. makes [Canada] extremely vulnerable in a way that pretty much nobody else is,” insists Juneau, pointing to the urgency of Carney’s task.
The Canadian government has set itself a goal is to “double non-U.S. exports in the next decade” as it seeks to expand trade with other markets.
In January, Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping to forge what he called a “new strategic partnership” to end Canada's economic reliance on the American market.
Canada is also currently in negotiations with India as it seeks to negotiate a new comprehensive economic partnership agreement with Delhi, and is in talks for a free trade agreement with the Philippines.
The diversification efforts extend into defensive measures. At the E.U.-Canada summit in June 2025, Canada established a new Security and Defense Partnership with the bloc. Canada later became the first non-European country to participate in the "Security Action for Europe” (SAFE) instrument, which provides low-interest loans to help member states purchase military and defense equipment.
Canada is seeking to further strengthen ties overseas by becoming the European Union’s first “associate member”—a goal European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has vowed to help make a reality. The proposed arrangement, the details of which have yet to be ironed out, would likely deepen cooperation on matters including trade, defense, AI, and Arctic security.
Carney made his pledge to E.U. lawmakers when he addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Sept. 17. Touting closer ties with the bloc, he said “Europe and Canada are stronger together” and insisted "we are not fair-weather allies, we believe that our prosperity grows when it is shared."
Juneau warns that despite Carney’s current push to diversify trade and defense away from the U.S., the results of these deals may take a long time to truly stand up, as "in practice, diversifying trade and security relationships is measured in years and decades."

 Sometimes the term “phenomenology” is used to refer to the subjective character of one’s experiences or, as it is often glossed, their “what-it’s-likeness”. Used in this way, one may, for instance, focus on the what-it’s-likeness of a sharp pain one is currently experiencing and perhaps attempt to describe the subjective character of that pain – its phenomenology. Russian Finance Ministry sets Hormuz opening scenario for $50/bbl oil price in budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:26:37 UTC
03:26:37 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Setting the base oil price in the budget at $50 per barrel means that the Russian Ministry of Finance is already factoring an open Strait of Hormuz scenario into its forecast, Igor Yushkov, an expert from the Financial University and the National Energy Security Fund, told TASS.
"The Ministry of Finance has taken a very conservative approach to assessing future oil and gas revenues, making it a bet on stability," the expert noted. "Essentially, the Ministry of Finance is now factoring in a Strait of Hormuz opening scenario to ensure it does not depend on this factor," he said.
The global oil market was highly volatile in 2026, Yushkov said. In January, the price of Russian Urals crude stood at $41 per barrel, but in March, following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, it jumped to $77, after which prices fluctuated sharply amid Middle East instability.
The ministry in this connection is deliberately budgeting a rather low oil price to mitigate the risks of unexpected deficits and the need to revise the budget throughout the year, the expert added.

Israeli elections: Ben-Gvir gains as Lieberman and Winter lose ground in latest i24NEWS poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:21:58 UTC
03:21:58 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- i24NEWS poll: Ben-Gvir gains as Lieberman and Winter lose ground
i24NEWS poll: Ben-Gvir gains as Lieberman and Winter lose ground
Likud holds steady at 27 seats, while Gadi Eisenkot’s Yesh! party places second. The poll puts the coalition bloc at 60 seats
Likud would win 27 seats if an election were held today, unchanged from last week’s i24NEWS poll.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yesh! party would place second with 22 seats, according to the survey conducted by Direct Polls and published Thursday.
Otzma Yehudit, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, gains one seat to reach eight. Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu falls by one seat to seven, while Ofer Winter’s Amach Yisrael loses one seat and would win four.
Together remains at nine seats, while the Democrats fall by one to nine. United Torah Judaism holds steady at eight seats. The Joint List and Shas each remain at seven. Religious Zionism and Zehuta each hold six seats, while Ra’am gains one to reach six.
The poll puts the coalition bloc at 60 seats, the opposition at 47 and the Arab parties at 13.
Direct Polls, headed by Tzuriel Sharon, surveyed 537 Israeli adults on September 24 using a digital questionnaire and panel. The poll reports a sampling error of ±4.2 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

One dead after security forces open fire during Ebola burial in Congo, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:21:41 UTC
03:21:41 KST

One dead after security forces open fire during Ebola burial in Congo, sources say
Sept 24 - One person was killed and several others wounded after security forces fired shots to contain unrest during the burial of a suspected Ebola victim in northeastern Congo on Thursday, two sources said.
• The incident occurred at Katula-Paida cemetery in Beni, a city in North Kivu province, which has recently seen a surge in Ebola infections.
• The burial team was preparing to bury the body in line with Ebola safety procedures when residents demanded to see the deceased, questioning whether the person had died of Ebola, according to a member of the Ebola response team in the city.
• Tensions escalated and security forces escorting the burial team opened fire as they sought to contain the unrest, the source said.
• At least one person was killed and several others were injured, according to the response team member and a health official who asked to remain anonymous.
• Investigations are underway to establish the full toll and circumstances of the incidents, two health officials said.
• The incident is the latest in a series of attacks on burial teams and other Ebola responders, underscoring persistent mistrust among the population.
• The outbreak, declared on May 15, has infected 7,820 people and killed 3,779, according to government data released on Wednesday. REUTERS

Ethiopian army says 272 Tigrayan fighters killed as conflict escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:19:03 UTC
03:19:03 KST

Ethiopian army says 272 Tigrayan fighters killed in Amhara
Tigray People’s Liberation Front says in a ‘situation of full-blown war’ with Ethiopia’s government.
Ethiopia’s army says it has killed at least 272 fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) in a counter-offensive in the country’s northwest Amhara region.
The Ethiopian National Defence Force said on Thursday that another 260 Tigrayan fighters were wounded and several were captured.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can Ethiopia’s seven-group rebel alliance challenge Abiy Ahmed?
- list 2 of 3Ethiopia warns of ‘destruction’ as Tigray rebels launch offensive
- list 3 of 3Fighting widens across Ethiopia as Tigray clashes escalate
“Government forces launched a counter-offensive that inflicted heavy personnel and equipment losses on the TPLF” after the group and its allies attacked several areas of North Wollo, a region of Amhara that borders Tigray, the army said in a statement on Facebook.
The intensification came days after TPLF and six other armed groups from across Ethiopia announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, which committed itself to removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
The coalition brought together the newly-formed Amhara Fano National Movement, the Oromo Liberation Army and other movements from the Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regional states.
‘Full-blown war’
“We are in the situation of full-blown war now,” TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa told AFP news agency on Thursday.
He confirmed that Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.
The alliance marks a striking realignment that had been almost a year in the making, bringing together armed groups with very different histories and grievances against the central government, including forces with histories of conflict among themselves.
In a statement issued as the fighting widened on Wednesday, the alliance said the federal government was attacking its forces on several fronts and presented their response as part of the broader struggle that had brought the coalition together.
Meanwhile, the escalation has disrupted air travel, as Tigrayan forces seized three local airports in the region.
Flights to Lalibela, a UNESCO-listed site in Amhara known for its medieval rock-hewn churches, were suspended on Thursday, according to Reuters news agency.
AFP also received reports of fighting around Lalibela, causing its airport to close. The area has often been targeted by the Fano, a local armed group that is now operating alongside the TPLF.
Wider regional rivalries
TPLF last went to war with the Ethiopian federal government in 2020, leading to a devastating two-year conflict that ended with a peace deal in 2022.
In his address at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Ethiopia’s President Taye Atske-Selassie Amde blamed the escalation on “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”.
He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.
Analysts say the Tigray rebels have support from Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea.
The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”
Ethiopia’s domestic conflicts are becoming harder to separate from wider rivalries in the Horn of Africa, particularly Addis Ababa’s deteriorating relationship with Eritrea and Sudan’s civil war.
Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has visited Asmara twice since July for talks with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, while Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, reportedly visited Addis Ababa in late August.

Lavrov, Grossi discuss Israel’s, US’ strikes on Iran’s peaceful nukes — Foreign Ministry
Unknown

Zelenskyy broke confidentiality with N. Korea POWs disclosure: S. Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:13:00 UTC
03:13:00 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy broke a confidentiality agreement by disclosing publicly that Kyiv had sent North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, the East Asian country's president said Thursday.
The remarks by President Lee Jae Myung came after Zelenskyy told the United Nations that two North Korean soldiers had been recently sent to South Korea after being captured while fighting for Russia in the war against Ukraine.
"These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die," Zelenskyy said in his speech.
Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be captured alive since the country joined the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
Zelenskyy said at the time that he would hand them over to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to send them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishment the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
The revelation prompted South Korea's political opposition to criticize the Lee administration for allowing a foreign leader to inform them of the prisoners' arrivals.
South Korean president said it was "deeply regretful" that Ukraine had made the transfer public, adding that the two sides had agreed not to disclose it.
"I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing," Lee said on the social media platform X.
"The issue of bringing North Korean prisoners to South Korea is a highly sensitive one that could have a major impact on diplomacy, security and the situation on the Korean Peninsula," he said.
Lee said there had been calls to disclose the arrivals, but "given the problems that could arise from making it public, we agreed that keeping it confidential was the right thing to do."
Zelenskyy's aide Dmytro Lytvyn told journalists that Ukraine was "an open country" and that it would have been strange to hand over the soldiers in secret.
"From the entire story – which is long and detailed – we reported only the fact itself, that they were sent to the Republic of Korea," he said.
A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South.
Under South Korea's constitution, all Koreans, including those living in the North, are considered citizens, and officials have said this would apply to any North Korean troops captured in Ukraine.
The transfer comes as South Korea has voiced support for efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea and U.S. President Donald Trump has renewed his willingness to engage with Pyongyang.
Opposition politicians in South Korea questioned why Seoul had not announced the matter first.
South Korean opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told reporters on Thursday that the two men had left Ukraine last weekend, transited through a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days ago, Yonhap News Agency reported.
"While their exact location is unknown, I believe our intelligence agencies are protecting them," Yu was quoted as saying.
South Korea said in June it would accept any North Korean prisoners of war captured after fighting for Russia and opposed their repatriation to either Russia or North Korea.
In his address, Zelenskyy criticized North Korea's deployment of troops to support Moscow.
"This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return," he said.
North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000-15,000 troops to support Russia's war since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Pyongyang has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, as well as ballistic missiles, long-range artillery systems and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.

UN chief asks to tackle root causes of sea-level rise by capping emissions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
02:12:18 CST
03:12:18 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Thursday called for efforts to tackle the root causes of sea-level rise, primarily by capping greenhouse gas emissions.
"Any overshoot of the 1.5-degree limit (on man-made global temperature increase) must be as small and short as possible. Global emissions must peak immediately, and fall 60 percent by 2035," he told a high-level meeting on sea-level rise.
"We must triple renewable energy, double energy efficiency, slash methane emissions, halt and reverse deforestation, and transition away from fossil fuels -- fast and fairly," he said. "The G20 (Group of 20) must lead, and COP31 (UN Climate Change Conference) in Türkiye must deliver."
Guterres also stressed the importance of protecting people from rising waters -- by embedding sea-level rise resilience in national adaptation plans, development budgets, infrastructure and land-use decisions; and drawing on science, data, and the knowledge of indigenous peoples and local communities.
Around 770 million people live less than 5 meters above the high-tide line. Without significant adaptation and mitigation, the risks facing coastal cities and communities could increase tenfold by 2100, he said.
Sea-level rise is a threat multiplier. It batters economies, trade, infrastructure, and food systems; erases cultural heritage and identity; fuels instability; and it threatens the territorial integrity of some nations, he said.
Guterres also called for closing legal gaps.
The International Court of Justice and the International Law Commission stated that continued statehood is possible, even if territory is lost. States have called for maritime zones and boundaries to be preserved as coastlines shift. People's rights do not disappear because their homes do. And those people must be protected, he said.
"We need legal clarity consistent with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea -- and international cooperation is essential to reach the arrangements that affected states and local communities deserve," he said.
Rising seas are sinking futures. In 2024, the global sea level rose almost 6 mm, the highest annual increase ever recorded. And the pace is accelerating.
According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, even in the best-case scenario, sea levels are projected to rise by as much as half a meter by century's end. Without drastic emissions cuts, that rise could reach a meter. Meanwhile, Greenland and West Antarctica are losing ice faster, risking irreversible change, Guterres said.
Sea-level rise is measured in millimeters. But its toll is measured in millions of shattered lives, uprooted communities, and stolen futures. Those on the front lines must be front and center in every decision, he said. "We cannot allow countries and cultures to vanish beneath the waves -- or leave the aspirations of billions dead in the water. The SOS has gone out. The world must answer." ■
