Taiwan’s minimum monthly wage is set to rise to NT$30,900 next year from NT$29,500, exceeding NT$30,000 for the first time following a decision yesterday by the Ministry of Labor’s Minimum Wage Deliberation Committee.
The minimum hourly wage would also increase to NT$205 from NT$196, with both increases pending Cabinet approval.
The new rates are scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1 next year.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
According to the Ministry of Labor, around 2.61 million workers in Taiwan, including 414,400 migrant workers, are expected to benefit from the minimum wage hike.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) in April said that he could “guarantee” the minimum monthly wage would exceed NT$30,000 next year.
The minimum wage increases would not apply to migrant workers employed as live-in caregivers or domestic helpers, as they are not covered by the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法).
The meeting, which began at 10am, continued until 5:30pm due to disagreements between labor and management representatives over the scale of the increase.
It was the second-longest minimum wage review on record, trailing only a nine-hour negotiation session in 2018.
The 4.745 percent hike marks the 11th consecutive year in which the minimum wage has increased.
Since 2016, the monthly wage has climbed 47.4 percent from NT$20,008 to the current NT$29,500, and the hourly wage has risen 63.3 percent from NT$120 to NT$196.
During the negotiations, the committee referenced a ministry research report that projected the consumer price index (CPI) would increase by 2.07 percent this year, while the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics had revised its estimate for the nation’s GDP growth this year to 11.05 percent.
Prior to the meeting, Chinese National Federation of Industries executive director Sam Ho (何語) cited customs export data to highlight a heavy imbalance in industrial development, saying that many sectors would struggle to absorb a uniform wage hike.
Chinese National Association of Industry and Commerce secretary-general Chiu Yi-cheh (邱一徹) urged the committee to base its decision on the CPI while considering the practical financial pressures faced by various industries.
However, Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) said that the wage adjustment must reflect inflation to maintain the purchasing power and basic living standards of low-income workers.

Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
If a borough resident had not brought the matter to the party’s attention, voters would not have known about the candidate’s conduct, as it would not have appeared in the election bulletin, the chairwoman said.

Kaohsiung had the largest number at 22, followed by New Taipei City with 17 and Tainan with 11, she added.
Taiwan Statebuilding Party Taipei City councilor candidate Wu Hsin-tai (吳欣岱) said that as of Wednesday, election-related offenses accounted for the largest category at 36 cases.
Illegal claims for public funds or false reporting of campaign expenses, and violence or intimidation each accounted for 21 cases, followed by eight cases involving drunk or drug driving and traffic offenses.
Taiwan Obasang Political Equality Party (TOPEP) Taipei city councilor candidate Lee Hui-hsuan (李惠喧) said there were seven people involved in cases of attempted sexual assault, forced indecency, profiting from premises that provide prostitution, sexual harassment, and stalking and harassment.

TOPEP executive Chen Wan-yu (陳宛毓) said there were eight offenses involving bribery and 25 related to illicit relocation of household registrations.
Green Party Taiwan general convener Kan Chung-wei (甘崇緯) said 19 candidates were involved in 21 cases involving the misuse of public funds.

ASIAN GAMES: Teams slam Games organizers over ‘chaos’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:32 UTC
01:38:32 KST

Several teams yesterday rounded on the organization of the Asian Games in Japan, with Thailand likening it to a “chaotic” game of “musical chairs” and South Korea saying “they deserve a failing grade.”
The biggest issue at the Aichi-Nagoya Games has been a shortage of rooms for the 17,000 participants, while some athletes have complained of cramped accommodation.
That was compounded by delays at airports and hours-long waits to board a cruise ship acting as a floating hotel. Erratic transportation services have seen competitors’ buses to training and venues turning up late or, in some cases, not at all.
No traditional athletes’ village has been built as a cost-cutting measure. Teams have instead been staying in temporary container-style huts, hotels and the Costa Serena cruise ship moored in Nagoya Port.
“It remains a problem from the beginning until now,” said Chalitrat Chandrubeksa, deputy secretary general of the National Olympic Committee of Thailand.
“The number of [rooms available on] cruise ships and hotels does not match our actual number of athletes. On the peak day, we required 201 beds on the cruise ship, but they provided only 170,” Chalitrat said.
“When athletes checked in and found their names missing from the list, they had to be placed somewhere else and when the new athletes arrived, the previous ones had to move out and look for other hotels,” he said.
“It’s like musical chairs,” he added.
Frustrated athletes have made their feelings known online, with complaints also about some of the food.
“We are solving the problem by finding replacement accommodations ourselves,” Chalitrat said.
The shortages meant the Thailand team had to put some staff far away from the Games epicenter in the city of Nagoya.
“Our medical team has to stay about one hour 30 minutes from Nagoya,” Chalitrat said. “We had to rent additional vehicles from Tokyo so they could travel to look after the athletes. “It has been chaotic.”
South Korea said that the problems were “affecting athletes’ performances,” Yonhap news agency reported.
“If I were to give them a grade, it would be an F,” South Korean Sport and Olympic Committee president Ryu Seung-min said.
Asian Games organizing committee spokesman Hiroshi Koshizuka told reporters that there had beem issues with transport, but added that “there had been no significant impact on the Games and no event has been delayed.”
“We have set up a system to respond to complaints and we will address them in a sincere manner going forward.”
However, the the complaints keep coming.
Taiwan’s Olympic committee spokesman Steven Chen said that experience prepared them for the worst.
They booked 100 extra rooms at hotels in case there was a shortage of beds.
“We were informed at the last minute before departure that there weren’t enough beds. That was a major blow to every country,” he said.
Chen said that the “biggest headache” was with transport, with schedules frequently changing at the last minute.
“When our team had an evening flight, they suddenly informed us that the afternoon bus to the airport was changed to pick us up in the morning, which caused us a lot of trouble,” he said.

Southwestern Mexico on Wednesday braced for heavy rain and mudslides after Polo, a powerful Pacific cyclone, became a major hurricane. Forecasters also warned another system headed for Hawaii could cause catastrophic flooding later in the week.
Hurricane Polo, an “extremely dangerous” storm, is expected to skirt Mexico’s Guerrero state, submerging coastal areas with 10cm to 15cm of rain through yesterday, the US National Hurricane Center said.
Guerrero has been repeatedly pummeled by hurricanes in the past few years.
Photo: AFP
Farther out in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Nolo was churning about 475km south of South Point, Hawaii. The storm was forecast to become a hurricane by last night and expected to approach the Big Island as early as today.
Hawaiian Governor Josh Green’s office said public schools and state and county offices on the Big Island would close yesterday and today, while Maui County would shutter them today ahead of the threat of heavy rain, winds and flooding.
Forecasters said the storm could drop up to 51cmof rain.
Concepcion Lopez Villegas was busily bolstering her seaside restaurant in Lazaro Cardenas, Michoacan, against the expected onslaught of rain.
Strong waves were already hitting some beaches and Lopez Villegas said she feared the storm could destroy the small business she worked decades to build.
“We’re worried and trying to protect our businesses,” she said. “And of course, we’re sad because it’s our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed.”
Guerrero state was particularly at risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, the hurricane center said.
In the resort town Acapulco, rough surf pounded the shoreline, rain swept across the bay and strong winds bent palm trees. Merchants reinforced stall roofs as boats remained anchored in the bay.
“As they gave us a warning yesterday, I started getting my documents in order and half-packed my things, just in case,” local resident Andrea Tenorio said.
A nearby elementary school had been opened as a temporary shelter, she said.
Asked whether she was afraid, Tenorio said memories of Hurricane Otis still haunted residents.
“With Otis, we were left with trauma,” she said. “We haven’t been able to overcome it.”
Hurricane Otis slammed into Acapulco in October 2023 as a Category 5 storm, killing dozens and flattening the coastal town.

====================================================================================================

Lessons from the Mataian disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

On Sept. 23 last year, an overflow from a Mataian River (馬太鞍溪) barrier lake devastated Hualien County’s Guangfu Township (光復).
In the aftermath, tens of thousands of people boarded trains with their shovels, rain boots and tools to travel to the disaster site and help clear away the mud. The so-called “shovel heroes” quickly became one of the most celebrated and moving images of Taiwanese civil society. One year on, what the occasion calls for is not simply another celebration of that generosity, but an examination of how much has actually changed since the disaster.
The government has been reviewing its disaster preparedness and prevention systems based on lessons learned from the flood, rapidly expanding training programs for disaster relief volunteers, and making amendments to the Disaster Prevention and Protection Act (災害防救法) regarding responsibility management, local coordination and barrier lake risks.
However, the most pressing question still remains: When the next disaster arrives even faster and harder than the last, would we still be waiting on an organization of volunteers to rush to the scene, or have we found a way to harness civic power, such as those shown by the shovel heroes, into a mobilizable force of national resilience?
Guangfu showed us that Taiwan has the people. The next step is to prove whether it has the systems.
Extreme weather events this year have only heightened the issue’s urgency. Bouts of short, but intense rainfall have repeatedly broken records, while the limits of river dredgers, drainage systems, box culverts, water pumping stations and flood detention facilities are beginning to be tested.
The water management system’s measures for success can no longer just be about how much silt has been cleared and how many flood retention ponds have been built; we must start seriously stress testing for extreme climate conditions. When rainfall over 24 hours exceeds flood control standards, the government should be clear on which communities might experience flooding, which bridges might break, which power stations and cell towers might fail, and which hospital and care facilities need protection.
How we think about disasters must change: We need system-level thinking about drainage, water storage, flood detention and diversion and pre-emptive evacuations. True social resilience does not mean that cities would never flood; it means that when the limits of defenses are breached, the government knows where people should evacuate, supplies should be sent and equipment should be deployed, while ensuring essential services continue to operate.
Even more important to consider is the institutionalization of professional engineering capacity. In 2018, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) converted the Chinese People’s Armed Police Force Hydropower Corps into China Anneng Construction Group, a centrally owned engineering and emergency-rescue enterprise. Taiwan does not need to replicate that system, but it could learn from some of its strengths and establish a national engineering emergency response system compatible with a democratic system.
We already have a legal framework for requisitioning professionals, private vehicles and engineering equipment; the armed forces and reserve system also offer an institutional basis for supporting disaster prevention and response. What truly needs to be strengthened is the ability to use those resources when disaster strikes.
The central and local governments should establish a national engineering disaster response resource database, recording the locations and mobilization times of excavators, bulldozers, cranes, low-bed trailers, dump trucks, water pumps, generators and their operators. Personnel that specialize in engineering, communications, medical care, transportation, water, electricity, civil engineering and drones should also be incorporated into a reserve and civil coordination units.
Disaster response preparations should follow the logic of military operations: During normal times, resources are organized, drills are conducted, equipment are readied and chains of command are established, so that resources could be mobilized properly when a disaster strikes, instead of scrambling for personnel and equipment during the emergency.
The most precious lesson the Mataian disaster gave Taiwan is that the nation has a powerful societal capacity for spontaneous mutual aid. However, the state cannot treat people’s goodwill as a disaster response plan, nor could it expect another group of shovel heroes to swoop in each time a major disaster strikes.
On their first anniversary, we should turn the civic miracle of the shovel heroes into the starting point for reform. Taiwan should reassess capacity during extreme rainfall, establish specialized disaster response units, create a disaster mobilization database for civilian equipment, and connect volunteers, businesses, local governments, the armed forces and the central government’s disaster response system.
In the face of disasters, Taiwan last year saw that Taiwanese were willing to step in. Now, the state must demonstrate that before torrential rain falls, roads are cut off or infrastructure is damaged, it already knows what to do next. That is the true meaning of treating disaster response like combat, and what shovel heroes have left for Taiwan to fulfill.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

Brave Eagle AJT production completed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

Taiwan has completed production of all 66 domestically developed Brave Eagle (勇鷹) advanced jet trainers (AJT), with Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (AIDC) chairman Tsao Chin-pin (曹進平) yesterday personally piloting one of the final two aircraft to the Air Force Academy in Kaohsiung’s Gangshan District (岡山).
The two aircraft, No. 1165 and 1166, took off at about 11am, circled Ching Chuan Kang Air Base (清泉崗基地) and made a low pass over AIDC’s Shalu plant in Taichung, where employees waved to the aircraft.
They landed at 11:36am, marking the completion of a nine-year program to develop and mass-produce the new trainer.
Photo: CNA
Although 66 Brave Eagles have been produced, the air force currently has 65 after one crashed into waters off Taitung County in February last year.
The pilot ejected safely from the aircraft.
The Brave Eagle is designed to replace the decommissioned F-5E/F and AT-3 aircraft, enabling the air force to adopt a “three-stage, two-aircraft” pilot training system that also involves the T-34 trainer aircraft.
The Brave Eagle serves advanced and operational flight-training roles, allowing pilots to transition more efficiently to frontline fighters such as the F-16V Block 20 and Block 70 aircraft.
The advanced jet trainer program was launched in 2017 through contracts involving the air force, government-funded weapons developer National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) and the AIDC.
AIDC was the prime contractor, overseeing aircraft design, component production, assembly and testing, while more than 200 domestic suppliers participated in the program.
Derived from Taiwan’s Indigenous Defense Fighter (IDF), the Brave Eagle has more than 80 percent of its components redesigned from those of the IDF, with changes to its aerodynamics, exterior and fuselage. Its domestic content reached 55 percent.
The first prototype was unveiled on Sept. 24, 2019, and named Brave Eagle by then-president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文).
AIDC completed the aircraft’s design and conducted its first flight within three years and two months, the company said.
Mass production began in 2021, but was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, international conflicts and geopolitical tensions that disrupted global supply chains.
AIDC said it overcame shortages of imported systems and key components by developing some of them domestically in cooperation with government research institutes and local manufacturers.
Despite those disruptions, AIDC delivered 14 Brave Eagles each last year and this year, it said.
Completing the program has also strengthened its experience and capabilities in aircraft development, systems integration, mass production and supply chain management, which would support future military aircraft maintenance, upgrades and logistics programs, AIDC said.
With the Brave Eagle production completed and plans for a next-generation primary trainer or fighter jet still undetermined, experts warned of a potential talent drain in the domestic aerospace industry.
Chi Li-ping (齊立平), former head of the institute’s Aeronautical Systems Research Division, urged the government not to repeat the mistake it made after the IDF program in the 1990s, when a halt in development led to a decades-long technology and talent gap.
Maintaining an indigenous aircraft platform is the lifeblood of national defense autonomy, Chi said, adding that while Taiwan could integrate its domestically developed missiles onto the IDF, the US would never open the interfaces of purchased F-16s or MQ-9B drones to accommodate Taiwanese weapons.
Institute for National Defense and Security Research research fellow Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌) suggested that pivoting to develop advanced combat drones could be a viable path to sustain the local industry’s manufacturing capabilities, although it would require significant financial and personnel investments.

Retail, food, beverage sales hit record highs for August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

Retail and food and beverage sales last month hit record levels for August, rising annually for the seventh consecutive month, although growth moderated from the previous month, data released on Wednesday by the Ministry of Economic Affairs showed.
Retail sales increased 6.5 percent from a year earlier to NT$416.8 billion (US$13.12 billion), as holiday purchases, new department store openings and sales of new mobile phones bolstered consumer spending, the ministry said.
Last month’s growth slowed from the previous month’s 7.8 percent, but was within the ministry’s 5 to 8 percent growth forecast.
Photo: CNA
Sales of cars, motorcycles, auto parts and accessories increased 5.8 percent, while purchases at convenience stores, big-box stores, department stores, e-commerce and mail-order platforms, and computer and home appliance stores grew from 8.4 percent to 10.9 percent from a year earlier, the ministry said.
Even with purchases of cars, motorcycles, auto parts and accessories excluded, retail sales still grew 6.6 percent annually last month — slightly higher than overall sales growth, indicating that consumer demand remained strong, it said.
In the first eight months of this year, retail sales rose 4.9 percent to NT$3.298 trillion, a record for the period, ministry data showed.
Food and beverage sales rose 1.8 percent to NT$95 billion last month, meeting the ministry’s 1 to 4 percent annual growth projection, but was lower than the previous month’s 2.5 percent increase, the report said.
In this sector, restaurants and beverage shops posted sales growth of 0.3 percent and 7.4 percent respectively, while sales of catering and group meal services providers increased 11 percent, it said.
From January to last month, food and beverage sales rose 3.7 percent to NT$737.2 billion, also a record for the period, ministry data showed.
However, firms expressed reservation regarding their business outlook this month, as consumer spending typically slows after the summer holidays.
The ministry’s diffusion index — a gauge of companies’ sales expectations for the following month — declined to 49.8 for the retail sector and 33.7 for the food and beverage sector, both of which were below the neutral threshold of 50.
As a result, retail sales this month are expected to grow 3.6 to 6.6 percent year-on-year to NT$410.4 billion to NT$422.3 billion, and food and beverage sales are projected to increase 3 to 6 percent to between NT$85.4 billion and NT$87.9 billion, the ministry said.

OpenAI agent hacked government health site: Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:26 UTC
01:38:26 KST

An OpenAI agent breached an Australian government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, Australia said yesterday, in what could be the first known instance of an artificial intelligence (AI) agent hacking a government Web site.
The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the US, coming on top of several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents that have alarmed governments and companies.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he was extremely concerned about the June 18 incident in which the OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the medical statistics portal of Medicare, Australia’s universal health insurance program, while conducting research on public medical spending.
Photo: EPA
The portal hosted aggregate data about health spending and drug subsidies and is popular with researchers and academics.
No personal information had been accessed, the government said.
Albanese made the breach public following a telephone conversation with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. Both are in New York to address the UN General Assembly.
Altman was among heads of major AI firms who in speeches on Wednesday pleaded with the UN to save the world or at least its people by somehow regulating the fast-expanding technology that they have been designing.
“Today I spoke with ... Altman to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” Albanese told reporters. “I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.”
OpenAI notified Australia of the breach in an e-mail to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, he said.
OpenAI in a statement said it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.”
An inquiry looking into the security breach would examine whether OpenAI could be criminally charged, Albanese said, adding that three other government health-related Web site might have been affected.
The inquiry would also investigate how Australian security agencies failed to detect the breach before OpenAI revealed it.
Albanese said he assumed there were commercial reasons for the AI investigation of how much was being spent on particular medicines and where expenditures were changing.
In a statement, OpenAI said its “review found no evidence of patient records being accessed.”
It added that it “identified activity involving several Australian government Web sites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend.”
The breach adds to tensions between Australia and the largest US-owned technology companies. Canberra has already drawn criticism from social media firms and Washington after introducing a world-first ban on social media for children younger than 16 and new rules that force tech firms to let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
Australia considered the breach serious.
“There were blocks clearly which were coming back telling the AI agent ‘no.’ The AI agent found a way around those blocks — didn’t accept no for an answer,” Albanese told reporters.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the incident was the first time that an AI agent was known to have gained unauthorized access to the Australian government’s information technology systems.
“This is a warning about the technology being developed without safeguards and without guardrails in place,” Marles said.
OpenAI was engaging with the government, but the situation was “fundamentally unacceptable,” he said.
When the agent was denied information, it engaged in “misaligned behavior” to gain unauthorized access, he said.
Marles used an analogy of the information sitting behind a fence.
“It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence ... and the point is it was unintended. It wasn’t asked to. That’s our concern here,” Marles said.

Rubio later told reporters that Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments — both countries are major exporters — and on each country’s energy sectors, which have been targeted in escalating drone and missile attacks.
Reaching even a partial deal would be difficult but worthwhile, Rubio said, adding that Zelenskiy had publicly endorsed such a plan and the US would be willing to help make it happen.
Russia’s foreign ministry made no mention of a partial deal on grain shipments in a statement after the Lavrov-Rubio meeting. The statement reiterated that the root causes of what it calls its “special military operation” must be addressed.
At the Security Council, Lavrov said Russia would not “pause” its military action, claiming Europe would use it to “pump” Ukraine with weapons.
He also made no mention of any kind of grain and energy deal, called Ukraine’s government “terrorists” and said Moscow’s military operation aims to ensure Russia’s security and the rights of Russian speakers.
Zelenskiy cast doubt on Russia’s interest in ending the fighting.
“Something always seems to stop Putin from saying: ‘That’s it. Enough. Peace,’” Zelenskiy said. “Can you even imagine him without war? He is ‘patient zero,’ the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further.”
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.
Zelenskiy also said in his speech that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
“Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” he said. “These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself, and he was shocked that fate did not let him die.”
Zelenskiy did not provide more details about the return. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia’s Kursk region in January last year. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be apprehended alive since the country joined the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
South Korean Representative Yu Yong-weon yesterday told reporters that the two North Koreans had left Ukraine last weekend, transited through a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days ago, Yonhap News Agency reported.
“While their exact location is unknown, I believe our intelligence agencies are protecting them,” Yu was quoted as saying.
Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian delivered his speech at the General Assembly, displaying images of the late Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict.
He said his country had been the “victims of terrorism” by the US.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
Turning toward the US, Pezeshkian added: “Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee.”
Pezeshkian addressed world leaders a day after US President Donald Trump used the same stage to suggest that he might “annihilate” the Islamic republic if an agreement was not reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.

Pentagon probes how China got parts for F-35s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:21 UTC
01:38:21 KST

The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the US’ most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet on Wednesday reporting that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the US Department of Defense are aware of “a shipment issue” with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Photo: AP
UPS was shipping a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door from an Australian military F-35 that was being sent to the US for inspection and possible repair or disposal in late May, said people briefed on the incident, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.
Both parts, supplied by Lockheed Martin Corp, were coated with radar-absorbing material that enhances their stealth capabilities, two of the people said.
The plane stopped in South Korea en route to the US and from there it was routed to Hong Kong, one of the people said.
It is not clear why the plane stopped in South Korea or why it was diverted to Hong Kong, or whether the parts were intentionally diverted or by mistake.
The Chinese government later took possession of the parts, and has not returned them, two of the people said.
Australian Minister for Defence Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred,” he said.
A Chinese embassy spokesman declined immediate comment, while the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday said it was “not aware of the situation.”
Disclosure of the incident comes at a politically sensitive time for the two countries. Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) arrived in the US on Wednesday evening for a state visit hosted by US President Donald Trump.
At least two congressional committees are investigating how the parts fell into Chinese hands.
China’s possession of the parts, the stop in South Korea and the fact that UPS was used to transport them had not been previously reported. Politico reported earlier that the parts had been unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
“The juxtaposition is hard to miss,” US Senator Elissa Slotkin said on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power. “The Chinese are holding some of our most sensitive technology and we are rolling out the red carpet for their president.”
Slotkin said she had not received a briefing on the issue.
“When it comes to intelligence and military issues, China is a competitor and an adversary. They are always seeking information about our military equipment, sensitive information,” she said.
China has for years targeted the F-35 in its espionage efforts. Concerns that China could learn valuable intelligence about the jet were one reason why a US bid to sell F-35s to the United Arab Emirates, announced in Trump’s first term, later collapsed.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” said Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington-based think tank.
Bowman in November last year said that US military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35’s technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service.
The plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat, Bowman said.
The Pentagon said it was working to retrieve the parts.
Officials “are aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 components. We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” it said in a statement.
A Lockheed Martin spokesperson in Australia yesterday said in a statement that “the components in question are unserviceable and deemed low risk for exploitation.”
“It’s always best when your adversaries have to guess at your capabilities,” said J.J. Gertler, a former aviation analyst for Congressional Research Service who is now director of The Defense Concepts Organization. “You never want to hand them evidence.”
UPS disclosed the incident to the US Department of State’s Directorate of Defense Trade Controls, which enforces export control laws, out of an abundance of caution. Company spokesman Malcolm Berkley declined to comment.
During a closed US Senate Committee on Armed Services F-35 hearing on June 23, defense department program office officials expressed their hope the components would be returned, people familiar with the exchange said.
The diversion is being reviewed by two House congressional panels — House Foreign Affairs and Armed Services committees.
House Armed Services Committee spokeswoman Heather Vaughan said the “committee is aware of this issue and we’ve received multiple briefings on it.”
The Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Airland also “is aware of the reports and is currently looking into the matter,” spokesman Dave Vasquez said.

Trump invites Putin to Miami G20: Why that matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:32:56 UTC
01:32:56 KST

Trump invites Putin to Miami G20: Why that matters
US Secretary of State Rubio said the summit would be an ‘opportunity’ for Putin to engage with other world leaders.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced that Washington has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 meeting in Miami amid efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
Following a meeting with Russian Foreign Secretary Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Rubio said the US remained open to speaking with Moscow about Ukraine.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3The view from Russia: ‘No party can be antiwar’ in parliamentary election
- list 2 of 3Trump-Xi summit: Here’s what’s on the agenda, and why it matters
- list 3 of 3China vs US: Who is winning the AI race, in four charts
“We’ve just invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” Rubio said.
Trump and Putin last met, face to face, in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025, but failed to reach any agreement over Ukraine. Putin has not visited the contiguous United States since he invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Here’s what we know.
What is the G20?
The G20, or Group of 20, is a forum bringing together the world’s major and emerging economies. A summit is held annually – this year in Miami, Florida, in the US.
Those countries or groups of countries are:
- Argentina
- Australia
- Brazil
- Canada
- China
- France
- Germany
- India
- Indonesia
- Italy
- Japan
- Mexico
- Russia
- Saudi Arabia
- South Africa
- South Korea
- Turkiye
- United Kingdom
- United States
- African Union
- European Union
While many G20 countries, such as Germany, France, and the UK, are allied with Ukraine, others have closer ties with Russia – including China and India.
If he accepts the invitation, it would be Putin’s first in-person attendance at a G20 summit since 2019.
In 2021, the Russian leader attended the G20 summit virtually and spoke by video feed, but in 2023, when the summit was held in India, Putin sent Lavrov in his place.
What has Russia said?
On Thursday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said no decision had been taken about Putin’s attendance at the December summit.
When asked what the two leaders might discuss, Peskov told reporters, “It is premature to speak about this right now.”
“No decision has been made yet. We certainly appreciate this kind invitation, we value it, and it will be reviewed and coordinated, after which an appropriate decision will be reached.”
The spokesperson reiterated that Russia is seeking a peace settlement, not a temporary ceasefire.
How are US-Russian relations?
While the US maintains contact with Moscow for dialogue over the war in Ukraine, relations between the countries are strained.
Last week, Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 into law, which grants the president sweeping powers to sanction buyers of Russian energy, in a bid to pressure Moscow to end the war.
The legislation, named after the late hawkish Republican lawmaker, also sanctions President Vladimir Putin, senior officials and oligarchs, along with Russian banks and financial institutions.
However, this week, Trump appeared to contradict this approach when he called on Ukraine to agree to an “energy truce” with Russia whereby both sides stop launching strikes on each other’s energy facilities and infrastructure. In comments to reporters at the UN headquarters, Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt strikes on Russian energy facilities if Moscow stopped targeting Ukraine’s energy systems, as well.
Trump has blamed the Ukraine-Russia war for the current record rise in diesel prices in the United States, which has become a major issue as the country approaches midterm elections in November, adding that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian diesel facilities were “hurting the world”.
But observers said Trump is placing pressure on the wrong actor in the war.
“It is Russia’s – not Ukraine’s – responsibility to end the attacks,” Marnie Howlett, an associate professor of international relations in Eastern Europe and Eurasia at the University of Oxford, told Al Jazeera. “The Russian Federation has repeatedly broken ceasefire agreements, so the war will continue until it agrees to recognise Ukraine’s territorial sovereignty.”
“The ongoing sales of Russian fossil fuels continue to finance Russia’s war against Ukraine,” Amanda Paul, senior policy analyst at the European Policy Centre (EPC), said.
“Rather than putting the emphasis on the impact of Ukrainian strikes on fuel prices, Trump should be putting greater pressure on Russia to end its attacks and bring the war to an end,” she said. “Trump himself is responsible for stoking high energy prices, due to the repercussions of the US-Israel war on Iran and the subsequent blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Was the G20 invitation for Putin expected this year?
Last month, US media reported that the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), John Ratcliffe, travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks.
According to CBS News, news of his trip came only after an Air Force Boeing C-17 Globemaster III transport plane was spotted flying into a Moscow airport.
While the CIA did not comment on his trip, Peskov told reporters in Moscow that Ratcliffe had spoken to Russian intelligence officials, but did not meet Putin. Then, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS that Washington had told Ukraine that a US delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to pause its attacks until the delegation left.
On Wednesday, citing two sources familiar with the matter, the Reuters news agency reported that Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev would go to the US to meet special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
According to one source, the visit aims to keep Russia-US dialogue and peacekeeping efforts going. Economic cooperation, energy issues and a peace settlement in Ukraine will also be on the agenda.
Will Putin’s visit trigger the International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant for his arrest?
No.
In March 2023, the ICC issued a warrant for Putin’s arrest for the alleged war crime of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children to Russia.
Under the Rome Statute, the international treaty that established the ICC, signatories are obliged to carry out the warrant if a person with a warrant for their arrest enters their territory.
However, the US is not a signatory to the Rome Statute and will therefore not abide by it. Furthermore, the Trump administration is reported to be preparing sanctions against the ICC, which has also issued a warrant for the arrest of Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on suspicion of war crimes in Gaza. The US has previously also placed sanctions on ICC officials.
The new US sanctions would prohibit most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday. If imposed, the measures would bar US citizens and companies from providing the ICC with money, goods or services without a licence from the US Department of the Treasury. Banks and other companies often take an especially cautious approach to US sanctions because they rely on access to the US financial system.
On Thursday, Trump urged all countries that are members of the ICC to quit and said it was “out of control”.
“The United States is equally opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the International Criminal Court,” he told the United Nations General Assembly. “I call on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.”
How have other countries responded to Putin’s invitation to the G20?
Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s high representative for foreign affairs, criticised the invitation and said she would raise it with other members of the G20.
“We need to discuss this together with colleagues, but it’s clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalise people who are starting wars, who are going against the UN charter, who are killing and giving orders to kill civilians, to ignore the international humanitarian law, to cause as much damage and suffering to people that they can,” she added.
“By normalising this, believe me, we will have more of it around the world.”
On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, a Ukraine ally, said inviting Putin to the Miami summit could encourage Moscow to continue its attacks on Ukraine.
“If inviting Putin to the G20 could bring us closer to a just peace, I would be absolutely in favour of it,” Tusk told a news conference.
“However – and this is both my concern and what my experience tells me – at this stage, Russia might well view it as an encouragement to continue its aggressive policies. That is what I fear.”

Unknown

2026-09-24
16:31:09 UTC

Police arrested a high school principal in the Negev on suspicion of slapping and biting a student during a brawl. Following questioning, the principal was released to five days of house arrest under restrictive conditions. Police at the Ayarot station are continuing to investigate the circumstances of the incident. The case was first reported by Reshet News.
The principal was the one who called police more than a week ago to report the brawl. The investigation found that his son and nephew were also suspected of being involved in the altercation. Investigators took statements from those involved, with one student saying the principal shoved him, bit him and slapped him. The principal was questioned under caution and later released to his home.
The principal gave his account in a letter sent to fellow school principals. He said: "Several days ago, a 12th-grade student called my son at night and began making serious threats against him and me, while also hurling curses and insults at us. We did not understand the reason for his behavior. That same night, I contacted the student's parents but did not receive an adequate response. Immediately afterward, I reported the threats to Israel Police and requested a police presence at the school the following morning."
The principal continued: "The next day, despite an agreement with the parents that the student would be barred from school, he arrived at the school, ambushed my son and brutally attacked him solely because he is the principal's son. He later tried to reach my office to physically harm me, and only the quick thinking of teachers at the school prevented him from doing so. Police arrived only after the attack, and I filed a formal complaint. At the end of the school day, I was asked to come to the Ayarot police station to give a statement."
'Fingerprinting in a humiliating and degrading manner'
The principal, who is suspected of assaulting the student, said he was surprised to discover at the police station that he was being detained and questioned under caution.
"My cellphone was taken from me, and I was placed in a detention cell with other detainees," he said. "I underwent identification procedures, was photographed and had my fingerprints taken in a humiliating and degrading manner. Only during questioning did I learn that the student who attacked us had filed a baseless assault complaint against me. The investigator treated me dismissively and did not listen to my account."
The principal added: "At the end of the questioning, I was released on bail to five days of full house arrest, while the violent student remains free. The following day, when my two sons went to the police station to file a complaint, they were arrested and also placed under house arrest. After looking into the matter, I learned that someone had posted content criticizing the student on TikTok. The student demanded that I, as principal, remove the post. When that did not happen, he decided to take revenge on my children and me.
"I am now sitting at home with very difficult feelings. In dealing with the police, the Education Ministry, the Teachers' Association and the local council, I feel completely alone. We acted properly, followed the law and made all the required reports, but in the end, they turned us — the victims — into criminals. It is an upside-down world devoid of justice.
"After a quarter-century devoted to education, working day and night for the sake of our students, I have reached the painful conclusion that in today's crazy reality — with no institutional support and violence running rampant — it simply does not pay to be a school principal."

Russian budget deficit to be 2.2% of GDP next year — Finance Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:28:53 UTC
01:28:53 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The Russian federal budget deficit in 2027 will amount to 2.2% of GDP, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said at a Russian government meeting.
"Expenditures will total 48.8 trillion rubles ($574.1 bln), while revenues will stand at 43.3 trillion rubles ($509.4 bln). The budget deficit is set at around 2% of GDP for the next three years. In 2027, the budget deficit will amount to 2.2% of GDP. In conclusion, I would like to note that the prepared budget is balanced, which is important for maintaining macroeconomic stability, lowering inflation and interest rates, and driving the growth of real disposable public income, which will reach 1.4% next year," the minister said.
A smooth transition to the fiscal rule will be achieved by 2029, Siluanov noted. During the transition period in 2027-2028, the maximum expenditure limit will exceed the structural level by 1.5 trillion and 0.5 trillion rubles ($17.6 bln and $5.8 bln), respectively, the minister added.
"The budget is resilient to various scenarios. Starting next year, the base price of Urals crude oil is factored in at $50 per barrel for a three-year period. This means all obligations will be funded at this oil price level. If market conditions are more favorable, we will replenish the National Wealth Fund," Siluanov said.

U.K. prime minister teases possible return of booze to soccer matches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:27:19 UTC
01:27:19 KST

Could U.K. soccer fans get their beers back? Prime Minister Andy Burnham teases possible end of 40-year ban
London — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called the ban on alcohol in the stands at high-level men's soccer matches in the U.K. "discrimination," teasing fellow fans with a possible reversal of a more than 40-year-old ban.
"I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out," Burnham told reporters in New York on Wednesday, where he is attending the United Nations General Assembly.
He hinted at a trial to reintroduce alcohol consumption in stadium seating.
The U.K. government, under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, banned alcohol in the bleachers at men's soccer games in England and Wales in 1985.
Home Secretary Leon Brittan said at the time that booze was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behavior" in soccer stadiums.
Since then, fans attending men's soccer games in the top five divisions have not been allowed to drink alcohol in view of the pitch. People can still buy and drink alcohol in the concourse before games and during halftime, but they cannot carry it back to their seats.
No other sports are subject to such a ban in the U.K.
At some older, less well-equipped soccer grounds, lines for pints of beer can get so long during halftime that fans will leave their seats before the referee blows the whistle.
In a statement, the Football Supporters' Association said Thursday that it has "always argued that it's unfair to criminalize football fans for having a pint while watching the match," and it argued that many clubs are in favor of a reintroduction of alcohol, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated."
After a successful pilot run in the Women's Super League, the highest level of English women's soccer, fans of the women's game have been allowed to drink in the stands since the beginning of the current season.
Burnham, who's a season ticket holder at Premier League club Everton, criticized the restriction shortly before becoming prime minister.
Asked Wednesday if he still held the same view, he said: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different … And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis."
"I'm not going to back away from what's been a long-held view of mine," he said. "I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."
The ban was imposed with reason, however.
Soccer hooliganism in 1970s and 1980s England — sometimes referred to as the "English Disease" — involved fans in rival gangs linked to soccer clubs fighting each other and vandalizing areas in and around stadiums.
Several high-profile deaths linked to hooliganism, including that of a 14-year-old boy who died when fans were pushed into a wall by police after violence between Birmingham City and Leeds United fans, led to the alcohol ban.
Police have long supported the legislation.
"Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behavior from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behavior," a spokesperson for the U.K.'s Football Policing Unit said, according to CBS News' U.K. partner network the BBC.
"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games," they said, adding that it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area."
A fan-led review of U.K. laws around soccer in 2021 called for the legislation to be reviewed, however.
In Scotland, which also has a history of soccer-related violence, alcohol has been banned from soccer stadiums since 1981, but recent trials have seen it reintroduced, and fans can now buy booze at games at Hampden Park, the country's national soccer stadium.

16:26:47 UTC
01:26:47 KST

President Donald Trump and Chinese Leader Xi Jinping are meeting at the White House on Thursday for high-stakes talks focusing on trade, artificial intelligence and the Iran war — in between displays of military fanfare and a lavish banquet.
Trump said in an arrival ceremony speech that the two countries have been "working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship," and that the leaders plan to discuss "pressing issues" around security, technology and AI.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday evening that the countries have agreed to extend their temporary trade truce, which lowered U.S. tariffs and suspended Beijing's controls on exports of rare earths and critical minerals, among other stipulations. That agreement, which was set to expire in mid-November, will be extended by two months to Jan. 10, Bessent told Fox News.
"The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," Trump said in Thursday's remarks.
Xi joined in the bonhomie. "China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation," he said in his own remarks, which were translated live.
"We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses," he said.
Xi also engaged in the Chinese specialty of "panda diplomacy," announcing that two pandas will be coming to Georgia's Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
While China analysts broadly predict the leaders' personal relationship and policy goals will result in a cautious summit that yields few major deliverables, their latest face-to-face nevertheless carries real geopolitical risk.
Pomp and circumstance
That significance was on display the moment Xi arrived Wednesday evening at Maryland's Joint Base Andrews, where he was greeted on the tarmac by Trump — who met him at the airplane stairs after walking down a red carpet that U.S. service members had rolled out. The White House arrival ceremony Thursday morning included military members lining the south portico stairs holding alternating U.S. and Chinese flags, while trumpets played a fanfare.
It was Trump's first time traveling to the base to welcome a foreign leader, a source familiar confirmed to CNBC on condition of anonymity to discuss the president's plans for the summit. The last president to make the gesture was Barack Obama, who greeted then-Pope Francis on the Andrews tarmac 11 years ago this week.
Before leaving the tarmac, Xi was treated to a military flyover of two B-1 bombers while cannons fired and a U.S. Air Force band played the national anthem.
Chinese media was blanketed with images of Xi's arrival, holding up the red-carpet treatment as further proof of Beijing's vaunted global standing.
The flattery extended to social media. "I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit - Better than ever," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday morning.
AI takes focus
In another Truth post, Trump confirmed that AI will be at the top of the agenda — but asserted that neither the U.S. nor China want to change how the rapidly growing sector is handled.
"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion," Trump wrote, using the term he picked to try to rebrand AI amid a crescendo of concerns about the risks posed by the increasingly powerful technology.
"But I want to leave it exactly where it is," wrote Trump, who has bristled at calls to slow AI growth on the belief that the U.S. must beat China in the race to AI dominance.
"That is China's position also," Trump said in the post, suggesting Xi also opposes new AI regulations and apparently precluding any possibility of an agreement to strengthen safety precautions.
He added that the U.S. "guardrail" is the Department of Justice, reiterating the Trump administration's stance that sufficient regulatory safeguards are already in place.
But Xi has previously acknowledged the risks of AI and the importance of keeping it under human control.
In remarks after arriving at the White House, Xi said that the U.S. and China have "both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people."
China's Iran ties
Trump has also confirmed the Iran war will be a topic of discussion with Xi. "I'll be talking about that and many other subjects but it's all coming along, including that," he told reporters Wednesday evening after returning to the White House.
The U.S. last month launched "Operation Economic Outcast," its effort to harm Iran by targeting its financial enablers with secondary sanctions. The plan raised questions about whether the U.S. would take action against China, Tehran's top trading partner and oil buyer.
The Trump administration has said no country is exempt from potential sanctions, but it has not directly targeted Beijing.
Trump has also shied from unreservedly criticizing China over its reported Iran ties in the run-up to the Xi meeting. Asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Chinese entities supplied Tehran with satellite imagery that it used to carry out deadly attacks on U.S. troops in Jordan in July, Trump said of Beijing's surveillance activities, "They basically do what we do."
Summit schedule
On Thursday morning, Trump and first lady Melania Trump welcomed Xi and Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan at the White House for an arrival ceremony. It is Xi's first visit to Washington since September 2015, coming to the capital city right after the pope.
The leaders then headed to the Rose Garden for a military review, after which Trump and Xi will hold a bilateral meeting, while Melania Trump and Madame Peng branch off for a separate event.
In the evening, Trump and the first lady will host the Chinese delegation for a state dinner in the White House's East Room, with both countries' leaders expected to give remarks at the top of the event.
A slew of U.S. business executives are slated to join the dinner. Reuters had reported that Xi was expected to bring along his own crew of CEOs, but that entourage did not materialize. The South China Morning Post reported Thursday morning that a small group of Chinese CEOs flew to the U.S. separately from Xi, even though they have not yet found out if they will be able to join the events.
On Friday, the presidents and first ladies will hold a private tea at the White House, then take a tour of the National Archives before Xi's departure.
"President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told CNBC in a statement.
This is developing news. Please check back for updates.
— CNBC's Eunice Yoon contributed reporting.

Xi says ready to work with Trump to steer China-U.S. ties on steady course

U.S. President Donald Trump holds a welcome ceremony for Chinese President Xi Jinping, who is on a state visit to the United States, at the White House in Washington, D.C., the United States, Sept. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Ye)
WASHINGTON, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Thursday that he is ready to work with U.S. President Donald Trump to steer the giant ship of China-U.S. relationship on a steady course toward the future.
Addressing an arrival ceremony at the White House, Xi said that he is visiting the United States at Trump's invitation to carry on their friendship, expand cooperation and promote the well-being of the two peoples.
China and the United States should strengthen communication, cooperate with sincerity and coexist in peace, he noted.
Xi said he and Trump encourage government departments, such as those in charge of foreign affairs, economic matters, financial cooperation, law enforcement and people-to-people exchanges, to catch up on strengthening contact.
China-U.S. cooperation may not solve every problem in the world, but without it, it would be hard to solve many of the world's problems, Xi said.
China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business in China, Xi said. "We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States. Working together, we can lengthen the list of cooperation and shorten the list of issues."
Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence (AI), Xi said, noting that the two countries have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people.
On counternarcotics and law enforcement, the Chinese side is willing to strengthen cooperation with the United States, Xi said. "Our two sides may also increase direct flights to facilitate two-way travel and trade."
China and the United States do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but the competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds, he said, adding that it should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses.
China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation, Xi said. "We can certainly find the right path for our two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home."
Chinese and U.S. militaries should maintain regular dialogue and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention, Xi said, adding that the Thucydides Trap can be overcome.
Xi announced an invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study in the coming five years. He also declared that in a few days, a pair of pandas will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people. ■

Rwandan coffee generated 148.6 mln USD in 2025/2026 financial year: official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
00:26:28 CST
01:26:28 KST

KIGALI, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Rwanda's coffee generated a record 148.6 million U.S. dollars in the 2025/2026 financial year, a senior official said Thursday.
Rwandan Minister of Gender and Family Promotion Consolee Uwimana made the remarks while opening a global coffee conference in Kigali, the Rwandan capital city.
The conference, due to close on Friday, brought together women coffee producers, buyers, roasters, policymakers, researchers, investors, and industry partners to connect, exchange ideas, and build meaningful partnerships and solutions.
The global coffee conference was convened by Sustainable Growers Rwanda, an organization focused on unlocking the potential of women smallholder coffee farmers in East Africa.
The minister said the revenues generated from coffee demonstrate the strength and potential of the country's coffee sector in economic development.
"But this growth must be reflected in the pockets of our women. Women may produce coffee and create its value, yet remain excluded from the decisions, capital and market that determine who will receive it. Participation is not ownership, and producing value is not the same as having a stake in it," Uwimana said.
More than 250 participants from Africa, Europe, Asia, North America and Latin America convened to learn from the farmers behind the coffee before discussing the future of the industry, according to organizers.
It provided a platform to explore new opportunities, share knowledge, and advance a more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable future for coffee. ■

China beats Maldives in football friendly

Unknown Publisher

01:26:20 KST

CHONGQING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China beat the Maldives 3-0 in the opening match of the CFA Team China International Football Competitions Chongqing on Thursday, with Wang Ziming scoring a second-half hat-trick.
Neither side found the net in the first half, as China struggled to find its rhythm, managing nine shots with only two on target.
China made nine changes after the break and quickly found the breakthrough. In the 50th minute, substitute Wang Shangyuan threaded a through ball to Wang Ziming, who raced clear and fired a low shot into the net.
Six minutes later, substitute Chen Pu delivered a cross for Wang Ziming to head home for his second.
Wang completed his hat-trick on the hour mark, applying a deft finish near the six-yard box after Wang Gengrui's cross from the flank.
Many players made their senior national team debut, while high school student Zhao Songyuan became the youngest player ever to represent China's men's national team.
Head coach Shao Jiayi is expected to use the four matches to experiment his squad and assess new players ahead of the 2027 AFC Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia.
At the post-match press conference, Shao said that the team had carried out its pre-match plans well in terms of achieving its objectives, adding that China had not played a competitive match for nearly three weeks, and that it would take time for the players to get back in sharp form.
In other action on Thursday, Palestine and New Zealand played out a 2-2 draw. ■

Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine Tour' after Sheeran split
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Breadcrumb
Macklemore hits back with 'Free Palestine Tour' after Sheeran split
US rapper Macklemore, who was dropped from British pop star Ed Sheeran's tour after saying 'Free Palestine', comments, announced Thursday he will instead perform on his own "Free Palestine Tour."
Macklemore, who was opening for Sheeran's "Loop Tour," shouted "Free Palestine!" and told Palestinians they were "not forgotten" during two concerts earlier this month in New Jersey.
The "Thrift Shop" star was quickly booted from the US tour -- a decision that Sheeran said was made by tour promoters, not him -- provoking outrage among musicians and pro-Palestinian activists.
"What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," Macklemore, 43, said in an Instagram post.
"When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention," he added.
Macklemore announced three shows in London, Paris and Dublin for late October, with US dates also planned, and said all proceeds will benefit pro-Palestinian organisations.
"It's 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn't work anymore," he said.
"People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it."
Macklemore's removal has opened a can of worms for the Grammy-winning Sheeran, who says he steers clear of making "political" statements, despite performing at a benefit concert in support of Ukraine after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Last weekend at a show in Philadelphia, he opened the performance with a statement on the controversy, calling the 7 October attacks on Israel "horrific" and describing the situation in Gaza as "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate". Sheeran also described the situation in Palestine as the "most complex political issue on the planet", drawing further criticism from pro-Palestine activists.
"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry," an emotional Sheeran told his audience, who responded with cheers. At the end of the show, Sheeran tearfully said "the one thing I would like to apologise for is the first bit of the show where it wasn't about music and I had to talk."
Four other supporting artists, including American singer Finneas, have also pulled out of Sheeran's tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.

Copper boom to boost Russia's export revenue, to attract investments — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:26:04 UTC
01:26:04 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Rapid growth in global demand for copper opens up opportunities for Russia to increase its export revenue and attract investment into domestic mining and metallurgical companies and projects, Pavel Gamov, an expert on the mining and metals industry at the Stolypin Institute for Growth Economics, told TASS.
Earlier, Kirill Dmitriev, Russian Presidential Special Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), called copper the "new gold."
"For Russia, the copper boom represents a direct boost to export revenues and the investment appeal of Nornickel, UMMC, RMK, Udokan, and the Baimsky GOK," Gamov said.
According to him, the growing need for the metal is linked to developments in the energy sector and artificial intelligence technologies, while options to expand production are limited.
"Demand is being driven by electrification, power grids, renewable energy sources, and AI data centers, whereas supply is constrained: it takes 12-15 years to build a new mine, and mature deposits are becoming depleted," the expert explained.
The expert noted that Russia supplies about 4% of the world's refined copper - roughly 1 million tons annually, with exports accounting for approximately 600,000 tons.
"By 2040, global demand for copper could rise by approximately 50%, while the deficit could reach 10 million tons per year," Gamov noted.
At the same time, the expert pointed out that high prices do not eliminate the impact of sanctions, increased logistics costs, difficulties with banking settlements, and discounts for Russian suppliers. "Rising metal prices also drive up the production costs of cables, electrical equipment, and the construction and modernization of grids within Russia," Gamov concluded.

Full text: Xi's remarks at arrival ceremony at the White House
China

WASHINGTON, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday gave remarks at the arrival ceremony at the White House in Washington, D.C., the United States.
The following is the full text of the remarks:
Honorable President Donald J. Trump and Mrs. Melania Trump,
Ladies and Gentlemen,
Dear Friends,
I'm very glad to pay a state visit to your beautiful country, the United States of America. Thank you, President Trump and Mrs. Trump, for the warm hospitality you have extended to me and my wife. On behalf of the 1.4 billion and more Chinese people, I wish to begin by extending sincere greetings to the American people and warm congratulations on the 250th anniversary of the U.S. independence.
Both China and the United States are great countries, and both the Chinese and American peoples are great peoples. I am visiting the United States at President Trump's invitation to carry on our friendship, expand cooperation, and promote the well-being of both our peoples.
Facing the changes in our world, in our times, and of historical significance today, China and the United States, as two major countries, shoulder a historic responsibility of advancing human development and progress.
Mr. President, during your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and this is widely welcomed by the people of our two countries and the international community. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of China-U.S. relationship on a steady course toward the future.
-- We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust. President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch. We encourage our government departments, such as those in charge of foreign affairs, economic matters, financial cooperation, law enforcement and people-to-people exchanges, to catch up on strengthening contact, and we support our legislative bodies in increasing exchanges.
-- We should cooperate with sincerity. The interests of China and the United States are deeply intertwined, and there is plenty of room for us to work together. China-U.S. cooperation may not solve every problem in the world. But, without our cooperation, it would be hard to solve many of the world's problems. China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business there. We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States. Working together, we can lengthen the list of cooperation, and shorten the list of issues. Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence. We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people. On counternarcotics and law enforcement, the Chinese side is willing to strengthen cooperation with the United States. Our two sides may also increase direct flights to facilitate two-way travel and trade.
-- We should coexist in peace. As I have said many times, China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses. China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for our two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention. The Thucydides Trap can be overcome.
Ladies and Gentlemen,
Dear Friends,
During the Second World War, Chinese and Americans fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression. Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people. The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in our people, and its future lies with the young. I am glad to announce an invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study in the coming five years.
The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans. Here, I have a piece of good news. In a few days, two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people.
Ladies and Gentlemen,
Dear Friends,
Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand. Let us meet the people's expectation and show our historical initiative. Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world!
Thank you. ■

Egypt seeks closer business cooperation with China: minister

Egyptian Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh attends a press conference in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 24, 2026. Egypt welcomes Chinese investment and seeks to expand business cooperation in areas including desalination, artificial intelligence and digitalization services, Egyptian Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh said at a press conference on Thursday. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
CAIRO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Egypt welcomes Chinese investment and seeks to expand business cooperation in areas including desalination, artificial intelligence and digitalization services, Egyptian Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh said at a press conference on Thursday.
Responding to a question from Xinhua, Saleh praised the performance of some Chinese companies in Egypt, citing their entry into industries such as fiberglass, which he said had not previously been represented in the country.
He said Egypt welcomes investors who comply with its laws and regulations and seeks to support them while ensuring a level playing field for all.
Saleh said the number of Chinese companies operating in Egypt had risen significantly, estimating that it had exceeded 3,000.
The minister highlighted trade missions and exhibitions as ways to expand bilateral cooperation, adding that Egypt was seeking to identify specific projects for further cooperation.
He said the government was working to address both broader challenges affecting the business environment and specific difficulties faced by individual companies.
Saleh said the government welcomed greater cooperation between the two countries' private sectors and saw its role as creating the platforms and conditions to facilitate such partnerships.
Egypt is working to facilitate such cooperation through exhibitions, trade and investment missions, and other business-to-business initiatives, he added. ■

Darden Restaurants stock falls as Olive Garden reports slower growth
