Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has outlined Türkiye’s positions on a wide range of regional and international issues, including reform of the United Nations, the Gaza crisis, tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, Black Sea security and Türkiye-US defence cooperation.
Speaking to journalists at Turkevi in New York on Wednesday, Erdogan also discussed the Terror-Free Türkiye process, relations with Iraq and Greece, the Development Road Project, climate change and Türkiye's preparations to host the COP31 climate summit in Antalya.
He said the UN system needed to become more representative, criticised the veto power of its five permanent members and called for a stronger General Assembly.
Erdogan also reiterated Türkiye's opposition to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, called for a return to negotiations between Iran and the US, and said Ankara was stepping up diplomatic efforts to revive the Black Sea grain corridor.
He said Türkiye expected the US to take concrete steps towards its return to the F-35 programme, while stressing that Ankara would continue developing its domestic defence capabilities, including the KAAN fighter jet.
Below is the full Q&A:
QUESTION: You published an article in Bloomberg in which you wrote that the United Nations needs reform and that this reform can no longer be postponed. This is not the first time you have said this, but in that article you also stressed that Türkiye is ready to play its part in reforming the United Nations.
As I understand it, you emphasised the idea of a regional United Nations, in which different regions have different problems and therefore require solutions tailored to their circumstances. What kind of UN do you envision, Mr President? What kind of UN would you like to see?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
First and foremost, we are talking about a United Nations in which the will of more than 190 countries is constrained by the veto power of five countries.
It is impossible for this unjust structure to maintain global stability and peace, remain faithful to the fundamental principles it upholds, and fulfil its promise to humanity.
The issue is not simply about Türkiye having a greater say. It is about Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Muslim world, Europe and all other regions being fairly represented in this global system through their own experiences and their own will.
That is why we say the veto mechanism should be abolished. We should move away from a United Nations model that protects only five members and towards a mechanism that embraces all members.
We should strengthen the General Assembly and make it more powerful and effective.
The new structure should be fairer, with elected members serving for defined periods and those seeking re-election having to regain the confidence of the international community.
The world's problems should be addressed and decisions made not by five members, but by all members.
Because the world no longer needs new walls; it needs new bridges.
QUESTION: You have delivered your 16th speech to the UN General Assembly. From your first speech until today, you have also been a voice for the oppressed and for the pursuit of a fairer world.
In your latest speech, you said, “As long as I live, I will continue to speak about these truths from this podium.”
Looking at the long journey from your first speech to today's address, and at where the world has reached today, how would you assess that journey?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
This journey has been one of standing firm.
When we first took to the podium of the UN General Assembly, whatever we said and wherever we stood, we remain, thankfully, in the same place today.
What has happened in Syria, Iraq, the Russia-Ukraine war, Africa, Myanmar and, most recently, Gaza has repeatedly demonstrated the truth of what I have been saying.
The foundations of the Russia-Ukraine war were laid in those years. Many issues in our region grew because of wrong steps taken at the time; sparks effectively turned into fires.
If the world had listened to what we were saying at the time and taken measures, so many lives would not have been lost.
If UN reform had been carried out in those years, preventing the conflicts and wars we see in our region and around the world today would not have been beyond our reach.
The fact that Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas was unable to attend the United Nations for two consecutive years is, in itself, an indication of how deeply injustice has become entrenched in the international system.
Our issue is not being against any country. Our issue is being against injustice.
We are happy that, from those days to today, we have always stood on the right side of history and have not taken a single step that would bring shame upon our nation.
Today, the world is moving towards the position we expressed from the very beginning.
QUESTION: Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is declining sharply. The steep fall in the number of vessels passing through the region shows that the crisis is no longer just an issue concerning Iran, but has become a global energy and trade issue.
Does Türkiye have a concrete plan to bring the US and Iran towards a ceasefire? What are you proposing to the parties?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz shows that this is no longer simply an issue between Iran and the United States.
We have made our position on this matter very clear. We oppose the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to maritime traffic. Freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz must be protected.
Every tension in the Strait of Hormuz affects not only the countries of the region, but also Europe, Asia, energy markets, transport and the daily lives of millions of people.
The dramatic decline in commercial shipping in recent days clearly demonstrates the scale of the issue. The Strait is vital to global energy security and international trade.
Hormuz must be opened as a key to resolving problems through dialogue and negotiations.
We are telling all our interlocutors that we need to return to the negotiating table as soon as possible.
What needs to be opened are not new fronts, but new channels of diplomacy.
QUESTION:
While the world is focused on Hormuz, the war between Russia and Ukraine has also intensified again in the Black Sea. Attacks on commercial vessels have also increased again.
As a result, grain ships are waiting at ports. Could a new security mechanism similar to the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which was established through your efforts, be created and the corridor revived?
Are you hopeful following your discussions with the parties on this issue? Did this issue come up during your meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
The issue of security in the Black Sea is extremely important both for us and for our region.
The Black Sea is not a front in this war, and it must never become one.
In our talks with the parties, we are explaining in detail the need to restore the safety of navigation.
This would have two benefits: ensuring food security and preventing the war from spreading.
We have made it clear that we do not accept attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, whoever carries them out, and that we expect the parties to act responsibly.
We have now stepped up our efforts to re-establish the grain corridor. We are also accelerating our diplomatic efforts to this end.
I raised the issue once again with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and the response I received from him was positive.
QUESTION: There are already various challenges at an early stage regarding the Mecca Defence Alliance. There is particularly some pressure on Saudi Arabia.
What would you like to say about the future of the alliance?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
The Mecca Defence Agreement is a strong step in the right direction.
If you undertake such an important initiative in such a challenging region, it is hardly surprising that you encounter some challenges.
If you say something new and demonstrate a new will, there will naturally be those who are uncomfortable with it.
We are not a state that was established yesterday. We are a state with enough experience not to be provoked or fall into traps.
I have no doubt that we will move forward more strongly once the institutionalisation efforts are completed.
The foundations have been laid for a platform that will produce regionally driven solutions to the region's problems.
We have all seen that those who come from outside and prescribe security solutions for our region often leave behind greater instability.
The sapling we have planted will soon grow and become a great tree.
We have confidence in our country and our nation, and we have confidence in our brothers and sisters.
QUESTION: Last year, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, there was a meeting attended by the Gulf countries, US President Donald Trump and yourself.
As an outcome of that meeting, Trump launched his Gaza plan in Sharm el Sheikh.
A similar meeting was held this year. You touched on part of this in your opening remarks, but will this second meeting produce an outcome soon, as the meeting in Sharm el Sheikh did?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
There can be no lasting peace in the Middle East without stopping the bloodshed in Gaza, making the ceasefire permanent and ensuring that Palestinians can have a dignified future in their own homeland.
The will that has emerged within the framework of the peace plan is important and valuable.
For lasting peace, tranquillity and stability in Gaza, almost everyone, including Hamas, has taken positive steps and expressed their desire for a solution.
However, Israel continues its aggression and is undermining peace.
The international community, led by the United States, must make Israel understand that it has to comply with this plan.
It is not enough simply to say, “Let the war in Gaza stop.”
We need to establish mechanisms that will prevent the war from starting again, accelerate the reconstruction of Gaza and guarantee the political future of the Palestinians.
The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza remains there even as the world looks away.
I am talking about people struggling to survive among the ruins.
And this has not been happening for one day, one week, one month or one year, but for years.
This is an issue that concerns the shared conscience of humanity.
QUESTION: We also listened to your address to the UN General Assembly. We would particularly like to congratulate you on your messages regarding Gaza, which once again attracted considerable attention.
My question is about the F-35s.
US President Trump had made a commitment regarding the F-35s. However, months have passed and we see that there has still been no progress.
Could you give us an update on the situation?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We also discussed this issue with Mr Trump at NATO.
He expressed a positive will regarding Türkiye's return to the F-35 programme.
We now expect this will to translate into concrete steps. We are continuing our contacts on this issue. I believe we will achieve a result.
My relationship with Mr Trump has also given momentum to Türkiye-US relations.
Cooperation between the two countries has made considerable progress compared with the previous administration.
I believe we will not stop here and will reach even more ambitious goals.
Of course, what is important for us is our domestic defence industry. This is extremely important to us.
We want to produce our own fighter aircraft, air defence systems and defence industry capabilities, particularly the KAAN.
Meanwhile, we also met with the British prime minister. Our efforts and work on the Eurofighter are continuing with them as well.
Türkiye has security requirements, defence needs and strategic objectives.
We will work towards our goals and, God willing, we will not take a step backwards.
QUESTION: I would like to ask for an update on the stage reached in the Terror-Free Türkiye process.
First of all, could you share the latest information with us on whether the organisation has entered the stage of laying down its arms?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
Terror-Free Türkiye is not a day-to-day issue for us.
This is about Türkiye overcoming a problem that has existed for nearly half a century.
As you know, the Turkish Grand National Assembly has established the legal framework. The relevant mechanisms have been established or are being established.
Our relevant institutions are on the ground and are carrying out the necessary monitoring.
For the framework law to be implemented, the organisation must actually lay down its arms and complete the disbandment process.
It is also clear how this will be determined and verified.
The process is moving forward step by step under the supervision of our relevant institutions.
Our parliament will also contribute to the process within the framework defined by the law, and Türkiye will, God willing, close the chapter on terrorism in unity and solidarity.
There are, of course, those who are trying to obstruct this process.
Those involved in the terrorism industry naturally do not want these chapters to be closed.
But we will not give them the opportunity they are waiting for.
As the People's Alliance and as the state, we are determined on this issue.
In short, we have received no indication of any problem.
The process is moving forward and, God willing, we will achieve the desired result before long.
QUESTION: Iraq's new Prime Minister Ali Zaidi visited Türkiye some time ago.
There have also been a number of developments between the two sides in both energy and the Development Road Project, which had been stalled for many years but is now gaining momentum.
How do you assess the positive atmosphere in relations between Ankara and Baghdad, both in terms of regional stability and perhaps stability within Türkiye?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
As you know, Prime Minister Ali Zaidi made his first visit to Ankara.
I can say that we have made a good start to the new era.
I believe we will develop relations between the two countries and achieve mutual gains.
Indeed, today we also met with Mr Ali Zaidi and his colleagues here at Turkevi.
As you know, the Iraqi government's authority will now prevail in the Sinjar region, where the PKK has been based in Iraq for a long time.
Today, we discussed with the Iraqi authorities how control of the area will be organised once it has been cleared of terrorism.
We also discussed the handover of Bashiqa.
With our neighbour Iraq, we now want to talk not about terrorism, but more about the Development Road, increasing our bilateral trade volume, stability, peace and prosperity.
The process is moving forward positively.
We have gained good momentum.
God willing, the outcome will also be positive.
QUESTION: Mr President, elections are approaching in Greece. There will be elections in May.
Once again, Türkiye is a major issue on the agenda.
You previously warned Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis against taking our bilateral disputes to other countries, but there are once again statements concerning the sale of F-35s and Türkiye's need to acquire F-35s.
Could this current course of events put the atmosphere of rapprochement and negotiations at risk?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We have no intention of getting involved in the domestic politics of Greece or any of our other neighbours.
There may be elections in Greece, governments may change and opposition parties may change; these are not our concerns.
Our concerns are Türkiye's rights and security, and preserving peace and stability in the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Let me make one thing very clear: Türkiye is not Greece's enemy. It is its neighbour and an ally under the NATO umbrella.
Relations between the two countries are too delicate and important to be turned into election material.
This is how we view these debates.
We are focused on our own agenda and are now attending to our own affairs.
QUESTION: Mr President, at the beginning of your speech you referred to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
What will Türkiye's main priorities be at COP31, which we will host in Antalya in November?
There are also demands from developing countries, particularly regarding climate finance.
What messages will you deliver on this issue?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We simply cannot ignore the problems created by climate change.
This is extremely important to us.
At COP31, we will set out our measures and road maps, as well as what we plan to do to address the adverse effects of climate change in different parts of the world.
Indeed, in my speech at the United Nations today, I addressed not only the General Assembly but also climate change in a separate speech.
I also focused on these issues there.
The world is our home, and protecting it from pollution is our responsibility.
COP31 is not merely a climate conference; it is also a platform where developing countries can make their voices heard, set out their expectations and discuss concrete outcomes.
It is the responsibility of developed countries to stand by and support countries facing financial difficulties.
Combating climate change now requires action, not just words.
Disasters know no borders. Fires, floods and droughts do not distinguish between countries.
We, too, must remove borders when it comes to solving these problems.
I believe the COP31 summit we will hold in Antalya will be an important crossroads on this long journey.
QUESTION: If you allow me, I would like to ask the final question.
One of the main issues occupying the agenda in recent days is a situation known publicly as the “fund crisis”, which directly affects 455,000 investors.
The investigation is continuing. There have been detentions and arrests.
What message would you like to give investors, and could you give us some perspective on the road map ahead?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We are talking about a problem that has emerged in a limited area of the capital markets and in a certain number of funds.
In other words, there is no risk to our financial system or the Turkish economy.
Portraying this as a problem affecting the entire market would be unfair to the Turkish stock market.
All necessary steps are being taken and will continue to be taken within the principles of the capital markets and the framework of the law.
Our relevant institutions are pursuing the matter with determination.
Our judiciary has likewise launched a comprehensive investigation, and there have been a number of detentions and arrests.
I want everyone to know this: whoever is responsible will be held accountable before the law.
There should be not the slightest doubt about this.
Regardless of the circumstances, no one has the right to engage in a race to profit from the situation at the expense of others or to cause anxiety among our people.
Of course, given the nature of the capital markets, it is important that the process be conducted both transparently and with the utmost sensitivity.
That is also our instruction.
In addition, we will ensure that whatever measures are needed, including legal and administrative regulations, are implemented to prevent a similar problem from occurring again.

(China Economic Roundtable) Xinhua Headlines: From barbecue to immersive theater, diverse consumption scenarios bring new vitality to China's consumer market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:38:32 CST
00:38:32 KST

* Across China, consumers are increasingly seeking cultural experiences, leisure activities and services alongside goods, creating new opportunities for businesses to meet more diverse demand.
* China's National Bureau of Statistics began releasing the broader indicator of combined retail sales of consumer goods and services in June to provide a more complete picture of the changing consumption market.
* For local businesses, the changing demand is prompting efforts to turn temporary popularity into sustained consumption through improved services and more diverse experiences.
BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- At a barbecue restaurant in Badaju Market in Zibo, east China's Shandong Province, the dining experience now extends beyond sizzling skewers and local delicacies to performances that introduce visitors to the city's history and culture.
"If visitors come just for the food, their visit is too short for them to get to know Zibo better," said Zheng Feng, who runs the restaurant.
The approach is part of a broader transformation at Badaju, a traditional neighborhood market that became an internet sensation in 2023. Since then, it has expanded its offerings to include cultural performances, handicrafts and creative products.
Over the past three years, the market has received more than 18 million visits annually on average, with over 430 merchants offering more than 100 business formats.
Across China, consumers are increasingly seeking cultural experiences, leisure activities and services alongside goods, creating new opportunities for businesses to meet more diverse demand.
In the first eight months of 2026, China's combined retail sales of consumer goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year, with retail sales of services increasing 4.9 percent, compared with 1 percent growth in retail sales of goods, official data showed.
As incomes rise, service consumption is growing faster than goods consumption, a trend consistent with broader economic development, said Lin Jian, vice president of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce, on China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency.
Lin noted that per capita spending on services accounted for 46.1 percent of China's total per capita consumption expenditure in 2025, up 3.5 percentage points from 2020, and expected the share to surpass 50 percent during the 2026-2030 period.
China's National Bureau of Statistics began releasing the broader indicator of combined retail sales of consumer goods and services in June to provide a more complete picture of the changing consumption market.
For local businesses, the changing demand is prompting efforts to turn temporary popularity into sustained consumption through improved services and more diverse experiences.
Zhang Weihua, deputy head of Shandong's provincial culture and tourism department, said Badaju's continued appeal lies in its combination of consumer trust, local culture and interactive experiences.
The market has introduced clearer pricing, consumer complaint services and infrastructure improvements, while incorporating local cultural traditions into commercial activities and retaining its functions as a neighborhood market.
A similar change is taking shape in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, where small theaters and immersive performances are creating new spaces for cultural consumption.
At the city's Houhu Ximatou theater, an immersive street play titled "Changsha" takes audiences back to the 1990s, telling a story of friendship and entrepreneurship through scenes from the city's past.
Actors interact directly with audiences in recreated neighborhood settings, with some spectators even offering tissues to performers during emotional scenes, said Jin Xingzhou, an actor in the production.
Changsha had established 111 new performing arts venues by the end of June this year, with performances at these venues totaling 14,000 in the first six months and attracting 3.63 million audience visits, according to local cultural authorities.
Zhang Dandan, head of the Changsha New Consumption Research Institute, attributed the emergence of new consumption formats to changing consumer needs, which are driving innovation in products, services and business models.
At the national level, China's consumption expansion plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) calls for expanding service consumption, upgrading goods consumption, developing new consumption scenarios and improving the consumption environment.
The plan aims to boost China's total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan (about 8.89 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030. It also calls for expanding high-quality cultural and tourism offerings, improving the supply of performing arts products, and supporting the development of immersive and interactive venues for consumers.
Efforts similar to Zibo and Changsha are taking shape across China, with 50 cities participating in a national pilot program to develop new consumption formats, models and scenarios.
These cities have a combined resident population of over 480 million and account for more than half of China's total retail sales of consumer goods, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
As of early July, the pilot cities had collected proposals for more than 6,000 projects, with the potential to attract over 300 billion yuan in investment, the ministry said.
Lin said cities should develop distinctive consumption offerings based on their own cultural, ecological and industrial resources, supported by better services, consumption facilities and the business environment.
"Events attract consumers, supply turns interest into spending, and a supportive environment sustains long-term appeal," said Lin.
(Video reporters: Yang Shiyan and Zhao Jiale; Video editors: Yang Zeyi, Roger Lott, Zhao Xiaoqing and Hong Yan) ■

Feature: Japanese teenage swimmer Ohashi breaks world record at Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:38:27 CST
00:38:27 KST

By sportswriters Gao Meng, Qian Zheng
TOKYO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Shin Ohashi may spend his spare time on his phone, enjoy junk food and, according to his coach, resemble an ordinary Japanese high school student.
In the pool, the 17-year-old is anything but ordinary.
Ohashi broke the men's 200-meter breaststroke world record at the 2026 Asian Games on Thursday, clocking 2 minutes, 4.83 seconds to become the first swimmer to set a world record at the Games.
"I was able to put into the race what I had been training for, so I think it was a perfect race," Ohashi said.
The performance has attracted the attention of some of swimming's biggest names, including France's Leon Marchand.
"I'm scared. I'm very scared of him," Marchand said with a laugh. "He's still so young. His coach is really good. I think his entourage, the people around him, are really good, so I hope he's going to keep improving."
"His breaststroke is amazing, and I'm very excited, also stressed about it, to race him," the Frenchman added.
Ohashi's rise has been rapid. At the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in August, he clocked 2:08.27 in the 200m breaststroke. Just over a month later, he had lowered that mark by more than three seconds.
His preparation for the Asian Games was far from ideal. Ohashi developed a fever in the days before the competition and subsequently tested positive for COVID-19.
According to his coach Shin Ota, there was no wholesale rebuilding of Ohashi's training program between the Pan Pacific Championships and the Asian Games. Instead, the biggest change came in the teenager's approach to training.
Ohashi had previously been reluctant to undertake some breaststroke training but became more disciplined in his preparation, continuing to complete the assigned work even when his training times were unimpressive.
The plan for Thursday's final had been to control his pace over the first half before maintaining his speed down the stretch. Instead, Ohashi attacked from the start.
"Once I saw that his technique hadn't broken down, I knew his time would be very good," Ota said.
At 1.69 meters tall, Ohashi is relatively small by the standards of elite male swimmers. Ota said his build led the coaching team to identify a high stroke rate as one of the qualities that could become a major strength.
But Ota believes Ohashi's greatest asset lies elsewhere.
"He may look carefree, as if he doesn't think about much, but he really loves swimming, and he really likes to study it," Ota said.
Ohashi regularly analyzes his own swimming, makes adjustments and experiments with different ways of moving through the water. Ota said the teenager often works out technical changes for himself rather than relying on constant instruction from his coach.
Away from the pool, however, the newly crowned world-record holder remains recognizably 17.
Ota said Ohashi enjoys spending time on his phone and eating junk food, adding that "overall, I think he's just an ordinary high school student you could find anywhere."
Ohashi's ambitions are considerably less ordinary.
His immediate goal is gold at next year's World Championships, followed by the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Asked which swimmer he hopes one day to emulate, Ohashi named Kosuke Kitajima, Japan's four-time Olympic breaststroke champion.
Ota said Kitajima's ability to deliver victories under the weight of expectation was particularly difficult to replicate, and that Ohashi still needs experience and greater mental strength before reaching that level.
For now, Ohashi sees little conflict between the sacrifices required to become an elite swimmer and experiencing life as a teenager.
"Swimming really is my life," he said. "Because of swimming, there may have been times when I couldn't go out and play. But it is also because of swimming that I have been able to get to where I am today. So I don't look at those things so negatively." ■

Unique pyramid-shaped Roman-era tomb discovered in SW Egypt
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:37:56 CST
00:37:56 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- An Egyptian archaeological mission discovered a unique pyramid-shaped tomb dating to the Roman period (30 BC-395 AD) in the southwestern province of New Valley, the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said Thursday.
In a statement, the ministry said the tomb, discovered at the Bir al-Shaghala archaeological site in Dakhla Oasis, was built of mudbrick and used to bury a man and his wife.
The tomb features distinctive architecture and rare funerary inscriptions that shed light on the oasis' burial practices and religious and cultural life during the Roman period, the statement said.
Among the finds were a stone funerary stele bearing a 19-line Greek-language lament, an offering table, a sandstone purification basin, pottery vessels and a bronze coin depicting Roman Emperor Constantine.
The tomb is accessed by a 14-step staircase leading to a sandstone entrance decorated with recessed hieroglyphic inscriptions and funerary spells. Its lintel bears a rare scene depicting the seventh hour of the "Amduat," a major ancient Egyptian funerary text that serves as a twelve-hour map of the underworld recounting the sun god Ra's nightly journey.
The entrance leads to a mudbrick vaulted hall and two burial chambers beneath the pyramid-shaped superstructure.
The funerary stele commemorates a man who may have served as a judge, according to the statement. ■

China Focus: Tech giant Tencent launches payment app for inbound visitors as "China Travel" surges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:37:54 CST
00:37:54 KST

SHENZHEN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's tech giant Tencent on Thursday launched TenPayGo, a payment app for overseas users traveling to China. This new platform is designed to make payments more convenient for inbound visitors as the country sees a growing number of international travelers.
The app supports bank cards issued overseas by seven major international card organizations including Visa and Mastercard, as well as Apple Pay and overseas e-wallets such as Starryblu, Tencent said.
After linking a payment method, users can scan and pay directly through TenPayGo, according to Tencent. The company unveiled the app at an international payment services launch event in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province.
TenPayGo will also enable overseas visitors to activate a ride code for Shenzhen's buses and metro, with no phone number or transit card required.
In addition, TenPayGo will further expand its in-app services, pledging to connect payment with consumption scenarios, such as departure tax refunds and AI-powered translation of menus, the Shenzhen-based company added.
Dong Ximiao, chief economist at Merchants Union Consumer Finance Company Limited, noted that TenPayGo allows inbound visitors to travel across China with a single smartphone, which is set to further improve their travel experience.
The launch of TenPayGo came after Tencent announced in May a landmark integration of its extensive payment network with PayPal, enabling U.S. visitors to pay like locals in China via QR codes. The partnership connects Tencent's cross-border payments platform TenPay Global with PayPal World, a global platform connecting the world's largest payment systems and digital wallets.
Tencent's WeChat, which serves as a multifunctional app beyond social media and messaging, offers digital payment services known as Weixin Pay in the Chinese mainland.
The launch of TenPayGo by Weixin Pay comes amid a surge in foreign visitor spending. Data from Weixin Pay showed that in the first eight months of this year, the value and number of overseas e-wallet transactions in China increased by 80.6 percent and 81.8 percent year on year, respectively.
The payment growth came as "China Travel" surged, driven by the country's measures to facilitate inbound tourism, including the expansion of visa-free policies and improved departure tax refunds.
Official data showed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period, up 19.5 percent from a year earlier. Visa-free entries accounted for 23.72 million of the total, up 26.8 percent from a year earlier.
To better cater to the increasing payment demand, Tencent said it will carry out cooperation with domestic online payment-clearing house NetsUnion and work to connect more overseas e-wallets with its payment network, in a bid to enable more overseas users to scan to pay when traveling in China. ■

In a press statement issued late Wednesday, the 55-member continental organization said AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf expressed "deep concern" over renewed tensions and military escalation in northern Ethiopia.
The AU highlighted the seizure and occupation of airports in the East African country's Tigray regional state, as well as the detention of federal personnel by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the ensuing disruption of civilian air services.
The chairperson also voiced "grave concern" over reports of escalating hostilities in parts of Tigray and Afar regions, along with recent developments involving the formation of new political and military alliance that risks further destabilizing the situation and reversing the gains made to silence the guns since 2020, the statement read.
Youssouf reaffirmed that the Agreement for Lasting Peace through a Permanent Cessation of Hostilities, signed in Pretoria in November 2022 between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF under the auspices of the AU, remains "the cornerstone of sustainable peace, stability and reconciliation in Ethiopia."
He said the seizure and occupation of civilian airports in Mekelle, Axum, and Shire by Tigray forces is inconsistent with the commitments and obligations under the above agreement and risks eroding hard-won gains achieved in the pursuit of lasting peace and stability.
The AU Commission chief called for "utmost restraint and immediate cessation of all actions that could further escalate tensions," while urging the immediate resumption of direct talks within the framework of the Pretoria agreement.
He also called upon all neighboring countries of Ethiopia to refrain from actions that could contribute to further escalation and to actively support de-escalation, dialogue, and confidence-building.
The latest developments come amid heightened tensions in Ethiopia's northernmost Tigray region, following Sunday's announcement of a new alliance formed by seven Ethiopian opposition and armed groups, according to local media.
Amid rising security concerns, the national flag carrier Ethiopian Airlines temporarily suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum, and Shire, effective Wednesday, citing the "current situation" in the region.
Also on Wednesday, Getachew Reda, minister advisor to the Ethiopian Prime Minister on East African Affairs, said TPLF forces launched "an all-out offensive" against government positions in Afar and Amhara regions, adding that TPLF forces have taken over previously federally-controlled airports in Tigray.
Tigray was at the epicenter of a two-year conflict between Ethiopian federal forces and TPLF-loyal troops from November 2020 to November 2022, which left millions in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, before the two parties signed the landmark Pretoria peace accord. ■

The 29-year-old, a two-time Asian championships winner who broke the Chinese national record several times last year, was visibly emotional after the victory.
"It's been more than 20 years since China last won the title. Now we've brought it back," Abuduaini said. "I'll call my family and friends when I get back to my hotel, and then have a good sleep."

"I weighed around 113 to 114 kilograms in 2023, and now I'm 140 kilograms," he said. "I made that sacrifice to improve my performance. Adding more than 20 kilograms has made me more stable in all aspects."
Bahrain's Winfred Yavi, the Olympic and world champion in the women's 3,000-meter steeplechase, won the women's 10,000 meters in 32 minutes and 39.18 seconds for her first international major title over the distance.

"It feels so special because it's my first 10k at the Asian Games and I did it for the first time in my life in a competition," Yavi said. "It felt so good, entering in such an event and getting a gold medal."

Bahrain's quartet won the mixed 4x400-meter relay in an Asian Games-record 3:12.87.

"I am extremely happy now because I never expected to reach this result," the 20-year-old said. "My initial goal was around 10 seconds."
It was Boonson's second sub-10-second run of the season. He set his personal best of 9.94 seconds last year.
The Hangzhou Asian Games silver medalist said he was confident ahead of the final and hoped to win gold for Thailand.
China's Zeng Keli, who ran in the same heat as Boonson, advanced in 10.22 seconds. Defending champion Xie Zhenye won another heat in 10.30 and also progressed to the semifinals.
In the women's 100 meters, 17-year-old Chinese sprinter Chen Yujie won the first heat in 11.41 seconds to post the fastest time in the preliminaries.
Chen said she was not satisfied with the result after having targeted 11.40 seconds or faster before the race.
"Before the race, I had a conversation with the coach. I estimated that I would aim for a time of 11.40 seconds or less," she said.
Chen set an Asian junior record of 11.08 seconds at a domestic championship in August, also the fastest women's 100-meter time in Asia this season.
Defending champion Ge Manqi, another member of China's team, suffered leg cramps during the fourth heat and finished in 12.13 seconds, failing to advance. ■

Belarus president Lukashenko frees 15 more prisoners in wake of US talks
Sept 24 - Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko pardoned 15 prisoners in a decree on Thursday that follows talks last week with an envoy for US President Donald Trump.
Trump's envoy John Coale has been negotiating with Lukashenko for more than a year, so far obtaining the release of hundreds of prisoners including opposition figures, activists, journalists and lawyers, in return for removing some US sanctions.
Banned human rights group Viasna says 883 political prisoners remain in Belarus, convicted on charges such as extremist activity, incitement to hatred or insulting the president.
Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has ruled Belarus since 1994. He denies there are any political prisoners in the former Soviet state, but has engaged with the Trump administration in order to get sanctions relief and ease his international isolation.
Lukashenko's office said the 15 newly pardoned people included 10 women, and 13 of them had "committed crimes of an extremist nature". It said the pardons were granted after they asked for clemency and expressed remorse.
The releases represented further gradual progress towards Coale's stated goal of freeing all the remaining prisoners this year.
During his visit last week, he won the release of 25 people including prominent journalists and activists — far fewer than the 250 who were freed during his previous trip in March.
Analysts say Lukashenko is taking a tougher line in the talks, frustrated that the removal of some US sanctions — especially on potash, a key export earner for Belarus — has not been matched by the European Union.
Lukashenko has also demanded the release of $43 million to $44 million of frozen Belarusian assets that he says are "stuck" in Citibank, and Coale promised last week to address this. Citi has declined to comment. REUTERS

The Story of Bhutan’s UN Membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:36:00 UTC
00:36:00 KST

Aside from Bangladesh, the youngest nation of South Asia born in December 1971, Bhutan is the second-to-last state from the region to gain membership in the United Nations. India is a founding member of the U.N., followed by Afghanistan (1946), Pakistan (1947), Nepal and Sri Lanka (1955), and Maldives (1965). Bhutan finally joined on September 21, 1971.
Bhutan’s King Jigme Dorji Wangchuk had formally applied for U.N. membership on December 10, 1970, mainly seeking the sovereign equality the global body offers to small nations like Bhutan. In a letter addressed to then-U.N. Secretary-General U Thant, the king wrote, “The Government and people of Bhutan area acutely aware of the proven value of the United Nations Organization to small and developing nations off the world and consequently attach great importance to membership.”
Bhutan’s Permanent Mission to the U.N. holds the same attitude today. Its website says: “The United Nations, with its universal scope and global membership and the spirit of multilateralism that the United Nations fosters, forms an integral part of Bhutan’s foreign policy.”
Two months after Bhutan’s formal application to the U.N., on February 10, 1971, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted to favorably recommend Bhutan’s membership at that year’s 26th General Assembly. Bhutan was thus formally recognized as a U.N. member state on September 21, 1971.
Bhutan’s accession to the United Nations in 1971 was a great diplomatic achievement for a small state in South Asia. In the same decade, forget joining the U.N., the Kingdom of Sikkim had lost its very nationhood and merged into India in 1975. In 1971, the same year that Bhutan became a U.N. member state, Pakistan lost the “East Pakistan” part of its nation, which became the independent state of Bangladesh. Amid the making and breakings of nationhood in South Asia in this tumultuous decade, it was a diplomatic victory for a tiny Himalayan nation like Bhutan to become a part of the U.N. body.
Despite the tensions in the region, Bhutan’s entry into the world body wasn’t a part of controversy like nearby Nepal’s. Nepal applied for membership in 1949, but its ambition was delayed for six years mainly owing to the Soviet Union’s veto. Moscow’s obstruction, however, wasn’t really about Nepal. The USSR was seeking a broader diplomatic deal to win approval for five new U.N. member states that were in the Soviet camp: Hungary, Albania, Romania, Bulgaria, and Mongolia.
This was not the case for Bhutan. In the February 10, 1971 meeting of the Security Council, Bhutan’s ally India spoke in favor of its membership application. To do so, India requested permission to participate in the UNSC discussion, as New Delhi was not a member at the time. India’s U.N. representative, Samar Sen, said that the Security Council’s “decision to support Bhutan’s candidature… was but a final manifestation of Bhutan’s independent stature and nationhood.” Sen also noted that India “had, at Bhutan’s request, given it as much help as possible regarding the application for United Nations membership.”
In the same meeting of the UNSC, China’s U.N. Representative Liu Chieh said he “had been happy to vote for the admission of Bhutan.” In Liu’s words, “Bhutan had had a long history of independence… although in foreign relations, it had agreed to be guided by India.” However, China here means the Republic of China (or Taiwan), not the People’s Republic of China. The PRC government would gain China’s seat in the U.N. in October 1971 – one month after Bhutan entered the United Nations. That means Bhutan has been a U.N. member longer than the PRC.
Pakistan, like India, requested and was granted the right to participate in the UNSC session. Its diplomat, Agha Shahi, also voiced his support for Bhutan’s membership and welcomed the country to the “mainstream of international life.” He added that “Bhutan, although smaller than the other countries of the region, played a valuable role and would, he was sure, maintain harmonious relations with its neighbors in the interest of peace and stability.”
Japan, which held a non-permanent seat on the UNSC at the time, also approved Bhutan’s U.N. accession, saying that “Bhutan and Japan were closely connected by ties of the Eastern Asian civilization,” especially Mahayam Buddhism.
Other members of the UNSC in 1971 to support Bhutan’s membership included Argentina, Belgium, Burundi, France, Italy, Nicaragua, Poland, Sierra Leone, Somalia, the Soviet Union, and the United Kingdom. The session was chaired by the U.S. representative, Charles Yost, who concluded the session by pointing out that Bhutan “had long prided itself on its cultural traditions and its strong sense of national identity.”
Bhutan thus became the 128th member of the United Nations, with support from rivals like the U.S. and the Soviet Union, as well as India and Pakistan. Today, the number of U.N. member states has jumped to 193.
Bhutan’s major achievements in the U.N. include its graduation from Least Developed Country status in 2023 and its emphasis on “gross national happiness.” Bhutan also has a reputation as a voice for green growth, thanks to its global image as a “carbon negative” nation.
Beyond the U.N., Bhutan’s global diplomatic engagements remain limited. Interestingly, Bhutan does not have formal diplomatic relations with any of the five permanent U.N. Security Council members: China, France, Russia, the U.K., and the U.S. Bhutan does maintain a Permanent Mission to the U.N. in New York, where its U.N. representative also serves as Bhutan’s ambassador to Canada and Brazil.
Meanwhile, only three countries operate embassies in Bhutan: India, Bangladesh and Kuwait. Bhutan doesn’t host an embassy of Australia, the nation where reportedly 1.5 percent Bhutanese have migrated.
In the second week of June 2026, I was in Thimphu on my first tour to the fellow Himalayan nation. I talked to some tourism entrepreneurs, political figures, and ordinary citizens I met there and found that none of them were concerned about the few embassies in the Buddhist kingdom of around 800,000 people.
“In the age of digital visa and hyperconnectivity, we don’t need physical embassies of all important nations,” said a hotelier based in Paro, Bhutan’s third largest city which hosts the international airport. He added, “Even the U.S. and China don’t have embassies in all United Nations member nations.”

UN rights chief says civilians are bearing the brunt of fighting in Yemen
Unknown

00:34:25 KST

Civilians are being hardest hit by surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, the UN human rights chief said on Thursday.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said his office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement, without giving a breakdown of who was responsible for the casualties.
A total of 125 people were documented by his office as killed or wounded in the latest flare-up in the conflict. Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
The statement said the UN human rights office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi terrorists, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
It was not immediately clear if the UN toll included any deaths or injuries from those incidents.
Houthis deny UN allegations
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities.
He cited what he said was the targeting of inmates at a correctional facility in al-Hazm in al-Jawf province, as well as homes and schools in several areas. He said the UN allegations were false and unsupported by evidence.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years. Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen. Saudi Arabia's diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump-Xi meeting outside UNGA spotlight tests world body's clout - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:34:03 UTC
00:34:03 KST

While world leaders gather at the United Nations for their annual diplomatic ritual, the two biggest power brokers in global politics will sit down in a different venue on Thursday: the White House.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping will meet for the second time this year, hoping to keep the world's most consequential bilateral relationship steady as both leaders grapple with a host of domestic and global issues.
The split-screen moment highlights an existential question for the UN: does the world body, established after the calamity of two world wars, still matter?
While UN delegates discuss "multilateralism" and hold panels on the world's conflicts, Trump and Xi – what the US president calls the "G2" – will talk AI, trade, and defense.
"It's pretty notable that Xi Jinping is coming to Washington in the same week as the General Assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York," said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
"I think a lot of people will say, 'Where is the real center of decision-making?'"
Xi rarely travels to New York for the General Assembly.
The questions about the UN's role are hardly new, but have acquired fresh urgency as the organization struggles with deep financial problems, divisions among major powers and limited influence over conflicts from Ukraine to the Middle East.
Those concerns have gained new relevance since Trump's return to office last year. The US leader has pulled the US out of dozens of UN agencies and slashed Washington's budgetary contributions to the organization, pushing it to the brink of bankruptcy.
In his speech on Tuesday, Trump accused the UN of "imposing the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected."
UN facing deepening financial woes
The UN has a persistent budget shortfall, forcing it to cut the budget of its Secretariat by 9.2% for 2026. It laid off thousands of staff, sent peacekeepers home, and cut back on humanitarian and human rights work.
The United States, which has for years withheld much of its dues, is part of that problem.
The Trump administration last week paid $725 million for the regular budget, preserving its vote at the assembly, but still owes $1.3 billion to the regular budget and $2.9 billion for peacekeeping operations, the UN said.
The organization's problems extend beyond money, however.
Gridlock has long defined the UN Security Council, where five veto powers, including China, Russia and the US, rarely agree on anything substantive.
"There are two main challenges that the UN faces today: the first is its dire financial situation," said Eugene Chen, a former UN official.
"This is linked to a second, broader, challenge – the fact that member states no longer agree on what the form or function of the UN ought to be at a time of mounting global challenges," he said.
Outgoing Secretary-General Antonio Guterres launched a reform task force last year, known as UN80, which seeks to cut costs, remove duplication, move jobs to locations cheaper than New York and Geneva and improve efficiency.
It includes a 21% reduction in posts at the Secretariat and a review of more than 600 series of mandated Secretary-General's reports, aiming to reduce reporting by about 700,000 words in 2026.
Trump decries 'craven hypocrites' of UNHCR
Unlike in 2025, Trump did not use his Tuesday speech to complain about escalators or teleprompters and largely stuck to a script that focused on defending his record in the war with Iran and on the US economy.
Still, he inveighed against the "craven hypocrites" of the UN's Human Rights Council who "want America to open our borders to gangs and criminals from the world’s most dangerous places," and zeroed in on UNESCO, saying "these globalists are actively destroying the greatest cultures and most extraordinary heritage in history."
The UN has defended culture and education agency UNESCO's work as "unanimously acclaimed by major specialized organizations,” and the Human Rights Council as playing "a very important role in the promotion and protection of human rights worldwide."
Xi has sought to capitalize on Trump's often bellicose rhetoric by presenting China as a reliable partner on the global stage, especially for developing nations, and by using the UN as a platform to advance that message.
Over 1,000 meetings planned over UNGA week
For all the criticism of the UN, its annual meeting remains a forum for high-volume diplomacy. This week, member states planned more than 1,000 bilateral meetings, according to UN data.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines on Tuesday, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
The European Union's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters the UN remained relevant, but she too criticized the organization for being "paralyzed when it comes to preventing or ending conflicts."
Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky used the venue to hold talks with Trump on ending the war with Russia, including a potential ceasefire on energy-related targets.
He was asked by a journalist whether years of meetings at the UN have brought any concrete results. He answered in English: "Today it helps us to meet. Maybe it's not too much, but it's something."

According to the corporation's press service, the Rosatom stand was attended by Darmawan Prasodjo, head of Indonesia's state-owned power company PLN; Haendra Subekti, Deputy Chairman for Nuclear Safety Assessment at Indonesia's Nuclear Energy Regulatory Agency (BAPETEN); as well as other representatives of Indonesian government bodies, partners, and experts from the nuclear industries of Indonesia and ASEAN countries.
"For ASEAN nations, nuclear energy is no longer a matter for the distant future. It is a practical tool for long-term energy planning. ASEAN representatives acknowledge that there is no one-size-fits-all solution: each country develops its own model based on its energy system structure, geography, industrial demand, and national priorities. We are collaborating productively with partners in Indonesia and stand ready to share our expertise with neighboring countries in the region to foster a more effective and comprehensive dialogue regarding the future energy mix of ASEAN nations," the press service quoted Anna Belokoneva, Head of Rosatom’s representative office in Indonesia, as saying.

So Long, Pave Hawk: Air Force’s HH-60G Combat Rescue Helicopter Completes Final Flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:31:21 UTC
00:31:21 KST

The Air Force’s HH-60G Pave Hawk helicopter made its final flight earlier this month.
The 129th Rescue Wing retired its last HH-60G with a final flight and ceremony on Sept. 10 at Moffett Air National Guard Base, Calif. The Pave Hawk is being replaced by an updated model, HH-60W Jolly Green II.
Tail number 27045 is the last operational HH-60G in the entire Air Force, a service spokesperson said, noting that a few remaining G-models are still in the inventory for now and will be processed out by Sept. 30, the end of the fiscal year.
Often called the “Golf,” the HH-60G entered service in 1982, was the Air Force’s combat search and rescue helicopter for more than 40 years until the updated “Whiskey” models began to supplant it in 2022. Both are UH-60 Black Hawk variants.
In addition to CSAR, the Air Force used the Pave Hawk for disaster relief, humanitarian missions, and casualty and medical evacuations. Capable of carrying eight-plus passengers, it could fly at speeds of 180 miles per hour with a range of 580 miles and be aerially refueled. It was equipped with two guns, a cargo hook that could lift up to 8,000 pounds, and folding rotor blades allowing it to be transported in cargo aircraft like the C-5M Galaxy.
The Pave Hawk played a key role in events like the military’s humanitarian response to Hurricane Katrina in 2005, operations during the Global War on Terror in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the noncombatant evacuation out of Afghanistan in 2021. Airmen were decorated with Distinguished Flying Crosses and Presidential Unit Citations for their actions in the Afghanistan evacuation, where they faced small arms fire from the ground as they evacuated scores of people ahead of the Taliban’s advance.
“When you’re flying the [Pave Hawk], you kind of become one with that machine,” Lt. Col. Benjamin Buchta, HH-60 pilot and commander of the 129th Rescue Squadron, said in a statement. “The Golf feels like home when I sit in it.”
At its peak, there were more than 100 HH-60Gs in the Air Force inventory, split among Active, Guard, and Reserve units. By 2024, units across the globe were saying their final farewells to the Golf—Kadena Air Base in Japan retired its last Golf in August 2024, Gabreski Air National Guard Base, N.Y., followed in October 2024, and Kirtland Air Force Base, N.M., and Aviano Air Base, Italy, both completed the switch in December 2024. The Air Force Reserve’s last HH-60Gs left Patrick Space Force Base, Fla., in September 2025.
The Air Force’s fiscal 2026 budget funded the final 11 Pave Hawk divestments. The Alaska Air National Guard retired its last HH-60G in July 2026, setting the stage for the California Air Guard to follow in September, just ahead of the new fiscal year on Oct. 1.
In tributes to the HH-60G, rescue units across the Air Force credited the Golf with helping them save thousands of lives over the years.
The new HH-60Ws have fully digital glass cockpits, improved hot weather/high-altitude performance, on-board self-defenses capable of defeating higher-end threats, larger cabins, and double the internal fuel capacity of the Gs. The Air Force asked for more than $200 million in the 2027 budget request for Whiskey upgrades, including for self-protection against shoulder-fired rockets and conversions to transport VIPs around Washington D.C., which will be a new mission for the HH-60.
All told, the service plans to field 102 Whiskeys, including 11 test and developmental aircraft, with the final delivery due in January 2030, according to budget documents.

China gets F-35 parts containing sensitive US technology – Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:18:17 UTC
00:18:17 KST

China gets F-35 parts containing sensitive US technology – Bloomberg
China has obtained potentially sensitive components from the F-35, the US military’s most advanced stealth fighter jet, after the parts were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the US, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people briefed on the incident.
The incident first reported by Politico last week occurred earlier this year, when a shipment of allegedly unserviceable F-35 parts from Australia that was bound for the US was inexplicably rerouted.
US shipping giant UPS was transporting an F-35 canopy and weapons-bay door from the Australian Air Force to the US for inspection and possible repair or disposal, people familiar with the incident told Bloomberg. The two components, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, were coated with radar-absorbing material designed to enhance the aircraft’s stealth capabilities, according to two sources cited by the outlet.
One of the sources said the transport aircraft stopped in South Korea on its way to the US, after which the shipment was rerouted to Hong Kong. It remains unclear why the aircraft stopped there, why the shipment was sent to Hong Kong, or whether the rerouting was intentional or accidental, the source said. Two sources added that Chinese authorities subsequently seized the components, which have not been returned.
The F-35, one of the world’s most advanced fighter jets, is operated by around 20 countries, including South Korea, Japan, Singapore and Australia. Australia serves as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific for storing spare parts and maintaining F-35s operated by nearby US allies.
At least two congressional committees are investigating the latest incident, the news agency noted. Earlier this week, Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles confirmed that Canberra was working with the US and Lockheed Martin to examine its role in the shipment blunder. Marles stressed that the missing components were not sensitive.
According to a Lockheed Martin spokesperson in Australia, “the components in question are unserviceable and deemed low risk for exploitation.”
The disclosure of the incident comes at a politically sensitive time for the two countries, as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit with his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
China’s Foreign Ministry said it was not aware of the incident, while the Hong Kong government declined to comment on specific cases.

Cancer-linked ‘forever chemical’ found in blood of residents near UK factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:17:52 UTC
00:17:52 KST

Burak Bir
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Elevated levels of a cancer-linked “forever chemical” have been found in blood samples from dozens of residents living near a factory in the UK, a law firm said Thursday.
Blood tests on residents of Thornton Cleveleys living near a large chemical factory revealed increased levels of PFOA, a type of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS), Leigh Day said in a statement.
The results showed that of the 49 residents tested, nearly 70% had elevated PFOA levels, placing them at higher risk of health problems associated with the chemical, including high cholesterol and some cancers.
PFOA is part of the PFAS group of chemicals, known as “forever chemicals” because they resist breaking down in the environment and can accumulate in human tissue.
The statement said the participants live near an industrial site operated by AGC Chemicals, where PFOA was historically used until 2012.
“The site was previously operated by ICI until 1992. It is estimated around 178 tonnes of PFOA has been released by the site since the 1950s,” it noted.
Wyre Council, in conjunction with the Environment Agency (EA), has carried out soil testing in the area, with samples from residents’ properties and nearby allotments showing elevated levels of PFOA, the firm said.
Leigh Day has also been investigating PFAS contamination in the area, working with experts led by Dave Megson at Manchester Metropolitan University (MMU).
The blood testing was carried out during the summer of 2026 by an expert team from MMU, with the results relayed to participants on Sept. 23.
“The results showed levels of PFOA above 20 nanograms per millilitre (ng/ml) in 69.4% of participants, placing them in the high-risk category, with the overall average at 26 ng/ml.”
The statement said the findings were comparable to those recorded among residents in Ohio living near a DuPont factory in the case adapted into the film Dark Waters, where an average level of 32.9 ng/ml was recorded.
“The results of our testing project in Thornton Cleveleys are hugely concerning,” said Sarah Moore, a Leigh Day partner who leads the firm’s investigations.
She added: “The available evidence suggests that PFAS exposure can lead to serious health impacts, including cancers, when it reaches elevated levels.”

leaning timber frame anchors shrine office in japanese mountain valley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:15:09 UTC
00:15:09 KST

Sobokuya builds The Shrine Office in mountain valley in Hokuto
Set within a mountain valley in the precincts of Fujitake Shrine, in Hokuto, Japan, The Shrine Office by Sobokuya is conceived around the way natural materials change and deepen with age. Two generous openings bring light and air through the interiorof the timber building, casting shifting shadows across the tatami as the seasons change, from spring light and summer greenery to autumn air and crisp winter conditions. Deep eaves and hand-finished lime plaster walls give the office a restrained, ceremonial character.
Niho-Korobi and Ishiba-Date techniques form the timber frame
The building’s structure by Sobokuya Studio combines ishiba-date, an ancient technique in which column bases sit directly on stone, with niho-korobi, where columns lean uniformly outward in two directions. Unlike conventional timber framing, the inclined columns require each beam to be calculated across three dimensions, marked, and drawn at full scale before being cut.
The resulting frame distributes loads along diagonal vectors. Because the columns are left unfixed at their stone footings, the structure can absorb seismic movement instead of resisting it, functioning as an early form of base isolation. The roof is clad in Corten steel, whose oxidizing surface will develop a deeper character over time.
The Shrine Office sits within a mountain valley at Fujitake Shrine
Larch timber structure connects the interior to the landscape
Above, an open roof structure exposes larch felled on the slopes of the Yatsugatake mountain range. Struts and red pine taiko beams form a geometric framework shaped by the natural properties of the timber, while the scent of wood remains present throughout the interior.
Sobokuya designed and handmade the joinery in-house, allowing the exterior landscape to become part of the interior. When the panels are opened, wind and natural light pass directly through the room, maintaining a physical connection with the surrounding valley.
deep eaves frame the office and protect its lime plaster walls
The sumo ring at Mizu-waka-su Shrine informs the design
The building’s formal starting point is the sumo ring at Mizu-waka-su Shrine on Oki Island in Shimane Prefecture, a site associated with the cultural legacy of the exiled Emperor Go-Toba. Sobokuya founding principal Hisashi Imai visited the island during the design process, and the austere character of the ring informed the building’s restrained spatial expression.
Hand-chiseled surfaces add another layer of individuality to the architecture, with marks from the carpenter’s tools remaining visible in the finished work. The use of natural materials, traditional construction techniques, and handmade details is intended to allow the building to age alongside its mountain setting over the long term.

Russia stands for early entry into force of CTBT — Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:11:22 UTC
00:11:22 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Russia supports an early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), one of the core parts of the global security, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
"The Russian Federation has consistently considered the CTBT as one of the key elements of the international security architecture and supports an early entry into force of the CTBT. This requires the consolidation of efforts of all states, a remarkable political will and a willingness to put common interests above market considerations. We are ready to continue actively contributing to the achievement of this goal," Lavrov said in a congratulatory telegram to Robert Floyd, executive secretary of the Preparatory Commission for the CTBT, on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the treaty's opening for signature.
Lavrov said that the treaty became a visible expression of the collective responsibility of states to preserve global stability and security for future generations.
"Its importance cannot be overestimated: the nuclear test ban is not only an arms control measure, but also a powerful political signal about the priority of peaceful development and dialogue in international affairs. The principles laid down in the CTBT remain topical today," the telegram says.
Lavrov also praised the efforts that Floyd and his colleagues are making to universalize the treaty.
"Your work is a daily contribution to maintaining trust between states and creating conditions for preserving the international architecture in the field of arms control and non-proliferation of nuclear weapons, a clear example of how professionalism, dedication and teamwork can ensure the relevance of important agreements even in difficult political conditions," Lavrov said.
About the agreement
To date, the CTBT was signed by 188 states and ratified by 179. For its entry into force, mandatory ratification is required by the 44 states listed in the annex, which are countries with nuclear weapons or potential capabilities to create them (their list is based on IAEA data).
Currently, 35 nuclear-weapon states, including the United Kingdom and France, ratified the document. "The "nuclear club" members - the United States, China, Egypt, Israel and Iran - signed, but not ratified it, while the three "young" nuclear powers - India, North Korea and Pakistan - did not sign it.
Russia signed the treaty in 1996 and ratified it in 2000. However, in 2023, Russia withdrew its ratification, as the document was never ratified by the US Congress. The law on Russia’s withdrawal of ratification was passed by the State Duma on October 18, 2023; the Federation Council approved it on October 25; and on November 2, it was signed by the president.

UN rights chief says civilians are bearing the brunt of fighting in Yemen
Civilians are being hardest hit by surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, the UN human rights chief said on Thursday.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said his office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement, without giving a breakdown of who was responsible for the casualties.
A total of 125 people were documented by his office as killed or wounded in the latest flareup in the conflict. Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
The statement said the UN human rights office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi movement, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
It was not immediately clear if the UN toll included any deaths or injuries from those incidents.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities.
He cited what he said was the targeting of inmates at a correctional facility in al-Hazm in al-Jawf province, as well as homes and schools in several areas. He said the UN allegations were false and unsupported by evidence.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years. Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen. Saudi Arabia's diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Israel uproots 400 olive trees in occupied West Bank as harvest season approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:10:03 UTC
00:10:03 KST

Qais Abu Samra, Ikram Kouachi
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
The Israeli army uprooted 400 olive trees and bulldozed 31 dunams (3.1 hectares, 7.6 acres) of Palestinian-owned land Thursday in Beit Rima in northwestern Ramallah in the occupied West Bank as harvest season approaches.
Sources told Anadolu that bulldozers cleared the land and uprooted the trees, two days after Israeli authorities issued a military order targeting two areas of land in the town.
They added that the military order demanded “removing wild vegetation and uprooting olive and other trees from the targeted areas.”
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said Tuesday that Israeli authorities issued five military orders targeting the uprooting of trees and removal of wild vegetation from 533.5 dunams of Palestinian land in the Jenin, and Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorates in the northern and central West Bank.
Since the beginning of 2026 through Sept. 22, Israel has issued 51 orders to remove trees and vegetation in the occupied West Bank, targeting 2,093 dunams of land, according to data from the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
The uprooting operation comes as the olive harvest season approaches. Olive trees are a major source of income for thousands of Palestinian families. Bulldozing and uprooting operations cause losses to farmers and threaten their ability to access and cultivate their land.
Afrah Qadura, 65, from Beit Rima, told Anadolu that residents learned of the military order two days ago and saw a map at the municipality building showing the areas targeted for the removal of olive trees.
He said landowners were given 12 hours to remove trees before the Israeli army would implement the order. “How can we remove trees planted by our fathers and uproot them with our own hands?” he asked rhetorically.
Qadura said the olive trees had been planted over decades, beginning in the late 1960s and continuing through the 1970s and 1980s, as well as trees planted in the 1990s.
He said some of the trees uprooted Thursday had become highly productive for years, adding that olive trees are a primary source of livelihood for residents.
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are preparing for the olive harvest season, which usually begins in October.
Thousands of Palestinians rely on olive trees and their crops as a source of income, alongside their connection to the land and agricultural heritage passed down through generations.
“We are proud of those trees like our children,” said Qadura, noting the years he and his father spent cultivating the land, caring for the trees and watering them.
He added that he used to bring water from a well to water the saplings and follow their growth during the years. “My father worked hard planting the trees, and we also worked hard caring for them.”
He said his family continued to tend, clean and care for the trees until they became part of their lives. Losing them in this way was, for him, like losing one of his children.
Qadura said uprooting the trees would not force his family to abandon their land, stressing that he and his family intend to replant the trees uprooted by the Israeli army.
“We will continue planting trees like my father did, and our children will continue after us,” he said, citing his family’s connection to the land and its cultivation across generations.
Abdul Rahman al-Rimawi, mayor of Bani Zeid al-Gharbia, which includes Beit Rima and other towns, told Anadolu that everybody was surprised Thursday when Israeli army bulldozers began uprooting mature olive trees in the town in an area of 31 dunams.
Rimawi said the trees “are hundreds of years old,” and that uprooting them not only destroys the trees, but also affects the livelihoods of Palestinian families that depend on them.
He said the operation comes as the olive harvest season approaches, describing it as part of “arbitrary Israeli practices against people, trees and stones.”
Rimawi said the residents of Beit Rima “are not isolated from this people” and what Palestinians are subjected to in terms of harassment, killings, displacement and the uprooting of olive trees.
 
He implored international institutions and relevant parties to work to halt the decision to uproot the trees, noting that there is ongoing communication with the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission to that end.
Rimawi said Israeli authorities had not, according to him, explained the grounds for implementing the decision, and that what is happening represents “Israeli practices against all members of the Palestinian people” in the occupied West Bank.
