What the World Owes the Marshall Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:09:08 UTC
00:09:08 KST

This week, the U.N. General Assembly affirmed that statehood endures the loss of land. My country, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, will persist despite rising seas. The question is how Marshallese people go on living here safely.
Our nation consists of narrow strips of land on 29 low-lying coral atolls scattered across more than 750,000 square miles of the central Pacific Ocean.
For many, adapting to rising seas may mean moving communities to higher ground. In the Marshalls, we have no higher ground to move to. That fundamental difference shapes what climate adaptation means for us and how we must act.
As we prepare for another El Niño, our people know its rhythms well, but the severity with which these forces now arrive is worsening.
First, the rains come heavily. Then they stop. Water tanks empty, wells run dry, crops fail, and ocean conditions shift. We begin shipping water to communities with none.
These changes are the reality behind the historic diplomatic achievement taking place this week. The U.N. General Assembly adopted the first Sea-Level Rise Declaration by consensus. In a year of fractured diplomacy, that is worth celebrating.
The Republic of the Marshall Islands has never wavered in its position. Sea level rise will not alter the statehood, sovereignty, or maritime zones of any state. But while the legal status, rights, and maritime zones of my country and its people are now secure, our physical safety is not.
That distinction must guide what comes next. The world must respond to the impact of sea level rise on coastal communities, heritage, and cultures, and the lands that have nourished our ancestors for generations. We must start by preventing as much sea level rise as we can.
Island nations have long fought for climate action. The Alliance of Small Island States, the High Ambition Coalition (which the Marshall Islands convenes), and other progressive forces fought hard for the 1.5°C temperature limit within the Paris Agreement.
And last year, inspired by a campaign led by Pacific youth, the International Court of Justice affirmed in its advisory opinion on climate change that every country's emissions reductions must align with 1.5°C. The Court also affirmed that the continued licensing, subsidy, production, and consumption of fossil fuels may constitute internationally wrongful acts.
Yet earlier this month, the United Nations Environment Programme released a report indicating that an overshoot of 1.5°C is now almost certain. Crossing the threshold cannot be an excuse to abandon the target. Every fraction of a degree means greater risks, higher seas, and more lives and livelihoods lost. Our responsibility is to make that overshoot as small and short-lived as possible.
In the Pacific, we know that fossil fuel dependency hurts not only the planet but also our health, security, and economies. That is why, earlier this month, Pacific leaders set out our vision for a fossil fuel-free Pacific.
If the world does not follow science, international law, or the Pacific by phasing out fossil fuels as swiftly as possible, the harm to the roughly one billion people who live on the world’s coasts will be devastating. What’s more, the costs of adaptation will rise exponentially. For the Marshallese people, the desire to stay in the land of our ancestors is deeply felt. We demand action from major emitters as we also adapt to rising seas.
Adaptation is a huge technical challenge. We are mapping our atolls from the air, meter by meter, because available satellite elevation data has a margin of error nearly three times the height of most of our nation. We cannot determine which land to raise or whose drinking water can survive a drought from inaccurate data. Precise information is also essential to develop credible proposals and access climate finance.
We know what practical adaptation looks like. Our National Adaptation Plan is complete; funding it is not. Effective adaptation costs money—$310 billion to $365 billion per year to manage worsening climate impacts—which is why the call in the Declaration on Sea Level Rise to streamline and simplify access to finance matters. Pacific leaders in Palau put it plainly: what this region needs is climate finance, and finance that actually reaches people on the ground. We need states to invest in helping communities adapt, protecting livelihoods, allowing people to remain safely on their lands for as long as possible, and ensuring that those who move can do so with dignity.
The Marshall Islands is proud to lead the champions launching the Rising Nations Institute, which aims to translate the principles we have fought for into practical solutions for communities confronting rising seas.
Despite geopolitical challenges, UNGA’s Sea-Level Rise Declaration shows that the world is committed to climate action and to the protection of countries threatened by sea level rise. We now have legal frameworks capable of enduring physical change and inspiring action. The next challenge is to ensure that our systems of finance, planning, and adaptation can do the same.
We cannot completely hold back the rising seas. But we can do a lot more to limit that rise and to choose how we meet it.

Heavy rains hit Mexico as Hurricane Polo tracks offshore, expected to make landfall on Sunday night
Sept 24 - Heavy surf and rain lashed southwestern Mexico as "extremely powerful" Hurricane Polo crawls northwest offshore the mainland, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said in a bulletin on Thursday.
With maximum sustained winds near 155 miles per hour (250 kph) Polo has been classified last as a Category 4 storm, a notch down from level 5, the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale, which it had previously reached.
As the NHC keeps adjusting the storm's force, it said it could see some near-term strengthening and is expected to remain a major hurricane for the next few days.
AccuWeather, a private forecaster, expected Polo to make landfall late Sunday night into Monday, to lose some steam and to reach a Category 2 hurricane as it tracks across the Baja California peninsula north of Cabo San Lucas, where local authorities have already begun restricting beach access and closing the local harbor.
The NHC said that Polo's outer rainbands are spreading onshore and producing heavy rains. Tropical-storm-force winds are likely occurring along the coast of southwestern Mexico, it said.
Polo's hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 40 miles (65 km) from the center and tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 125 miles (205 km).
Additional rainfall totals of 2 inches to 4 inches (50.8 mm to 101.6 mm), with isolated maximum totals up to 6 inches, are expected across across coastal portions of the Mexican states of Michoacan, Colima, northern and southern Jalisco, and Nayarit.
"These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf, rip currents, and coastal flooding," said the NHC.
AccuWeather hurricane expert Nicholas Arman said that if the hurricane stays on the expected track, some rain and moisture can be pulled into Texas.
“This is textbook El Niño impacts where the strong tropical development in the Pacific ultimately pushes moisture into the southwestern US,” he said
How much rain and moisture reaches Texas depends on the storm’s ability to cross the Sierra Madre mountains, a major mountain range system which runs northwest–southeast through northwestern and western Mexico, and along the Gulf of California.
“The Sierra Madre often act like a cheese grater to an organized system, shredding it apart and preventing any organized tropical feature from staying together,” Arman added. REUTERS

Canada studied ‘extreme’ US military scenario – Carney
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has revealed that his government carefully examined the possibility of US-led military action against his country, despite President Donald Trump having ruled out using force against America’s northern neighbor.

Carney’s disclosure comes just days after he traveled to the EU to deepen ties with the bloc.
Addressing the European Parliament last week, Carney argued that economic integration was increasingly being “weaponized,” with tariffs used as leverage and supply-chain dependencies exploited as vulnerabilities – remarks widely seen as an implicit reference to Washington’s economic pressure on Ottawa.
Defense was also part of Carney’s talks in Strasbourg, where he and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen discussed expanding Canada-EU military cooperation and joint procurement to strengthen what Carney called their “strategic autonomy.”
That cooperation is already taking shape through the EU’s €150 billion ($170 billion) SAFE defense procurement program, in which Canada has become the first non-European country to participate. 7 Fall Yard Habits That Help Pollinators Survive Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:04:12 UTC
00:04:12 KST

A few years ago, Katie Costanzo and her students went curbside shopping for trash. They collected eight bags of leaves that homeowners around Buffalo had raked up for disposal, then sifted through them to see what—if anything—was hiding inside.
The bags were anything but empty. They contained insects from more than 25 families, representing every stage of life from eggs and larvae to pupae and adults. There were bees, wasps, lacewings, hoverflies, beetles, and more—all tucked into material their human landlords had deemed garbage. The class exercise was later published in American Entomologist.
That’s the problem with what we call “fall cleanup.” Costanzo, an ecologist and entomologist at Canisius University, wishes people would stop viewing leaves, stems, and wood as trash. “This is part of the ecology of our system,” she says. “This could be habitat or resources.” Much of what looks dead, messy, or finished for the season is still serving as food, shelter, or a nursery. And leaves are only the beginning.
Queen bumblebees may be tucked just beneath the soil in your yard. Native bees and ladybugs can shelter inside hollow stems you might otherwise have snipped and stuffed into a yard-waste bag. Beetles, flies, and other insects hide in spent flower heads, while birds return to those same plants for seeds. Once cold weather arrives, a yard might look like it’s closed for the season, but “all this business is happening” through the winter, says Mary Phillips, head of native plant habitat strategy at the National Wildlife Federation.
Pollinators are animals that move pollen from one flower to another, allowing plants to reproduce. In an American yard, that group includes native bees, butterflies, moths, beetles, flies, and some wasps—not only the honeybees most people picture. The same habitat also supports plenty of beneficial creatures that aren’t technically pollinators, including predators and decomposers that help keep an ecosystem functioning.
Kim Eierman, an ecological landscape designer and author of The Pollinator Victory Garden, encourages homeowners to think differently about even the smallest patch of land. “You have an ecosystem,” she says. “It may be a really tiny one. Maybe you’re lucky and have a lot of land—but you have an ecosystem, so we need to start treating our landscapes that way.” That means reconsidering some familiar features, including the closely cropped lawn she calls a “green desert.”
Here are seven fall habits pollinator experts practice in their own yards—and how to make each one manageable.
Choose one corner where cleanup stops
Before you pick up a rake, divide your yard mentally into zones. Continue maintaining the high-traffic areas where kids play, pets run, or people gather, as well as walkways and other spots that need to remain clear. Then identify one quieter space—under a tree, behind shrubs, alongside the house, or at the back of a garden bed—where leaves, stems, and a few branches can remain.
Costanzo does this in her own yard. “You don’t have to manage your entire property the same,” she says. Her family keeps recreational areas usable and designates other spots for pollinator gardens and small piles of natural material. Someone with a suburban lot might preserve only a few sticks and one bed of leaves. That still counts. “Anything—any change—is good change,” she says.
If you’re worried that neighbors will mistake habitat for neglect, put up a sign explaining what you’re doing. “I have a pollinator sign. I have a native-plant sign,” Eierman says. “It’s a clue to neighbors and passersby that we’re gardening a little differently—and we’re gardening with a purpose.”
The same zoning strategy applies to the lawn: “I start to cut back—not cut the lawn back, but cut back on how often I mow,” Phillips says of the turf her family still uses. As growth slows in the fall, she spaces out mowing and leaves the grass a little taller. A patch set aside as habitat is different: Once insects have settled in, leave it undisturbed through the winter rather than mowing it down.
Rake leaves into beds instead of bags
Eierman would like to rebrand “leaf litter” as “nature’s gold.” Fallen leaves insulate bumblebee queens near the soil surface where they hibernate and shelter butterflies, moths, caterpillars, and many other invertebrates. As the leaves break down, they also return nutrients to the soil, suppress weeds, and become free mulch and compost. “Nature knows what it’s doing,” Costanzo says. “We don’t have to clean it up.”
The most practical approach isn’t necessarily to leave every leaf exactly where it lands. The National Wildlife Federation recommends moving leaves off turf, pavement, driveways, and other places where a thick or slippery layer would create problems. Rake them beneath trees or into garden beds, aiming for a layer about 3 to 5 inches deep. If you still have extras, pile them in a little-used corner and let them slowly become leaf mold. Lightly spray newly placed leaves with a hose to keep them from blowing away on a windy day.
If you plan to shred fallen leaves with a lawn mower and leave the pieces on the grass, do it early in the season, before many insects have settled in for winter, Eierman says. “If you leave all those leaves and then start chopping them up, you’re chopping up lots of invertebrates, too,” she says. When you send occupied leaves to the curb, “you’re throwing away a part of your ecosystem,” Costanzo adds.
There are exceptions: Diseased plant material and invasive plants may need to be removed; ask a local extension office how to dispose of them. Leaf litter can harbor ticks, so keep it away from play spaces and heavily used paths, and follow local public-health guidance. In wildfire-prone regions, habitat advice never outranks defensible-space rules. For example, CAL FIRE advises removing leaves and other combustible debris from the first 5 ft. around structures and maintaining additional cleared zones beyond that. Regional rules vary, so check with your local fire authority.
Leave stems and seed heads standing
When an aster, ironweed, Joe-Pye weed, or native grass turns brown, resist the urge to shear it to the ground. Hollow and pithy stems can serve as nesting or overwintering sites; flower heads shelter small beetles, flies, and weevils; and seed heads become winter buffets for birds. Eierman has watched goldfinches descend on the plants in her yard to pry out seeds.
“They look dead to you,” she says. But they haven’t clocked out yet.
The easiest option is to leave most plants standing through the winter. Phillips’s Joe-Pye weed grows so high that they’re “taller than me,” she says. To keep those lanky stalks from toppling, she gathers them with twine, transforming them into an architectural feature rather than a botanical pileup.
You can shorten especially unruly stems, but don’t cut them all the way down: Leave at least a foot standing. Eierman trims only some hollow or pithy stems and varies their heights, creating openings for stem-nesting bees of different sizes. Leave plenty untouched, too. The point is variation—not precision pruning with a ruler.
Diseased plants are the exception. Remove affected material rather than preserving it alongside healthy stems, and use local extension guidance to determine whether it should be trashed, burned where legal, or processed another way. Normal browning at the end of the season isn’t itself a disease.
Uncover a little bare ground
Bee housing doesn’t always resemble a charming wooden hotel. Many native bees nest in the ground, burrowing a few inches into exposed soil and spending much of their lives there. A landscape sealed beneath thick wood-chip mulch offers them fewer entrances.
Look for a quiet spot where you can pull back the mulch and leave a modest patch of soil exposed and undisturbed. It doesn’t need to dominate the garden. Even small openings between plants can help, especially when they aren’t covered with plastic sheeting, landscape fabric, or another barrier. The Xerces Society offers guidance on recognizing and preserving ground-nesting habitat.
If you like mulch because it suppresses weeds and looks polished, keep using it where you need it; just don’t smother every square inch. “Everybody’s situation is different,” Costanzo says. The goal is to create access, not a moonscape.
Save a few logs and branches
A fallen limb doesn’t automatically need to leave the property. Decaying logs, sticks, and small brush piles provide structure and shelter for insects and other wildlife; birds also forage there for food. “Keep some of the sticks, keep some of the larger pieces of wood,” Costanzo says. “It really does provide structure and habitat that’s so important in the winter.”
That doesn’t mean every branch must remain exactly where it lands. “You don’t leave them where they fall necessarily,” Phillips says. She moves dead branches, logs, and brush into a corner of her yard—like behind shrubs, where they’re less conspicuous. “Sometimes a pile like that can be really helpful,” she says.
Start small: Place a log along the back of a garden bed, tuck a few sticks beneath a shrub, or build one restrained brush pile in a low-traffic area. Keep dead wood away from the house, and don’t leave a damaged tree standing if it could fall on a person, building, power line, or neighboring property. The National Wildlife Federation has additional guidance on dead wood and wildlife habitat.
Plant one native species this fall
Fall isn’t only a season for leaving things alone. In many parts of the country, it’s an excellent time to plant: Cooler temperatures can reduce stress on new plants, and nurseries may discount perennials that look tired but have perfectly viable roots. “Here in the Northeast, our optimal times for planting are September, October,” Eierman says. “That’s what I’m doing right now.” The ideal window varies, so check local recommendations and leave enough time for roots to establish before the ground freezes.
Start with one or two species rather than redesigning the entire property by sundown. Choose plants native to your region and suited to the site’s sunlight, soil, and moisture. Costanzo’s family has added everything from oaks, dogwoods, and redbuds to Joe-Pye weed and black-eyed Susans. “We’ve seen such a difference,” she says. “We have so much diversity.” Last year, seven bird species nested on their property.
Some plants pack an especially powerful ecological punch. “The oak tree is the superstar,” Phillips says: Across the U.S., oaks support hundreds of species of butterfly and moth caterpillars. If you don’t have room for a giant tree, native shrubs, grasses, and flowering perennials still count. Enter your ZIP code into the National Wildlife Federation’s Native Plant Finder to see locally useful options. The right list will look very different in Pennsylvania than it does in Arizona or Oregon.
Native plants can be pricey, but fall bargain-hunting may pay off. Phillips looks for end-of-season markdowns at nurseries that carry them. “They may not look good, to be honest,” she says. You might put one in the ground and immediately cut it back—but “then they’ll come back the next year.”
When shopping, ask whether a cultivated variety still produces pollen, nectar, and seed. “You don’t want sterile plants,” Eierman says. “You want plants that actually produce seed.” Some cultivars provide nectar for pollinators but no seeds for birds, making them less useful than they first appear.
Fall is also seed-collecting season. Gather mature seeds from native plants you already grow and spread them elsewhere on your property. Phillips does this with plants she wants to expand into other parts of her yard. Some seeds, including those of many milkweeds native to cold-winter regions, need a period of low temperatures before they germinate. Plant them in fall, Phillips says, and winter will handle the chilling for you.
Stop spraying just in case
Treat the problem, not the calendar. Pesticides and herbicides should answer a specific need—not arrive automatically with the turning leaves.
Broad-spectrum insecticides don’t distinguish between a mosquito and the many insects you want to keep. Costanzo recommends using them “in response to something rather than proactively,” and only when truly necessary. “They kill every insect,” she says. “They’re not specific.”
Herbicides create a different problem: They eliminate clover, violets, dandelions, and other plants that can provide food for insects. “Your lawn doesn’t have to look like a carpet,” Costanzo says. Keep turf where you need it for recreation, but consider allowing more plant diversity elsewhere.
That doesn’t mean never treating a genuine infestation or health threat. Identify the problem first, then use the most targeted approach available rather than spraying preventively across the entire property. Follow the label exactly. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency recommends using pesticides only when necessary and treating only the specific area that needs treatment.
Also reconsider the assumption that every nibble is damage. A chewed leaf can be evidence that a native plant is feeding the ecosystem exactly as intended. When Costanzo notices signs of hungry insects, she reminds herself: “I’m supporting the ecosystem. I’m so glad these insects are finding a resource here.” A few holes usually won’t kill a healthy plant, she adds—and flawless foliage isn’t much use to a caterpillar.
These changes benefit the gardener, too. In an August 2026 National Wildlife Federation survey of more than 1,000 wildlife gardeners, 96% said the practice had improved their mental health, and 93% reported physical-health benefits. Respondents most often described the joy of seeing wildlife, a lift in mood, and the satisfaction of knowing they were making the world a little better. Unlike many long-term environmental problems, the payoff can appear surprisingly quickly. “Within a season, you’re seeing the wildlife come,” Phillips says. “You’re seeing the butterflies. You’re seeing the birds; you’re hearing the birdsong.”
For Eierman, that ability to take action—and see it rewarded—is part of the appeal. “There are very few things we have control over in our lives—particularly the ones that give us a lot of pleasure,” she says. “This is one. The effort that you put into it comes back to you in a big way.”

HANGZHOU, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The global digital trade sector has demonstrated resilience amid multiple external pressures, with export value hitting 7.75 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025, a 7.1 percent year-on-year increase, according to a report released Thursday.
The export value accounted for 22.2 percent of total exports of global goods and services, up 2.6 percentage points from 2021, continuing to outpace total global trade growth, said the report titled "Global Digital Trade Development Report 2026" unveiled at the ongoing fifth Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province.
The report presents the scale and structure of global digital trade, technological transformation and innovative practices, while exploring future industry trends.
Digitally delivered trade exports reached approximately 5.26 trillion U.S. dollars, representing 67.9 percent of the total, with cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence services leading the growth. Meanwhile, digitally ordered trade exports stood at 2.49 trillion U.S. dollars, according to the report.
For the first time, the report compiles 20 global digital trade innovation achievements from economies at different development stages, spanning diverse scenarios including AI empowerment, cross-border payments, green trade and digital intellectual property.
China's digitally deliverable service trade value expanded at an average annual rate of 11.2 percent between 2016 and 2025, outpacing the global average by 1.8 percentage points.
The fifth Global Digital Trade Expo, an event dedicated to promoting digital trade and industrial cooperation, is being held from Sept. 23 to 27.
The expo features 170,000 square meters of exhibition space, with international exhibitors accounting for over 20 percent of the total. The number of overseas pavilions has already exceeded the combined total of all previous editions.
According to a guideline on boosting reform and innovative development of digital trade released in November 2024, China expects the share of digitally deliverable service trade in total service trade to exceed 45 percent by 2029 and 50 percent by 2035. ■

Interview: China rising as global robotics powerhouse, industry leader says
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:51:08 CST
23:51:08 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China is emerging as a global powerhouse in robotics, driven by the rapid adoption of robots across industries, a large and increasingly diverse domestic market and a national strategy supporting the development of robotics and artificial intelligence, said Susanne Bieller, Secretary General of the International Federation of Robotics (IFR).
"From our last visits to China, it was really impressive to see the speed of adoption and the interest across a broad range of industries, but also among people," Bieller told Xinhua in an exclusive interview on Tuesday, coinciding with the release of the IFR's latest World Robotics report.
The IFR, based in Frankfurt, Germany, represents robotics manufacturers and research institutes worldwide and provides industry data and analysis on the development of robotics. It publishes the World Robotics report annually, tracking global trends in industrial robot adoption.
According to the IFR's newly released World Robotics 2026 report, China installed 354,000 industrial robots in 2025, up 20 percent from the previous year and accounting for 59 percent of global installations. The figure was nearly 60,000 units higher than the previous annual record, further consolidating China's position as the world's largest market for industrial robots. Its vast manufacturing base continues to generate strong demand for robots across a wide range of applications.
Bieller said several factors were driving demand for robots in China, including industrial modernization, demographic changes and the country's industrial policy and national strategy for robotics.
"There are certain drivers for the demand for robots in China. First of all, the industrialization of the industry and the need for more technology to replace or encounter the demographic shift the country is facing in the years to come," she said.
"There is also the strong industrial policy and the national strategy for robotics, bringing robotics into the market in China. That's driving the demand, as it really looks into which application areas and industries need robots and how to best foster those industries to take up the technology."
Bieller said China's development of robotics was also closely linked to its broader effort to modernize its industrial system. "There is a well-thought-through strategy behind that, and companies are embracing the technology and looking into new ways to use new technologies, as we see from the humanoids right now," she said.
According to Bieller, the IFR sees China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) as placing greater emphasis on technological self-reliance, the modernization of traditional industries and the application of artificial intelligence in the physical world.
The Chinese industrial robot market also has considerable room for further growth. IFR projections indicate that the market could maintain average annual growth of around 5 percent to 10 percent through 2029.
China's domestic robot suppliers have also strengthened their position in the market. Their installations rose 15 percent in 2025 to 195,000 units. According to the latest IFR data, domestic suppliers accounted for about 55 percent of the Chinese market in 2025.
"Chinese companies have grown in competitiveness over the last decade, and the domestic share has increased dramatically," Bieller said. She noted that the growth was not confined to a small number of industries, with "huge opportunities" in sectors that have not invested as heavily in automation as automotive.
She cited logistics as one area with strong potential and said vehicles beyond passenger cars, as well as food, textiles and paper, could also see further growth in robot adoption. The characteristics of the Chinese market are also encouraging manufacturers to develop robots tailored to specific industrial needs, she said.
"Chinese companies have learned to develop robots that are just fit for the purpose," Bieller said, calling this a strength of Chinese suppliers in developing solutions tailored to specific markets and applications.
The development of China's robotics industry is also reflected in the changing role of manufacturing companies.
During a visit to Shenzhen in April, Bieller visited electric vehicle manufacturer XPeng's factory and saw robots being used in vehicle production. She said XPeng was also developing quadruped and humanoid robots.
"They are a customer of robots for their electric vehicle factory, but at the same time they are developing their own quadruped and humanoid robots," she said. ■

Asian Games | Day 5: Japan shines in table tennis and swimming as China's gold rush continues
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:50:56 CST
23:50:56 KST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Asian Games witnessed a day where host nation Japan delivered historic breakthroughs, while China maintained its gold medal march on Thursday.
Japan ended China's quest for a ninth consecutive title in the men's table tennis team final following a narrow 3-2 win, clinching its first gold medal in the event since 1966.
The team tie was ultimately decided in the fifth match, where 19-year-old Wen Ruibo fell 3-1 to fellow teenager Sora Matsushima. Earlier in the contest, China faced strong resistance from Japan's Tomokazu Harimoto. Harimoto defeated Wen 3-1 and later swept Wang Chuqin 3-0 to level the overall score at 2-2.
However, China women's table tennis team quickly restored order, sweeping Japan 3-0 to claim the women's team title. Sun Yingsha, Wang Manyu, and Kuai Man all secured victories in their respective matches.
Japan also shone in the pool as Shin Ohashi shattered the men's 200m breaststroke world record in 2:04.83, trimming 0.65 seconds off Qin Haiyang's previous mark. His compatriot Kotomi Kato triumphed in the women's 200m breaststroke in 2:22.57.
China's young swimmers made waves as 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo claimed his sixth Asiad gold, winning the men's 800m freestyle in a Games-record 7:42.49. He then helped China win the men's 4x100m freestyle relay with an Asian-record 3:10.60, ahead of South Korea and Japan. China also dominated the women's 4x200m freestyle relay in 7:49.37, beating Japan by 10.16 seconds.
Wu Qingfeng won the women's 50m freestyle in a Games-record 23.98, missing the Asian record by just 0.01 seconds. Bahrain's Mikhail Arkhangelskiy won the men's 50m butterfly with an Asian-record 22.91, followed by Japan's Shoon Mitsunaga and China's Wang Changhao. This was also Bahrain's first gold at the Games.
Also in the pool, China beat Japan to win the women's water polo title.
China reclaimed the Asiad badminton women's team title with a 3-0 sweep of Japan, ending a gold-medal drought that spanned the last two editions of the Games. In the men's team final, China suffered a 3-2 defeat to Indonesia, missing out on the gold medal.
Out on the water, China claimed two golds and two silvers in the canoe sprint. In the women's kayak double 500m, Yin Mengdie and Yu Shimeng took gold with a time of 1:45.010, finishing 3.130 seconds ahead of Kazakhstan. Meanwhile, Ji Bowen and Wu Shengyue secured the men's canoe double 500m title in 1:40.741, beating Uzbekistan by 2.137 seconds. In rowing, China won nine out of 14 gold medals on offer.
China's Wu Zhifan and Liang Zhenglan finished 1-2 in the women's mountain bike cross-country. Since the event became an official Asian Games sport at Bangkok 1998, China has won all available gold medals in the women's cross-country.
Across other venues, Chinese shooters added two gold medals to the tally, winning the men's 10m air pistol team and the mixed skeet team.
In gymnastics, China's Qiu Qiyuan won the women's uneven bars, while Lan Xingyu topped the men's rings. In weightlifting, China's Yang Yang won the men's 60kg title, while He Yueji broke the men's 65kg snatch world record but settled for a silver.
In athletics, China's Huang Yingying and Li Yi took silver and bronze in the women's triple jump respectively. The gold medal went to Uzbekistan's Sharifa Davronova with a personal best of 14.35 meters.
China secured a 1-2 finish in men's discus throw, with Aduduaini Tuergong winning gold with 64.26m and Wu Nanjun taking silver with 61.58m.
Bahrain's Winfred Yavi claimed the women's 10,000m title in 32:39.18. ■

Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:50:29 UTC
23:50:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
On 30 March, Kosovo’s government approved the deployment of Kosovo Security Forces personnel to Gaza as part of the proposed International Stabilisation Force (ISF) backed by the United States and envisioned under President Donald J. Trump’s peace plan.
Then on 7 September, Pristina formally signed an agreement to join the United Nations-mandated force, according to a statement posted on social media by the Board of Peace.
The decision places Kosovo at the centre of a wider international effort to establish security and support reconstruction in Gaza, while also raising questions about the mission’s role, its legal and political implications, and Kosovo’s ties with the United States and Israel.
Kosovo's strategic calculation
Kosovo’s decision to join the Board of Peace and the ISF underscores Pristina’s commitment to the United States. The small Muslim-majority Balkan state has long regarded Washington as its most important international partner.
This is particularly because of the US role in supporting Kosovo during and after the Kosovo War (1998–99) and in backing its independence, which the US under the George W. Bush administration formally recognised in February 2008 as one of the first countries in the world to do so.
But Dr Ramadan Ilazi, head of research at the Kosovar Centre for Security Studies (KCSS), said Kosovo’s decision should not be understood solely as an attempt to please Washington.
He described the motivation as a combination of principle, pragmatism, and strategic interest, arguing that Kosovo also wants to demonstrate that it can contribute to international security after more than two decades as a recipient of international assistance.
“There is now a strong desire to demonstrate that it can also be a contributor. Kosovo remains grateful for the international engagement that helped end the war in 1999, supported post-war reconstruction, and continues to provide security through KFOR. Participating in the ISF is therefore also a way of expressing solidarity and giving something back,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Lily Lynch, editor-in-chief of the Balkanist Magazine, holds that participating in Trump’s initiative sends a message that Kosovo’s relationship with the United States is intended to remain strong regardless of which political party controls the White House.
This is quite significant given concerns in Kosovo that a Trump administration could potentially be more accommodating toward Serbia.
“Kosovo decided to join the Board of Peace and [ISF] as a demonstration of its fidelity to the United States. The decision indicates that regardless of who is in the White House, Kosovo's commitment to its relationship with the United States is ironclad,” she told The New Arab.
“Some foreign policy commentators see Kosovo's existence as an independent state as a product of Clintonite foreign policy and liberal internationalism; there was concern among some in Kosovo that a Trump presidency would give Serbia an advantage,” added Lynch.
“But participation in the Board of Peace and ISF suggests that Kosovo wants to make clear that its commitment to a strong relationship with America transcends party politics.”
The Kosovo-Gaza comparison and its limits
Prime Minister Albin Kurti has framed the decision through Kosovo’s own experience with international peacekeeping. In announcing the government’s support for the deployment, Kurti pointed to the fact that Kosovo itself has benefited from international forces since 1999.
The analogy is also linked to the continued presence of NATO’s KFOR mission, which has provided security in Kosovo for more than two-and-a-half decades.
Lynch sees this as a deliberate attempt by Kurti to explain why Kosovo should now contribute to an international mission elsewhere, based on the argument that international forces helped provide security in Kosovo, and therefore Kosovo can now use its own experience and capabilities to assist another population.
Kosovo’s Security Forces have developed expertise in areas including search-and-rescue operations and demining, which policymakers in Pristina say could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
But the comparison between Kosovo and Gaza is also one of the most contested aspects of the decision because the circumstances surrounding NATO’s intervention in Kosovo and the proposed Gaza mission differ in fundamental ways.
In Kosovo, international intervention followed a war between Serbian forces and the Kosovo Albanian population and ultimately preceded Kosovo’s declaration of independence in 2008. Questions remain over whether Kosovo’s experience can straightforwardly serve as a model for the Gaza initiative. This distinction is important because Kurti’s comparison is not simply historical. It is also political.
Jelena Novakov, a Belgrade-based geopolitical analyst who writes for Kosovo Online, said the comparison is understandable given Kosovo’s own experience of conflict and international protection, but argued that it also contains a significant contradiction.
“For a young country that is still struggling with international recognition and, in a way, remains a recipient of international assistance through KFOR, this represents a significant demonstration of improved stability, even if largely symbolic,” she told The New Arab.
“What is debatable is the decision to participate in an initiative launched by the country that is largely responsible for the devastation in Gaza, after Kosovo itself experienced aggression,” Novakov added.
Dr Ilazi noted that Kosovo’s experience could provide a point of reference but cautioned against treating it as a model for Gaza.
“Kosovo and Gaza have different histories and political circumstances. Our experience cannot tell Palestinians what their future should look like. It can, however, remind us that people need both physical security and a say over how they are governed,” he said.
He also pointed to Kosovo’s own experience with international administration, arguing that this provided another lesson that could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
“We also know the frustrations of international administration, as we had our own share of that with [the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo (UNMIK)], and these include decisions made far from the people affected, unclear accountability, and arrangements described as temporary that become very difficult to change. That experience is worth sharing too,” Dr Ilazi said.
Kurti appears to be carefully framing his message to reassure Kosovar Albanians who may be uneasy about Kosovo’s involvement in Trump’s Gaza initiative. With 4,600 KFOR troops stationed in Kosovo, at least as of earlier this year, the southeastern European country continues to depend on international peacekeeping troops.
“Kurti is trying to say, ‘international peacekeeping troops have helped keep us safe, so now we can use our own unique expertise to help others.’ Kurti is also undoubtedly trying to communicate Kosovo’s unique value to Trump’s putative peace effort. Of course, all of this would be far more meaningful if Trump’s plan for Gaza actually benefited the people of Gaza the way NATO helped Kosovar Albanians,” Lynch explained to The New Arab.
"I would say this is the main problem with Kurti's framing: He’s right that international forces helped the [Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA)] force Serbian troops out of Kosovo in 1999. This was a prerequisite for Kosovo’s eventual declaration of independence in 2008. That’s the difference here,” she noted.
“By Kurti’s own analogy, what’s happening with Trump's Gaza peace plan is much more akin to what would have happened in 1999 if NATO troops had helped Serbia retain control of Kosovo and had helped Serbian forces keep Albanians in submission.”
By invoking Kosovo’s experience with international protection, the country’s prime minister is presenting participation in the ISF as an extension of a principle that Kosovars know personally, which is the idea that international forces can provide security to a population emerging from conflict.
Whether that principle applies to Gaza, however, remains a matter of significant disagreement.
Between Palestinian sympathy and strategic necessity
The decision is also likely to be viewed through the lens of Kosovo’s domestic politics. With many citizens of Kosovo sympathetic to Palestinians, there is tension between public sentiment and Pristina’s strategic interests.
Kosovars who oppose Trump’s Gaza plan or support the Palestinian cause may nevertheless view participation as a necessary cost of maintaining the United States as Kosovo’s closest ally, which can be understood as a limitation faced by a small state.
Novakov said, however, that the issue has so far generated little sustained public debate in Kosovo. She attributed this partly to the country’s wider political and economic problems, including prolonged political instability, inflation, stalled negotiations with Belgrade and the EU, deteriorating relations with Washington, and the legal proceedings involving former KLA leaders.
“There is currently no large-scale public conversation about this issue in Kosovo,” Novakov told The New Arab. “There is support for Palestine among Kosovars, but the government’s alignment with the US is rarely raised as one of the main issues during demonstrations.”
Dr Ilazi cautioned against assuming that political support for the deployment necessarily translates into broad public support for every aspect of the mission. Although he stated that the parliament’s 89-0 vote on 17 April to approve the government’s earlier decision to deploy Kosovo’s forces to the ISF “shows broad political support for participation,” Dr Ilazi stressed that it does “not tell us how the public will respond to every task the mission might undertake, and I would avoid claiming a public majority without reliable polling.”
As he explained, much will depend on what people see unfolding in Gaza.
“Clearing unexploded ordnance, helping aid reach families and making neighbourhoods safer are contributions the government can explain clearly. Public confidence would be harder to sustain if Kosovo’s soldiers became associated with restricting Palestinian movement or protecting arrangements that leave people displaced,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Kosovo has relatively little ability to influence major international conflicts and may therefore prioritise maintaining relationships with powerful allies, chiefly Washington. The result is a complicated political position in which criticism of the Gaza policy can coexist with acceptance of Kosovo’s participation, according to Lynch.
“The majority of Albanians are sympathetic to Palestinians, though there are some very vocal Zionist Albanians as well. But even those who support Palestine and deplore Trump’s Gaza plan are likely to accept the Kosovo government's decision to participate as a necessary cost of keeping America as their closest ally. The prevailing thought in Kosovo is ‘we’re a small country, there’s not much we can do to shape major world events and distant conflicts, so we will accept this arrangement because this is what our closest ally wants,’” she told The New Arab.
For Novakov, the calculation is ultimately rooted in Kosovo’s continuing reliance on international support. Around 100 countries have yet to recognise Kosovo’s independence, including five European Union members (Cyprus, Greece, Romania, Slovakia, and Spain), while Russia and China remain opposed to its statehood.
With Brussels’ focus increasingly shifting towards Ukraine, she argues, maintaining a close relationship with Washington remains particularly important for Pristina.
Questions over responsibility and accountability
Beyond public opinion, the deployment raises questions about legal and reputational responsibility. There are valid concerns to raise about the possibility that Kosovo’s involvement could expose its personnel or government to scrutiny if the wider operation were associated with forced displacement, the consolidation of Israeli control over Gaza, or other conduct that violates international law.
Lynch argues that these concerns deserve particular attention because of Kosovo’s own experience with international justice and accountability. The recent conviction and 25-year sentence of former Kosovo political and military leader Hashim Thaçi on war crimes charges has already placed questions of wartime responsibility at the centre of public debate.
Against that background, participation in a controversial international operation could create additional scrutiny if Kosovar personnel became associated with actions later determined to be unlawful.
Dr Ilazi distinguished between the legal and reputational risks Kosovo could face.
“I would also separate legal responsibility from reputational damage. Establishing legal responsibility requires evidence about particular actions and circumstances. Public trust can be lost much earlier if a mission is seen as facilitating abuse or denying Palestinians control over their future,” he told The New Arab.
He also argued that Kosovo should establish clear limits on what its personnel can be asked to do.
“Those restrictions need to shape operational planning, with legal review, reporting to the Assembly and a credible option to suspend or withdraw the contingent. We should not leave individual soldiers to resolve political ambiguities that their government failed to address,” commented Dr Ilazi, who also argued that the perspectives of Palestinians themselves should receive greater attention in discussions about the force.
“One issue that deserves more attention is how Palestinians themselves view the force. Most discussions focus on Washington’s intentions and the calculations of contributing countries. Yet the people expected to live alongside this mission need meaningful influence over the arrangements it supports. From Kosovo’s experience, we should understand how much that matters,” he argued.
A new test for Kosovo's foreign policy
Ultimately, Kosovo’s decision to participate in the Gaza stabilisation effort highlights the difficult choices facing a small state whose security and international standing have been closely connected to the United States for many years.
For Kurti’s government, participation offers an opportunity to demonstrate continued commitment to Washington and to portray Kosovo as a country capable of contributing to international security rather than simply receiving international assistance.
At the same time, the decision places Kosovo between competing pressures, including domestic sympathy for Palestinians, its strategic partnership with the United States, questions about the nature of the Gaza mission, and concerns about legal and reputational consequences.
As the deployment moves forward, the central question will be whether Kosovo can maintain its strong relationship with Washington while avoiding becoming entangled in the contentious political and legal disputes surrounding Gaza.
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics.

9-year-old Israeli boy dies after rare brain-eating amoeba infection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:50:18 UTC
23:50:18 KST

A nine-year-old boy who was hospitalized earlier this month after contracting a rare infection caused by a brain-eating amoeba died on Thursday at Rambam Medical Center in northern Israel.
The boy, Baruch Neria from Pardes Hanna-Karkur, had been hospitalized in serious condition for about two weeks while under sedation and on a ventilator. According to the Health Ministry, an epidemiological investigation found that he had swum at Kursi Beach on the Sea of Galilee, a lake in northern Israel, a week before his hospitalization.
Neria's brain infection was caused by Naegleria fowleri, a microscopic amoeba found primarily in warm freshwater. In extremely rare cases, it can cause a severe central nervous system infection.
Only about 500 cases of infection have been documented worldwide, according to the Health Ministry, but the disease has a fatality rate of about 97 percent.
Three cases have been recorded in Israel in recent years. In July 2024, a 26-year-old man died and a 10-year-old boy was left in a vegetative state after exposure to the amoeba at a water park near the Sea of Galilee. In 2022, a resident of northern Israel died after becoming infected in a freshwater reservoir in the north.
Most infections occur in the United States, but the disease is rare even there: 31 cases were reported between 2012 and 2021, while 151 infections were reported between 1962 and 2020, of which only four patients survived.
Last week, a teenager from North Carolina and an eight-year-old girl from Louisiana died from infections caused by the amoeba.
Climate change could lead to an increase in infections, as the amoeba is surviving in places where it had not previously been observed. 
For example, an infection was reported in Minnesota, a relatively cool state where the amoeba would not ordinarily be expected to survive. Rising temperatures can also lower water levels in reservoirs, resulting in higher concentrations of the amoeba in the water and increasing the risk of infection.
How does infection occur?
Infection can occur when water containing the amoeba enters through the nose, allowing the amoeba to travel to the brain. The disease is not caused by drinking water and is not transmitted from person to person.
According to the Health Ministry, to reduce the risk when swimming in warm freshwater, people should avoid getting water into their noses as much as possible, particularly when jumping, diving or submerging their heads. They can close their nostrils or use a nose clip. They should also avoid digging into or stirring up the bottom in shallow water, where the amoeba may be present in higher concentrations.
When should you seek medical attention?
After exposure to warm freshwater, medical attention should be sought if symptoms such as fever, severe headache, nausea or vomiting develop. Symptoms such as a stiff neck (difficulty bending the neck forward), confusion, unusual drowsiness or altered consciousness require urgent medical attention.
The Health Ministry advises telling medical staff about any water exposure when seeking care. Although the disease is extremely rare, it can cause rapid deterioration.

‘Israel is destroying the two-state solution’: Abbas alleges in UN address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:50:06 UTC
23:50:06 KST

Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas addressed the United Nations General Assembly by prerecorded video Thursday after the United States denied him a visa to attend the annual gathering in New York for the second consecutive year.
Speaking from his office in Ramallah in the West Bank, Abbas opened his address by criticizing the Trump administration's decision and calling on Washington to reverse its restrictions on Palestinian officials.
“Preventing me from coming to address the General Assembly is a violation of UN procedures,” Abbas said. He called on the United States to “lift the sanctions and return to dialogue and respect” and to discussions aimed at advancing a two-state solution.
The General Assembly voted 152-3, with four abstentions, last week to allow Abbas to address the gathering remotely after he was denied entry. The United States, Israel and Paraguay opposed the measure.
Abbas used much of his speech to sharply condemn Israel's conduct in the Gaza Strip and West Bank.
“In Gaza, the Palestinian people are being subjected to killing, destruction, starvation, attempted displacement and a genocidal war that has created a major humanitarian catastrophe,” Abbas said.
Israel rejects accusations that its military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide, saying it targets terrorist groups and operates in accordance with international law.
Abbas also accused Israel of accelerating settlement expansion in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, which Palestinians seek as the capital of a future state.
“Israel's policies, in violation of international law, are destroying the two-state solution,” Abbas said. “The danger is growing and threatens the existence of the Palestinian people on their land.”
He characterized Israeli policies in Gaza and the West Bank as a “colonial plot” intended to force Palestinians from their land and warned world leaders against allowing what he described as another Nakba, the Arabic term for “catastrophe” used by Palestinians to describe the mass displacement that accompanied Israel's establishment and the 1948 Arab-Israeli war.
“Do not allow violent gangs, with the approval of the Israeli army, to burn communities,” Abbas said, referring to attacks by extremist Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
Settler violence and settlement expansion have drawn growing international criticism. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said this week that settler violence was rising at an alarming rate and reiterated the UN's position that Israeli settlements in the West Bank violate international law. Israel disputes some international legal characterizations of the territory and says the status of settlements should be resolved through negotiations.
Barred from New York for second year
The U.S. State Department rejected Abbas' visa request for this year's General Assembly after taking the same step in 2025, again forcing the 90-year-old Palestinian leader to participate remotely.
The United States, as host country of the UN headquarters, generally has obligations to facilitate access for foreign delegations attending UN meetings, though Washington retains authority over visas and has imposed restrictions in some cases involving officials with whom it has serious disputes.
The Trump administration has accused the Palestinian Authority and Palestine Liberation Organization of undermining peace efforts, including through attempts to secure international recognition and pursue cases against Israel in international courts. Palestinian officials have rejected the U.S. restrictions.
The visa dispute comes as Abbas faces mounting pressure over the Palestinian Authority's political future and the question of who would govern Gaza under any long-term settlement of the conflict.
The Palestinian Authority exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank under agreements reached with Israel in the 1990s. Hamas seized control of Gaza from Abbas' Fatah movement in 2007.
The Israeli-Palestinian conflict has again emerged as one of the dominant issues at this year's General Assembly, where a series of leaders have criticized Israel over Gaza, West Bank settlements and Palestinian statehood.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan used his address to condemn Israel's conduct in Gaza and urge greater international pressure on Israel while calling for broader recognition of a Palestinian state.
Other leaders, including Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, have also accused Israel of genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly rejected that charge, saying Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack and subsequent military operations are central to understanding the war and accusing critics of ignoring the threats it faces.
Abbas' address came hours before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was scheduled to speak before the General Assembly, setting up sharply contrasting presentations of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict from the two leaders.
Netanyahu is expected to defend Israel's conduct and address threats facing the country, including Iran, amid an unusually brief visit to New York and plans for protests surrounding his appearance.

Was Hitler behind niece's death? Documents raise questions about alibi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:49:50 UTC
23:49:50 KST

Hitler's possible role in niece's death under scrutiny after documents raise questions about alibi, report says
Newly unearthed records in a Munich archive have cast doubt on Adolf Hitler's whereabouts at the time of his niece's suspicious 1931 death, according to news magazine Der Spiegel.
Hitler's unusually close and controlling relationship with his niece, Geli Raubal, has long been the subject of speculation and rumor, and newspaper reports at the time suggested that Hitler may have played a role in her death.
Raubal died from a gunshot wound to the chest from a pistol belonging to Hitler, in what was officially determined to be a suicide.
According to the official account, Hitler's personal servant, Georg Winter, discovered the 23-year-old Raubal's body on the floor inside her locked room in Hitler's apartment in Munich on Sept. 19, 1931, a Saturday.
Hitler, who at the time was a prominent far-right extremist but had not yet seized power in Germany, was away in the city of Nuremberg that day, giving him what appeared to be a strong alibi.
But according to an article in Der Spiegel, historian Harald Sandner recently discovered documents in archives in Munich casting doubt on that account — and raising questions about whether Nazi sympathizers in the police may have falsified records to protect Hitler.
 Two death notices and an entry in an official local death registry all put the date of the discovery of Raubal's body to Sept. 18, a full day earlier, when Hitler was known to still have been in Munich.
 
Strange relationship
Hitler's relationship with Raubal, the daughter of his half-sister Angela Raubal, was the subject of intense speculation. Some contemporaries believed Hitler had been abusive or had pursued a sexual relationship with his relative.
Hitler reportedly strictly controlled nearly every aspect of Raubal's life after she moved to Munich in 1927.
She reportedly argued intensely with Hitler just before her death after Hitler refused to allow her to move to Vienna.
Sandner told the magazine the discrepancy in the documents over the date of Raubal's death may point toward a cover-up by the police, though there is no decisive proof.
Days after Raubal's death, a left-wing Munich newspaper reported Hitler had been in a heated argument with his niece, that injuries had been found on her body and that Nazi officials held crisis meetings regarding how to present the matter to the public.
Other newspapers suggested Hitler might have had Raubal killed — or killed her himself — though the Nazi leader publicly denied those allegations in a statement.

France says ICC warrant posed no obstacle to Netanyahu overflight
PARIS, Sept 24 - France defended its decision to let Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's plane cross its airspace en route to the United Nations on Thursday, saying international law did not require action despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against him over alleged war crimes.
France is a signatory of the ICC's founding Rome Statute and is formally bound to cooperate with the court, including arresting suspects who enter its territory. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux told reporters the clearance was "in full conformity with international law".
"The Rome Statute does not impose any obligations regarding overflights of its territory by a state plane which has a passenger who is targeted by an arrest warrant," Confavreux said.
Netanyahu is unable to travel to many countries because of an International Criminal Court arrest warrants issued against him and his then-defense minister as well as the then-military commander of Hamas in 2024.
Israel rejects the jurisdiction of the Hague-based court and denies war crimes in Gaza, where it waged a military campaign it says was aimed at eliminating Hamas following the deadly attack on Israel by the militant Palestinian group on October 7, 2023. It is contesting the warrants against Netanyahu and his former defence chief Yoav Gallant.
Flight-tracking app Flightradar24 showed Netanyahu's plane flew over Greece, Italy and France. A spokesperson for Italy's Foreign Ministry said they could not immediately answer whether Israeli authorities had sought permission for an overflight.
Last year Netanyahu flew a circuitous route to New York to skirt the airspace of several European countries, including France, media reported at the time.
Washington has announced a campaign to isolate the court. US President Donald Trump this week urged ICC members to quit what he called an "out of control institution". France has said it condemns the threats against the court.
Netanyahu was making an unusually short visit to the US for his address to world leaders at the UN General Assembly. He arrived in New York around 9 a.m. ET (1300 GMT) and was expected to fly back later in the day after delivering his speech. REUTERS

UK government spending with the domestic defense industry rose 3.2% to a record £34.1 billion ($45 billion) in 2025-26, the government said Thursday.
In a statement, the Defense Ministry said investment in the UK defense sector reached its highest level since records began.
Direct spending with smaller firms also increased to £1.3 billion ($1.7 billion) annually, the ministry said.
Northern Ireland recorded the largest percentage increase in defense spending, up 63%, followed by the East of England at 24.7% and the East Midlands at 21%, as investment reached communities across the UK, it added.

The ministry said the figures build on the Defense Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion ($393 billion) to UK defense over the next four years.

Marineland dolphin dies at Spain aquarium in latest death after rescue

Marineland dolphin dies at aquarium in Spain in latest death after rescue
A dolphin rescued from the troubled theme park Marineland Canada has died weeks after it was taken to an aquarium in Spain. Several other animals from Marineland, including three beluga whales, have died at their new homes in recent weeks.
Oceanogràfic València, Europe's largest aquarium, said Thursday that the dolphin, known as Echo, arrived from Marineland with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, including blindness, that "required individualized attention."
Echo was taken to the facility's medical pool and cared for by veterinarians after beginning to exhibit respiratory problems and difficulty swallowing, the aquarium said. Her health "deteriorated rapidly" throughout Wednesday before she died that night, the aquarium said.
The aquarium said its staff and pathologists from a nearby university will conduct an autopsy to determine the cause of death.
Echo is one of four dolphins rescued from Marineland Canada. The facility said the other animals are "still progressing favorably" under the care of Oceanogràfic València staff.
Another beluga whale rescued from Marineland, known as Jelly Bean, died at Oceanogràfic València in July. The facility said it is still investigating what caused the whale's death.
Marineland Canada shut down in 2024 after its owners died, but remained in possession of its animals, including dolphins and 30 beluga whales. In October 2025, the theme park warned it would have to euthanize the animals if they couldn't be relocated.
In July 2026, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced an international relocation plan that would send 28 beluga whales to accredited aquariums in the United States. The other two beluga whales were sent to Oceanogràfic València.
Several other animals rescued from Marineland Canada have died in recent weeks. Three beluga whales taken from Marineland to the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago died within a month of each other, raising questions about how medically fragile the animals were when they were rescued. A fourth beluga whale, a longtime member of the Shedd's beluga pod, also recently died at the aquarium.
Even before Marineland Canada closed, it was under scrutiny for its treatment of animals. Twenty whales, including 19 belugas, have died there since 2019. Inspectors previously declared that all animals in the theme park were in distress due to poor water quality. In a letter to American aquariums, NOAA noted that the whales from Marineland "are health-compromised."
Staff at the Shedd Aquarium are also conducting investigations and medical exams to determine the whales' cause of death.

People & Power
Forever Chemicals: Ground Zero
Pervasive, persistent and poisonous: How one US company helped pollute the world with forever chemicals.
When scientists discovered a new class of chemicals in the 1940s, they knew they had struck gold. Polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS, are nearly indestructible – resistant to heat, cold, oil and water. They’ve been used in everything from cookware to cosmetics and from pizza boxes to pesticides. But they also don’t biodegrade in the environment, and some of them are toxic. US corporate giant 3M was the first to mass-manufacture PFAS and allowed them to pollute the environment around its facilities for decades despite being aware of their harmful effects.

Saudi Arabia 'threatens to quit Quad' amid US-Sudan UN visa row

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia 'threatens to quit Quad' amid US-Sudan UN visa row
Saudi Arabia has threatened to withdraw from the Quad mechanism for Sudan amid tensions over Washington's refusal to grant Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan a visa to attend the United Nations General Assembly, according to a report on Thursday.
Washington's refusal to issue the visa was part of an apparent attempt to pressure al-Burhan into accepting a ceasefire proposal, The Africa Report reported.
According to the report, Riyadh criticised Washington's actions, accusing US officials of engaging in "political blackmail" and attempting to besiege Sudan's leadership.
The dispute reportedly prompted Saudi Arabia to threaten to withdraw from the Quad, a diplomatic grouping aimed at mediating an end to Sudan's war that also includes the US, UAE and Egypt.
Riyadh also reportedly threatened to reject decisions "that have thwarted diplomatic efforts and undermined joint action from within".
The report said Saudi criticism was followed by condemnation from UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and UN member states, amid accusations that Washington was exploiting its position as the UN host country to settle political scores.
However, the Saudi government has not publicly confirmed that it threatened to leave the Quad or announced any decision to withdraw.
Neither the Sudanese government nor the US State Department has commented on the report regarding the alleged Saudi threat.
The claims emerged as the Quad met in New York on Wednesday alongside the Quintet, which comprises the UN, African Union, European Union, Arab League and Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the regional body covering the Greater Horn of Africa.
Reports first emerged on Tuesday that Washington had withheld a visa from al-Burhan, who had been scheduled to address the General Assembly in New York on Thursday.
Al-Burhan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, in a war that has killed tens of thousands of people and triggered the world's largest displacement and hunger crises.
He has addressed the General Assembly twice since the conflict began.
According to reports, Washington made the issuance of al-Burhan's visa conditional on his acceptance of a 90-day ceasefire proposed by US Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos.
AFP, citing two diplomatic sources, also reported that Washington had refused to issue the visa. One source described the move as a "clear violation of the UN's agreement with the US", while another said the visa had been "conditioned" on al-Burhan accepting the three-month truce.
Meanwhile, Reuters reported that Sudan's UN ambassador, Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith, had written to Guterres requesting the UN's "immediate intervention" with US authorities.
In a statement, Stephane Dujarric, a spokesman for Guterres, said the UN chief was "deeply concerned" that the visa had reportedly not been issued.
He said the UN Secretariat had urged the US, as the host country, to ensure visas were issued in accordance with its obligations under the UN Headquarters Agreement and in time for al-Burhan to participate in the General Assembly.
The State Department issued a statement on Tuesday questioning al-Burhan's legitimacy but did not directly address whether his UN visa was being withheld.
Spokesman Tommy Pigott said neither the Sudanese army nor the RSF "nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan".
He added that the US would "seek to raise the cost of continued conflict on all belligerents".
Sudan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded on Wednesday by calling on Washington to engage positively with the country's government.
Any peace initiative, it said, must "be grounded in respect for Sudan's sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity, and legitimate national institutions".
"It must also address the root causes of the war's continuation – foremost among them, negative foreign interference," the ministry added.
Dispute over US ceasefire proposal
Introduced in June, the US plan called for an immediate 90-day humanitarian truce, followed by negotiations towards a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led transition.
However, the Sudanese army has objected to the proposal, particularly over the terms governing the RSF's withdrawal from territory it controls.
The army has demanded that the RSF withdraw from all cities it has occupied since May 2023, rather than making the more limited withdrawals outlined in the US proposal.
Al-Burhan has also rejected what Sudanese officials describe as a take-it-or-leave-it approach, arguing that previous pauses in fighting allowed the RSF to regroup.
The disagreement spilled over into the UN General Assembly as al-Burhan prepared to travel to New York.
Washington has also refused visas to Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas and some members of Iran's delegation to the UN.

AI generated
PHILADELPHIA – While US President Donald Trump is “Chinamaxxing”, rolling out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s first White House visit in more than a decade, US analysts are wondering where the US will draw a line.

“China’s sovereignty, security and development interests cannot be violated, and four red lines – the Taiwan question, democracy and human rights, development paths and systems, and development rights – cannot be challenged,” he said in a Sept 23 op-ed for the official People’s Daily.
These are well-rehearsed Chinese positions that are often aired before, during and after visits by key US officials. Xi had outlined them himself in November 2024 when he met then President Joe Biden in Lima.
If those are China’s red lines, what is the US asking China to stop doing?

Typically, the red lines are related to China’s industrial policy, its desire to reunify Taiwan, the South China Sea disputes, and human rights, said Scott Kennedy, a China analyst at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Those items are hard to find in the Trump administration’s approach now, he added. “Instead, they want an avoidance of war. They want to keep markets up, and anything that makes President Trump look good. Very different kinds of red lines that the US now has than in the past.”
Grieco said she did not see a radical departure from the US red lines, pointing out that the Trump administration has opposed Chinese coercion in the South China Sea, including reaffirming its defence commitments to the Philippines, maintaining joint maritime patrols, and conducting military exercises.
“On maritime disputes and China’s support for Iran, I’d look more closely at actual policy decisions rather than changes in rhetoric,” she said.
“Some analysts are conflating the administration’s effort to avoid needlessly provocative rhetoric with a substantive retreat from US commitments. Those are two very different things,” she added.
It would not hurt if both countries talked more openly about their red lines.
“Clarifying the two sides’ red lines could be helpful to stabilise relations, particularly to avoid misperceptions and the dangers of accidental or inadvertent escalation,” she said.

French-Lebanese man files legal complaint over Israel's uprooting of 600 olive trees
A French businessman of Lebanese origin has filed a legal complaint against unknown individuals over alleged war crimes, accusing the Israeli military of uprooting 600 centuries-old olive trees owned by his family, his lawyers told AFP on Wednesday.
The 37-year-old Frenchman, who has not been publicly named, said in the complaint that some of the trees were up to 500 years old and had been uprooted from land cultivated by his family for 250 years in the village of Zawtar al-Sharqiya, his birthplace in southern Lebanon.
According to the civil complaint, filed over theft, destruction and damage to property that it alleges amount to war crimes, the trees were uprooted from the ground.
The plaintiff, who states in his complaint that he is "not a member or supporter of Hezbollah" – the armed group fighting Israel – said he suspects the trees were transported to Israel. The complaint adds: "There is no evidence to indicate that Hezbollah was using the house or agricultural fields for military purposes".
Israel has often claimed that its attacks in southern Lebanon, Beirut’s southern suburbs or other parts of the country are targeting Hezbollah bases and operatives. Close to 9,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Lebanon since the conflict erupted in October 2023.
According to the plaintiff, a digital entrepreneur, his family home was completely destroyed in an Israeli airstrike just hours before a ceasefire was announced in southern Lebanon in April 2026.
He said that the Israeli army took full control of his village a few weeks later, followed by the uprooting of the olive trees, after Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement in late June, which Israel has failed to uphold.
The complaint argues that "the destruction and uprooting of olive trees is evidence of war crimes committed by Israel in southern Lebanon," citing in particular a report by Amnesty International.
"These events are part of a broader context of ethnic cleansing and the destruction of numerous villages by Israel in southern Lebanon. Our client expects the French justice system to do everything in its power to identify those responsible and bring them to justice," his lawyers told AFP.
Lebanese officials, NGOs and local residents have condemned the systematic destruction of farmland, particularly through burning, by Israel in southern Lebanon.
The Israeli military has used white phosphorus, banned under international law.
Southern Lebanon is home to a significant share of Lebanon’s olive groves, an important part of the country’s agricultural sector, which has been significantly impacted by the war.
Since invading Lebanon in October 2024, just a year after the start of hostilities with Hezbollah, Israel has widened its occupation to include large swathes of the south along the entire border.
Dozens of towns and villages have been razed or largely devastated in the so-called "Yellow Line," a security zone established by the Israeli military which it says is to push Hezbollah back from the border.
Despite a lull in fighting since the June agreement, Israeli attacks have continued across the south, including home demolitions.
Other complaints have been filed in Paris against the Israeli military over alleged war crimes in Lebanon, including one brought by French-Lebanese artist Ali Cherri, who lost his parents in an Israeli airstrike on a residential building in Beirut in April, and another filed in July by a French-Lebanese man who lost his mother, sister and two nephews in Israeli airstrikes.
Israel conducted more than 100 strikes in 10 minutes on Beirut and across Lebanon on 8 April, a day after the US-Iran ceasefire was announced, massacring more than 350 people in what has become locally known as 'Black Wednesday'.
Israel has refused to leave Lebanon before Hezbollah is fully disarmed, but the Iran-backed group has refused to surrender its weapons as long as the occupation continues.

"We have adapted the logistics scheme for shipments from Ankara, keeping the rail leg to Gebze and changing the port of destination in Russia to ensure stable deliveries from central Turkey for our clients. Today, FESCO is the only container operator offering direct intermodal delivery from the Turkish capital to St. Petersburg," said German Maslov, the Deputy CEO of Fesco.
