In terms of this indicator, we are currently at the level of 2017-2019 with steady economic growth and low inflation. This means the economy is generating profit."
Labor shortages, access to technology, and the investment climate are factors constraining the Russian economy: "We see among the factors holding back economic and investment growth are not so much the impact of interest rates, but rather labor shortages, access to technology, and the investment climate. There are sectoral issues, including structural deterioration in conditions for our export industries. This all should be taken into account in building our credit policy, of course."
Banking sector
There are no problems with banking liquidity on the market, this is a "far-fetched" issue, which is being "whipped up for some reason": "There is no shortage of banking liquidity. Banking regulations are responsible for this. Banks are meeting them with a comfortable margin, and we are keeping an eye on it."
The Central Bank’s banking regulation measures are not aimed at influencing monetary policy, but at ensuring the long-term stability of banks: "We do not aim to influence monetary policy. The instrument we use to influence monetary conditions is the key rate. This is our key tool we use. We apply regulations to ensure the stability of the banking system."
National Payment Card System
It is not required that only financial institutions be National Payment Card System (NSPK) shareholders: "We would like to attract not purely financial investors interested in returns from monopolistically set payment service fees. Our goal is to attract a high-quality investor, essentially a partner."
The Bank of Russia is actively discussing the sale of "a fairly large stake" in the NSPK with market participants: "We plan to start consultations with potential buyers as early as October."
In preparing for the NSPK sale, the regulator "assessed the possibility of reducing existing fees for banks," and it intends to gradually lower them: "After we reviewed the situation, we made a fundamental decision to gradually reduce fees for banks."
The Central Bank believes the NSPK should "remain profitable, self-sustaining, and capable of investing in development projects."
Demand for cash
The Bank of Russia sees a certain rise in demand for cash, but its share has risen only slightly and the situation is stabilizing: "We see an increase in demand for cash, but we need to have a broader, macroeconomic view of the economy. The money supply is also growing. Indeed, the share of cash in the money supply structure fell significantly in previous years because banks offered very attractive rates. As the rate is going down the situation is returning to normal to some extent. The share of cash in the money supply structure has risen slightly.".

Iran threatens to hit back at countries that ban its airlines

Breadcrumb
Iran threatens to hit back at countries that ban its airlines
Iran's national security chief has threatened to hit back at countries that cooperate with US attempts to cripple its aviation industry as route cancellations gather pace.
A handful of countries have suspended Iran-operated flights in recent days after the Trump administration threatened to target them with sanctions if they continued to deal with Iranian airlines.
"If you stand by America, we will not simply watch you … your airports will have no flights," Mohsen Rezaei, the head of the Supreme National Security Council, said on state TV on Wednesday.
The US earlier this month imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airliners, including state-owned Iran Air and Mahan, Iran's largest carrier, as part of its efforts to crush the country's economy.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that any organisation that continues to work with airlines after 23 September would be frozen out of the dollar financial system. That includes any company that provides services, such as ground handling and ticketing, as well as airport operators.
Several countries have suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers since the announcement, including Turkey, Oman, Azerbaijan and Georgia.
The most recent was the United Arab Emirates, which Iranian media said on Thursday had cancelled all flights operated by Iranian airlines.
As of Thursday, Mahan was also no longer listing flights to India and Malaysia. Neither of the countries has officially announced that flights would be suspended.
A handful of countries have yet to comply with the sanctions, including China and Iraq.
Beijing has opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal under international law.
Iraq, among the top destination countries for Iranian travellers, has not officially announced that it would ban Iranian airlines, though anonymous government officials have said flights would be suspended. As of Thursday morning, Mahan was offering tickets to Najaf and Baghdad.
The airline is also continuing to list flights to Russia, Pakistan and Thailand.
International travel was already heavily restricted for Iranian passengers before the latest sanctions. Flights to key destinations in the region such as Turkey and the UAE had been curtailed by the war, and many major international carriers had suspended routes to Iran.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the rebel group at the centre of Ethiopia's 2020-2022 war, has said that it had launched an attack against the Ethiopian army in the country's north.
In a statement, the TPLF-led Tigray regional government said federal forces had launched an attack on Wednesday and that its forces had been ordered to enter what it described as a “defensive” war.
The group also claimed that federal forces had launched a large-scale offensive from several directions, using infantry and mechanised units as well as drones and other air assets.
Local media reported clashes between federal forces and TPLF-affiliated forces in parts of Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
Getachew Reda, a former head of Tigray's interim administration who now serves as a federal government adviser, accused the TPLF leadership of launching a large-scale attack on government positions in Afar and Amhara.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie said his country had exercised “immense restraint” despite what he described as interference by “adversarial elements.”
Renewed fears of war in Tigray
The latest escalation follows reports that TPLF forces had taken control of Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray.
Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire in the Tigray region from Wednesday, citing the security situation.
The African Union called for restraint as military tensions increased, saying the Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, signed in November 2022, remains the foundation of the peace process.
The United Nations also expressed concern over the deteriorating situation.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged the parties to de-escalate tensions and return to dialogue under the 2022 Pretoria agreement.
The TPLF and Ethiopia's federal government fought a two-year war that began in November 2020. The conflict, which was centred in Tigray and drew in forces from neighbouring regions, is estimated to have killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The war ended with the Pretoria agreement, which halted major fighting but left several issues unresolved, including the status of disputed areas in western Tigray, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of TPLF forces.
The TPLF, which dominated Ethiopia's political system for decades before Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018, has remained a major political and military force in Tigray.
Last week, seven armed and political groups from different parts of Ethiopia, including the TPLF, announced that they had allied to coordinate their opposition to the federal government led by Abiy.

Ozdemir, who leads the environmentalist Greens in a coalition in Stuttgart, accused the Left Party of tolerating “antisemitism” in its Berlin branch and said some remarks from the party’s regional organization during the election campaign in recent months were deeply concerning.
Ozdemir drew a parallel between the anti-immigrant AfD and the Left Party in an interview with Politico’s podcast, claiming both answers to accusations after controversial remarks by party figures were unsatisfactory and that they should be held to the same standard.

Eralp voiced support during the campaign for Berlin’s Palestinian community and sharply condemned the war crimes of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in the Gaza Strip. She criticized the outgoing CDU-led coalition under governing Mayor Kai Wegner for canceling pro-Palestinian events and using disproportionate police force against peaceful demonstrators.
Eralp pledged that a Left Party-led state government would end repressive police measures against peaceful pro-Palestinian protests in the capital.
The head of Germany’s Central Council of Jews voiced opposition Sunday to a Left Party-led government in Berlin and urged other parties not to enter into coalition talks with the socialist election winner.
Josef Schuster said he was concerned about the Left Party’s solidarity with pro-Palestinian demonstrators protesting the Israeli government. He accused the party of antisemitic statements and said a Left Party-led coalition would promote the “ongoing normalization of hatred against Jews.”

Rubio warns of Iraq ‘Balkanisation’: Is that a real threat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:04:43 UTC
23:04:43 KST

Rubio warns of Iraq ‘Balkanisation’: Is that a real threat?
The US secretary of state’s warning comes after he and Trump met the Iraqi PM on the sidelines of the UNGA.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has warned that Iraq risks “Balkanisation” unless its armed factions are brought under state control.
He made the remarks to reporters at the Palace Hotel in New York City on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, after meeting Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi Tuesday night.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran cancels Baghdad, Muscat flights as US aviation sanctions take effect
- list 2 of 4US, Iran hold mediated UNGA talks on ending war, opening Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
- list 4 of 4Turkiye agrees to gradual handover of Bashiqa base to Iraq
Rubio said Washington had no doubt about al-Zaidi’s commitment to disarming Iraqi armed groups, but called it a massive and difficult challenge.
He said at least three armed groups had disarmed and joined the national government, while at least one had been far less cooperative.
Bringing all weapons under state control, he said, would mean Iraq no longer had “independent forces operating and balkanising the country”.
So what does Rubio really mean? And is the breakup of Iraq a real threat? Here’s what you need to know:
What does ‘Balkanisation’ mean?
It means a country breaking up into smaller, rival units, usually along ethnic or religious lines.
The term comes from the fragmentation of the Balkans as the Ottoman Empire collapsed in the early 20th century.
In Iraq’s case, it has often been used to describe concerns that the country could split along ethnic and sectarian lines.
However, what Rubio was pointing to was “fractures within the Iraqi state system” caused by Iran-aligned armed groups, Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera.
These groups act as rivals to one another, “but also by serving as arteries for pro-Iranian regime interests inside Iraq by wielding parallel economic channels, political influence, and oil smuggling networks”, she said.
Is Iraq at risk of breaking up?
Not imminently, although interpretations differ on how seriously to take Rubio’s warning.
“Balkanisation as Rubio framed it means more that Iraq risks failing to become a centralised, stable state that can wean off Iranian interference – not that it faces imminent territorial partition,” Ozcelik said.
She described the armed groups as a “festering, now structural” challenge, and said they have “operated inside federal Iraq with near impunity”.
Zeidon Alkinani, a Middle East political analyst and founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, was more sceptical.
He told Al Jazeera that Rubio’s remark could be read “either as a pressure tactic to push the Iraqi government forward on the disarmament process, or as a sign of the administration’s limited understanding of Iraq and the wider region”.
He said disarmament was “a major turning point” in Iraq’s post-2003 politics, but “far from the greatest challenge Iraq has faced”, pointing to the 2003 United States invasion, the sectarian strife of 2006–2007, the war against ISIL (ISIS) from 2014 to 2017 and the 2017 Kurdish independence referendum as far graver threats to the country’s unity.
What do we know about Trump and Rubio’s meetings with al-Zaidi?
Very little.
Rubio told reporters he first met with the Iraqi prime minister, and then US President Donald Trump met with him on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday evening.
Al-Zaidi’s office said in a statement that they discussed political, economic and investment cooperation as well as regional security.
Why is the timing of the meeting important?
It was the second meeting between the two leaders since July, when al-Zaidi promised at the White House that armed factions would have no justification after September 30.
That deadline has since slipped; al-Zaidi told The New York Times that disarmament would now run until June 30, 2027.
Alkinani said that the government is in “a highly delicate position”, as many Iraqis strongly support disarmament, having long seen armed groups outside state institutions as a central pillar of corruption, and as a way to curb Iranian influence.
That could give Baghdad “some breathing room” from both Washington and Tehran, he said, but “it remains an extremely difficult transformation that demands patience and political sensitivity; without them, the process could quickly unravel”.
The meeting also came days before the remaining few hundred US troops are due to leave Iraq on September 30.
Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that “there’s been no discussion” on extending that timeline.
Who are Iraq’s armed groups?
Most of Iraq’s armed groups come under the umbrella of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), a mostly Shia body formed to fight ISIL (ISIS).
The PMF was formally brought into Iraq’s security forces a decade ago, but many of its factions keep their own command structures and maintain close ties to Iran.
Several groups say they have complied with the government’s push.
Saraya al-Salam, Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib al-Imam Ali have reached understandings with Baghdad to hand over their weapons or regularise their status.
Saraya al-Salam, the armed wing linked to Shia leader Muqtada al-Sadr, was formally integrated into the security forces at a ceremony in Samarra in June.
But Ozcelik cautioned that “full disarmament of any group has not really been fully, successfully implemented yet”.
The most powerful Iran-aligned factions have refused. Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba say they will keep what they call “resistance weapons”.
Hadi al-Amiri, the leader of the Badr Organisation, one of the oldest and largest factions, said last month that bringing weapons under state control was an Iraqi decision, not one imposed from outside, and ruled out any clash between the state and “the resistance”.
Ozcelik said the challenge now is “discerning which of these groups – they have their own sets of interests, pockets, and incentives – can credibly be incorporated and which cannot by the disarmament deadline”.
A key test, she added, will be whether al-Zaidi can “Iraq-ify these groups, meaning a transition to an Iraq-first or Iraqi-Shia identity”.
Have the armed groups played a role in the Iran war?
Yes.
Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba have both previously targeted US forces in Iraq and have attacked Gulf states during the US-Israel war on Iran.
On Wednesday, Rubio said recent strikes on energy infrastructure in the region were probably carried out in part by Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq, not only by Yemen’s Houthis.
“Pro-Iran militias have directly played a destabilising role in the US-Iran confrontation,” said Ozcelik, citing reports that Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline was targeted from southern Iraq.
Are Iranian airlines still flying to Iraq?
Not entirely.
New US sanctions threaten to cut off any airport or company that refuels, services or sells tickets for Iranian airlines.
Iran says Baghdad has stopped accepting its flights and is trying to reroute them to Najaf, where flights to Iran are continuing, and no suspension order has been received.
Najaf, home to the shrine of Imam Ali, is a major destination for pilgrims, and local travel companies depend heavily on routes to Iran.

Feature: China-supported project helps improve livelihoods in Sudan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:04:39 CST
23:04:39 KST

ROME, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- For families living through conflict, a small amount of assistance can go a long way.
Liang Xiao has seen living proof of this through her work with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) headquartered in Rome, where she has helped coordinate a poverty reduction and agricultural assistance project in Sudan's Red Sea State.
Supported by China and launched in Suakin in May 2025, the project provides much-needed assistance to local communities while helping them build more sustainable livelihoods. So far, more than 40,000 people have benefited from the project, including a family in Red Sea State who made a living by raising sheep.
Years of drought had degraded local pastures and made livestock feed increasingly difficult to find. The conflict made things worse, disrupting markets and livelihoods. When the family could no longer afford animal feed, they had to give their sheep sorghum stalks and other crop residues.
Through the project, the family received 100 kilograms of concentrated animal feed so that the sheep could produce milk for the children. Any extra milk could be sold at local market, bringing in some income for the household.
"What may look like just a bag of seeds or animal feed can seem insignificant to many of us," Liang told Xinhua. "But for a family affected by a conflict, it can become a turning point, helping them resume production, improve their livelihoods and rebuild confidence in the future."
The project also focused on helping women. It provided small cold-storage units for 200 women who earn a living by selling fish, according to Liang. This allows the women to keep fish fresh for longer and sell it farther afield.
The project has also trained women to make fishing nets, providing them with another skill and a potential new source of income.
"The project didn't just give me a fishing net. It gave me dignity," said one of the women.
Many of these projects, Liang said, are "small yet impactful". Instead of large infrastructure projects, they focus on practical needs in agriculture and people's daily lives, including production supplies, technical training and livelihood support.
Carrying out the project in Sudan has been far from easy. The ongoing conflict has disrupted transport and markets and pushed up procurement costs, while differences in local social and cultural practices have also brought challenges. Project teams have had to adjust their plans, find alternative ways to deliver supplies and work closely with local organizations to make sure that assistance reaches those who need it.
"China has funding, technology and development experience that can help meet the needs of developing countries," Liang said. "FAO provides a platform to bring them together."
"We hope more people can benefit from these projects and that they can contribute to better production, better nutrition, a better environment and a better life," she added. ■

German institutes raise 2026 growth forecast to 1.3 pct

23:04:36 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Germany's leading economic institutes on Thursday raised their growth forecast for the country's economy this year to 1.3 percent, up 0.7 percentage points from their spring projection, citing a stronger-than-expected recovery in the first half of 2026.
The German economy has been on an upswing since late 2025, with exports and manufacturing value added performing strongly in the first half of this year, the institutes said in their joint autumn forecast.
The stronger recovery was supported by resilient global growth and the worldwide artificial intelligence boom, they added.
"However, the recovery rests on a narrow foundation, as high energy prices and structural problems continue to weigh on economic activity," said Oliver Holtemoeller, head of macroeconomic forecasting at the Halle Institute for Economic Research, one of the institutes that prepared the report.
Growth is expected to slow temporarily in the third quarter to just 0.1 percent from the previous quarter, as low water levels in summer hampered industrial production and higher energy prices continue to erode household purchasing power.
The institutes expect the upswing to continue in 2027, when gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to grow by 1.1 percent. Growth would then slow to 0.4 percent in 2028 as population aging reduces labor supply and weighs on Germany's potential growth rate.
Inflation is forecast at 2.8 percent this year before rising to 3.2 percent in 2027 and easing to 2.0 percent in 2028, respectively, the report said. ■

China Focus: China to build on inbound tourism boom with easier travel, richer experiences
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:04:15 CST
23:04:15 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on promoting high-quality development of culture and tourism during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Cai Yang)
BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- As more overseas visitors come to experience China firsthand, the country plans to make inbound travel easier and offer more ways to explore its culture over the next five years, a senior culture and tourism official said Thursday.
China recorded 154 million inbound tourist trips in 2025, up 17.1 percent from a year earlier. Spending by inbound travelers surpassed 130 billion U.S. dollars, up nearly 40 percent from the previous year.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), authorities will continue to improve inbound tourism services, making visas, payments, tax refunds, guided tours, accommodation and transport more convenient for international visitors, Vice Minister of Culture and Tourism Wang Jianhua told a media conference.
Authorities will also develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life, while expanding cultural programs overseas. Wang said the aim is to help foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China.
China has steadily expanded measures to facilitate inbound travel in recent years. Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries, allowing eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days.
In a separate move, authorities extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam were added to the program last month, bringing the number of eligible countries to 57.
In March, Chinese authorities released a package of measures to improve tourism services, including optimizing departure tax refund services, encouraging everyday service apps to offer multilingual versions and further improving visa procedures.
In July, China set its inbound tourism goals. The country's 2026-2030 tourism development plan proposes attracting 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030, with annual inbound tourism spending exceeding 150 billion U.S. dollars.
Beyond policy measures, China's appeal as a travel destination has also been gaining visibility overseas. Video clips and other online content about traveling in China and experiencing the Chinese lifestyle have gained traction, with hashtags such as "China Travel" and "Chinamaxxing" going viral.
GLOBAL CULTURAL COOPERATION
The push to attract more international visitors comes as China's domestic tourism market reaches new highs and its cultural industry continues to grow.
Domestic travelers made a record 6.52 billion trips and spent 6.3 trillion yuan in 2025, Wang said. The cultural industry generated 20.8 trillion yuan in revenue, averaging 8.4 percent annual growth from 2021 to 2025.
The country also staged 640,000 commercial performances last year, generating 61.6 billion yuan in box-office revenue. Both figures rose by more than 6 percent year on year.
Wang said China will also deepen cultural and tourism cooperation with countries around the world through bilateral and multilateral mechanisms, guided by the Global Civilization Initiative.
The ministry will make greater use of the six Silk Road international alliances covering theaters, museums, arts festivals, libraries, art museums and tourism cities, as well as platforms such as the China International Travel Mart, to promote cooperation among cultural institutions and tourism businesses, he said.
China will also strengthen cooperation with international organizations, host a UNESCO conference on intangible cultural heritage, pursue nominations for world heritage and intangible cultural heritage listings, and support more Chinese villages in seeking recognition under the UN Tourism Best Tourism Villages initiative, Wang added. ■

====================================================================================================

Psilocybin restores social drive in an autism mouse model even under anesthesia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:00:31 UTC
23:00:31 KST

New research provides evidence that a single dose of psilocybin can durably increase social behavior in mice with genetic traits related to autism. The findings indicate that these behavioral benefits occur even if the mice are anesthetized during the drug’s acute effects, which suggests the subjective psychedelic experience is not strictly required. The study was published in Nature Communications.
Psilocybin is the primary psychoactive compound found in certain species of hallucinogenic mushrooms. In recent years, medical research has explored its potential to treat conditions like depression, anxiety, and addiction. Some experts also wonder if it could improve sociability, which refers to the innate drive and capacity to interact with others.
Reduced sociability is a prominent characteristic of autism spectrum disorder. It is also a feature sometimes observed in other conditions, such as schizophrenia and major depressive disorder. When considering how psychedelics alter brain function, scientists sometimes look at the idea of physiological set points. According to a 2026 review, psychedelics can push brain activity away from a rigid set point, making neural pathways more adaptable even after the drug wears off. This perspective suggests that psilocybin might help shift an out-of-balance behavioral state toward a more typical one.
Another ongoing debate in psychiatric research revolves around the psychedelic trip itself. The intense sensory and emotional alterations induced by psilocybin can be challenging to manage in clinical settings and sometimes provoke adverse psychological reactions. It has remained unknown whether this conscious experience is biologically necessary to achieve the drug’s long-lasting behavioral effects.
“We wanted to examine the lasting effects of a single dose of psilocybin beyond its established effect on depression as previously reported in the human literature,” Chenchen Song, a principal investigator at Nanyang Technological University Singapore, told PsyPost. Song led the research alongside Thomas Knöpfel, director of the JC STEM Laboratory for Neuronal Circuit Dynamics at Hong Kong Baptist University. “We conduct basic preclinical research, so we examined the lasting effects using a mouse model of altered sociability; the model was established by other labs and used by many independent labs internationally.”
“A long-standing debate in the psychedelic field is whether an awake subjective experience is required during the acute psychedelic phase (commonly known as a ‘psychedelic trip’) to achieve the therapeutic effects,” the researchers explained. “Since bad psychedelic trips have been linked to unfavorable behavioral outcomes, understanding this may have real-world implications for how psychedelic-assisted therapies are delivered.”
The researchers utilized a well-established group of mice bred without the Cntnap2 gene. In humans, variations in this gene are associated with autism. Mice lacking this gene naturally display lower levels of social interaction, hyperactivity, and repetitive behaviors. The team injected 30 adult mice with a single dose of either psilocybin or a saline solution to serve as a baseline comparison.
“We use social behavior as a behavioral readout of altered brain state,” the researchers noted. “Therefore we needed a mouse model that show altered social behavior that can potentially show an improvement in behavior, if any, upon treatment. It is for this reason that we used an established mouse model of autism which is known to show altered social behavior in the hands of many independent laboratories internationally.”
They emphasized that their focus was on understanding brain flexibility, not discovering a cure for a specific human condition. “The goal of this study is not to find a therapeutic intervention for autism per se, and we are not suggesting that autism, in and of itself, should be treated,” the team added.
The team assessed the animals’ social behavior using a standard three-chamber test. This behavioral measure records how much time a mouse chooses to spend near a cup containing an unfamiliar mouse compared to an empty cup. The psilocybin-treated mice displayed an increased preference for the social cup compared to the saline-treated mice. This enhanced social drive was detectable one day after the injection and lasted for at least two weeks.
“The sociability promoting effect of psilocybin in mice that show a low baseline sociability was an original discovery of our lab (first in the prenatal valproate exposure mouse model of autism and now in a genetic model of reduced sociability),” Song pointed out.
The differences in the total amount of time the mice spent exploring both cups and their overall movement around the testing area were not statistically significant. This indicates that the drug specifically improved the animals’ social motivation rather than merely increasing their general desire to explore. To ensure the animals were not just learning how to navigate the test over time, the researchers tested a separate group of 19 mice for the very first time two weeks after treatment and observed the same social enhancements.
To determine if psilocybin acts as a universal social enhancer, the researchers repeated the exact same procedure with 18 isogenic wild-type mice. These are genetically identical control mice that possess normal Cntnap2 genes and exhibit typical social behaviors. In these animals, a single dose of psilocybin did not increase sociability. In fact, the treated control mice showed a tendency toward reduced social behavior one day after the injection.
“Even though we observed therapeutic effects in the model mice (of altered social behavior), we observed a lack of beneficial effects in control mice that do not have a deficit to begin with,” the researchers explained. “We therefore think that psychedelic use in the absence of behavioral alterations have limited beneficial effects.”
“Further, given that a significant portion of preclinical psychedelic research is done using wild-type mice, we should highlight that we think it important that the therapeutic effects of psychedelics should be examined using models of altered states as different effects/mechanisms may be involved,” they added.
The team also looked at other behaviors associated with this genetic model, specifically repetitive self-grooming and hyperactivity. During the observation periods, mice lacking the Cntnap2 gene groomed themselves much more frequently and traveled greater distances than the typical control mice. Psilocybin treatment did not alter these specific behaviors. The hyperactive and repetitive actions remained at the same elevated levels one day and one week after the drug was administered.
Psilocybin is known to exert its primary effects by activating a specific serotonin receptor in the brain, known as the 5HT2A receptor. To confirm this biological pathway, the researchers gave a group of mice a drug that blocks 5HT2A receptors fifteen minutes before administering the psilocybin. The blocking agent completely prevented the long-term increases in sociability.
The blocking agent also stopped the mice from exhibiting head twitches, which are rapid side-to-side head movements that scientists use as an indicator of a psychedelic hallucination in rodents. Interestingly, the frequency of a mouse’s head twitches right after receiving psilocybin had no correlation with how much its sociability improved weeks later. This hint led the researchers to a final, more definitive test.
To directly test if an active, awake experience is necessary for the long-term benefits, the researchers designed an experiment where mice were given psilocybin while unconscious. The animals were placed under light isoflurane anesthesia, maintaining a steady breathing rate with no movement or conscious awareness, for two hours. During this window, the animals received their injection and experienced the entirety of the drug’s acute chemical effects without an awake psychological trip.
When these anesthetized mice were later tested awake, they still exhibited the exact same long-lasting increases in sociability as the mice treated while awake. This provides evidence that the drug’s ability to rewire social behaviors is driven by basic chemical receptor interactions, rather than profound psychological realizations.
“Our observations suggest that psilocybin – even when given under anesthetized state – can have long-term therapeutic potential,” the researchers noted. However, they cautioned that “our preclinical work is no substitute for human studies. As far as we are aware of, human studies at various institutions are also underway for examining the therapeutic effects when psychedelics are given under anesthesia, for different psychedelic compounds.”
These animal findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that autistic adults often reported increased social engagement and reduced distress after impactful psychedelic experiences. However, that previous study relied on human self-reporting, whereas the current research measured physical approach behaviors in an animal model.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Animal models cannot perfectly replicate complex human conditions like autism spectrum disorder. Additionally, the three-chamber test relies on measuring the physical time an animal spends near another mouse, but it cannot reveal the nuance of that interaction, meaning researchers cannot easily tell if an approach is driven by friendly interest or territorial aggression.
“The lasting effects of psychedelics remain understudied, especially at the mechanistic level,” Song said. “Nevertheless there is overwhelming evidence for the existence of lasting effects across species and across components of behavior. This is something that one should be generally aware of, especially with the increase of recreational psychedelic use.”
“Next we hope to look more mechanistically at how the lasting effects are achieved/sustained,” the researchers concluded. “Our preliminary observations suggest that epigenetic mechanisms are involved.”
The study, “Psilocybin enhances sociability only in altered behavioural state and does not need an awake experience to be effective,” was authored by Chenchen Song, Tinya Chang, Tobias Buchborn, and Thomas Knöpfel.

VP JD Vance named as official behind Politico article used to justify White House press ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:58:01 UTC
22:58:01 KST

US Vice President JD Vance was allegedly the anonymous senior administration official behind a Politico report that the White House later cited as an example to justify stripping the outlet of its press access, media newsletter Status reported Wednesday.
The identification adds a new element to the dispute over President Donald Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The administration accused the outlets of publishing false or misleading reporting and, in Politico's case, pointed to six articles that it said had threatened national security or spread falsehoods.
One of those articles, published in June, quoted an unnamed "senior administration official" who assessed the likelihood of reaching a preliminary agreement with Iran at between 80% and 85%. According to Status, the official was Vance, who had spoken to reporters during a background briefing authorized by the White House. Status was not a participant in the call and therefore was not bound by the briefing's anonymity agreement, the publication said. The White House declined to comment on Status's identification of Vance.
The Washington Post separately established that the remarks did not originate from an unauthorized leak. The Post reviewed a White House invitation to the briefing and a recording of the call, reporting that a White House aide instructed participating journalists that the discussion was "on background, attributable to a senior administration official."
The Post did not independently identify the official as Vance. It updated its report after Status published its account, attributing the identification of the vice president to the media newsletter.
Vance reportedly behind White House press pool ban on CNN, MS NOW, Politico
The distinction is significant to the sourcing dispute because Politico's anonymity was imposed as a condition of the White House-organized briefing rather than independently granted by the outlet to a source who approached it privately. Other news organizations, including the Associated Press, Bloomberg, and CNBC, also reported comments from the same call while identifying the speaker only as a senior administration official, according to the Post.
The White House's letter to Politico was filed in federal court as part of the administration's defense of its decision to revoke the outlet's access. The letter accused Politico of failing to meet professional standards and cited its use of anonymous sources, publication of alleged falsehoods involving national security, and publication of sensitive or classified information. The June Iran report appeared on a six-item list of examples.
Trump announced the ban on September 18, accusing CNN, MS NOW and Politico of repeatedly reporting what he called "fake news." Reporters from the affected organizations were subsequently denied entry to the White House grounds and had their credentials deactivated.
CNN, MS NOW, and Politico then filed a federal lawsuit challenging the restrictions, arguing that the administration had violated their First Amendment rights and deprived them of due process.
The administration maintained in court that access to the White House is a privilege rather than an entitlement and argued that the president has authority to suspend media organizations' access. Vance separately defended the administration's action earlier in the week, saying the outlets remained free to report on the White House but were not entitled to what he described as special access.
The legal dispute shifted again on Thursday, when US District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the administration to immediately restore the three organizations' White House press passes and temporarily blocked enforcement of the ban for 14 days. Kelly said the record did not support the administration's argument that allowing the outlets back into the White House would endanger national security.
The ruling means CNN, MS NOW and Politico are set to regain White House access while their lawsuit proceeds, even as the circumstances surrounding the Politico article cited by the administration have raised a separate question over the White House's use of background briefings and its subsequent criticism of anonymous sourcing.

Man charged with assault after Swedish man died following punch in Copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:56:59 UTC
22:56:59 KST

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.

Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.

Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.
The United States will pay for any new American military bases established in Greenland under a new security and defense agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen says.
“To the extent that the Americans are to build American bases in Greenland, that is of course something that the Americans finance,” Løkke told Ritzau.
At the same time, Løkke said the agreement contains “no financing elements”.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that an agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland was being reached without costs for the United States.

He also emphasized that the US pays for improvements at Pituffik Space Base, the only US military base currently in Greenland.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.

The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.

“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.

Despite its positive assessment of the agreement, Berlingske also warned that uncertainty remains because Trump is president.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office said the agreement would strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We do not surrender sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I will never do that as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told DR and Danish broadcaster TV 2.
More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.

Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.
