États-Unis. Amnesty International demande la suppression de l’ICE après avoir établi les violations généralisées des droits humains lors des opérations anti-immigration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:43:18 UTC
22:43:18 KST

In a new report released today, Amnesty International documented widespread human rights violations committed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and other federal agencies during the Trump administration’s large-scale, militarized immigration enforcement operations in Chicago, Minneapolis-St. Paul, New Orleans and Washington, DC.
The report, “We Had Whistles, They Had Guns”: Human Rights Violations in U.S. Immigration Enforcement Operations and the Case to Abolish ICE, demonstrates that the Trump administration is implementing a mass detention and deportation system, fueled by racist, xenophobic and false narratives, whose objective is to detain and deport as many migrants, asylum seekers and refugees from the United States as possible and spread fear throughout immigrant communities more broadly.
“Our report documents a chilling pattern of human rights violations across the U.S. intended to instill fear within migrant, asylum seeker and refugee communities,” said Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA. “ICE’s record of violating human rights is nothing new, but our report shows many of these abuses have reached a perilous new level.”
Our report documents a chilling pattern of human rights violations across the U.S. intended to instill fear within migrant, asylum seeker and refugee communities.”
Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA.
The Trump administration has committed a host of human rights abuses, including unlawful killings, some of which may amount to extrajudicial executions; arbitrary and discriminatory incommunicado detentions, including possible enforced disappearances, in some cases in conditions of confinement that may violate the prohibition on torture; violent repression of peaceful protests, and more. Based on these findings, Amnesty International is joining the chorus of community voices calling for ICE to be abolished, immediately.
ICE must be abolished
Amnesty International’s findings demonstrate that the violations documented across the four operations were not isolated or exceptional incidents, but part of recurring patterns of abuse with devastating consequences for immigrants and entire communities.
“Masked and armed federal agents attacking people in the streets with impunity doesn’t make our communities safer — it puts everyone in danger,” said Daar. “ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed. For the U.S. government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.”
ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed. For the U.S. government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.”
Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA.
ICE was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001 attacks, and an extremely problematic security framework was adopted in the years following. Amnesty International and other organizations have documented human rights violations committed by ICE and a troubling lack of oversight and accountability since its creation in 2003. However, the scale and horror that we have witnessed since January 2025, fueled by billions of new dollars and persistent impunity, has reached new levels.
Human rights violations
The four operations resulted in human rights violations against immigrants, asylum seekers and refugees, people profiled as immigrants, Black and Brown communities, and those who came to their aid and challenged the conduct of the Trump administration. They also created a pervasive climate of fear that extended throughout entire communities.
Across all four operations, Amnesty International documented:
· Racially discriminatory immigration enforcement operations and arbitrary detention
· Harassment, intimidation, degrading treatment and unjustified use of force by federal agents
· Use of lethal force and unlawful killings by federal agents, which should be investigated as extrajudicial executions
· Repression of protests and use of less lethal weapons, including tear gas
and pepper spray, by federal agents
· Unlawful surveillance and facial recognition technology
· Inhumane detention conditions and denial of due process, which should be investigated as torture
· Unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance
As the report documents, ICE agents operated within an institutional environment – openly supported and expanded by the Trump administration – in which violent and racially discriminatory immigration enforcement practices were encouraged by senior government officials, including President Trump. Agents frequently operated with masks and without identification; safeguards intended to prevent and address misconduct were weakened or dismantled; and human rights violations were rarely followed by meaningful investigation or accountability.
The report details an account from Minnesota State Representative Liish Kozlowski, who is Obijwe-Latine, who said: “My cousin was in her car going to work with her husband. ICE rolled up, literally looking for Black and Brown people. They smashed her window at gun point. They roughed her up; she was pregnant. Her husband yelled ‘She’s Native American, here’s her Tribal ID card’. An ICE agent responded, ‘That doesn’t [expletive] matter, this is our land now’.”
“My cousin was in her car going to work with her husband. ICE rolled up, literally looking for Black and Brown people. They smashed her window at gun point. They roughed her up; she was pregnant. Her husband yelled ‘She’s Native American, here’s her Tribal ID card’. An ICE agent responded, ‘That doesn’t [expletive] matter, this is our land now’.”
This is just one example from dozens in the report where ICE agents appeared to be engaging in explicit racial profiling.
“Racially profiling and snatching people off the street, separating families and arbitrarily detaining people are not only unlawful, cruel practices, but profoundly damaging,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International. “These practices violate human rights and cause fear and psychological distress and long-lasting health concerns to children, other family members and entire communities.”
Racially profiling and snatching people off the street, separating families and arbitrarily detaining people are not only unlawful, cruel practices, but profoundly damaging,”
Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International.
The report also highlights how communities came together to resist and protect one another. These networks played an essential role in documenting human rights violations, and being there for their neighbors, through mutual aid networks, constitutional observer trainings, rapid response networks, walking school buses, and more in order to stand by and protect those most directly impacted. Protests were one important tool of resistance, but were frequently met with additional acts of lawlessness by ICE and Border Patrol agents.
For example, in Chicago, the Broadview facility became a focal point for protesting against ICE and Border Patrol’s actions in the city. Reverend David Black, who frequently went to the Broadview facility to do ministry, said, “The escalation of violence by ICE and CBP at Broadview when we were just praying and chanting was terrifying.” During one ministry service he led at the facility, Reverend Black, who was dressed as Clergy, was calling on three federal agents who were standing on the facility’s roof to repent, when the agents suddenly shot him in the face, arms and torso with exploding pellets of pepper spray. He is one of the numerous people whose experiences are documented in the report.
The report highlights numerous additional human rights violations during these cruel immigration enforcement operations. Amnesty International researchers interviewed 154 people across the four locations, allowing the organization to analyze how immigration enforcement operations affect diverse communities across different political, legal, and historical contexts, and to conclude that the human rights violations documented reflect broader national patterns rather than being isolated local incidents.
“It is heartbreaking to see the pain and suffering caused by this Administration as it criminalizes and demonizes immigrants,” said Daar. “I’m also hopeful – communities have rallied around those targeted and in some instances forced the Trump administration to back down. We must hold accountable those government officials responsible for this reign of terror, and we must keep fighting for an immigration system that is grounded in human rights and dignity, not cruelty.”
It is heartbreaking to see the pain and suffering caused by this Administration as it criminalizes and demonizes immigrants. US no longer ally it once was, Belgian foreign ministry document says: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:42:29 UTC
22:42:29 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Belgium's foreign ministry said in an internal document that the US is “no longer the ally it has been in the past,” the Financial Times reported Thursday.
The paper, prepared by the ministry's Americas and Caribbean unit in October 2025 and seen by the newspaper, calls for a “thorough re-evaluation” of Belgium's and the EU's relationship with Washington.
It also warns that developments in the US could compromise vital Belgian and EU interests.
The document recommends maintaining engagement with the Trump administration while calibrating Belgian officials' visits and public actions to protect the country's interests. It says Brussels should seek areas of cooperation without being seen by Washington as hostile.
Contacts with US states and major cities should be “significantly reinforced,” the paper says, while also recommending continued discussions with Democratic politicians, engagement with Congress and efforts to identify emerging figures in both parties who could influence future US policy.
The document notes that Trump respects royal families. Since it was drafted, Belgium's King Philippe has visited the US, while Queen Mathilde accompanied Belgian ministers to New York for this week's UN General Assembly, according to the FT. 
Trade, defense, security
The ministry identifies economic relations, military spending, migration and cooperation against drug trafficking and organized crime as key issues in managing ties with the US.
On trade, the document warns that deeper engagement could leave Belgium more exposed to disputes and possible US protectionist measures.
“Diversifying our partnerships is more essential than ever,” it concludes.
The document says purchases of American weapons are viewed favorably by the Trump administration but recommends increasing purchases of European military equipment as well.
It identifies the fight against drug trafficking and organized crime as a promising area for cooperation. Belgium is a major entry point for cocaine trafficking through the port of Antwerp, according to the EU Drugs Agency.
However, the leaked document also raises concerns about differences between US and European approaches to drug gangs, surveillance and counterterrorism. It warns that US foreign aid cuts could strengthen criminal organizations by reducing other sources of employment, according to the report.
A Belgian foreign ministry spokesperson told the FT that the paper was an “internal working document” and should be distinguished from an agreed government strategy.
Assessing how changes in US policy affect Belgian interests is part of the ministry's regular work, the spokesperson added.
The White House did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment.

Germany pledges to phase out fossil fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24

22:33:22 KST

Germany pledges to phase out fossil fuels
Germany has presented a roadmap for completely phasing out fossil fuels by 2045. The government is sticking to its green transition policy, despite Chancellor Friedrich Merz earlier acknowledging that the country is going through “an energy crisis.”
Germany abandoned Russian pipeline gas, on which its energy-intensive manufacturing sector had been built, after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. The US-Israeli war on Iran this year, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, accounting for some 20% of global crude oil trade, has further complicated the situation for the country’s businesses and households.
The German economy contracted in both 2023 and 2024, marking its first back-to-back annual decline in more than two decades, while 2025 only saw a weak growth of 0.2%. Over the past few years, leading German companies such as BASF, Bosch, and Volkswagen have been forced to shut down factories or announce major staff cuts.
In the document released on Wednesday, Merz’s government for the first time explicitly promised to get rid of coal, oil, and gas altogether. Previously, it only committed itself to “carbon neutrality.”
According to the roadmap, the proportion of renewable energy obtained from windmills and solar panels should increase from 55% to 80% in electricity generation by 2030.
It also envisages a reduction of methane emission by 30% by 2030 in line with the global methane pledge signed by Berlin in 2021.
The plan to phase out fossil fuel is being rolled out at a time when Merz’s approval ratings sank to a record low of 10%, with even the majority of supporters of his own Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party disapproving of his policies, according to the latest polls.
Speaking about the roadmap at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider called the 19-year deadline feasible, saying that the plan “combines independence, affordability, and climate protection.”
“Our roadmap is intended to set an international example. I am sure that many other countries will follow,” Schneider insisted.
Germany is only the third country after France and the Netherlands to publish such a plan.
Greenpeace energy expert Mira Jager welcomed the roadmap, but noted that “at the same time, the federal government is subsidizing the oil industry, breaking the heating transition, and slowing down the expansion of renewables,” as cited by Deutsche Welle.
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD), which delivered crushing defeats to the CDU in two local elections this month, warned in a post on X on Wednesday that “the German middle class dies” if the fuel price climbs from the current €2.3 ($2.6) per liter to €3 ($3.4).
“We demand the reduction of EU energy taxes as well as value-added tax. In addition, the immediate abolition of the CO2 levy on gasoline and diesel,” it said.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel, who has been a strong opponent of Germany’s green transition, previously called wind turbines “the windmills of shame.” She also repeatedly argued that restoring economic ties with Moscow and bringing back Russian gas is key to reviving the German economy.

UN rights chief says civilians are bearing the brunt of fighting in Yemen

UN says Yemen violence struck camps and health centres
GENEVA, Sept 24 - Displacement camps and health centres have been attacked during surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, UN agencies said on Thursday, deploring a growing civilian death toll which includes children.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce, as well as a widening of the conflict that has grown out of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said his office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi movement, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
He said these attacks on August 7, September 7 and September 9 in the Marib region caused dozens of casualties and killed five children.
Overall, Turk's office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes. They were among 125 people killed or wounded in the latest flareup in the conflict - a figure his office said was likely an undercount due to access constraints and insecurity.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement.
The World Health Organization said some health facilities had been "directly attacked" and an ambulance driver and a medic were killed in Lahj on September 18, without attributing blame.
INFLUX OF DISPLACED CAUSES NEW ACUTE AID SHORTAGES
Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial and that its allegations were false, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities including a correctional facility and homes and schools.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years. Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians, saying the government warnings of attacks did not remove the protections they should have.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen. Saudi officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Aid groups are ramping up their response to the crisis in a country where 18 million people, or roughly half the population face acute food insecurity.
The World Health Organization has stepped up distribution of medical supplies, including blood bags as well as trauma and surgery kits, and is deploying emergency teams as injuries rise, the statement said.
But many people lack support and a UN refugee agency plan for Yemen was less than 20% funded before the renewed violence caused a surge in needs.
An internally displaced mother of four, Aisha Ahmed, told Reuters in the Taiz camp that the influx of people in recent weeks is causing shortages. "We need water and everything else, we have nothing," she said. REUTERS

Gaza economy has entered world's 'most severe crisis on record': UN report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:31:02 UTC
22:31:02 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Gaza's economy has entered the world's "most severe crisis on record," with recovery and reconstruction needs reaching $71.5 billion amid widespread destruction of productive capacity, according to a UN report.
The report by the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said the assessment was based on the peak-to-trough decline in real GDP per capita and the projected duration of recovery.
Gaza's annual real GDP per capita stood at just $212, or $0.58 per day, in 2025, equivalent to just 17% of its already low 2022 level.
Israeli military operations since October 2023 have left 92% of Gaza's economic establishments damaged or destroyed, "bringing productive activity to a near-total halt across all sectors," the report said.
Agricultural and industrial output each plunged 94% compared with 2022, while construction output collapsed by 99%.
The labor market has also been devastated, according to the report, with only 123,300 Gazans employed in 2025, leaving more than 90% of the working-age population without work.
Prices in Gaza remained 274% above 2022 levels in 2025, with food prices "spiraling." Potatoes, for example, cost more than 20 times their pre-conflict level.
Physical infrastructure damage was estimated at $35.2 billion, more than 2.5 times the pre-conflict real GDP of Gaza and the West Bank combined, alongside $22.7 billion in economic and social losses.
UNCTAD said total recovery and reconstruction needs had reached $71.5 billion by early 2026 and "will continue to increase until a sustainable ceasefire is achieved."
Gaza's share of the Palestinian economy had fallen below 4% by 2025, while GDP per capita stood at just 5% of the level in the occupied West Bank, down from near parity three decades ago.

How Gaza's dental crisis is putting treatment out of reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's dental crisis: Families forced to choose between treating their teeth and feeding their children
For many families in Gaza, a visit to the dentist is no longer simply about treating a painful tooth. It has become a question of whether they can afford to pay for treatment or whether that money is needed for food, shelter and other basic necessities as Israel's genocidal war continues across the Strip.
As a dentist, I see this every day at the International Dental Centre in Al-Nuseirat refugee camp, one of Gaza's busiest and most crowded camps, where displaced Palestinians are supposed to be safe.
One of the patients I see is 38-year-old Maha El Masry, a mathematics teacher who previously worked on a temporary contract with UNRWA.
When I examine her painful teeth, I can see the exhaustion on her face. But instead of asking whether her teeth can be saved, she asks me one question: how much will the treatment cost?
Maha lost her job after UNRWA contracts were suspended during Israel's war. She has also been displaced from Sheikh Radwan to Deir al-Balah, while several of her teeth have begun causing her severe pain.
"My family partly relies on financial assistance from one of my siblings abroad. But restrictions on banking services and money transfers mean that the money may arrive only once every six months. When it does, it may cover little more than two months of the family's expenses," Maha tells The New Arab.
I know that Maha's teeth can still be saved through root canal treatment followed by crowns, but the estimated cost is around $1,200.
For her, that is far beyond what she can afford. "I am forced to consider a cheaper alternative: extraction," Maha notes.
'My daughters come first'
Maha's situation is similar to that of many other patients in Gaza. They come to the clinic needing treatment, but the cost forces them to think about what else their families need before deciding whether they can afford to save a tooth.
Forty-year-old Mahmoud Al Ataar from Al-Nuseirat lost his front teeth, from canine to canine, as a result of the war and needed urgent dental treatment.
He required dental implants, which cost around $4,000, or a fixed bridge costing about $1,650, but neither option was possible for him.
When Mahmoud learned how much the treatment would cost, he knew he had to put his family first.
"My daughters come first, and keeping a roof over their heads to shelter and protect them is all that matters to me," he says.
In the end, Mahmoud chose a removable denture costing around $165. Its quality does not match that of a fixed bridge, but it improved his appearance and helped him eat. It was the option he could afford in his family's circumstances.
Even getting the denture was not straightforward. One of the few dental laboratories still operating needed plaster and acrylic, two materials that have become very difficult to obtain. It took about two weeks just to find them.
Before Israel's war, the same denture cost around $100 and could be completed in about five days.
The problems Mahmoud faced with his teeth are also part of a much wider struggle. His house was damaged in a previous bombardment, and he suffered an injury that led to the amputation of several of his fingers.
After part of his home was destroyed, Mahmoud initially moved into a tent. The harsh conditions eventually led him to repair what he could of the house and cover it with tarpaulins.
"They provide my family and me with much better protection than staying in a fragile tent," Mahmoud explains.
Mahmoud has two daughters, ages 7 and 13, and four sons. With the family struggling financially, he says much of his time is now spent moving between organisations and charities looking for basic assistance.
"I spend my entire days moving between organisations and charities, trying just to secure a food coupon to feed my family," Mahmoud adds.
For him, paying for dental treatment was another expense to weigh against his family's basic needs.
"The choice was not between treating my teeth or leaving them; it was a critical choice between treating myself or meeting the basic needs of my daughters and family," he says.
'My grandchildren need milk first'
The same problem is visible with other patients around the besieged enclave, who sometimes choose to treat only the tooth causing the most pain while leaving other dental problems untreated.
One of those patients is 50-year-old Um Ahmed, who needed three dental crowns costing around $500. She did not have enough money to pay for them.
Um Ahmed called her son, Ahmed, before deciding what to do. He told her that the family could not afford the full cost and asked her to treat only the tooth causing her pain, at the lowest possible cost.
She followed his advice and treated just one tooth after her circumstances were taken into account and the price was reduced.
The single tooth was saved, but her other dental problems were left untreated.
For Um Ahmed, the family had more urgent needs. She has been a widow for five years, and her home was bombed during the Israeli invasion of Deir al-Balah, forcing her to flee.
"I didn't have a single shekel to treat my teeth. At the same time, my son Ahmed was struggling to provide milk for his infant and desperately needed to buy a tarpaulin to cover our tent and protect us from the upcoming winter rains. How could I think of my teeth when my grandchildren need milk first?" Um Ahmed shares.
Um Ahmed now lives in a tent inside a shelter in Al-Nuseirat with her eldest son, Ahmed. Her three married sons all lost their jobs during the war and now rely on working at street stalls to provide for their families.
She has no income herself and relies entirely on the charity of others.
Smiles hidden behind masks
For younger patients, the same financial pressure seems to affect their decisions about dental treatment.
One of them is 30-year-old Fedaa, who needed cosmetic fillings costing around $330. When she learned the price, she decided she could not afford the treatment.
"When they told me the cost, I was shocked. This amount would require about two months of hard, continuous work for me to save. My siblings are far more important than my teeth and my appearance. Putting them before myself is not a sacrifice; it is my duty. Now, I prefer to wear a mask all the time to hide my smile rather than deprive them of anything," Fedaa says.
Fedaa lost both of her parents during the war and is now responsible for her younger siblings. She lives in a tent in the Mawasi Khan Younis area with three of them, aged between 14 and 20.
She does not have a high school diploma, so she found work at a hairdresser's to help support her siblings.
She receives some limited assistance from her uncle, who also supports his own family. This means the money Fedaa earns from working is spent on feeding and clothing her siblings.
For Fedaa, spending money on cosmetic dental treatment is therefore not something she can justify.
A severe shortage of supplies in clinics
The stories of Maha, Mahmoud, Um Ahmed, and Fedaa show how difficult it has become for families to afford dental care. But the problem is not only the lack of money.
Inside Gaza's dental clinics, I am also dealing with shortages of materials, damaged facilities and rising costs.
Since Israel's war began, I have watched the cost of dental treatment rise sharply at my dental centre in Al-Nuseirat camp.
The rise in treatment costs is directly linked to the severe restrictions on the import of dental materials into the Gaza Strip.
Since the beginning of the war, new supplies of dental materials have been largely blocked by Israeli authorities from entering the Strip, leaving dentists to rely on what was already available before.
The supplies have also been affected by poor storage conditions, damage to dental supply warehouses and the destruction of facilities.
Together, these problems have reduced the amount of usable material by nearly half.
This shortage is evident in the cost of even basic dental treatment. A filling that once cost between $23 and $33 now costs between $66 and $83, while root canal treatment has risen from around $33 to approximately $100.
As prices have gone up, fewer patients have been able to afford treatment. The number of patients coming to my clinic has fallen to around a quarter of what it was before Israel's war.
The financial pressure has also affected the dental centre itself. I struggle to pay staff salaries, while some dentists have left their jobs to look for other sources of income.
The dentists who have stayed have also seen their share of earnings fall. In some months, fixed prosthetic treatments had to be halted because dental laboratories could not operate or obtain materials such as zirconia, acrylic, and dental plaster.
The clinic itself has also been damaged. A nearby bombing damaged the premises, leaving dental chairs and other equipment unusable.
These shortages affect the treatment patients receive. What their teeth need is only part of the decision; what they can afford has become just as important.
The remaining supplies are also being used by licensed dentists and dental students from Al-Azhar University and the University of Palestine.
With so many people relying on the same limited stock, the materials have become increasingly hard to find.
Some dentists have tried to bring supplies in from outside the Gaza Strip. But these materials often have to be obtained through expensive arrangements, and suppliers sell them to dentists at prices far higher than before the war.
The higher cost then reaches patients. Dentists have to pass on a significant part of the increase, which pushes up treatment fees and makes procedures that were once routine too expensive for many people.
The result is a chain of problems: restrictions limit supply, shortages drive up prices, and patients end up bearing the financial burden.
Ultimately, as a dentist working in Gaza, I see how the war has turned dental care from a basic need into a luxury, with patients delaying treatment, choosing cheaper options or living with pain because food and shelter come first, leaving me to see not only damaged teeth but also the economic and psychological scars of war.
For many of these patients, the shortage of dental materials and rising costs are forcing them to live with problems that could otherwise be treated, as families are left choosing between looking after their health and simply having enough to survive.
Dr Liza Hassouna is a dentist and writer based in the Gaza Strip. She has previously worked with UNRWA and now practices at a dental centre. She has also written for Al Jazeera Blogs, documenting the human toll of the war on healthcare in Gaza

====================================================================================================

Constitutional Reform as the Lee Jae-myung Administration’s Political Watershed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

On September 18, President Lee Jae-myung convened a press conference. Unlike his other public appearances, this one was devoid of smiles. There were no pleasantries floated. He just trudged to the podium in his crisp dark navy suit, his presence and the ambience made heavier by the royal blue of the presidential office draped in the backdrop.
“I have been lacking fear and humility,” he said. “I shall revive the fear for the people and tackle every task more meticulously and fiercely, from a lower position of service.”
The administration’s poor performance in opinion polls prompted this sense of crisis and humble words. Lee’s approval ratings have been taking a steady dive since the June local elections.
Until late August, the two main factors behind the slide had been the government’s controversial housing policy and the Democratic Party’s much more controversial judicial reform, which entrusts all investigative powers to the police. That change seems premature, or even inappropriate, given the recent barrage of anecdotes of police corruption and incompetence.
In September, Lee’s approval ratings plummeted still more following his ill-fated Cabinet nominations. Back in 2021, Kim Seung-won, Lee’s pick for the justice minister, allegedly streamlined the drug approval process for a pharmaceutical company on behalf of his friend. This allegation resurfaced during nomination hearings.
Meanwhile, Lee picked Yong Hye-in, the only parliamentarian from the Basic Income Party, to lead the gender equality ministry. Yong’s insistence on holding both positions, however, garnered opprobrium.
As opposed to constituency legislators – those who won the most votes from their districts – proportional representatives like Yong owe their positions to their parties. South Korea’s proportional representation ballot, designed to give minor parties a chance at lawmaking, accounts for 46 out of the National Assembly’s 300 total seats. Legislators in these seats are expected to resign when they take up another government job since someone else from their party can replace them without tarnishing the voters’ mandate. It seemed apparent that Yong had no other reason to retain her legislative seat than to enjoy the perks of being a lawmaker.
Kim and Yong both withdrew from their ministerial nominations after much damage to the Lee administration. And now they are both under investigation, the former for alleged sexual harassment of his former staff and the latter for allegedly funneling her political funds to her husband.
The public smarts all the more to questionable behavior by liberal figures. Lee’s approval ratings in major polls hit a nadir in mid-September, dropping to 33.8 percent in a poll by Realmeter and 37 percent in another by Gallup.
So, Lee’s press conference was a revolving door of apology and resolution to do better on all the factors shaving his approval ratings. But the most emphatic point he made – and the one that received the most headlines – was his assertion that “I have no intention whatsoever for a second presidential term.”
The Problematic Presidency
The current South Korean constitution allows the president to serve a single five-year term. In 2025, when Lee was running for the snap presidential election following Yoon Suk-yeol’s impeachment, one of his campaign policies was to amend the constitution so that the president can serve two four-year consecutive terms. At the time, almost two thirds of the voters approved of such reform.
South Korea’s system of a single five-year term for the president has come under much flak. The populace has to wait too long until they can pass judgment on the president through ballots. Besides, without the prospect of another term, the incumbent president has no incentive to behave responsibly when it comes to their government. How frequently the people can make their voices heard through voting and how much accountability with which the president leads the country determine the soundness of democracy. And South Korea has been poor in this aspect.
On top of that, the strong, centralized nature of South Korea’s presidency – often called an “imperial presidency” – has exacerbated the problem. Consider the president’s monopoly on administrative decisions; the government’s monopoly on funding for the rest of the country; the president’s power to appoint some 10,000 top government agency and QUANGO posts; the president’s authority to wield some $400 billion through their budgetary decisions; their decrees overriding local government ordinances; and the National Assembly’s inability to monitor and check the president’s executive arms.
Yoon’s presidency manifested everything that could go wrong, from rampant corruption due to lack of auditory mechanisms to toxic control over law enforcement. South Korea’s presidency depends too much on the good will of that one person at the top.
Naturally, constitutional reform to trim down the imperial presidency and beef up the parliament and local government has been expected to materialize sometime soon. But the speaker of the National Assembly sparked an intense controversy in late July when he said that “the question of allowing the incumbent president to serve consecutively is ultimately up to the public.” The opposition People Power Party (PPP) immediately raised the possibility that Lee could be plotting “treason” by assuming another term.
In fact, the current constitution bars any constitutional reform – whether that’s to prolong the presidential tenure or introduce multiple terms – from applying to the incumbent president. Immediately after, the speaker admitted his error in legal interpretation.
The presidential office also clarified to the press that, when it comes to Lee running for re-election, “our constitution doesn’t allow it, the people won’t condone it, and it’s realistically impossible.” Lee, while visiting France on September 10, mentioned again that “the constitution clearly confines my term.”
Still, the controversy had gained enough traction to drag down his approval ratings ever since. Hence Lee’s forceful, articulate reminder during the September 18 press conference that the notion of him serving consecutive terms “is not only constitutionally impossible but also never have I thought of it.”
Lee then proposed to collaborate with the National Assembly to amend the constitution to allow for consecutive presidential terms – for future presidents, not for himself – and more even distribution of powers among the parliament and the central and local governments. He also didn’t fail to point out that this would require “bipartisan discussion and public opinion and ideas.”
Political Opposition
Despite Lee’s fairly categorical stance, the PPP is deliberately incredulous. “Lee says he has ‘no intention’ of serving another term. Why is it so hard for him to say ‘I will not serve another term?’” wrote Jang Dong-hyuk, the PPP leader, on his social media. To him, Lee didn’t promise anything, therefore “he hasn’t given up the dream of a second consecutive term.”
The PPP floor leader, Jeong Jeom-sig, also made it clear that the PPP wouldn’t partake in any discussion for constitutional reform during the Lee administration. “The PPP is telling you now: There will be no constitutional reform during this administration,” he said to much applause among fellow PPP legislators. Like Jang, Jeong suspects that Lee has an ulterior motive to amend the constitution and run for a second term. (The president is immune from indictment, which is why the trials in various legal cases against Lee are currently on hold.)
But the real reason behind the PPP’s refusal to hash out a constitutional reform could be that it can’t take the lead in remolding the constitution to its taste. Constitutional amendment requires 200 votes in favor. The PPP only commands 109 out of 300 parliamentary seats. Meanwhile, the liberal camp comprises more than 180 seats, with the DP holding the parliamentary majority alone with its 161 seats. The PPP would manage to eke out only a piecemeal compromise at the negotiating table.
Besides, history would only remember the Lee administration, not the PPP, for having reformed the constitution. The PPP is loathe to serve Lee and the DP such an enormous political cachet on a silver platter.
In spite of the PPP’s intransigence, the DP is plowing ahead. On September 20, the DP launched a constitutional amendment committee. “It’s time to stop picking at diction but start discussing constitutional reform,” said Kim Min-seok, the DP’s new leader.
Granted, the timing is convenient for the Lee administration. Public discourse and political haggling over constitutional amendment could overshadow any other agenda. In the process, the government’s sore spots could be covered and even forgotten.
Plus, constitutional reform is not a distant possibility. Although the PPP opposes talk for tweaking the constitution, the conservative bloc is fractious anyways. Quite a sizable pocket despises Jang and the PPP leadership. Breakaway participation and votes are possible for constitutional amendment. Hearsay has it that some in the PPP are already stirring to join the discussion for constitutional amendment.
Notably, Kim Tae-ho, a four-term PPP legislator, sounded the bugle of reason this time after Lee’s press conference. “We should end this war of attrition over this consecutive terms controversy,” he said on his social media, alluding to the PPP’s pathological distrust of Lee. He then underlined the need to reform the constitution “in order to disperse the authority channeled into the president and overcome the political polarization.”
But in the end, it is this “political polarization” that will be hindering the very first step needed to heal this polarization. According to Realmeter’s September 22 survey, 5 out of 10 South Koreans were still dubious about Lee’s true intentions for wanting to introduce a consecutive presidential tenure. No matter how well-meaning and earnest the government may be about reforming the constitution and the polity, if the public isn’t convinced and comforted, no talk of constitutional reform, nor any resulting constitution, would be viable.

Sudan slams US challenge to government’s legitimacy

Sudan slams US challenge to government’s legitimacy
Sudan’s army-backed government has rejected US remarks questioning its legitimacy, insisting that efforts to end the country’s civil war must respect its sovereignty and national institutions.
US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said on Tuesday that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the rival Rapid Support Forces (RSF), or their leaders, “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan.” He said “the conduct of each leader of the warring factions renders them ineligible to govern the country,” adding that Washington seeks “to restore peace and give power back to the Sudanese people.”
In a statement on Wednesday, Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said Khartoum “strongly rejects” the State Department’s remarks and “calls for positive engagement with the Sudanese government.” It warned that negotiations must not legitimize territory taken by the paramilitaries or “reward the rebellion for its crimes against civilians and state institutions.” It demanded the dissolution of militias and exclusive state control over weapons.
The dispute comes as Washington has reportedly withheld a visa for Sudan’s transitional leader, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, to attend the UN General Assembly in New York, making his attendance conditional on accepting a 90-day ceasefire, according to Reuters, citing sources.
Three years of war Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when a power struggle between Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo erupted into fighting. Burhan’s government relocated to Port Sudan on the Red Sea coast after fighting engulfed Khartoum. Prime Minister Kamil Idris announced its return to the capital earlier this year, following the army’s recapture of the city in 2025.
The army controls Khartoum and eastern Sudan, while the RSF dominates much of the western Darfur region. The paramilitary group and its allies established a rival administration last year in Nyala, South Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council and Mohammed Hassan al-Taishi serving as prime minister. The conflict has displaced millions of people and pushed parts of the country into famine. Repeated ceasefire efforts, including US-Saudi talks in Jeddah, have failed to halt the violence.
Mediation difficulties Burhan rejected a US-led proposal last November as “the worst yet,” arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The Quad – comprising the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the UAE – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce followed by a political transition toward civilian rule. The RSF said it accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement in mediation remains a major point of contention. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries.
On Wednesday, the Sudanese Foreign Ministry said peace remains the government’s “choice and strategic goal.” It affirmed Khartoum’s readiness “for positive and responsible engagement” with the US and other partners, including Russia, who it said are “working sincerely and impartially” to achieve stability in Sudan, “far from dictates and external interferences.”

When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:28:15 UTC
22:28:15 KST

When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory
- Summary:
- The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.
- Share:
Sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. New research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.
In a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.
The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together
Different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.
"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh says.
The researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.
Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree
To explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.
During the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.
The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions quickly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.
"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.
A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism
The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.
"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.
If dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.
The idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.
"While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Mitra Javadzadeh, Marine Schimel, Sonja B. Hofer, Yashar Ahmadian, Guillaume Hennequin. Reciprocal connections dynamically build consensus between neocortical areas. Nature Neuroscience, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02437-3

To ease developers' funding pressure, land transfer payments may be paid in installments, according to the guideline. ■

Distant time crystals can somehow fall into the same rhythm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:16:41 UTC
22:16:41 KST

Distant time crystals can somehow fall into the same rhythm
Physicists have discovered that separate time crystals can synchronize across surprisingly large distances inside a semiconductor.
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- TU Dortmund University
- Summary:
- Researchers have shown that multiple time crystals inside a semiconductor can synchronize their oscillations, much like pendulum clocks gradually falling into the same rhythm. The coupling is carried by spin-polarized electrons, allowing time crystals separated by up to 40 micrometers to lock to a common frequency. The discovery reveals surprisingly long-range connections between these exotic spin systems and could help researchers develop future spin-based devices.
- Share:
Physicists at TU Dortmund University showed in January 2024 that a continuous time crystal could persist inside a semiconductor, with its oscillations remaining stable for hours. Now, in a new study published inNature Communications, Prof. Alex Greilich and his colleagues have found that multiple time crystals can emerge within the same material and synchronize their electron-nuclear spin oscillations.
Time crystals are unusual physical systems whose internal behavior repeats in a regular rhythm over time, even though they are not being driven by a repeating external signal.
In the TU Dortmund experiments, the time crystals form inside a semiconductor made from gallium arsenide with small amounts of indium and silicon. These added elements create localized electrons within the material. At temperatures close to -270 °C, each electron interacts with roughly one million nearby nuclear spins.
To initiate the process, the researchers use a pump laser to align the electron spins. The electrons then transfer their polarization to the surrounding nuclear spins. When a weak magnetic field is applied, the polarization of those nuclear spins begins to rotate.
Feedback between the electron spins and nuclear spins keeps the oscillations going. A second laser allows the researchers to monitor how those oscillations develop over time.
Separate Oscillations Fall Into Sync
Different regions of the semiconductor are not perfectly identical at the microscopic level. Because of these local variations, time crystals that form in separate areas would normally oscillate at slightly different frequencies.
That changes when the researchers illuminate many regions at once with a broad laser beam. Under those conditions, the separate oscillations can lock together and begin operating at the same frequency.
The effect is reminiscent of an observation made by Christiaan Huygens in 1665 involving two pendulum clocks. Huygens noticed that clocks attached to the same support could gradually synchronize because of the weak mechanical interaction transmitted through that shared structure.
In the semiconductor, the connection works differently. Instead of mechanical vibrations, the time crystals become coupled through the movement of spin-polarized electrons.
Synchronization Across Surprising Distances
The team found that time crystals located as far as 40 micrometers apart could still synchronize. That distance is more than one thousand times greater than the characteristic size of a single oscillator.
Once the separation becomes larger, however, the individual time crystals no longer lock together and instead continue oscillating independently.
The findings demonstrate non-local coupling between spatially separated spin systems. They could also help lay the groundwork for future networks of controllable spin oscillators, potentially opening new possibilities for spin-based technologies.
Story Source:
Materials provided by TU Dortmund University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alex Greilich, Nataliia E. Kopteva, Vladimir L. Korenev, Philipp A. Haude, Linus Kunze, Ben W. Grobecker, Sergiu Anghel, Markus Betz, Manfred Bayer. Non-local synchronization of continuous time crystals in a semiconductor. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75714-1

Chinese analysts say Trump should "understand pressure doesn't work" on Xi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:12:11 UTC
22:12:11 KST

Chinese analysts say Trump should "understand pressure doesn't work," as he and Xi tackle thorny issues
Hong Kong — It was 11 years ago that Chinese President Xi Jinping last visited the U.S. capital, for a 2015 White House meeting with then-President Barack Obama. As he returns for a meeting on Thursday with President Trump, both Xi and China's role in the world have changed dramatically.
China is now regarded as America's chief geopolitical rival, and Xi arrived back in Washington Wednesday night projecting confidence and authority.
"I think after all these years, Americans should understand pressure doesn't work," Zhao Hai, an expert in Sino-U.S. relations and vice president of the Chinese Institute of Hong Kong, told CBS News ahead of the leaders' summit in Washington. "It doesn't work on Xi. It doesn't work on China, and it doesn't work on the Chinese people."
When President Trump visited Beijing in May, he and Xi agreed to pursue what they called "constructive strategic stability" — political-speak indicating a commitment to improve the world's most important bilateral relationship despite deep mistrust, suspicion and intense competition.
Four months later, Chinese analysts see little reason to hope for any major breakthroughs, and they say the bilateral relationship, far from easing, appears as strained as ever.
Extending the trade war truce
Xi will be keen to secure an extension of the fragile economic truce that has walked the world's two biggest economies back from last year's damaging trade war.
In late 2025, Mr. Trump backed down from threats to impose 100% tariffs on some Chinese imports after Beijing threatened to limit supplies of vital rare earth materials.
Later agreements reached during the summit in May, on the sale of U.S. soybeans, other agricultural products and Boeing aircraft to China, are likely to come up.
Beijing insists the relationship cannot be one-sided, and Xi is likely to push Mr. Trump to open up the U.S. market to more Chinese goods, potentially to Chinese electric vehicles.
In 2015, Xi traveled to the U.S. with the leaders of 15 Chinese companies, including Jack Ma, the boss of online retail giant Alibaba, and executives from tech giants Tencent and Baidu.
Professor Wu Xinbo, who advises China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told CBS News he believed Xi had intended to bring a similar contingent with him to Washington this week, but that the U.S. did not approve visas for some Chinese business leaders ahead of the trip.
As a result, Wu said China decided not to send a business delegation this week. China's state television network CCTV listed the members of Xi's entourage, and it included his wife and a number of high-ranking Chinese Communist Party officials, but no corporate leaders.
The AI race
Safety concerns over the breakneck pace of artificial intelligence advancement are also expected to feature prominently in the leaders' discussion, following warnings from industry leaders that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.
Many Chinese firms agree that AI must be regulated, Leia Wang, a nonresident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for Peace, told CBS News recently.
Yi Zeng, the dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance, wrote in a research paper shared with CBS News, meanwhile, that "the catastrophic risks posed by AI, and the hidden danger of human extinction, are growing by the day."
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has spoken out against regulating AI development, said in April that it was essential for U.S. and Chinese researchers to engage in dialogue, and he warned that such bilateral coordination by AI industry leaders "is glaringly missing because of the current [U.S.] attitude about China as an adversary."
Zhao also questioned Washington's commitment to engage in any genuine cooperation with its strategic competitors.
"This is not an American issue or a Chinese issue, this is a humankind issue, and it's very threatening," he told CBS News, adding that, in his view, "the Chinese government is much more concerned about the negative side of AI development and has more measures and tools to regulate AI development."
President Trump made it clear just before his meeting with Xi that he was not in favor of any guardrails on AI development despite concerns about the possible emergence of superintelligence - a theoretical AI agent smarter than any person — and he said China's leader was in agreement.
"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ," Mr. Trump said in a social media post.
Taiwan
Xi is expected to press President Trump to limit U.S. support for Taiwan — the Chinese leader's top priority. He's widely expected to urge Mr. Trump to halt all arms sales to the self-governed island and oppose Taiwanese independence.
That would effectively end the longstanding policy of refusing to state whether the U.S. would intervene militarily if China were to attack Taiwan, a practice known as "strategic ambiguity."
After their last summit in May, President Trump said he had made "no commitment either way" on whether to move forward with a pending arms sale to the island. Democratic and Republican lawmakers urged the arms package to be approved, but it has remained in limbo since Mr. Trump and Xi last met.
"This relationship is far from stable"
Mr. Trump, who has rejected multiple reports that Beijing supports Iran in its ongoing war with the U.S., is expected to again seek Xi's assistance in resolving the conflict and ensuring the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. How he does that could determine the outcome, according to Zhao.
"If the American side is only thinking about pressuring China, and particularly using financial tools to pressure China, I think that will be a deal breaker," he told CBS News.
"We should not be too ambitious about this trip," added Wu, calling the bilateral meeting taking place at all an achievement, given the two nations' differences.
Wu attributed the lack of progress on the key issues thus far, in part, to what he called a big disconnect between what Mr. Trump says, and what his administration actually does.
He pointed, as examples, to the Pentagon placing 54 Chinese companies on a blacklist over the last two months; the Department of Homeland Security placing Chinese universities (including the one where Wu teaches) and other institutions on a watchlist, and the Federal Communications Commission imposing new regulations on Chinese robotics and other electronics.
Those measures were taken "all to gain leverage for these talks," Wu argued. "So, basically, beneath the surface, this relationship is far from stable."

Croatian court allows extradition of Nord Stream blast suspect to Germany, media reports
Sept 24 - A Croatian court has ruled that a Ukrainian man suspected of being involved in the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline blasts can be extradited to Germany, Ukraine's Suspilne news portal reported on Thursday.
German prosecutors have said the man — identified as Vladimir Z. — was a scuba diver who was part of a group behind the blasts, which followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine earlier that year.
The explosions — described by Russia and Western countries as sabotage — damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, a vital route for Russian gas exports to Europe, as well as the Nord Stream 2 branch, which had yet to enter service.

Vladimir Z. was arrested in August in a hotel in the Croatian coastal city of Pula on a European arrest warrant. He has denied any involvement, his lawyers have said.
Another suspect in the case, former Ukrainian army officer Serhii K., was charged by prosecutors in July with orchestrating the blasts while acting on behalf of Ukrainian state entities.
That man — who was arrested in Italy in August 2025 and transferred to Germany in November — has also denied any involvement in the blasts near the Danish island of Bornholm.
The County Court in Pula confirmed on Thursday it had made a ruling, but said it could not go into details until the parties had decided whether to appeal. REUTERS

AI solves 79-year-old mathematical mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:11:03 UTC
22:11:03 KST

He’s done it again: mathematician Levent Alpöge, at Anthropic, has solved yet another open math problem using artificial intelligence. He had already tackled the Jacobian conjecture and found two new elliptic curves. Now add to these the 1947 Hopf problem. It asks whether a six-dimensional sphere can be completely described using complex numbers, which include the (seemingly impossible) square root of –1. According to Alpöge, the answer is yes, though the result remains unverified.
Some geometric objects, such as a regular sphere (a two-dimensional surface that lives in three-dimensional space), have a “complex structure.” This means that there’s a simple way to assign a different complex number to every point on the sphere. The advantage of this is that many more mathematical tools are available for complex numbers than the usual “real” numbers, which makes some calculations easier. The complex structure on the sphere has had far-reaching uses, such as connecting complicated, ugly equations that live on its surface to simple, polynomial equations.
In a 1947 paper, German mathematician Heinz Hopf posed the question: What about higher-dimensional spheres? He showed that, no, high-dimensional spheres don’t have a complex structure. But he couldn’t prove it for one case: the 6D sphere.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Ever since, numerous experts have grappled with this scenario. They’ve proposed evidence both for and against the hypothesis that a complex structure exists for the 6D surface of a sphere. But no one has managed to prove their case.
Now AI may have solved the problem. Alpöge used an internal version of Anthropic’s large language model, Claude, to do what humans could not. On August 23 Alpöge posted a 100-plus-page document with a purported proof that the 6D sphere does, in fact, have a complex structure. For the proof, the AI apparently generated a complex 3D structure and demonstrated that it exactly represents the 6D surface of a sphere.
Unfortunately, the full document was nigh-indecipherable—LLMs tend to explain their proofs in unhelpful ways, spending inordinate time on minor details while glancing past important steps.
Mathematician Ilka Agricola at the University of Marburg in Germany says this lack of transparency is typical of tech company announcements: “You don’t know how many prompts were needed to arrive at the result, how much human fine-tuning was required, and so on.” Then, he adds, the mathematical community must verify the claim.
And they got right to work. Within a few days, they’d reconstructed the proof. “There seems to be an emerging consensus that the construction is plausible,” says Duke University mathematician Robert L. Bryant. On August 27 Philip Engel of the University of Illinois Chicago posted a more pedagogical explanation of the LLM’s process on his website. Around the same time, OpenAI researcher Boris Alexeev managed to formalize the proof, verifying its correctness step-by-step using the programming language Lean.
“These examples of ‘new geometry’ have become very rare and precious,” Engel says. “There is a new geometric object in the world that we now know about and can explore.”
Meanwhile, Alpöge has continued to explore other mathematical mysteries. In separate work with mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, he made significant progress toward the Navier-Stokes problem, which made headlines recently when OpenAI claimed to have found a solution.

US President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping upon arrival at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on September 23, 2026. Xi is visiting the United States from September 23 to 25. (AFP Photo)
Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the White House on Sept. 24 for a day full of pageantry, as the U.S. president sought to set the agenda by saying that both sides agreed no new controls were needed on fast-evolving AI technology.

"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is," Trump said on social media, using his new moniker for artificial intelligence. "That is China's position also."
In another post, Trump said 73-year-old Xi looked "strong, vibrant, and fit," following recent rumors about the Chinese leader's health.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sept. 23 announced a two-month extension of a trade truce that was due to expire in November.
Both sides are keen to avoid plunging back into the trade war sparked by the U.S. president's sweeping global tariffs last year.
But while Trump, 80, boasts that he will get results from what he calls his "great relationship" with Xi — the latest in a series of authoritarian leaders he has befriended — few breakthroughs are expected.
Instead their third meeting since Trump returned to power is aimed at maintaining the broader detente.
Xi's first White House state visit in more than a decade will therefore be more about spectacle than substance.
The program includes a military inspection in the Rose Garden — which Trump recently paved over — and a gift-giving ceremony involving Trump's wife Melania and Xi's wife Peng Liyuan.
Trump and Xi will make remarks in the morning and again in the evening, though it remains unclear if there will be an opportunity for reporters to put questions to the two leaders.

Trump confirmed that his stalled Iran war would be discussed, despite earlier playing down reports that Beijing was giving Tehran intelligence.
"I'll be talking about that and many other subjects — but it's all coming along well," Trump said.
Artificial intelligence is a key focus due to growing fears that it is out of control and even risks wiping out humanity as China and the United States race for supremacy in the field.
Taiwan will also be on the cards, with Trump's words likely to be watched for any sign of diminishing U.S. support for the self-governing island that Beijing claims as its territory.
Xi's visit will wrap up on the morning of Sept. 25 when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the U.S. Declaration of Independence.
